title: The disclosure ledger's own schema nodes could be redacted, undoing a withdrawal or a supersession
claim: ledger_redact_node, ledger_redact_node_properties, ledger_redact_edge and ledger_redact_edge_properties checked the handle, the id, the reason and the leak, but not what the node or edge was. graphene's RedactNode deletes the node and its index entries, and disclosureWithdrawalOf and disclosureFind read through NodesByProperty. So a script holding the ledger could redact a Withdrawal and then issue a new grant to the recipient whose access was withdrawn, redact a Disclosure out of disclose_history, or strip a ReclassEvent's properties and disclose a superseded record. A property redaction clears the index entry too and has the same effect.
evidence: Reproduced in Stage B: after disclose_withdraw a second grant to Counsel was refused; after ledger_redact_node on the Withdrawal node, disclose_to_passphrase issued a new grant and disclose_history showed withdrawn 0. After ledger_redact_node_properties on the ReclassEvent node the superseded record was disclosed with no error. Stage C: TestNoSchemaNodeOrEdgeIsRedactable failed on the first schema node it tried (the Case), which ledger_redact_node removed. DISCLOSURE_POLICY.md promises 'Future grants stop.'
repro: builtin/ledger_schema_redact_test.go TestNoSchemaNodeOrEdgeIsRedactable: every node of the disclosure schema (Case, Actor, Record, Classification, View, Recipient, Disclosure, Withdrawal) and every edge touching one, through all four redaction builtins; before the fix ledger_redact_node removed the Case node.
impact: Anyone with write access to the ledger through a script could reverse a withdrawal or a reclassification and re-enable grants, or hide a disclosure from the history, while the ledger's redaction record was the only trace and no disclose_* builtin consulted it.
fix_proposal: Refuse a redaction whose subject belongs to the disclosure schema. Fixed: a script can only ever write custom types 0..127 (dbNodeTypeFromObject, dbEdgeTypeFromObject), so ledgerSchemaSubject treats any node or edge carrying a label outside that range -- graphene's built-in Case, the disclosure schema's custom 4096+ types, anything else no script wrote -- as protected, and a node redaction is also refused when its cascade would take such an edge. All four scopes check before anything is destroyed and the refusal says why and how a disclosure record is corrected instead (by appending). ledger_redaction_impact reports protected and protected_reason, so the preview never describes an act that will be refused. A script's own nodes and edges stay redactable, including a script edge that touches a schema node. DISCLOSURE_POLICY section 7 says so.

title: A disclosure the ledger refuses derived the grant's key material and asked for its passphrase before the refusal
claim: DISCLOSURE_POLICY section 3 says a withdrawal is checked before any new key is issued. disclose_to_passphrase called IssueGrant and then asked the examiner to choose and confirm the grant's passphrase; the withdrawn-recipient and superseded-record refusals ran only afterwards, inside disclosureWriteIssue. Nothing left the process on the refusal path, but per-segment key material for a recipient who must not receive it was derived and held in memory, and the examiner was prompted for a grant that was then refused.
evidence: Stage B: after a withdrawal, disclosing again to the same recipient was refused as withdrawn after one passphrase prompt (Purpose disclose_to_passphrase, Confirm true); the refusal of a superseded record also came after one prompt. Reproduced in Stage C by TestARefusedDisclosureIssuesNoKeyAndAsksForNoPassphrase: both refusals came after one IssueGrant call and one prompt.
repro: builtin/disclose_preflight_test.go TestARefusedDisclosureIssuesNoKeyAndAsksForNoPassphrase counts IssueGrant calls (through the disclosureIssueGrant variable) and passphrase requests on a withdrawn recipient and on a superseded record; before the fix each counted one of both.
impact: The documented ordering was false: key material for a refused recipient was derived in the trusted process, and the examiner was asked to choose a passphrase for a grant that would never be issued. No grant was returned, recorded or written.
fix_proposal: Refuse before IssueGrant and before the prompt; keep the re-check inside the ledger write. Fixed: the two refusals moved into disclosureRefusal, which disclosurePreflight calls under disclosureLedgerMu right after the view resolves, before the partition, IssueGrant and the passphrase prompt. disclosureWriteIssue asks the same question again under the same lock for a withdrawal or reclassification recorded in between. The disclose_to_passphrase metadata says both refusals come before any key material is derived or any passphrase asked for.

title: DISCLOSURE_POLICY says crypto-erasure is available; no builtin performs it
claim: Section 3 lists crypto-erasure as available, but no builtin erases or re-wraps a record key; the only route is deleting key files by hand.
evidence: No erase/destroy builtin in builtin/record.go or builtin/case_key.go; the builtin registry has none. Stage B 2026-09-24: DISCLOSURE_POLICY.md:92 says 'Crypto-erasure is available', and section 0 says nothing in the document is waiting to be built. The record key exists only wrapped in each .mrec header under the case key. case_key_rotate(mode case_key) keeps earlier generations (metadata.go:1188), and no builtin erases or re-wraps anything. Stage B 2026-09-25: The only name in builtin/names.go matching erase|destroy|shred|wipe|forget|purge|zeroize|delete_key|revoke|withdraw is disclose_withdraw, which stops future grants and destroys nothing. DISCLOSURE_POLICY.md:92 says 'Crypto-erasure is available', :303 lists it as an operation, and :26-27 says nothing described is waiting to be built.
fix_proposal: Stage E7: record_erase and case_key_erase, and rewrite sections 3 and 7 to state exactly what each destroys and what it cannot reach. Fixed: Stage E7c: record_erase overwrites the record key in one copy's header and records the erasure in the case's ledger with the file's digest before and after; case_key_erase erases every generation of the case key (the key file overwritten and removed) or one earlier generation, and a case is disposed of only after it. DISCLOSURE_POLICY section 3 now says crypto-erasure is two builtins and only case_key_erase reaches every copy, and the section 7 row says what each destroys and what is out of its reach (a grant already issued, a copy of the key file kept elsewhere). Each builtin's does_not_erase field names what it did not reach, and TestAGrantStillOpensAnErasedCopy holds the grant claim to what a grant does.
repro: TestB4NoEraseBuiltin: none of the 659 registered builtins has a name containing erase, destroy, shred, wipe, forget, purge, delete_key or zeroize. The only erasure possible is deleting every copy of the case key file by hand, which erases the whole case. Erasing one record's key is not possible without deleting every copy of that record.

title: A Withdrawal records no authority
claim: DISCLOSURE_POLICY says a withdrawal records on whose authority it was made; the Withdrawal node gets only WITHDREW and PERFORMED_BY edges.
evidence: disclosureWriteWithdrawal writes no AUTHORISED_BY edge and no authority property. Stage B 2026-09-24: disclosureWriteWithdrawal writes only WITHDREW and PERFORMED_BY edges (builtin/disclose_history.go:244-254). DiscloseWithdraw takes (ledger, disclosure, reason), so no authority can be supplied. DISCLOSURE_POLICY.md:90-91 promises 'Who withdrew what, when, and on whose authority'.
fix_proposal: Stage E1: disclose_withdraw takes {authorised_by}; the Withdrawal gets an AUTHORISED_BY edge to the authority's Actor node and the role recorded. Fixed: Stage E1 (L-4): disclose_withdraw takes an optional options hash, read first through secretOptionsArg, whose one key is authorised_by. Left out or naming the examiner recording it, the authority is the examiner's own (authority_basis self); otherwise it is the name given (named), refused when empty, not a string, or not valid UTF-8. The Withdrawal node carries withdrawal.authorised_by, withdrawal.authority_basis and withdrawal.actor_role, and gets an AUTHORISED_BY edge to the authority's Actor node (the same node as PERFORMED_BY when the authority is the examiner's own) carrying the basis; PERFORMED_BY carries the role. disclose_withdraw returns authorised_by, authority_basis and role, and disclose_history reports withdrawal_authorised_by, withdrawal_authority_basis (not recorded for a withdrawal written before 2.6.0) and withdrawal_role. DISCLOSURE_POLICY section 3 and section 13 say so.
repro: TestB4WithdrawalAuthority: the Withdrawal node's outbound edges are [WITHDREW PERFORMED_BY]. Its properties are withdrawal.{uid,unix_nano,at,bytes_recoverable,disclosure_uid,reason,recipient,record_uid}. There is no authority edge or property.

title: The disclosure guard's file list omits two files that hold key material
claim: builtin/custody.go (caseKey, classTagKey) and case_key_passphrase.go are not in DisclosureFiles, so the no-plaintext-rendering guard does not look at them, and nothing detects an omission.
evidence: DisclosureFiles lists 13 files; neither is among them. Stage B 2026-09-24: policy/disclosure_policy.go:33-51 lists 13 files, which it defines as 'the files that handle classified plaintext or the key material that opens it'. Three files that hold such material are missing: builtin/custody.go (session.caseKey and classTagKey at :178-179, zeroed at :748-750), case_key_passphrase.go (cached passphrases at :83) and credential/credential.go. None of the three has a finding today: scanDisclosureSource reports 0 findings for case_key_passphrase.go and credential.go, and 0 for custody.go at HEAD. The guard's own comment and DISCLOSURE_POLICY section 10 admit that an omission is not caught.
fix_proposal: Add both, and add TestEveryFileHoldingKeyMaterialIsGuarded so a file handling key material cannot be left off the list. Fixed: builtin/custody.go and case_key_passphrase.go are in DisclosureFiles, and both pass TestDisclosureCodeNeverRendersPlaintext. The new test walks every non-test Go file and requires any file naming key material (caseKey, classTagKey, IssueGrant, SealGrant, UnwrapRecordKey, openSegment, RequestPassphrase, SetPassphraseSource, recordClassification) to be listed; before the fix it named exactly these two. credential/credential.go is not listed: it reads the program's own password, which opens no classified record. Carrying the Classified mark (evaluator, VM, mutil, object) is not a marker, because those files render values by design. DISCLOSURE_POLICY section 10 states what the test catches and what it cannot.
repro: In my scratch copy I injected `_ = (&object.Bytes{Value: session.caseKey}).Inspect()` after builtin/custody.go:748. `go vet ./builtin` passed. `go test ./policy -run TestDisclosureCodeNeverRendersPlaintext` PASSED ('scanned 13 files ...; 0 findings'). My policy/zz_b4a_sec001_test.go, which runs scanDisclosureSource directly on custody.go, flagged 'builtin/custody.go:749 (CaseClose): calls Inspect'. I then injected `_ = fmt.Sprintf(string(session.caseKey))`: the guard still passed, but go vet, which the release gate runs, did flag the non-constant format. So only the Inspect rule is truly unguarded for these files. custody.go was restored byte for byte (cmp) after each run.

title: Anti-tamper probes route to a detail that says not implemented yet
location: security/antitamper_routing.go probeOne; security/antitamper_constants.go AntiTamperSupportedProbes; security/antitamper_detectors.go; builtin/security_status.go SandboxStatus
claim: Unrouted probes report AntiTamperDetailNotImplemented, a probe result that describes an absence of implementation rather than a measurement.
evidence: security/antitamper_constants.go:22 Stage B 2026-09-24: antitamper_routing.go:19-22 routes acpi_pci and gpu_feature to makeSignal(name,false,0,"not implemented yet"). A working detectACPIPCI exists at antitamper_detectors.go:131 but has no caller (git grep shows only its definition). detectLDPreload (antitamper_detectors.go:93-95) is hard-wired to 'env-based preload checks disabled'. All three are in AntiTamperSupportedProbes and requested by sandbox_status (security_status.go:90). docs/ANTITAMPER_PROBE.md section 4 lists acpi_pci and ld_preload as 'Implemented Probes (Current)', marking only gpu_feature as a placeholder, and section 6 says 'ld_preload reports active LD_PRELOAD markers'. Observed in WSL on the scratch build: sandbox_status().probe_signals printed `acpi_pci detected=false conf=0 detail=not implemented yet`, `gpu_feature ... not implemented yet` and `ld_preload detected=false conf=0 detail=env-based preload checks disabled`.
fix_proposal: Implement each routed probe or remove it from routing; nothing reports a result it did not measure. Fixed: acpi_pci, gpu_feature and ld_preload are unrouted and out of AntiTamperSupportedProbes, and sandbox_status no longer asks for them; each is now an unknown probe. None could be made honest under its name: detectACPIPCI (which had no caller) repackaged DetectSandboxType, which cpuid_hypervisor already reports, and read no ACPI table or PCI device; gpu_feature was never implemented; and ld_preload can see nothing in a CGO_ENABLED=0 release, which is statically linked and never runs the dynamic loader LD_PRELOAD works through. detectACPIPCI, detectLDPreload, AntiTamperDetailNotImplemented and the unused ACPIPCIConfidence* and ConfidenceLDPreload* constants are deleted. The test requires every supported probe either to measure (a detail that is not 'not implemented', 'disabled', 'placeholder', 'not supported' or unknown) or to say it did not (M26-TMP-018), and the three names to be unrouted; before the fix it failed on all three, and TestProbeOneNotImplementedSignals, which pinned the placeholder as correct, is replaced. ANTITAMPER_PROBE.md lists twelve probes and says why the three went.
repro: Scratch 7aeee5a, linux/amd64 build run in WSL: `./mutant probe.mu --dev --password-file pw.txt`, where probe.mut prints each sandbox_status()["probe_signals"] entry. The routing is platform-independent, so Windows behaves the same.

title: Bytecode is read with no size cap
claim: The artifact decode path reads its input with io.ReadAll and no bound, so an oversized or crafted artifact is loaded whole before anything checks it.
evidence: runner/runner.go:353 Stage B 2026-09-24: runner.go:345-351: zstd.NewReader with no WithDecoderMaxMemory, then io.ReadAll with no LimitReader, so the whole inflated buffer exists before gob sees it. os.ReadFile(srcpath) at :82 is also unbounded. The mechanism is real. Calibration: the bomb sits after AES-GCM authentication, so the crafter must know the password, or use --dev, whose artifacts are local-development only. Anyone who can produce a validly encrypted artifact can already ship a program that allocates without limit at run time (there is no VM memory or recursion cap; see VM.04). So the bomb adds no capability. It is a robustness defect: S4/P2, down from the ledger's S3/P1.
fix_proposal: Bound the read with a named limit and refuse beyond it. Fixed: readArtifact refuses a file larger than maxArtifactFile (1 GiB, above any standalone executable) from its Stat before reading, and bounds the read itself with a LimitReader for a file that grows; Run and HasStandalonePayload use it. maybeDecompressEncodedByteCode inflates with zstd.WithDecoderMaxMemory and a LimitReader at maxBytecode (256 MiB) and refuses past it, zeroing what it read. Before the fix a 227-byte zstd payload inflated to 2 MiB under a 1 MiB limit and a 4096-byte file was read under a 1024-byte one. Both limits carry //mutant:limit and appear in LIMITS_REFERENCE.md.
repro: My own scratch test runner/zz_b4_test.go TestB4ZstdBomb builds a correctly encrypted, self-signed artifact whose zstd frame inflates to 256 MiB of zeros, then calls decode(signed, "reviewpass"). It printed `bomb: artifact=22215 bytes, err=EOF, alloc=645MiB`. Fix: zstd.WithDecoderMaxMemory plus io.LimitReader under a named limit.

title: A crash during sealing leaves a torn record under its final name
claim: recordWriteFile creates the final path with O_EXCL and removes it only on a reported error, so a killed process leaves a partial .mrec where a complete one is expected; key files already write to a temporary file, sync and rename.
evidence: builtin/record.go:764 and :776 against builtin/case_key.go:665 Stage B 2026-09-24: recordWriteFile opens the final path with O_CREATE|O_EXCL (builtin/record.go:764) and removes it only through abandon() on a reported error (:774-778). By contrast, writeKeyFileAtomic (case_key.go:665) writes a temp file, syncs and renames.
fix_proposal: Seal to a temporary file, fsync, rename; a crash-child test proves no torn record survives. Fixed: recordWriteFile reserves the record's name with an empty O_EXCL file (so an existing record is still refused, never written over), writes the record to a .mutant-record-* temporary file created 0600 beside it, syncs and closes it, and renames it over the reservation; every reported failure removes both. recordLoad refuses an empty file by saying a seal was interrupted. The test re-runs the test binary with a -record.crashchild flag (not an environment variable), exits the child after the first segment through the recordSealInterrupt seam, and requires the name to hold nothing or an empty file the reader refuses: before the fix it held 825 bytes of a record. The record_seal metadata says what a killed seal leaves.
repro: Scratch builtin/zz_b4_torn_test.go, TestB4TornRecord: a child test process sealed a 400 MiB source and was killed once the destination passed 32 MiB. It left a 36,701,482-byte big.mrec at the final name. record_verify and record_open both refuse it with 'says it holds 419430400 bytes of plaintext and the whole file is 36701482 bytes'. Calibration: the torn file is detected by every reader and was never logged to the case, because custodyRecordArtifact runs only after success. Custody integrity is therefore not silently broken. The harm is a garbage file under an evidence name that blocks a re-seal to that name (O_EXCL), so S3, not S2.

title: Type uses across modules never reach the symbol graph
claim: lookupType is file-local, so a struct literal or enum reference to a type declared in another module is recorded as unbound and gets no USES_TYPE edge, although the compiler resolves it.
evidence: sema/graph_walk.go:378 notes UnboundType; the compiler resolves across the program in compile order. Stage B 2026-09-25: graph_query.go lookupType searches only this file's Types. program.go builds each module with BuildFile and never consults the program-wide type owner table. Own run: TypeOwner(Loc) ok=true, yet main.mut records 'Loc kind=type' and 'Dir kind=receiver member S' as unbound, and zero references reach a struct or enum.
fix_proposal: Stage D5: resolve such uses at export in compile order and count what cannot be resolved. Fixed: Stage D5: BuildProgram builds each module against the types of the modules compiled before it (typesBefore), the compiler's own reach -- structDefinitions/enumDefinitions are one table filled in post-order -- by claiming a module's types only after its graph is built. A struct literal or enum reference to such a type is a Ref into the declaring module; one to a type declared only later, or nowhere, is counted in ModuleGraph.UnresolvedTypeUses (an unbound x.y only when x is a program enum and y one of its variants). The parity test compiles seven programs for real, siblings in both import orders and a literal above its own struct statement among them. It also fixed an enum from an earlier module beside a local value of the same name, which the graph resolved to the value and the compiler to the enum. Ref.Role (use, construct, pattern) and Unbound.From/Role are new; the export writes cross-module type edges, CONSTRUCTS and MATCHES co-labels, the per-module misses in the module blob, and TypeUses/UnresolvedTypeUses in its summary. graph query gains types and type.
repro: sema/zz_verify_test.go TestZZLeadSem001: BuildProgram over lib/geo.mut (`struct Loc { a; b; }; enum Dir { N, S };`) and main.mut (`import "lib/geo.mut"; let l = Loc{a: 1, b: 2}; let d = Dir.S;`) gives typeRefs=0.

title: db_bfs and db_shortest_path misread their arguments
claim: An unknown direction silently means both; parallel edges are lost; neither walk has a budget; db_shortest_path ignores direction and returns an error where its metadata says an empty result.
evidence: builtin/db.go:448, :490, :598-607; builtin/metadata.go:2199 Stage B 2026-09-25: db.go:598-607 treats any unknown direction as both. "OUT", "outbound" and "sideways" all returned nodes [1 2 3], the same as "both". db_shortest_path(b,a)=[2 1] although the only edges run a->b, because graphene ShortestPath is undirected. With no path it returns 'ERROR: db_shortest_path: no path between nodes', but metadata.go:2199 promises an empty array. The dropped parallel edge (out gives edges=[1]) is weaker: that is BFS tree semantics.

title: Two ledger reads can be silently wrong

Stage B 2026-09-24: (a) ledger_query_nodes on a key that is not in the index returns count 0, comparison 'none' and no error. Reproduced on a Disclosure node whose blob holds disclosure.recipient=Counsel: the query {disclosure.recipient eq Counsel} returned ids []. (b) With one edge 1->2, ledger_path(2, 1, 'hops') returned found:true, hops:1. The rendered edge shows src:1 dst:2, and no field reports that the hop ran against the edge. Neither behaviour is documented in the metadata (:2378, :2403). Downgraded from S2/P1: ledger_add_node indexes every property (ledger.go:733-735), so for script-written data an empty answer on an unindexed key is correct (typo or never written). The silent miss is limited to the disclosure schema's blob-only keys, and the reversal is visible in the returned edges.
fix_proposal: Refuse or flag an unindexed key; mark each reversed hop. Fixed: ledger_query_nodes returns unindexed_keys, every filter key missing from graphene's NodePropKeys (an upper bound on the disk backend, so a key missing from it matches nothing for certain), and index_keys_known, false when the store cannot list its keys. A key that is indexed but has no matching value is not listed. ledger_path returns reversed_hops, the 0-based hops whose edge points from the node reached back to the node left, and directed, true only when none did. Before the fix a query on disclosure.recipient over a ledger holding a disclosure to Counsel returned count 0 with nothing else to say, and a path from an artefact back to its image reported two hops with no sign that both ran against their edges. The metadata of both builtins describes the new fields.

title: The label table is rewritten and fsynced on every disclosure write
claim: DeclareTypeNames runs on every disclosure, withdrawal and reclassification write, and graphene rewrites graphene.labels unconditionally.
evidence: disclose_ledger.go:533, disclose_history.go:199, disclose_reclassify.go:264 Stage B 2026-09-24: DeclareTypeNames runs on every disclosure write (disclose_ledger.go:533). I deleted <ledger>/graphene.labels (362 bytes) after the first disclosure, and it was recreated by the second disclosure under the same names, so the file is rewritten and fsynced unconditionally. Priority lowered from P2 to P3: a disclosure is a human-paced action that needs a passphrase, so an extra fsync per write has no practical cost.
fix_proposal: Declare the type names once per ledger session. Fixed: Stage D7: the three disclosure writes (disclosureWriteIssue, disclosureWriteWithdrawal, reclassWrite) declare the family's names through disclosureDeclareNames, which writes the table on the first write of a ledger session and records that on the session, under disclosureLedgerMu. A new session declares again, since it cannot know what happened to the file while the ledger was closed. The test backdates the table after the first disclosure and checks a second disclosure and a withdrawal leave it untouched, then that a reopened ledger's first write replaces it. A repeated reclassification went from ~4.0 ms to ~14 us per call, interleaved against 28dcd48.
repro: TestB4Lead003 in my scratch zz_b4a_cus_test.go.

title: Every read of a variable costs time in proportion to its size
claim: The VM keeps each variable encrypted and decrypts it on every load, so a loop that reads a large Bytes value pays for the whole value on each iteration. A script that walks a 3 MiB file with bytes_read_* takes about a minute.
evidence: examples/binary/static_bin_analysis.mut, which parses the 3 MiB examples/data/sample_win.exe, runs for 61.8 s at mutation 0 and fails the sweep's 60 s per-run limit. Two probes with the same 2000-iteration bytes_read_u32_le loop: over the whole 3 MiB file 47.2 s, over a 16 KiB slice of it 2.4 s (mostly start-up), about 23 ms per read at 3 MiB. Linux gate at 7aeee5a with the TEST-006 fix, 2026-09-24: static_bin_analysis was 'still running after 1m0s' at mutation 0 while nine audit agents shared the host, and about 27 s per run on the same host idle -- so until this is fixed the sweep's verdict on it depends on host load, not on the code. Stage B EVL.17 (CONFIRMED): Indexing an array in a loop is quadratic, because every load re-seals and re-opens every element with a fresh key derivation Stage B 2026-09-24: encryptForStorage/decryptForUse (vm.go:380-394) run EncryptObject/DecryptObject on every push, pop, global/local load and store, and on builtin arguments. A BYTES value is copied and ChaCha20-XORed in full each time (util.go:122-134), and containers are sealed element by element with a fresh key derivation per element. My TestB4LoadCost over examples/data/sample_win.exe (3,162,624 bytes) with bytes_read_u32_le in a loop: 10 reads took 433 ms and 100 reads took 2.33 s, about 21 ms per read. The same 100 reads over a 16 KiB slice took 80 ms. Building an array with `rs = push(rs, i)` took 0.75 s for 500 elements, 2.84 s for 1,000 and 11.0 s for 2,000, about 4x per doubling, so it is quadratic. Cost scales with value size and element count, as the lead says. Stage B 2026-09-25: I checked the code. SecureXORAt derives the key and nonce on every call (secure_random.go:59). encryptForStorage and decryptForUse (vm.go:380-394) are called on every load and store: OpGetLocal pushes decryptForUse(stack[slot]) and OpSetLocal re-encrypts. OpSetIndex decrypts the whole container and pushes the mutated copy (vm.go:1228-1236). My test, vm/zz_verify_test.go TestZZVerifyHashBuild, measured h[i]=i at 181 ms for n=200 and 685 ms for n=400, and s += a[i] at 79 ms for n=200 and 311 ms for n=400. That is about 4x per doubling, so both are quadratic, as the auditor's extension claims. I did not re-run the auditor's prototype fix. Its safety argument (cache the key and nonce, and move ciphertext instead of round-tripping it; do not cache plaintext, because execSetIndex mutates the decrypted copy) is consistent with the code I read.
repro: let data, err = fs_read("examples/data/sample_win.exe"); then for i in 0..2000 { bytes_read_u32_le(data, i * 4) }; compare with data = bytes_slice(data, 0, 16384). Compile with mutant gen and run each; wall time scales with the buffer, not the loop.
impact: Forensic scripts read large buffers in loops as a matter of course; this makes them quadratic in practice. It also fails the release gate's example sweep.
fix_proposal: Stage B PERF to establish where the time goes (decrypt, copy, or both) and design a representation that does not re-process an unchanged value on every load, without weakening what variable encryption protects against. Stage G adds a benchmark over a large Bytes variable.

title: A failed task's error names the instruction pointer, which changes with the mutation level
claim: A VM runtime error carries 'vm_runtime_error ip=N op=...'. When a spawned task fails, task_wait hands that text to the script as a value, so a program that prints it prints different output at different mutation levels, which breaks the promise that mutation rewrites the bytecode and not what a program prints. The ip also describes the mutated layout to whoever reads the output.
evidence: The --levels 0,5,10 sweep fails examples/concurrency/worker_pool.mut: line 18 reads 'vm_runtime_error ip=6 op=OpDiv' at mutation 0 and 'ip=12' at mutation 10. TestRuntimeErrorsIncludeInstructionMetadata requires the metadata, so it is deliberate for errors that end the program. Stage B 2026-09-24: runtimeErrorAt (vm.go:1537-1542) formats 'vm_runtime_error ip=%d op=%s', and builtin/tasks.go:208 hands task.failure.Error() to the script as a value. I compiled examples/concurrency/worker_pool.mut with `mutant gen --mutation M --seed S` and ran each .mu. Section 4 printed 'failure=ERROR:task failed: vm_runtime_error ip=6 op=OpDiv' for m0/s1, m10/s1 and m10/s3; ip=11 for m10/s2; and ip=12 for m5/s7. The same source prints different text depending on the build. vm/resource.go:88 (closeResource) also embeds the CallClosureSync error text, ip included, in a script-visible value.
repro: go run ./cmd/sweep --levels 0,5,10 examples/concurrency/worker_pool.mut
fix_proposal: Decide in Stage B whether script-visible error values carry bytecode positions at all; if not, task_wait (and any builtin that turns a VM error into a value) reports the source position only, and the ip stays in the fatal-error path and debug logs.

title: On Linux the parent-debugger check matches ordinary words in the parent's arguments
claim: isParentDebugger reads the parent's whole /proc/<ppid>/cmdline, arguments included, lowercases it and substring-matches linuxDebuggerPatterns against it. Short patterns such as 'rr', 'ida' and 'angr' occur inside ordinary words (error, current, concurrency, mirror, validate, candidate), so a parent whose arguments contain one is reported as a debugger. From vm/vm.go:810-822 (read, not run), a secure-mode run would then stop with ErrDebuggerDetected.
evidence: WSL at 07c737a: security_environment_report printed 'debugger detected: false' when the sweep's argv named only that example, and 'true' when it also named examples/concurrency/worker_pool.mut; security_diagnostics_example listed linux:parent_debugger_process. Stage B 2026-09-24: antidebug_linux.go:100-121 lowercases the parent's whole /proc/<ppid>/cmdline and substring-matches the patterns at :25-29 ('rr', 'ida', 'angr', ...). Reproduced in WSL with the scratch linux build. `sh -c './mutant probe.mu ... # concurrency'` gave debugger.detected=true methods=[linux:parent_debugger_process], and the control without the word gave false. With no comment at all, `sh -c './mutant cases/current/triage.mu ...'` gave detected=true, because mutant's own argument 'current' contains 'rr' and appears in the wrapper's argv (the same applies to sudo, which forensic users often need for raw devices). In secure mode, `sh -c './mutant hello.mu --password-file pw.txt ...; # terraform'` printed `event=debugger_detected stage=pre-decode action=terminate`, `detector=debugger signals=linux:parent_debugger_process` and `reason: secure mode does not run with a debugger attached to this process`. The comment at :99 names strace and ltrace, which are not in the list.
repro: Under Linux, run a program that calls security_diagnostics() from a parent whose argv contains 'concurrency'.
impact: A Linux user's program can be refused because of the words in the command that started it.
fix_proposal: Compare the parent's executable name (/proc/<ppid>/comm, or argv[0]'s base name) exactly against the list; never search its arguments.
reporter: Stage A Linux baseline WSL Ubuntu 24.04, go1.26.2, 2026-09-24

title: The pinned toolchain's standard library had 18 vulnerabilities the code reaches
claim: go.mod pinned go 1.26.2. govulncheck v1.8.0 (database of 2026-09-16) over ./... under go1.26.2 reported 18 vulnerabilities the code calls, all in the standard library (net/url, net/http, net/textproto, net/mail, net, crypto/tls, crypto/x509, encoding/asn1, encoding/xml, html/template), fixed across go1.26.3 to go1.26.6. A shipped mutant binary compiles the standard library in, so every release built on 1.26.2 carried them. golang.org/x/crypto v0.55.0 also had two ssh denial-of-service issues, fixed in v0.56.0, that the code does not call.

title: A function value prints its heap address, so a program that ends on one never prints the same thing twice

title: Four gate steps build with the host's cgo default, and the sweep builds with whatever go is on the PATH
claim: The gate exists to check what a release ships, and a release ships with CGO_ENABLED=0 built by the pinned toolchain. gendocs -check, the example sweep, govulncheck and the fuzz-target listing set no CGO_ENABLED in either script, so they take the host's default: on a host with a C compiler they check a cgo build no release is, and on a host with a compiler but no C headers they fail before checking anything. The sweep also builds its mutant binary with exec.Command("go", "build") (cmd/sweep/main.go:231), the go first on the PATH, not the gate's --go.
evidence: WSL at 7aeee5a after gcc was installed without libc6-dev: race, gendocs and sweep FAIL in 21s, 1s and 0s with 'runtime/cgo: fatal error: pthread.h: No such file or directory'. On the Windows host go on the PATH is go1.27.0 and go1.26.2 env CGO_ENABLED prints 1 (mingw gcc on the PATH), so the Stage A Windows sweep ran a binary built by go1.27 with cgo.
repro: policy/gate_guard_test.go TestEveryGateGoCommandChoosesCgo before the fix: 10 errors, one per unpinned go command in each script and one per sweep run without --mutant.

fix_proposal: Every compiling go command in both gates sets CGO_ENABLED=0 (1 for the race detector alone); the sweep step builds the binary with the gate's toolchain and -trimpath and passes it with --mutant; the PowerShell fuzz listing goes through Invoke-Logged so it can set cgo.

title: The pmap overlap test times its fixed setup cost against a budget meant for the overlapped work, so the race detector fails it
claim: TestPMapActuallyOverlapsWork times one whole runEncryptedVM call -- parse, compile, DerivePasswordFromInstructions, EncryptByteCode, a GlobalSize globals slice, then pmap -- and fails when that exceeds half the sequential sleep total (240ms). Only the pmap part is the overlap it means to measure; the fixed setup cost counts against the same budget, and the race detector multiplies it several times over.
evidence: Linux gate at 7aeee5a with the TEST-006 fix, race step (CGO_ENABLED=1 -race): 'pmap of 8 x 60ms took 246.9265ms; sequential would be about 480ms, so the work is not overlapping' -- the only failure in the race step, with zero data races reported. Without -race on the same host pmap takes about 63-73ms, so roughly 180ms of the 247ms was setup.
repro: In WSL: CGO_ENABLED=1 go1.26.2 test -race ./vm/ -run TestPMapActuallyOverlapsWork at 7aeee5a under the gate's load (the gate's race log, race_detector__test_binaries_only__.log).
impact: The Linux race step fails for a reason unrelated to concurrency, so a gate that must pass cannot, and a real overlap regression would be indistinguishable from load.
fix_proposal: Time map and pmap over the same callback; both pay the same fixed cost, so the test asserts that pmap saves at least half the sequential time. Checked both ways: under -race pmap 82-85ms vs map 485ms passes three times; with pmap forced to one worker it fails (485ms vs 482ms).
reporter: Stage B Linux gate run, WSL Ubuntu 24.04, go1.26.2, 2026-09-24

title: let defines its name before compiling the initializer, so `let s = s + 1` reads the new, unset slot (stale value from an earlier frame, nil crash, or hang)
claim: The single-name let path calls Define before compiling the value, so any reference to the same name inside the initializer resolves to the freshly allocated, never-written slot instead of the binding being shadowed (parameter, outer local, global or builtin). Inside a function that slot holds whatever an earlier frame left on the VM stack, so the program silently computes with a stale value. Verifier: The claim holds. The stale value is whatever an earlier frame left in the slot, so the exact wrong answer depends on the stack: 301/201 on the CLI, not 201/101. The `let len = len(xs)` case returned the argument array instead of hanging. The evaluator computes the intended value, so the VM also diverges from macro-time evaluation.
evidence: compiler.go:831-836: `if len(names) <= 1 { symbol := c.symbolTable.Define(node.Name.Value); if err := c.Compile(node.Value); err != nil {` -- Define (symbol_table.go:125-137) always allocates `Index: st.numDefinitions` and overwrites the store key, so `s` in the initializer now resolves to the new slot. The multi-name path (844-860) compiles first and defines after, so the two paths disagree. Repro results: `let g = fn(a, b) { return a + b; }; let f = fn(s) { let s = s + 1; return s; }; g(100, 200); f(1);` => INTEGER(201) (want 2). `let total = 10; ...; let f = fn() { let total = total + 1; return total; }; g(100, 200); f();` => INTEGER(101) (want 11). `let x = 1; let x = x + 1; x;` => RUN_ERR(recovered panic: nil pointer dereference). `let f = fn(xs) { let len = len(xs); return len; }; g(1,2); f([1,2,3]);` => hangs (go test -timeout 20s fired). Also: in the REPL a failed line `let x = no_such_name;` leaves `x` defined (Resolve(x) => GLOBAL index 0), so the next line `x + 1;` compiles instead of reporting `undefined variable: x`. Verifier: compiler.go:831-841: the single-name let calls c.symbolTable.Define(node.Name.Value) and only then compiles node.Value. Define (symbol_table.go:125-137) always allocates a new index and overwrites the store key, so the initializer resolves the name to the new, unwritten slot. The multi-name path compiles first and defines after. I ran it through the CLI in the scratch tree (mutant gen, then run the .mu with --compat): `let g = fn(a,b){return a+b;}; let f = fn(s){ let s = s + 1; return s; }; g(100,200); putln(f(1));` printed 301 (want 2). `let total = 10; ... let f = fn(){ let total = total + 1; return total; }; g(100,200); putln(f());` printed 201 (want 11). `let x = 1; let x = x + 1;` failed with vm_runtime_error: recovered panic: nil pointer dereference at 2:9. `let f = fn(xs){ let len = len(xs); return len; }` printed [1, 2, 3] (want 3). The auditor saw a hang here; the stale value depends on the stack. In my harness the evaluator gives INTEGER(2) for `let x = 1; let x = x + 1; x;`, so the two engines also disagree. Nothing in docs/ documents Define-first let or self-reference as unsupported. I only code-read the REPL sub-claim: repl.go:452-458 reuses symbolTable after a failed Compile and never rolls it back. Verifier's notes: The script author triggers it (trusted), but the result is a silent wrong value from an ordinary normalise-in-place idiom, so S2/P1 stands. It is not P0 because no published promise covers self-referential let. Define-first comes from the original Monkey design. Direct recursion does not need it, because the parser names function literals (FunctionScope).
repro: Scratch tree C:\Users\gaura\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\o--project-mutant\55290407-4e73-4476-84fe-dee8837b2290\scratchpad\stageB\b1\CMP\tree: go1.26.2 test ./reviewcmp -run 'TestReproLetShadowStaleSlot|TestReproLetSelfReference|TestReproReplFailedLetLeavesName' -count=1 -v; per-case: CASE=0..3 go1.26.2 test ./reviewcmp -run TestReproLetShadowOuter -timeout 20s -v (reviewcmp/harness_test.go compiles like the generator and runs the encrypted VM).
impact: The ordinary normalise-in-place idiom (`let name = lower(name);`, `let total = total + x;`, `let len = len(xs);`) silently returns a value from an unrelated earlier call, crashes, or hangs. For a forensic script that is a plausible wrong number with no error.
fix_proposal: Compile the initializer before Define whenever the name already resolves (own store, an enclosing scope, a parameter, a global or a builtin), so it reads the binding being shadowed. Keep Define-first only for a brand-new name, which is what lets `let f = wrap(fn(n) { f(n-1) })` refer to itself. The parser already names direct function literals (fl.Name), so direct recursion does not depend on Define-first. For the REPL, roll back the symbol table (numDefinitions and store) when a line fails to compile. Regression test: VM test: `let g = fn(a,b){return a+b;}; let f = fn(s){ let s = s + 1; return s; }; g(100,200); f(1);` == 2; `let x = 1; let x = x + 1; x;` == 2; `let t = 10; let f = fn(){ let t = t + 1; return t; }; f();` == 11; `let f = fn(xs){ let len = len(xs); return len; }; f([1,2,3]);` == 3; plus `let f = memo(fn(n){ f(n) })`-style self-reference for a fresh name still compiles.

title: break/continue inside a function literal nested in a loop back-patches the enclosing stream at the inner stream's offset, silently rewriting an unrelated instruction
claim: loopContexts belongs to the Compiler and is not saved or cleared when enterScope starts a function body. A break or continue inside a closure therefore finds the outer loop's context and records a jump position that is an offset in the closure's stream. The loop then patches that position in the outer stream, overwriting operand 0 of whatever instruction sits there. The closure keeps `OpJump 9999`. Verifier: The claim holds, and the failure modes are wider than reported: besides the silent wrong constant and VM faults at unrelated instructions, one shape (break in a closure inside a while loop) crashes the compiler with an unrecovered Go panic.
evidence: compiler.go:981-987: `case *ast.BreakStatement: if len(c.loopContexts) == 0 { ... } jumpPos := c.emit(code.OpJump, 9999); ctx := &c.loopContexts[len(c.loopContexts)-1]; ctx.breakPositions = append(ctx.breakPositions, jumpPos)`. enterScope (1287-1298) only pushes a CompilationScope and a symbol table. compileForStatement then does `for _, pos := range ctx.breakPositions { c.changeOperand(pos, loopEndPosition) }` (1822-1824), and changeOperand operates on `c.currentInstructions()`, which is the outer stream. Repros: `let marker = 1; let big = fn() { return [1000, ..., 1399]; }; for (let i = 0; i < 2; i++) { let f = fn() { break; }; } marker;` => INTEGER(1052) (want 1): the main stream's `OpConstant 0` became `OpConstant <loopEnd>`. Other shapes: for/while/for-in => `RUN_ERR(ip=0 op=OpConstant: constant index 60 out of range, len=6)`, and `RUN_ERR(ip=12 op=OpCaptureLocal: local slot 0 is not boxed)` when the closure is called. No compile error, and no LSP rule catches it. Verifier: loopContexts is a Compiler field (compiler.go:24). enterScope (1287-1298) neither saves nor clears it, so break/continue at 981-995 inside a function literal append an offset in the closure's stream to the outer loop's context. The outer loop then calls changeOperand on its own stream at those offsets. CLI repros at the default gen level: (a) `let marker = 1; let big = fn(){ return [1000..1399]; }; for (let i=0;i<2;i++){ let f = fn(){ break; }; } putln(marker);` printed 1055 (want 1), with no error; (b) `for (x in [1,2,3]) { let f = fn(){ continue; }; out = push(out, x); }` failed with `vm_runtime_error ip=0 op=OpArray: stack underflow for 19 elements`, blamed on line 1; (c) `while (n < 3) { let cb = fn(v){ if (v > 1) { break; } return v; }; n = n + 1; }` crashed `mutant gen` itself with a Go panic, `index out of range [0] with length 0` in code.Make via changeOperand <- compileWhileStatement, exit 2. No compile error is raised, and no lint rule covers break inside a closure (the only 'outside of for loop' checks are compiler.go:983/991). Verifier's notes: A plain mistake (continue inside a callback in a loop) silently corrupts an unrelated instruction, so S2/P1 is right. The fix is cheap: save and clear loopContexts around the function body.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./reviewcmp -run 'TestReproBreakInsideFnInsideLoop|TestReproBreakInFnSilentWrongConstant' -count=1 -v (scratch tree above)
impact: A common mistake, `continue` inside a callback passed to peach/pmap/a helper inside a loop, is accepted, and the compiler corrupts a different instruction of the program. The result is either a wrong constant loaded silently or a VM fault at an unrelated ip.
fix_proposal: Treat a function body as a loop boundary. In the FunctionLiteral case, save c.loopContexts, set it to nil before compiling the body, and restore it after leaveScope, on the error path too. Then `break`/`continue` in a closure with no loop of its own reports `break used outside of for loop`. Consider an LSP rule with the same wording. Regression test: Compiler test: `for (x in [1]) { let f = fn() { break; }; }`, `while (true) { let f = fn() { continue; }; }` and `for (let i=0;i<1;i++) { fn() { break; }; }` each return a compile error. A loop inside the closure (`fn() { for (y in ys) { break; } }` inside an outer loop) still compiles, and its break patches the closure's own stream.

title: break/continue from inside an expression leaves that expression's pending operands on the stack; an enclosing for-in then reads the wrong cursor
claim: A break or continue is compiled as a bare OpJump. When it sits in an if/match block that is an operand of a larger expression, the values already pushed for that expression (left operand, container, call arguments, array elements) are never popped. The for-in comment says every exit goes through the same pop and none leaks a stack slot. That holds only for statement-level breaks: a leaked value is popped in place of the cursor, the inner cursor stays on the stack, and an outer for-in reads it as its own. Verifier: The claim holds. The silent wrong answer needs break/continue inside an if/match that is an operand of a larger expression, inside a nested for-in. The single-loop for-in case fails loudly, and while/for loops return correct values while leaking stack.
evidence: compiler.go:1493-1497: `The cursor is left on the stack for the whole loop and dropped at end, which is also where break is patched to -- so every way out of the loop goes through the same pop and none of them leaks a stack slot.` Break emits only `c.emit(code.OpJump, 9999)` (985). Repro 1: `let out = []; for (a in [1,2,3]) { for (b in [10,20]) { let t = [0, if (b == 20) { break; } else { b }]; } out = push(out, a); } out;` => ARRAY([1]) (want [1, 2, 3]): the outer loop silently stops after one element. Repro 2: `for (k in ["a","skip","b","c"]) { score = score + match (k) { "skip" => { continue; }, "a" => 1, _ => 2 }; }` => RUN_ERR(op=OpIterNext: loop cursor was replaced on the stack), top level and inside a function alike. In while/for loops the leaked value simply accumulates, one per iteration (100k iterations leaked 100k slots without error). Verifier: Break and continue emit only OpJump (compiler.go:985/993) and never pop operands already pushed for the enclosing expression. The for-in comment at 1493-1497 ('none of them leaks a stack slot') holds only for statement-level exits. CLI repros: (a) nested for-in with `let t = [0, if (b == 20) { break; } else { b }];` printed [1] (want [1, 2, 3]), a silent truncation of the outer loop; (b) `score = score + match (k) { "skip" => { continue; }, "a" => 1, _ => 2 };` in a for-in failed with `ip=30 op=OpIterNext: loop cursor was replaced on the stack`; (c) the same shape in a while loop printed the correct 12 but leaks one slot per continue. Control: statement-level `if (b == 20) { break; }` in the same nested loops printed [1, 2, 3]. The language reference only says break/continue 'work in all of them'. Verifier's notes: Lowered from P1 to P2. The construct is unusual (a jump out of the middle of an expression), and only the nested for-in form is silent. The trigger is the trusted script author.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./reviewcmp -run 'TestReproBreakInsideExpressionLeaksStack|TestReproContinueInExpressionWhile' -count=1 -v (scratch tree above)
impact: The nested case silently truncates iteration over evidence, with no error. The non-nested case fails at run time with a message about the VM rather than about the program. Unbounded stack growth follows in long while/for loops.
fix_proposal: Track how many operands are pending while a sub-expression compiles: increment around Infix Right, Call arguments, Array/Hash elements, Index, assignment chains and similar, and record the count at loop entry. If a break or continue is compiled with more pending operands than the loop recorded, either emit that many OpPop before the jump or refuse with a compile error. Refusing is simpler and matches the refusal style used for impure assignment indices. Regression test: VM test: the nested for-in program above yields [1, 2, 3], or the compiler rejects it with an error naming break-inside-expression. The `score + match { continue }` program yields 5 or is rejected. `let v = if (c) { break; } else { 1 };` (nothing pending) still compiles and runs.

title: Compound assignment evaluates the last index twice: `a[next()] += 1` calls next() twice and writes one element with another's value
claim: `x op= v` is rewritten to an InfixExpression whose Left is the whole target node. For an index target, the last index is compiled once as the store index and again inside that rewritten value. The purity refusal covers only the hops before the last, so an impure last index runs twice and read and write can use different indices. Verifier: For an index target, compound assignment and ++/-- evaluate the last index expression twice (once for the store, once for the read), in both engines. There is no parity divergence. The behaviour is the literal desugaring the reference documents ('exactly x = x + y'), but it contradicts the same reference's 'the last index is compiled once' and the rationale behind the impure-hop refusal. The defect is a footgun plus a self-contradicting doc, not a broken implementation of a clear promise.
evidence: 1837-1843: `valueExpr = &ast.InfixExpression{ Token: node.Token, Left: node.Left, Operator: node.Operator, Right: node.Value }`. 1890: `for _, step := range steps[:len(steps)-1] { if step.index != nil && !pureAssignIndex(step.index) {` so the last hop is exempt. store() compiles `last.index` and then `emitValue()`, which compiles valueExpr and so node.Left's index again (2040-2046). The language reference says: `The last index is compiled once and is free to be anything, including a call.` Repro: `let calls = 0; let next = fn() { calls = calls + 1; return calls - 1; }; let a = [10, 20, 30]; a[next()] += 1; [calls, a];` => ARRAY([2, [21, 20, 30]]): next() ran twice and a[0] received a[1]+1 (want calls=1, a=[11,20,30]). Verifier: The CLI repro printed [2, [21, 20, 30]]: next() ran twice and a[0] got a[1]+1. `a[next()]++` gives the same result, and plain `a[next()] = 5` gives [1, [5, 20, 30]]. My parity harness shows the evaluator gives the identical ARRAY([2, [21, 20, 30]]): evalAssignedValue (evaluator.go:752-774) evaluates node.Left again, and its comment says it deliberately mirrors the compiler's desugaring. The language reference says both 'x += y is exactly x = x + y' (which, taken literally, evaluates the index twice) and 'The last index is compiled once and is free to be anything, including a call'. Verifier's notes: Lowered from S3 to S4. It needs a side-effecting last index, and one reading of the docs describes it.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./reviewcmp -run TestReproCompoundIndexDoubleEval -count=1 -v (scratch tree above)
impact: `hist[read_next_byte()] += 1` or `counts[next_record_key(h)] += 1` builds a wrong histogram or count table silently. This breaks a documented promise.
fix_proposal: For compound operators with an index as the last hop, compile that index once into a compiler-internal slot (internalSlot, as the value spill already does), and use the slot both in the rewritten read and in the store. Alternatively, refuse an impure last index when node.Operator != "", with the same message the earlier hops get. Regression test: VM test: the program above yields [1, [11, 20, 30]]. Also `a[0][next()] += 1` calls next once. The LSP assignmentTarget rule and the compiler must agree on whatever is refused.

title: `<` and `<=` evaluate their right operand first, reversing side-effect order and disagreeing with the evaluator
claim: To reuse OpGreater/OpGreaterEqual, the compiler emits Right before Left for `<` and `<=`, so side effects run right to left. Every other binary operator runs left to right, and so does the tree-walking evaluator that macro expansion uses. With side-effecting operands the comparison result changes. Verifier: The claim holds. Note that the reversal is documented in the internal IR doc (section 3.3). The defect is the user-visible side-effect order and the divergence from the evaluator used at macro expansion.
evidence: 687-698: `if node.Operator == "<" || node.Operator == "<=" { if err := c.Compile(node.Right); ... if err := c.Compile(node.Left); ... c.emit(code.OpGreater)`. Repro (VM vs evaluator.Eval on the same source): `let n = 0; let next = fn() { n = n + 1; return n; }; next() < next();` => VM false, evaluator true; `next() <= next()` => VM false, evaluator true; `next() > next()` => both false. Call-order log for `a() < b()`: VM [b, a], evaluator [a, b]. BYTECODE_IR.md:199 describes only the mechanism (`also used for < by swapping operands at compile time`), not this consequence. Verifier: compiler.go:687-699 compiles Right before Left for < and <=. Parity harness: `next() < next()` gives VM false, evaluator true. `next() <= next()` gives VM false, evaluator true. `next() > next()` is false on both. The call log for `a() < b()` is VM [b, a], evaluator [a, b]. BYTECODE_IR.md section 3.3 documents the mechanism ('right operand first ... (reversed!)') but not what it does to side effects, and the user-facing reference says nothing about operand order. Verifier's notes: Lowered from S3 to S4. It needs side effects on both sides of a less-than, which is rare, and the mechanism is documented internally. The parity divergence is real.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./reviewcmp -run TestReproLessThanOperandOrder -count=1 -v (scratch tree above)
impact: Comparing two sequential reads or counters gives the inverted answer. A value computed inside a macro differs from the same expression written inline, which the parity doc says must not happen.
fix_proposal: Append OpLess and OpLessEqual (the append-only rule keeps old bytecode valid) and compile Left then Right. As a stop-gap, swap only when both operands are side-effect-free (identifiers/literals, the pureAssignIndex test) and otherwise emit in source order with new opcodes. Regression test: Parity test: `next() < next()` and `next() <= next()` are true on both engines, and the call-order log for `a() < b()` is [a, b] in the VM.

title: Programs past the bytecode's operand widths crash the CLI with a Go panic instead of a compile error (257 locals, 65,536 literal occurrences, main stream over 64 KB)
claim: Operand-width overflow is enforced only as a panic in code.Make, and the comment calls it an internal invariant. But the indices come straight from the size of the user's program. Nothing in generator/main recovers, so `mutant run` dies with a goroutine dump and exit 2. Constants are never deduplicated (addConstant appends every literal and every field name), so the 65,536 cap counts literal occurrences across all linked modules. Verifier: The claim holds. The crash is loud and names the limit, so no wrong answer is produced, but a large valid program (for example an embedded IOC list of about 33k pairs) aborts the toolchain with a Go stack trace and no line.
evidence: code.go:261-263: `This is an internal invariant rather than a user error -- the compiler chose the index -- so it panics.`; code.go:276 `panic(fmt.Sprintf("code: operand %d of %s is %d, which does not fit ...` ; compiler.go:1158-1160 `c.constants = append(c.constants, obj); return len(c.constants) - 1`. No recover() in generator/, main.go, cli*.go or compiler/ (git grep). CLI repros, all exit 2 with `panic:` and a goroutine trace: a function with 257 `let`s => `operand 0 of OpSetLocal is 256 ... (limit 255)`; two IOC array literals totalling 66,000 strings => `operand 0 of OpConstant is 65536`; 12,000 top-level `let vN = N;` followed by an `if` => `operand 0 of OpJumpFalse is 80199` (from changeOperand). BYTECODE_IR.md:1233 already acknowledges `eventually panic inside code.Make`. Verifier: code.go:255-281 checkOperandFits panics by design, and nothing in generator/main recovers. My CLI runs of `mutant gen` all exited 2 with `panic: code: operand ...` plus a goroutine dump: 257 lets in one function (OpSetLocal 256), two arrays of 33,000 distinct strings (OpConstant 65536), 12,000 top-level lets plus an if (OpJumpFalse 79966 from changeOperand), and one array of 70,000 copies of the literal 7 (OpConstant 65536). The last confirms that constants are not interned (addConstant appends every occurrence). The panic text is explicit ('the program exceeds what the bytecode format can address') but has no source position. BYTECODE_IR.md:1233 only mentions the 256-local limit in passing. Verifier's notes: S3 because a large input crashes the tool with an undocumented limit. P2 because the trusted author triggers it, and the message is actionable.
repro: PowerShell in scratch tree\cli_repro: .\..\mutant.exe run locals257.mut --password-file pw.txt ; same for consts66k.mut and jump64k.mut (generated by the python snippet in the transcript). Each prints `panic: code: operand ...` plus a goroutine dump, exit=2.
impact: A large but valid script, such as a generated IOC list, a big linked module set or a long function, crashes the toolchain with a stack trace and no source position. The LSP gives no warning beforehand.
fix_proposal: Check operand fits in the compiler before calling code.Make (a checkEmit that returns an error), or recover the code.Make panic at the top of Compile and turn it into a compile error naming the construct and the current posLine:posCol. Intern integer/float/string constants and field-name strings, so 65,536 counts distinct values rather than occurrences. Document the limits (256 locals/params/args per function, 65,535 distinct constants and globals, 64 KiB per instruction stream) in the language reference. Regression test: Compiler tests: 257 locals, 256 call arguments, 65,536 distinct string constants and a 70 KB main stream with a trailing `if` each return a non-nil error (no panic) that mentions the limit and a line. 70,000 repetitions of the same literal compile once constants are interned.

title: Macro (and end) tables never record the return to 'no position', so every instruction after a macro expansion is reported as coming from the macro
claim: recordPosition passes macroLine=0 for code outside a macro, and LineTableBuilder.Add drops any line <= 0. The macro table therefore keeps its last macro entry in force, and LineTable.At, which returns the last entry at or before ip, attributes every later instruction in the stream to that macro. The same happens in the end table for a node with a start but no end. Verifier: The claim holds, but the impact is narrower. The reported line, column and caret are still correct; only the trailing 'expanded from a macro defined at ...' annotation is wrong for every later instruction in the same stream. The macro position is not exposed anywhere except the traceback text.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./reviewcmp -run TestReproMacroTableStale -count=1 -v (scratch tree above)
impact: After the first macro use in a stream, every runtime fault's report points the analyst at a macro definition that has nothing to do with the failing line. That is a confident wrong answer in the failure reporter.
fix_proposal: Give the macro and end builders a way to record a reset: when the previous entry was non-zero and the new position is zero, emit an entry with line 0, and have At report ok=false for a line-0 entry. The line table keeps its current drop-zero behaviour. Regression test: Compiler test: for the program above, MacroTable.At(ip) is !ok for every ip whose LineTable line is 6 or 7. The VM traceback for `c / 0` has MacroLine == 0.

title: ModuleLine maps into the wrong file: an empty path picks the first dependency (not the entry), and a line past a module's end lands in the next module
claim: moduleSpanFor("") returns span 0 and its comment says that is the entry module. But Link emits spans in post-order, dependencies first and entry last, so span 0 is the first import. ModuleLine also never bounds `line` by the next span's StartLine, so it is not the inverse of ModuleAt the doc says it is. Verifier: The claim holds. The empty-path case is reachable only when a DAP client sends a breakpoint with no Source.Path. The unbounded-line case is reachable from any breakpoint set past the last line of an imported module (for example the empty line after its final newline), which then binds into the next module while bp.File still names the first.
evidence: compiler.go:251-255: `if path == "" { // No file named: the first span is the program's entry module, which is what SourceFile names and what a single-module program means. return 0, true }`; module/link.go:59-60 `Modules are the graph's modules in link order -- dependencies first, entry last`. 243: `return bc.ModuleSpans[index].StartLine + line - 1, true` has no upper bound. Repros: a linked main.mut importing lib.mut gives SourceFile=mods\main.mut, spans=[lib.mut@1, main.mut@4], and ModuleLine("", 3) -> blob 3 -> ModuleAt = mods\lib.mut:3. With spans {lib.mut@1, main.mut@11}, ModuleLine("lib.mut", 15) = 15, ok=true, and ModuleAt(15) = main.mut:5. No test in compiler/ calls ModuleLine. Verifier: Go test in the scratch tree using generator.CompileForDebug on main.mut importing a 3-line lib.mut gives spans [mods\lib.mut@1, mods\main.mut@4] with SourceFile=mods\main.mut. ModuleLine("", 1..3) resolves via ModuleAt to mods\lib.mut:1..3, not the entry. ModuleLine("lib.mut", 4/5/9) returns 4/5/9 with ok=true, and ModuleAt maps those to main.mut:1/2/6. The moduleSpanFor comment (compiler.go:251-255) wrongly says span 0 is the entry, while link.go:59-60 says the entry is last. Caller: vm/debugger.go:606 resolve(). DAP only passes an empty path when the client sends Source.Path empty (dap/session.go:572-575). Verifier's notes: Debugger-only, no effect on program results.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./reviewcmp -run 'TestReproModuleLineEmptyPathIsNotEntry|TestReproModuleLineNotBounded' -count=1 -v (scratch tree above; uses generator.CompileForDebug on reviewcmp/mods)
impact: The debugger (vm/debugger.go:606) binds a breakpoint that names no file, or a stale line past the end of a file, into another module, then reports it verified at a line of the wrong file.
fix_proposal: For an empty path, return the span whose Path equals SourceFile (the last span). In ModuleLine, refuse when i+1 < len(spans) and StartLine+line-1 >= spans[i+1].StartLine. Add ModuleLine/ModuleAt round-trip tests. Regression test: For a two-module link: ModuleLine("", L) resolves via ModuleAt to the entry file. ModuleLine("lib.mut", lenOfLib+1) returns ok=false. ModuleAt(ModuleLine(p, l)) == (p, l) for every valid (p, l).

title: When padding declines on a large stream, the engine throws away that stream's line/end/macro tables even though the instructions are unchanged
claim: padInstructions returns (ins, nil) whenever it declines, for example when a repointed jump would pass 65535. spliceFillers remaps the tables through that nil map regardless, and Remap(nil) returns nil. A stream that was left exactly as compiled therefore loses all of its positions. Verifier: The claim holds. It affects only streams large enough (roughly 60-64 KB) that padding pushes a jump past 65535.
evidence: polymorphic.go:230-231: `if !rewriteJumpTargets(padded, remap, ownJumps) { return ins, nil }`; 142-143: `bytecode.Instructions, mainRemap = pe.padInstructions(...); bytecode.LineTable = bytecode.LineTable.Remap(mainRemap)`; linetable.go:127 `if len(t) == 0 || offsets == nil { return nil }`. Repro: 10,500 top-level lets plus a trailing `if` and `1 / 0` (63,028-byte main stream). At level 0 the line table is 31,518 bytes and the traceback reads `at <main> (line 10502:9)`. At level 10, seed 7, the line table is 0 bytes, opcodeMap is set, and the traceback reads `at <main>` with no position. Verifier: padInstructions returns (ins, nil) when rewriteJumpTargets declines (polymorphic.go:230-232). spliceFillers calls LineTable.Remap(nil) unconditionally (142-145, 154-157), and Remap returns nil for a nil map (linetable.go:127). CLI repro: 9,600 top-level lets plus an if and `v2 / z`. With `gen --mutation 0` the traceback reads `at <main> (c10m0.mut:9603:9)` with a caret. With `gen --mutation 10 --seed 7` the same source gives `at <main> (c10.mut)` with no line.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./reviewcmp -run TestReproPaddingDeclineDropsLineTable -count=1 -v (scratch tree above)
impact: Large programs built at the default mutation level lose every source position in fault reports, although nothing moved.
fix_proposal: In spliceFillers, remap the three tables only when the returned remap is non-nil, for both the main stream and each function. Otherwise leave them untouched. Regression test: Compiler test: a program whose padded main stream would exceed 65535 still has LineTable equal to the unmutated build's, and a runtime fault reports its line at level 10.

title: Struct-literal initialisers run in declaration order, not source order (hash literals in sorted-key order)
claim: compileStructLiteral compiles the field expressions in the order the struct type declares its fields, so side effects in the initialisers run in an order the source does not show. Hash literals likewise run their key and value expressions sorted by key text. Verifier: The claim holds, and it is also an engine-parity divergence: the tree-walking evaluator (used at macro expansion) runs struct initialisers in source order, the VM in declaration order. The hash-literal half has the same root as LEX.04/EVL.11 (unordered Pairs map); the struct half is unique.
evidence: 2268-2276: `for _, field := range typeDef { expr, exists := fieldExprByName[field.Value] ... if err := c.Compile(expr); err != nil {`. Repro: `struct H { size, magic }; ... let h = H{magic: next(), size: next()}; [h.magic, h.size];` => ARRAY([2, 1]) (source order gives [1, 2]); `{"z": next(), "a": next()}` => z=2, a=1. Verifier: compileStructLiteral (compiler.go:2267-2276) compiles fields in declaration order. Parity harness, three runs: `struct H { size, magic }; ... H{magic: next(), size: next()}; [h.magic, h.size]` gives VM [2, 1] and evaluator [1, 2]. Hash `{"z": next(), "a": next()}` gives VM [2, 1] (sorted-key order) and evaluator [1, 2] in these runs (map order, random per EVL.11). Arrays and call arguments are [1, 2] on both engines. No doc states the evaluation order for struct literals. Verifier's notes: Raised from P3 to P2 because the VM and evaluator disagree. It stays S4: it needs side-effecting initialisers (gets, channel receive, counters).
repro: go1.26.2 test ./reviewcmp -run TestReproStructLiteralOrder -count=1 -v (scratch tree above)
impact: `Header{magic: read_u32(h), size: read_u32(h)}` against a struct declared `{size, magic}` silently swaps the two fields' values.
fix_proposal: Compile initialisers in source order (node.Fields order) into internal slots, or into a stack order that a reordering opcode can permute, then push them in declaration order for OpMakeStruct. At minimum, document the evaluation order for struct and hash literals in the language reference. Regression test: VM test: the struct program above yields [1, 2].

title: The compile-time refusal to assign to the enclosing function's own name only looks one closure deep
claim: emitStoreOnly checks whether the free variable's immediate original is FunctionScope. Two closures deep, that original is itself a FreeScope symbol, so the check passes and the write fails at run time with the opaque error the comment says the check exists to prevent. Verifier: The claim holds. The run-time failure is deterministic and points at the offending line, so the only cost is that the refusal arrives at run time with a less direct message.
evidence: 1463-1469: `Writing it is refused here rather than at run time, where the failure would be an opaque type error about a closure. if original, ok := c.symbolTable.freeOriginal(symbol.Index); ok && original.Scope == FunctionScope {`. Repro: `let f = fn() { let g = fn() { f = 1; }; g(); return 0; }; f();` => COMPILE_ERR(cannot assign to the name of the function being defined: f). `let f = fn() { let g = fn() { let h = fn() { f = 1; }; h(); }; g(); return 0; }; f();` => RUN_ERR(op=OpSetFree: captured variable 0 is not assignable storage). Verifier: emitStoreOnly (compiler.go:1463-1469) checks only the immediate freeOriginal. CLI: `let f = fn(){ let g = fn(){ f = 1; }; g(); return 0; };` gives the compile error `cannot assign to the name of the function being defined: f`. One level deeper (`... let h = fn(){ f = 1; }; ...`) compiles and fails at run time with `op=OpSetFree: captured variable 0 is not assignable storage`, with a full traceback pointing at `f = 1`. Verifier's notes: Lowered from S4 to S5. The program is refused either way, and the shape is unusual.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./reviewcmp -run TestReproAssignFnNameTwoDeep -count=1 -v (scratch tree above)
impact: The error arrives late and is opaque, but only for an unusual program.
fix_proposal: Follow the chain outward: while the original is FreeScope, look it up in the Outer table's FreeSymbols, and refuse if the chain ends in FunctionScope. Regression test: Compiler test: the three-level program above returns the `cannot assign to the name of the function being defined` compile error.

title: Reintroducing the documented ReadOperands offset bug passes every code, compiler and vm unit test
claim: The comment on ReadOperands says the old read-every-operand-from-ins[0] bug survived because the tests used OpClosure 0xFFFF/255, where operand 0's high byte equals operand 1. TestReadOperands still uses exactly that pair, and no other owned test checks a {2,1} or {2,2} decode, so the bug can come back unnoticed. Verifier: The owned packages (code, compiler, vm) have no test that decodes a multi-operand instruction whose operands differ byte-wise, so the documented ReadOperands bug would pass them. The repository suite as a whole would catch it: parity/forin_parity_test.go fails four cases. It is a package-local coverage gap, not a regression that could ship unnoticed.
evidence: code_test.go:74 `{OpClosure, []int{65535, 255}, 3},` is the only multi-operand case; code.go:356-360: `Reading every operand from ins[0] happens to give the right answer ... for the one two-operand case the tests used (OpClosure with 0xFFFF and 255 ...) which is why it stood`. Mutation run: after changing ReadOperands to read `ins[0]` for both widths in the scratch tree, `go test ./code`, `./compiler` and `./vm` all report ok. A two-binding for-in then fails at run time: `for (i, v in [10, 20])` => RUN_ERR(op=OpIterNext: stack underflow reading the loop cursor), because changeOperand re-emits the corrupted binding count. Verifier: In the scratch tree I mutated ReadOperands to read ins[0] for both widths. `go test ./code ./compiler ./vm` passed (ok / ok / ok). Under the mutation a two-binding for-in fails (`for (i, v in [10, 20])` gives RUN_ERR unsupported types INTEGER, ITERATOR), while a one-binding loop still gives 30. But `go test ./parity` FAILS under the same mutation: 4 cases of TestForInSemantics (forin_parity_test.go:78) report VM refused / stack underflow reading the loop cursor. I restored the file and confirmed it is byte-identical to git archive. Verifier's notes: Lowered from S4/P2 to S5/P3 because go test ./... detects the regression.
repro: In scratch tree: patch code/code.go ReadOperands cases to use ins[0]; go1.26.2 test ./code ./compiler ./vm -count=1 => all ok; go1.26.2 test ./reviewcmp -run TestReproForInTwoBindings -v => RUN_ERR; original file restored afterwards (cmp against git archive).
impact: A regression in the helper that changeOperand and boxCapturedLocals depend on, one that corrupts every for-in with two bindings, would pass the unit suites.
fix_proposal: Add ReadOperands round-trip cases where the operands differ byte-wise: OpIterNext {0x1234, 2}, OpClosure {7, 3}, OpMakeStruct {0x0102, 9}, OpEnumValue {0x0A0B, 0x0C0D}. Add a compiler test that changeOperand on OpIterNext preserves the binding count. Regression test: The cases above, asserted operand by operand along with the bytes read.

title: Instructions.String loops forever on an undefined opcode byte; ReadOperands' 'test-only' comment is false; OpCall's name is spelled 'Opcall'
claim: On a Lookup error, String writes an ERROR line and `continue`s without advancing i, so any stream containing an undefined byte (for example the 0xFF polymorphic marker) never returns and grows the buffer without limit. The comment on ReadOperands says it is only used for testing, but compiler.changeOperand and boxCapturedLocals use it in production. The definitions table names OpCall "Opcall", which is what runtime errors print (`op=Opcall`), while the docs say OpCall.
evidence: code.go:320-323: `def, err := Lookup(ins[i]); if err != nil { fmt.Fprintf(&out, "ERROR: %s\n", err); continue }`; code.go:351 `// ReadOperands function is only used for internal code/compiler testing purposes` versus compiler.go:1232 and 1402; code.go:141 `OpCall: {"Opcall", []int{1}},` (vm/vm_test.go:618 pins `op=Opcall`). Repro: `code.Instructions{byte(code.OpTrue), 0xFF, 0x05}.String()` did not return within 2 s. Verifier: code.go:320-323: on a Lookup error, String writes an ERROR line and continues without advancing i. My test `code.Instructions{OpTrue, 0xFF, 0x05}.String()` had not returned after 2 s. code.go:351 says ReadOperands is only used for testing, but compiler.go:1232 (changeOperand) and 1402 (boxCapturedLocals) use it in production. code.go:141 names OpCall "Opcall" (Lookup returns "Opcall"), while BYTECODE_IR.md:212 says OpCall. git grep finds no production caller of Instructions.String.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./reviewcmp -run TestReproInstructionsStringHang -count=1 -v (scratch tree above)
impact: A test that stringifies a mutated or corrupted stream hangs instead of failing, and the comments mislead maintainers. There are no production callers of String today.
fix_proposal: Advance i by 1 (or break) after an unknown opcode. Rewrite the ReadOperands comment to name its production callers. Rename the definition to "OpCall" and update the one test that pins it. Regression test: String() on [OpTrue, 0xFF, 0x05] returns within the test deadline and contains `ERROR: opcode 255 undefined`.

title: Dead exported API in the owned packages: code.ReadUint16/ReadUint8, SymbolTable.IsCaptured, SymbolTable.ModuleNames
claim: code.ReadUint16/ReadUint8 have no callers, and they are the only reason package code imports mutant/security; the VM has its own cached equivalents. SymbolTable.IsCaptured has no callers. SymbolTable.ModuleNames is called only by a test, although its doc says `Editor completion behind ns. wants exactly this list`.
evidence: git grep: `ReadUint16|ReadUint8` appear only at their definitions and in a vm.go:632 comment; `IsCaptured(` has 0 non-test and 0 test callers; `.ModuleNames(` has 0 non-test callers and 1 test (module_scope_test.go:167). sema/facts.go:378: `This is what SymbolTable.ModuleNames has always returned to nobody`. Verifier: git grep: code.ReadUint16/ReadUint8 appear only at their definitions (code.go:377-401) and in a vm.go:632 comment, and they are the only uses of the security import in package code (code.go:382, 395). SymbolTable.IsCaptured (symbol_table.go:376) has no callers. SymbolTable.ModuleNames has only the test caller module_scope_test.go:167, and sema/facts.go:378 says it 'has always returned to nobody', which contradicts its own doc ('Editor completion behind ns. wants exactly this list').
repro: git -C O:/project/mutant grep -n 'ReadUint16\|ReadUint8\|IsCaptured\|ModuleNames' -- '*.go'
impact: The unused secret-taking decode helpers and a completion API with a false doc invite misuse and keep an unnecessary security dependency in the bytecode-format package.
fix_proposal: Delete ReadUint16/ReadUint8 (and the security import), IsCaptured, and ModuleNames with its test, or point ModuleNames' doc at sema's replacement. Regression test: None needed beyond the build. An exported-symbol usage check could flag it next time.

title: Polymorphism tests that cannot fail: TestOpcodeMappingDifferentSeeds only logs, TestPolymorphicWithSeed never compares its two builds
claim: TestOpcodeMappingDifferentSeeds reports identical mappings with t.Logf rather than failing. TestPolymorphicWithSeed says same-seed transformations should be reproducible but asserts only that both streams are non-empty and carry the marker. Verifier: The claim holds. The main-stream properties are covered elsewhere (TestTheSameSeedProducesTheSameBytecodeAtEveryLevel, TestADifferentSeedProducesDifferentBytecode), so these two tests are redundant rather than the only guard. The real gap is constant order and function streams.
evidence: opcode_mapping_test.go:110-112: `if differences == 0 { t.Logf("Warning: Different seeds produced identical mappings (possible but rare)") }`; polymorphic_test.go:114-129 has no comparison of bytecode1 and bytecode2. seed_reproducibility_test.go covers main-stream bytes only; it compares constant-pool length, not order, and not function streams. Verifier: opcode_mapping_test.go:110-112 only calls t.Logf when the mappings are identical. polymorphic_test.go:91-130 (TestPolymorphicWithSeed) asserts non-empty streams and the marker, never compares bytecode1 with bytecode2. seed_reproducibility_test.go:58-70 compares main-stream bytes and constant-pool length, but not constant order or function streams. The CMP.06 repro shows that gap is real: two distinct same-seed builds that this suite does not detect.
repro: Read-only: inspected assertions. Both tests contain no t.Error/t.Fatal path for the property they name.
impact: They give false assurance. A seed that stopped reaching the opcode permutation, or a non-deterministic constant shuffle, would pass.
fix_proposal: Make TestOpcodeMappingDifferentSeeds fail on zero differences, since the seeds are fixed and the result is deterministic. Make the seed test compare Instructions, OpcodeMap and each CompiledFunction's Instructions and constant order. Regression test: The tightened tests themselves.

title: audit_verify passed a log whose first entries were deleted, against the manifest's own head
claim: auditWalk never checked where the chain starts. The first entry's prev was taken on trust even when the document said nothing was dropped, and seq was never compared with first_retained_seq or the entry count. The head is the hash of the last entry, so deleting any number of leading entries left it unchanged: links_intact, head_matches and anchor_matches all true. entries, dropped and chain_complete were copied from the document itself, which whoever deleted the entries could rewrite to pose as a capped log.
