evidence: A 5-entry log (dropped 0, first_retained_seq 1) with log[0:3] deleted, verified against the head sealed into the case manifest, returned anchor_matches true, head_matches true, links_intact true, chain_complete true, entries 5, links_checked 2, detail '2 links recomputed, all intact' -- with the counts left as written and with them rewritten to describe a capped log. The documentation named the manifest head as the remedy for truncation, and that head is exactly the check this passed.
repro: builtin/audit_test.go TestADeletedPrefixIsNotAnIntactLog (both variants) and TestACappedLogVerifiesAndACappedLogMissingMoreDoesNot failed before the fix: every doctored log verified.
impact: Whoever held the written log could remove early security events such as debugger_detected or integrity_failed, and the verifier built to detect edits still reported it as the log the case ran under.
fix_proposal: Derive where the log must start from what the head authenticates, check consecutive seqs, and recompute the counts. Fixed: the last entry's seq is inside its hash, and appendEntry's cap is a fixed rule (keep everything to 4096, then drop 1024 each time the run refills), so auditFirstRetainedFor(last seq) says which entry the log must begin with; a log beginning anywhere else breaks at its first entry with a detail naming the missing range. Entry 1 must follow the genesis, seqs must be consecutive, and entries, dropped and chain_complete are recomputed from the walk, never copied. A new test holds auditFirstRetainedFor to the chain's own behaviour at every length through 10240 events.

title: audit_verify reported a break at an entry with no seq as an intact chain
claim: auditWalk used the breaking entry's seq both as the break flag and as its position (links_intact was firstBroken == 0). An entry whose seq was missing, 0 or not an integer broke the walk with firstBroken = 0, so the result said links_intact true and detail 'N links recomputed, all intact'. Forged entries appended after the genuine last entry therefore verified, and the computed head stayed the genuine one, so the anchor matched too. A middle entry edited with its seq removed also reported links_intact true.
evidence: A forged {event: integrity_failed, prev: head, hash: deadbeef} appended to a genuine 2-entry log with no seq, seq 0, or seq "three" returned links_intact true, anchor_matches true, head_matches true, detail '2 links recomputed, all intact'. Removing the seq of a middle entry and editing it returned links_intact true with '1 links recomputed, all intact'.
repro: builtin/audit_test.go TestAnEntryWithoutAPositiveSeqBreaksTheChain (no seq, 0, "three", -1, 2.5, and a seqless middle edit) failed before the fix.
impact: Fabricated security events, or any other content, could be appended to a written audit log and the verifier still called it intact and anchored -- enough to discredit a run or bury real events in noise.
fix_proposal: Track the break with its own flag and position, and refuse an entry without a positive integer seq. Fixed: auditWalk records broken as a bool, broken_index as the 1-based position and broken_at as the seq (0 when the entry has none); auditEntrySeq accepts only a positive integer, so an entry without one is itself the break. audit_verify's result declares broken_index.

title: ledger_redactions shows the current session's actor name on every record, including redactions by other people
claim: ledgerRecordInto sets out["actor"] = session.actor, which is whoever opened the ledger now, next to the record's own actor_id. When ledger_redactions lists redactions made in earlier sessions by other examiners, every record is attributed by name to the person reading the ledger. Verifier: As stated. The name is correct only for records made by the session doing the reading. Every record from an earlier session by another actor is attributed by name to the reader, with no caveat.
evidence: ledger_redact.go:242 `out["actor"] = stringObj(session.actor)`, next to :243 `out["actor_id"] = stringObj(fmt.Sprintf("%d", record.ActorID))`. Repro: 'Alice Examiner' redacts node 1 and closes the ledger. 'Bob Reviewer' reopens it and calls ledger_redactions, which renders actor="Bob Reviewer" actor_id=14087193026670161088, which is Alice's id. Verifier: ledger_redact.go:242 `out["actor"] = stringObj(session.actor)` is shared by the redaction result and by LedgerRedactions (:549-551). Repro: 'Alice Examiner' redacted node 1 and got back actor=Alice Examiner, actor_id=14087193026670161088. She closed the ledger. 'Bob Reviewer' reopened it, and ledger_redactions rendered actor=Bob Reviewer, actor_id=14087193026670161088 on Alice's record. The metadata promises 'every redaction ... with the actor'. The doc comment's rationale ('the name the session asserted') holds only for a record made in the current session. Verifier's notes: Repro: TestB4CUS03ActorName. No attacker is needed: an ordinary multi-examiner ledger triggers it.
repro: TestReviewRedactionRecordsNameTheWrongActor (scratch).
impact: The record of who destroyed evidence content names the wrong person, in the output an examiner would quote. Only a reader who cross-checks the numeric actor_id can tell.
fix_proposal: Render the name only when record.ActorID == session.actorID. Otherwise use "", or a name looked up from a recorded Actor node, and say which in a field such as actor_source. Regression test: Open a ledger as A, redact, close. Open it as B and call ledger_redactions. Assert the row's actor is not B, and is A or empty. Fixed: Stage E1: ledgerRecordInto names a record's actor with ledgerActorName: the session's own name for the session's own actor id, else the name a disclosure-family Actor node pairs with that id, else empty. A new field actor_source says which (session, ledger, unknown). The reading session's name is never put on another actor's record. The records also report role and role_id, read from the record's own RoleID.

title: The redaction reason check reads the property index, so values stored only in the blob pass and are written into the non-redactable ledgers
location: builtin/ledger_redact.go:153-165, 396-399 (edge scope :436 has the same pattern)
claim: ledgerReasonLeak compares the reason only against NodePropertyEntries, the index rows. The disclosure schema indexes only lookup keys (disclose_ledger.go:128-138). Recipient names, withdrawal reasons and similar values are in the blob only. So a property redaction whose reason repeats the value being erased is accepted, and that value is published in the redaction ledger and the audit log, neither of which can be redacted. The file header promises 'Every builtin here reads the entity's properties first and refuses a reason that repeats one of them.' Verifier: The leak check misses blob-only values. In practice that means the disclosure schema's non-lookup properties, such as recipient.name, disclosure.recipient and withdrawal.reason. Script-written nodes are fully covered.
evidence: ledger_redact.go:396 `ledgerReasonLeak(session.graph.NodePropertyEntries(nodeID), reason, ...)`. Repro: disclose to 'Jane Q Counsel', then ledger_redact_node_properties(Recipient node, 'erasure request from Jane Q Counsel'). It was accepted, and ledger_redactions contains the name. Verifier: ledger_redact.go:396 compares the reason only with NodePropertyEntries, the index rows. disclose_ledger.go:128-138 indexes only lookup keys, so recipient.name stays in the blob only. Repro: I disclosed to 'Jane Q Counsel'. The Recipient node holds recipient.fp (indexed) and recipient.name (blob only). As a control, a reason containing the fp was refused with 'repeats the value of recipient.fp'. The reason 'erasure request from Jane Q Counsel' was accepted, and ledger_redactions now contains the name. This breaks the file-header promise that every builtin 'reads the entity's properties first'. Script nodes from ledger_add_node index every property, so the gap is confined to disclosure-schema nodes. Verifier's notes: Downgraded from S3/P1/security. It is a safety net against the examiner's own accident: the header says it 'catches accidents, not adversaries'. Nobody untrusted gains anything from it, so no embargo is needed. Repro: TestB4CUS04ReasonLeak.
repro: TestReviewReasonLeakMissesBlobOnlyValues (scratch).
impact: A GDPR-style erasure of a recipient's name writes that name permanently into two append-only records, which is the outcome the check exists to prevent.
fix_proposal: Build the comparison set from ledgerDecodeProperties(node.Properties) together with the index entries. Do the same for the edge scope with the edge blob. Regression test: Property-redact a disclosure Recipient node with a reason that contains recipient.name. Expect the refusal 'the reason repeats the value of recipient.name'.

title: A script can stop a withdrawal (or a disclosure) from being recorded by declaring a schema key unique
claim: The property index is shared between script nodes and disclosure schema nodes. ledger_add_node accepts any key, including withdrawal.disclosure_uid, record.uid and disclosure.recipient_fp. ledger_declare_unique then enforces uniqueness across all labels at commit. A script that writes an unlabelled node carrying a disclosure uid and declares the key unique makes every later disclose_withdraw for that uid fail. The same trick works on recipient_fp for disclosures and on reclass.superseded_uid for reclassifications. Verifier: A script, or a co-examiner with ledger write access, can block disclose_withdraw, and similarly disclosures, by writing a colliding schema key and declaring it unique. The failure is loud and names the id that holds the value. It is a denial of a safety action, not a silent bypass.
evidence: Repro: after a disclosure uid U, ledger_add_node({withdrawal.disclosure_uid: U}) and ledger_declare_unique('withdrawal.disclosure_uid','node'). disclose_withdraw(U, 'recalled') then failed with: 'the withdrawal could not be recorded: transaction op 1 (index-node): graphene: unique key "withdrawal.disclosure_uid" value "faa93648..." is already held by id 10'. Verifier: Repro: I added a script node {withdrawal.disclosure_uid: U} and ran ledger_declare_unique('withdrawal.disclosure_uid','node'). disclose_withdraw(U) then failed with 'transaction op 1 (index-node): graphene: unique key "withdrawal.disclosure_uid" value ... is already held by id 10'. Control: with the same script node but no unique declaration, the withdrawal succeeded. So the collision needs a deliberate declaration. disclosureFind filters by label, so the forged node alone fakes nothing. Verifier's notes: Downgraded from S3/P1/security. The script author is trusted, the error is visible and names the colliding node, and nothing is disclosed that should not be. It shares a theme with M26-CUS-001 (generic ledger builtins are not fenced off from the disclosure schema), but the mechanism and fix are separate (key namespace vs redaction guard), so it is not a duplicate. Repro: TestB4CUS05UniqueBlocksWithdrawal and TestB4CUS05ControlNoDeclaration.
repro: TestReviewUniqueDeclarationBlocksWithdrawal (scratch).
impact: Further grants to a recipient cannot be stopped until someone finds the forged node and redacts it. The refusal is visible, but it blames the ledger.
fix_proposal: Reserve the schema's key names: have ledger_add_node, ledger_add_edge and ledger_declare_* refuse keys with the disclosure.*, withdrawal.*, reclass.*, record.*, recipient.*, view.*, class.*, case.* and actor.* prefixes. Alternatively, namespace the schema's index keys so that no script key can collide with them. Regression test: ledger_add_node with a withdrawal.disclosure_uid property is refused. ledger_declare_unique on a schema key is refused.

title: ledger_declare_ordered can report order_differs:false while the declaration empties a query
claim: ledgerOrderDisagreement only compares stored values with each other. A range query's result also depends on how each stored value compares with the query's bound, and the two rules disagree there too. So order_differs:false does not mean the answers are unchanged, although the metadata calls it 'what that does to the answers'. Verifier: order_differs covers stored-vs-stored ordering only, as the returns description says. A range bound encoded differently from the stored values can still change a query's answer after the declaration. The summary's 'what that does to the answers' overstates it.
evidence: Values 10, 20, 30 with filter gt "9": before the declaration count 3, order_differs=false, after the declaration count 0. Using the repo's own 'safe' zero-padded example (0009, 0010, 0100) with bound "9": before 2, order_differs=false, after 0. Verifier: Reproduced three cases. Values 10,20,30 with gt "9": before 3, order_differs:false, after 0. Values 0009,0010,0100 with gt "9": before 2, order_differs:false, after 0. Values 0009,0010,0100 with gt "0009" (bound encoded like the values): 2 before and 2 after. The metadata's returns line documents order_differs as 'whether it reorders what is already stored', which the code does exactly. Its advice to 'encode values so byte order matches intent' covers the padded case once the bound is encoded the same way. Only the summary's phrase 'reports what that does to the answers' promises more than that. Verifier's notes: Downgraded from S3/P2 correctness to S4/P3 docs. With a consistently encoded bound the answer is unchanged. Repro: TestB4CUS06DeclareOrdered.
repro: TestReviewDeclareOrderedFalseAssurance and TestReviewDeclareOrderedPaddedValuesUnpaddedBound (scratch).
impact: An examiner who reads order_differs:false as 'safe to declare' loses matching records from later range queries with no error. This is the 'absence of evidence manufactured by a schema change' that the file header warns about.
fix_proposal: Document order_differs as covering stored-vs-stored ordering only. Also add a field saying that numeric-looking bounds of a different width or form will compare differently, or refuse to declare while any stored value parses as a number unless the caller confirms. Regression test: Values 10, 20, 30 and gt "9" must not produce an assurance that the answer is unchanged.

title: One case_note containing NaN or Inf stops case_write for the rest of the case
claim: case_note keeps objectToNative's output, which passes float NaN and ±Inf through (format_native.go:283). encoding/json refuses those values, so custodySeal cannot canonicalise, and case_write returns an error from then on, including after case_close. A timeline entry cannot be removed. Verifier: As stated. case_bundle is broken too. In-tree builtins record no evidence-derived floats in the timeline, so only the script author's own data can trigger this.
evidence: CLI nan.mut: `let ratio = empty / empty;` prints 'ratio: NaN'. case_note is accepted, then case_write fails with 'ERROR:case_write: the manifest cannot be canonicalised: json: unsupported value: NaN'. Writing again after case_close fails with the same error. Verifier: CLI (my nan.mut, built with go1.26.2): `let mean = zero / zero;` printed 'mean: NaN'. case_note was accepted. case_write failed with 'the manifest cannot be canonicalised: json: unsupported value: NaN'. After case_close, case_write failed the same way. The Go test also showed case_bundle failing identically, while case_manifest() and case_close succeed. convertToNative (format_native.go:283) passes the float through, and custodyCanonical's json.Marshal refuses it. Verifier's notes: Priority lowered from P1 to P2. The failure is loud, the trusted author's own value triggers it, and the workaround is re-running without the note, although that can be expensive. Repro: scratchpad/stageB/b4a/CUS/run/nan.mut and TestB4CUS07NaN.
repro: Scratch .../CUS/run/nan.mut compiled and run with mutant.exe (PowerShell). Also TestReviewNaNNoteBreaksCaseWrite.
impact: An ordinary statistic, such as the mean over an empty set, recorded in a note makes the signed manifest impossible to write, and hours of custody record can only be exported unsigned by hand.
fix_proposal: Refuse NaN and ±Inf in case_note data (walk the native value), or render them as strings. Apply the same rule to every custodyRecordArtifact data map. Regression test: case_note("x", {"v": 0.0/0.0}) must be refused, or case_write must succeed afterwards.

title: A malformed hash option silently opens an unhashed case
claim: The policy comes from optString(args[2], "hash", "none"), which returns the default when the argument is not a hash, when the key is spelled differently, or when the value is not a string. case_open(id, ex, "sha256"), {"hash_policy": "sha256"} (the field name the result and manifest themselves use), {"Hash": ...} and {"hash": ["sha256"]} all open with policy none and return no error. Verifier: As stated. The returned hash_policy honestly reports 'none'. The digest can still be added later with case_evidence(path, {hash: ...}) while record.Digest is empty.
evidence: custody.go:339 `policy = strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(optString(args[2], "hash", "none")))`. The repro printed 'option {hash_policy: sha256} -> hash_policy=none (no error)', and the same for the other three spellings. Verifier: custody.go:339 uses optString(args[2], "hash", "none"), and optString (secure_net.go:886) falls back to the default for a non-HASH argument, a missing key or a non-string value. Repro: "sha256", {hash_policy: sha256}, {Hash: sha256} and {hash: [sha256]} each opened with hash_policy=none and no error. {hash: "sha-256"} was correctly refused. Verifier's notes: Downgraded from S3 to S4. The script author is trusted, the result states the policy, and it can be recovered. Repro: TestB4CUS08HashOption.
repro: TestReviewCaseOpenMalformedHashOptionIsIgnored (scratch).
impact: Evidence the examiner asked to be digested at open is never digested. The case is reported as hash_policy none, which is honest but has already happened by the time anyone reads it.
fix_proposal: Require args[2] to be a HASH, refuse unknown keys, and refuse a non-string hash value. Regression test: Each of the four malformed options must return an error. Fixed: case_open and case_evidence read {hash} and case_write reads {sign} through secretOptionsArg and formatOptions, so a non-hash options argument, an unknown key (hash_policy, Hash, signed) and a value of the wrong type are each refused with an error naming what was accepted; before the fix all ten cases in the test opened, registered or wrote. The CHANGELOG records it under Changed.

title: A redaction reason that is not valid UTF-8 is recorded as different text in the ledger and in the manifest
claim: ledgerReasonArg only trims the reason. The raw bytes go into graphene's hash-chained redaction record, and the same reason goes into the case manifest timeline as JSON, where invalid bytes become U+FFFD. This is the trap custodyDocumentName exists to stop: a name used twice must be valid UTF-8.
evidence: Repro reason "order \xff\xfe 17": the ledger record holds the bytes ff fe, and the written manifest holds "reason": "order �� 17". Verifier: ledgerReasonArg (ledger_redact.go:135-145) only trims the reason. Repro reason "order \xff\xfe 17": the ledger record's reason holds the raw bytes \xff\xfe, and the written manifest timeline holds "order �� 17". Verifier's notes: Only the script author can trigger it. The manifest hash stays self-consistent. Repro: TestB4CUS10InvalidUTF8.
repro: TestReviewRedactionReasonInvalidUTF8 (scratch).
impact: The manifest's copy of the reason no longer matches the ledger record whose redaction_hash the manifest quotes, so a reader cannot recompute or match it.
fix_proposal: Call custodyDocumentName(op, "reason", reason) in ledgerReasonArg. Regression test: A reason with invalid UTF-8 is refused by all four redaction builtins.

title: case_evidence silently discards an explicitly requested digest algorithm
claim: When a source already has a digest under another algorithm, case_evidence(path, {hash: "sha256"}) reads and hashes the whole file and then throws the result away. It returns the old md5 digest with no notice. Verifier: As stated. The result does show hash_algo md5, so a reader who checks it can see that the requested algorithm was not recorded.
evidence: custody.go:550 `if digest != "" && record.Digest == "" {`. Repro: case policy md5, raw_open, then case_evidence(path, {hash: sha256}) returned hash_algo=md5 hash=a0c16616.... Verifier: custody.go:550 `if digest != "" && record.Digest == ""`. Repro: I opened the case with md5, then ran raw_open/raw_close and case_evidence(path, {hash: sha256}). It returned hash_algo:md5, hash:a0c16616..., and the sha256 that was computed was discarded without notice. Verifier's notes: Repro: TestB4CUS12EvidenceAlgo.
repro: TestReviewCaseEvidenceHashRequestIgnored (scratch).
impact: The examiner believes a SHA-256 was recorded when it was not, and a potentially very large read was wasted.
fix_proposal: Keep digests per algorithm (a map), or refuse, or at least report that the requested algorithm was not recorded. Regression test: After an md5-policy open, case_evidence with sha256 returns sha256 or an explicit refusal.

title: A witness time given in milliseconds overflows into a plausible wrong date
claim: Only unix <= 0 is refused. `UnixNano: unix.Value * 1e9` overflows int64 for any value above about 9.2e9. A value in milliseconds, a common slip, wraps silently.
evidence: Witness unix 1790270474000 gave last_anchored_unix=936298850 and last_anchored_at=1999-09-02T19:00:50Z, which also appears in graphene's 'witnessed at' gap text. Verifier: ledger_custody.go:765 `UnixNano: unix.Value * 1e9` has no upper bound (:752 refuses only values of 0 or less). Repro: unix 1790270474 gave last_anchored_at 2026-09-24T17:21:14Z, which is correct. unix 1790270474000 gave last_anchored_unix 936298850 and at=1999-09-02T19:00:50Z, which is silent int64 wraparound. Verifier's notes: The script author supplies the witness list. Repro: TestB4CUS13Witness.
repro: TestReviewWitnessUnixOverflow (scratch).
impact: The only field a witness contributes that the store could not have written itself is reported as a wrong but believable date.
fix_proposal: Refuse unix > math.MaxInt64/1e9, or any value far in the future, and say that the value looks like milliseconds. Regression test: A witness record with unix 1790270474000 is refused.

title: case_close clears custodyActive outside the lock and can switch off recording for a case opened concurrently
claim: CaseClose unlocks and only then stores custodyActive=false. A CaseOpen that runs in that gap sets true, and the late false leaves the new case open with the fast path off. Every evidence open, touch and artifact of that case is then silently skipped.
evidence: custody.go:752 `custodyStore.Unlock()` then :753 `custodyActive.Store(false)`. The stress repro (close in one goroutine, open in another) hit 'case B open but custodyActive false' in 34 of 20000 iterations. Verifier: custody.go:752-753 releases the lock (`custodyStore.Unlock()`) and only then runs `custodyActive.Store(false)`. CaseOpen stores true after its own Unlock (:369-371). My stress run of a concurrent close A / open B found case B open with custodyActive=false in 10 of 20000 iterations. Verifier's notes: It needs concurrent case_close and case_open from spawned tasks, so it is unlikely. Repro: TestB4CUS14Race.
repro: TestReviewCloseOpenRaceLeavesCaseUnrecorded (scratch).
impact: Needs concurrent case_close and case_open, for example from spawned tasks. Unlikely, but when it happens the loss is silent.
fix_proposal: Store custodyActive while holding the lock in both CaseOpen and CaseClose, or derive it from the session under the lock. Regression test: Keep the stress test and assert zero hits.

title: ledger_verify_chain never checks that the earlier root set binds, although its docs say both are checked
claim: graphene VerifyChain (disk/prove.go:299-311) checks only later.PrevRoot == earlier.Snapshot and bindSnapshotRoot(later). The earlier set's five components and its body_version are required by ledgerRootsFromHash but never checked. The metadata says a zero component 'would fail the snapshot root's own binding check', which is true of the later set only. Verifier: Only the earlier set's snapshot_root takes part in the chain check. Its components and body_version are required by the parser and then ignored. The metadata's stated reason for requiring them applies to the later set only. The chain answer itself is correct, because the earlier snapshot's identity is its root.
evidence: Earlier set with a genuine snapshot_root, five garbage components and body_version 200 returned chained:true. Verifier: graphene v0.9.0 disk/prove.go:299-311 VerifyChain checks later.PrevRoot == earlier.Snapshot and bindSnapshotRoot(later) only. Repro: an earlier set with its genuine snapshot_root, five garbage components and body_version 77 returned chained:true. The control, a later set with garbage components, returned chained:false ('the later snapshot root does not follow from its components'). Metadata :2243 justifies requiring every component because 'a zero component would fail the snapshot root's own binding check', which is true only of the later set. Verifier's notes: Downgraded from S4 to S5. An 'altered' earlier record changes nothing the chain check depends on. Repro: TestB4CUS15VerifyChain.
repro: TestReviewVerifyChainEarlierComponentsUnchecked (scratch).
impact: A retained record that has been altered or mis-transcribed is accepted as the predecessor without comment.
fix_proposal: Check that the earlier set binds too, or correct the docs to say only its snapshot_root is used. Regression test: An earlier set whose components do not bind is refused, or chained:false.

title: The behavioural read-only test covers 3 of about 16 evidence opener call sites and none of the filesystem libraries
claim: The file says it is the check that catches 'a third-party library writing through a handle Mutant gave it', and the manifest asserts evidence_read_only:true. The test exercises only raw_open, zip_open and tar_open. There are about 16 custodyRecordOpen/At call sites: archive 2, disk_image_parsers 3, disk_image_extents 1, filesystem_parsers 6, table_parsers 2, hive 1, registry 1. The six aoiflux filesystem openers, EWF/VHDI and table_open are never opened read-only.
evidence: grep of custodyRecordOpen callers, compared with the three cases in TestEvidenceOpensFromAReadOnlyFile. Verifier: git grep finds 16 custodyRecordOpen/At call sites outside tests: archive.go x2, disk_image_parsers.go x3, disk_image_extents.go x1, filesystem_parsers.go x6, table_parsers.go x2, hive_builtins.go x1, registry_forensics.go x1. TestEvidenceOpensFromAReadOnlyFile (evidence_readonly_test.go:99-158) covers raw_open, zip_open and tar_open. No other test chmods an evidence file read-only; the only other Chmod is case_key_test.go:640, on a key directory. The manifest asserts integrity.evidence_read_only:true (custody.go:1163) for every opener. Verifier's notes: This was verified with git grep and by reading the test. There is no runtime failure to reproduce. The static AST guard (policy/evidence_guard_test.go) still backs the claim on the source side.
repro: Code reading only. The test was not extended.
impact: The behavioural backing for the manifest's read-only claim is thinner than the comment says.
fix_proposal: Add the in-tree fixtures (usb_stick.img, fsagen images, VHD fixtures) to the table so every opener family is covered. Regression test: One case per opener family.

title: A ledger redacted before the disclosure schema was guarded could have lost a withdrawal, a disclosure or a reclassification, and nothing noticed
verifier: Stage E7a 2026-09-28 (a probe on 57132eb, then a failing test first)
location: builtin/disclose_ledger.go disclosureRefusal and disclosureWithdrawnFor, builtin/disclose_history.go DiscloseHistory and DiscloseForSegment (57132eb); graphene v0.9.0 disk.RedactionRecord, which keeps no labels
claim: M26-CUS-001's fix stops the ledger_redact_* builtins removing a node or edge of the disclosure schema. A ledger redacted by an earlier build may already have lost a Withdrawal, a Disclosure or a ReclassEvent: a whole-node redaction deletes the node, its labels and its index entries, and graphene's RedactionRecord keeps the node id, scope, cascaded edges and hashes but no labels, so the record cannot say afterwards that the removed node was a withdrawal. disclose_to_passphrase, disclose_history and the other disclose_* readers consulted none of it: a withdrawal removed that way let its record be disclosed again to the recipient it was withdrawn from, and the history no longer counted it.
evidence: disclosureWithdrawnFor (57132eb) found a withdrawal only through the recipient's Disclosure nodes (disclosure.recipient_fp) and then the withdrawal.disclosure_uid index, and a node redaction removes the node's index entries with it. ledger_redactions reported such a record with role "" and nothing else read the redaction records. Scope: the ledger family is new in 2.6.0 (added after the v2.5.0 tag), and every build that records a role on a redaction (8f4a39a onwards) already refused the schema (a41011b), so only a ledger redacted by a development build from before 8f4a39a can hold such a redaction.
repro: Probe test in builtin on 57132eb (scratch, deleted after): newDiscloseFixture; disclose to Counsel under the counsel view; disclose_withdraw; session.store.RedactNode(withdrawal node, RedactionRequest with RoleID 0), the path a build before the guard took; ledger_close and ledger_open again; disclose_to_passphrase(ledger, record, "counsel", "Counsel"). Result: redaction 1 (scope node, role id 0) removed the withdrawal, and the record was disclosed again to the recipient it was withdrawn from -- 1 grant issued, 1 passphrase prompt -- and disclose_history counted 0 withdrawn of 2.
impact: On such a ledger a withdrawn recipient could be granted the record again, a disclosure could be missing from disclose_history and disclose_for_segment, and a superseded record could be disclosed, with the ledger giving no sign. Each redaction is attributable (ledger_redactions lists its actor, time and reason), so this was a detection gap on a ledger already altered, not a live bypass: the redaction builtins refuse the schema since M26-CUS-001.
fix_proposal: Report the redactions that may have removed a disclosure record, add ledger_redactions_review(ledger, through_seq, reason) for an examiner to answer for them, and issue no grant until one has. Fixed: every redaction recorded with no role is in question, except a property redaction of a node or an edge a script wrote that the ledger still holds. disclose_to_passphrase refuses, before any key material or passphrase and again under the ledger lock, while one is not answered for by ledger_redactions_review(ledger, through_seq, reason): the next event of the ledger's one hash-linked chain of RedactionReview nodes, bound to the hash of the redaction record it names; a chain that forks, goes backwards or names a record the ledger does not hold counts for nothing. disclose_history, disclose_for_segment, disclose_reclassified and redaction_versions report unguarded_redactions; ledger_redactions marks each record unguarded and reports reviewed_through, unguarded_redactions, reviews_intact and reviews_reason. A withdrawal is now found by the record and the recipient it names, so one whose disclosure was removed still stops a new grant.
regression_test: builtin/ledger_redaction_review_test.go: TestAnUnguardedRedactionStopsGrantsUntilReviewed (the probe's path, refused before any key or prompt, then lifted by a review), TestEveryAnswerFromTheDisclosureRecordsNamesTheUnguardedRedactions, TestAWithdrawalOutlivesTheDisclosureARedactionRemoved, TestOnlyARedactionTheGuardMayNotHaveSeenIsInQuestion, TestAReviewAnswersForTheRedactionsItNamesAndNoMore, TestAReviewIsBoundToTheRedactionRecordItNames, TestARedactionReviewIsFoundByEachOfItsLookupKeys

title: A hash lookup trusted a 64-bit FNV digest and never compared the key, so two crafted strings shared one entry
claim: String.HashKey and Bytes.HashKey were the FNV-1a-64 digest of the value, Hash.Pairs is a map keyed by HashKey, and every insert and lookup in both engines indexed by that key alone without comparing the pair's own key. Two different strings, or buffers, with one digest were therefore one key: the later write replaced the earlier, and a lookup of either returned the other's value. unique, contains and index_of were not affected, because they compare Inspect.
evidence: Stage B: a distinguished-point search found "e38154aa4dee0878" and "c4272bece7a8573e", both FNV-1a-64 c5844c23d3d0fabc, in 27 seconds on 16 cores. Inserting both into a hash printed len 1, and {"e38154aa4dee0878": "clean.exe"}["c4272bece7a8573e"] printed clean.exe. Reproduced in Stage C in both engines by TestTwoNamesWithOneDigestAreTwoKeysInBothEngines: the count was 1, the lookup returned the other name's value, a second write replaced the first, a literal holding both had len 1, and two buffers holding the two names were one key.
repro: parity/hash_collision_parity_test.go TestTwoNamesWithOneDigestAreTwoKeysInBothEngines and object/hash_key_test.go TestTwoKeysWithOneDigestAreTwoKeys failed on all their cases before the fix.
impact: Hash keys in forensic scripts come from evidence -- file names, registry values, URLs, account names. Anyone able to plant two colliding names could make a per-name hash (a dedup set, a count, an allow-list, a verdict table) merge them with no error: one artefact vanished from a count or inherited another's verdict.
fix_proposal: Compare the real key, or key strings and buffers by their full value. Fixed: HashKey gains a Text field, and a map compares every field, so a key is equal only to an equal value with no call site changed. A string's key carries the string whole in Text (sharing its memory, so nothing is copied). A buffer's key carries its SHA-256 rather than the buffer, because a map key is an immutable string nothing can zero and a buffer may be classified plaintext; no SHA-256 collision is known. Integers, floats and booleans were already exact. Compiled artifacts carry no hash constants, so older .mu files are unaffected. BYTECODE_IR section 17.3 describes the key.

title: Struct.Inspect ranges a Go map, so struct equality, contains/index_of/unique and printing are random
claim: Struct.Inspect builds its field list with `for k, v := range s.Fields`, so field order changes from call to call. Inspect is the identity used for struct `==` in both engines (vm/vm.go:2203-2206 falls back to Inspect; so does evaluator/eval_expressions.go:92-95), for contains and index_of (builtin/collections_builtins.go:27), for unique's dedup key (collections_builtins.go:224), and for Error.Equals on related values. Two identical structs therefore compare unequal most of the time, and a printed struct differs between runs. Hash.Inspect already fixed this same problem for hashes (hashObj.go:52-62). Verifier: The claim is accurate and slightly understated. A struct is often unequal even to itself (`p == p` is false), because every Inspect call re-ranges the map.
evidence: `for k, v := range s.Fields { fields = append(fields, fmt.Sprintf("%s: %s", k, v.Inspect())) }`. repro/structeq.mut compared two structs built from the same literal 200 times and printed `equal: 30 unequal: 170`, then printed `P { b: 2, a: 1, f: 6, e: 5, d: 4, c: 3 }`. The parity harness gives BOOLEAN(false) for `p == q` in both engines. Verifier: object/struct.go:22 builds its field list with `for k, v := range s.Fields` and does not sort. Struct `==` falls back to Inspect in vm/vm.go (execComparison fallback) and in evaluator/eval_expressions.go (the `==` case). I ran rp/structeq.mut three times. Over 100 iterations, two structs built from the same literal compared equal 23/17/15/16 times. `p == p` printed false. len(unique([p, q, p, q])) printed 2 where 1 is right. The printed struct changed every run, e.g. `P { b: 2, a: 1, f: 6, ... }` then `P { f: 6, e: 5, ... }`. Verifier's notes: Downgraded from S2 to S3. The script author triggers it, not the evidence. Structs appear in only 3 examples and none of them compare structs. It is still a silent wrong answer to basic equality, and it makes printed output nondeterministic, which is the same class of defect Hash.Inspect was already fixed for. So P1. Related to VM.08 (Inspect used as identity) but a distinct root: map order.
repro: `struct P { a; b; c; d; e; f; };` then, in a 200-iteration loop, `let p = P {a:1,...,f:6}; let q = P {a:1,...,f:6}; if (p == q) {same++} else {differ++}`. Compile and run it with the scratch mutant.exe.
impact: The same question gets a different answer on each run for any struct with two or more fields. Scripts that compare, dedupe or look up structs get wrong answers with no error, and every report that prints a struct changes between runs, so goldens and diffs cannot be used.
fix_proposal: Sort the field names in Struct.Inspect, or render them in declaration order if the definition is kept. Give structs typed equality (same TypeName and field-by-field equal values) in execComparison, evalInfixExpression and objectsEqual, rather than comparing rendered text. Regression test: An object test asserts that Inspect of a six-field struct is identical over 100 calls. A parity test asserts that `p == q` is true 100 times in both engines and that unique([p, q]) has length 1.

title: A function is never equal to itself on the VM, and the evaluator answers the opposite
claim: Closure.Inspect renders the pointer. mutil.EncryptObject and DecryptObject build a new *object.Closure on every push, pop and store (mutil/util.go:234 `encObj = &object.Closure{Fn: closureObj.Fn, Free: free}`, and mutil/util.go:524). Each read of `f` therefore has a new address. Equality falls back to Inspect, so on the VM `f == f` is false, unique([f, f, f]) keeps all three and contains([f], f) is false. The evaluator's Function.Inspect prints the source, so it answers true, and even says two distinct closures with the same source are equal. TestEveryObjectFieldSurvivesStorage compares with reflect.DeepEqual and cannot see that identity is lost. Verifier: The claim is accurate. On the VM a function value never equals itself or an alias. The evaluator (macro expansion only) compares rendered source, so it calls two distinct closures with the same text equal.
evidence: repro/closure.mut printed false, false, 3, false. Parity harness: `let f = fn(x) { x }; f == f` gives evaluator=BOOLEAN(true), vm=BOOLEAN(false). `len(unique([f, f]))` gives evaluator 1, vm 2. Verifier: Closure.Inspect is `Closure[%p]` (closureObj.go:11). mutil/util.go's CLOSURE arm builds `&object.Closure{Fn: closureObj.Fn, Free: free}` on every seal, so each load gives a new pointer. On the VM, rp/closure.mut printed false (f == f), false (g == f), 3 (unique([f,f,f])) and false (contains([f], f)). My parity test zz_b4_test.go gave, evaluator vs VM: `f == f` true/false; `let g = f; g == f` true/false; len(unique([f,f])) 1/2; `fn(x){x} == fn(x){x}` true/false. Verifier's notes: Downgraded from S3. Comparing functions, deduping them and testing membership of them are rare in forensic scripts, and the evaluator side is reachable only from macros. This interacts with M26-EVL-002: fixing Inspect to print a name or parameter list would make distinct closures compare equal, so the identity fix has to be separate.
repro: `let f = fn(x) { x }; putln(f == f); let g = f; putln(g == f); putln(len(unique([f, f, f]))); putln(contains([f], f));`
impact: Callback tables, dedup of handlers and membership tests silently give wrong answers, and the two engines disagree, so an unquote in a macro and the same expression written inline differ.
fix_proposal: Compare functions by identity (the same *CompiledFunction and the same Free cells) in both engines' comparisons and in objectsEqual, independent of Inspect. Fix Inspect separately as M26-EVL-002 proposes. Its fix alone (a name or parameter list) would make distinct anonymous closures compare equal. Regression test: A parity test for `f == f` (true), `let g = f; g == f` (true), `fn(x){x} == fn(x){x}` (decided and pinned), and `len(unique([f, f]))` equal to 1 in both engines.

title: Float.Inspect rounds to six decimals, and Inspect is the identity for composite equality, unique, contains and hash-key order
claim: `func (f *Float) Inspect() string { return fmt.Sprintf("%f", f.Value) }` discards every digit below 1e-6. Anything that compares rendered text therefore merges distinct floats: array, hash and struct equality, unique, contains and index_of on composites, and Error.Equals. hashKeyLess (hashObj.go:110) orders float keys by the same text. That ordering is lexical, so 10.0 sorts before 9.0. When two keys render alike the sort.Slice result depends on map order, so printing a hash and iterating it with for-in (iterator.go:77) come out in a different order from run to run. Verifier: The claim is accurate. unique also collapses two distinct scalar floats, not only composites: unique([7.9999991, 7.9999994]) has length 1.
evidence: repro/floats.mut with a=7.9999991, b=7.9999994: `a == b` false, `[a] == [b]` true, `len(unique([a, b]))` 1, `contains([[a]], [b])` true, and `putln(0.0000001)` prints 0.000000. `{0.0000001: "first", 0.0000002: "second", 0.0000003: "third"}` printed `{0.000000: first, 0.000000: second, 0.000000: third}` on two runs and `{0.000000: third, 0.000000: first, 0.000000: second}` on the third. The parity harness gives BOOLEAN(true) in both engines for `[0.0000001] == [0.0000002]`. Verifier: object/float.go:10 formats with `%f`. hashKeyLess has no *Float case and falls back to Inspect text. rp/floats.mut with a=7.9999991, b=7.9999994 printed: a == b false, [a] == [b] true, len(unique([a, b])) 1, contains([[a]], [b]) true, putln(0.0000001) 0.000000. Four runs printing `{0.0000001: first, 0.0000002: second, 0.0000003: third}` gave three different orders. `{10.0: ..., 9.0: ...}` printed 10.000000 before 9.000000. Parity: `[0.0000001] == [0.0000002]` is true in both engines. Verifier's notes: The root is distinct from VM.08, which is about cross-type equality, although both come from the Inspect-as-identity fallback. No document states the six-decimal rendering.
repro: Compile repro/floats.mut and run it three times.
impact: Entropy values, timestamps with sub-second parts and scores collapse under unique and match the wrong element under contains. Tiny values print as 0.000000. Output that contains float-keyed hashes is not reproducible.
fix_proposal: Render floats with strconv.FormatFloat(v, 'g', -1, 64), the shortest form that round-trips, or at minimum use a lossless form wherever Inspect serves as identity. Add a *Float case to hashKeyLess that compares numerically. Regression test: Assert that unique([7.9999991, 7.9999994]) has length 2 and `[a] == [b]` is false in both engines, and that Hash.Inspect with three sub-1e-6 float keys is identical over 50 calls and sorted numerically.

title: The evaluator returns arithmetic and bitwise failures as error values instead of faults, so `1 / 0` does not stop a macro body
claim: When the fault type was introduced, bare *object.Error stopped being a fatal signal. evalInfixExpression still returns object.NumericInfix(...) (line 77) and object.BitwiseOperandError(...) (line 70) as they come, and evalPrefixExpression returns object.BitwiseNot(right) (line 33) the same way. All three return a plain *object.Error for division or modulo by zero, a negative shift or a non-integer bitwise operand. isError only detects *fault, so evaluation carries on with an error bound to the name. The VM stops the run for every one of these. TestEvaluatorVMOperatorParity cannot catch it: normalize maps a fault and an error value to the same "ERROR". Verifier: The claim is accurate. It is reachable only through macro bodies and unquote, because the evaluator's sole production role is macro expansion (evaluator.go package doc).
evidence: Parity harness. The evaluator gave INTEGER(5) and the VM stopped with vm_runtime_error for each of: `let x = 1 / 0; 5`, `let x = 1 % 0; 5`, `let x = 1 << -1; 5`, `let x = 1.5 & 1; 5` and `let x = ~"a"; 5`. `let x = 1 / 0; type_of(x)` gave evaluator STRING("ERROR_OBJ"). The macro `let m = macro() { let q = 10 / 0; quote(unquote(3)); }; m();` expanded and ran to INTEGER(3), where the same body written inline stops with an error. Verifier: evaluator/eval_expressions.go returns object.NumericInfix(...), object.BitwiseOperandError(...) and object.BitwiseNot(right) unwrapped. These return *object.Error (infixError), which isError (fault-only) does not detect. In my parity test the evaluator gave INTEGER(5) and the VM stopped with vm_runtime_error for `let x = 1 / 0; 5`, `1 % 0`, `1 << -1`, `1.5 & 1` and `~"a"`. `1 / 0; 99` gave evaluator 99. `let x = 1 / 0; type_of(x)` gave evaluator ERROR_OBJ. The macro `let m = macro() { let q = 10 / 0; quote(unquote(3)); }; m();` expanded and ran to INTEGER(3), while the same body inline fails in the VM. Verifier's notes: Downgraded from S3 to S4 because it is macro-only and the script author controls it. It still breaks the macro/inline parity promise stated in parity/parity_test.go's header.
repro: Scratch parity/zz_review5_test.go, TestReviewArithFaultParity: `go1.26.2 test ./parity -run TestReviewArithFaultParity -v`.
impact: Macro bodies and unquote expressions keep running after a failure the VM treats as fatal, so a macro can expand successfully from a computation that the same code written inline refuses. TestGenuineFaultsStillStopEvaluation (evaluator/fault_test.go) lists no arithmetic case, which is why this passes.
fix_proposal: Wherever the evaluator calls object.NumericInfix, BitwiseOperandError or BitwiseNot, turn a returned *object.Error into &fault{err: e}. In the parity harness, tell a fault from a value, for example by also running `let x = <expr>; 5` for every case. Regression test: Add `1 / 0; 99`, `1 << -1; 99` and `~"a"; 99` to TestGenuineFaultsStillStopEvaluation, and a parity case `let x = 1 / 0; 5` that both engines must refuse.

title: Evaluator loops stop at the first iteration whose body ends in an error value
claim: The for-in loop (line 522), the while loop (line 554) and the C-style for loop (line 597) end the loop when `result.Type()` is ERROR_OBJ. That test matches the fault and also any error value. So a body whose last expression is an error value ends the loop after one iteration. Examples are `error("e")`, or `errs[i] = e`, since an assignment yields the value assigned. evalBlockStatement was already fixed to test isError (evaluator.go:267-273); the loops were not. Verifier: The claim is accurate: the three loop forms treat an error value as a fault. It affects only macro expansion.
evidence: `case object.RETURN_VALUE_OBJ, object.ERROR_OBJ: return result`. Parity harness: `let n = 0; for (x in [1, 2, 3]) { n = n + 1; error("e") }; n` gives evaluator 1, vm 3. The while and C-style for versions do the same. `for (i, p in ["a","b","c"]) { n = n + 1; errs[i] = error(p); }` gives evaluator 1, vm 3. A macro running that loop in its body splices 1 where the inline code gives 3. Verifier: evaluator/evaluator.go:522 and :554 contain `case object.RETURN_VALUE_OBJ, object.ERROR_OBJ: return result`, and :597 contains `result.Type() == object.ERROR_OBJ`. evalBlockStatement (:267-273) was already changed to isError. In my parity test, evaluator vs VM: for-in / while / C-style for whose body ends in error("e") gave 1/3 for each. `for (i, p in ["a","b","c"]) { n = n + 1; errs[i] = error(p); }` gave 1/3. A macro running the for-in loop spliced INTEGER(1) where the same code inline gives 3. Verifier's notes: Downgraded to S4 because it is macro-only. The resulting macro expansion is silently wrong, so P2.
repro: Scratch parity/zz_review_test.go (TestReviewParityCandidates) and zz_review3_test.go (TestReviewMacroLoop).
impact: A macro body that collects errors in a loop silently processes only the first element.
fix_proposal: In the three loops, return early only for RETURN_VALUE_OBJ or isError(result), which detects a fault; let error values fall through as ordinary values. Regression test: Parity cases for all three loop forms whose body ends in `error("e")` and in `errs[i] = e`, expecting 3 in both engines.

title: Evaluator higher-order builtins raise faults for argument mistakes the VM returns as values, and the file header says the opposite
claim: The header (higher_order.go:16-17) says "Errors surface as *object.Error values". But arrayAndCallback, evalReduce, evalParallel and sortKeyLess all use newError, which returns a *fault that stops evaluation. The VM's versions (vm/higher_order.go:78-96, 150-161, 243) return *object.Error values that the program can hold. The evaluator also never checks the callback's arity (1 or 2 parameters; reduce needs exactly 2). It calls the callback with one argument and faults on the resulting arity error, where the VM reports the shape as a value. Verifier: The claim is accurate. It is macro-only, and the evaluator fails loudly where the VM returns an error value.
evidence: Parity harness. Evaluator ERROR, VM INTEGER(7) for each of: `let r = map(5, fn(x) { x }); 7`, `let r = reduce([1, 2], fn(a) { a }, 0); 7`, `let r = map([1, 2], fn(a, b, c) { a }); 7`, and `let r = sort_by([1, "a"], fn(x) { x }); 7`. As a macro body, the map case fails expansion with "wrong number of arguments. want=3, got=1". Verifier: The evaluator/higher_order.go header says 'Errors surface as *object.Error values', but arrayAndCallback, evalReduce and the others use newError (a *fault). In my parity test the evaluator produced a fault (surfaced as an error by Eval) and the VM returned 7 for: `map(5, fn(x){x})`, `reduce([1,2], fn(a){a}, 0)`, `map([1,2], fn(a,b,c){a})` and `sort_by([1,"a"], fn(x){x})`. As macro bodies, the map cases failed expansion ('wrong number of arguments. want=3, got=1' and 'map: first argument must be ARRAY'). Verifier's notes: Lowered to P3. It is macro-only, and the divergent direction is a loud expansion failure, not a silently wrong value. The misleading header comment is part of the fix.
repro: Scratch parity/zz_review_test.go and zz_review3_test.go (TestReviewMacroMapArgs).
impact: A macro that validates or probes collection calls stops at expansion time where the same code inline carries on, and the header comment misleads anyone keeping the two in sync.
fix_proposal: Return errorValue(...) rather than newError(...) for argument-shape errors in arrayAndCallback, evalReduce, evalParallel and sortKeyLess. Add the VM's parameter-count checks. Correct the header comment. Regression test: Extend a parity table with the four inputs above and require the same value in both engines.

title: Evaluator spawn records an error value as a task failure and records a fault as a successful result, which leaks the fault
claim: `if errObj, failed := result.(*object.Error); failed { CompleteTask(handle, nil, errors.New(errObj.Message)) } else { CompleteTask(handle, result, nil) }` gets both cases backwards compared with vm/spawn.go. In the VM a returned error is the task's value and only a runtime failure is a failure. Here an error value becomes a failure. A genuine fault is not an *object.Error, so it is stored as the task's result, leaves the fault's package boundary through task_wait, and stops the program at whichever later expression first touches it. Verifier: The claim is accurate. It is reachable only when a macro body calls spawn.
evidence: Parity harness. `spawn(fn() { return error("boom"); })` then task_wait: type_of(we) gives evaluator ERROR_OBJ, vm NULL; type_of(v) gives evaluator NULL, vm ERROR_OBJ. For `spawn(fn() { return len(1); })` then `let s = [v]; 5`: evaluator ERROR (the leaked fault), vm INTEGER(5). Verifier: evalSpawn (higher_order.go:292-297) contains `if errObj, failed := result.(*object.Error); failed { CompleteTask(handle, nil, errors.New(...)) } else { CompleteTask(handle, result, nil) }`. vm/spawn.go passes the closure's result as the value and only a runtime failure as the failure. In my parity test (zz_b4b_test.go), `spawn(fn() { return error("boom"); })` then task_wait gave type_of(we) ERROR_OBJ in the evaluator and NULL on the VM, and type_of(v) NULL in the evaluator and ERROR_OBJ on the VM. For `spawn(fn() { return len(1); })` then `let s = [v]; 5`, the evaluator surfaced the leaked fault ('argument to `len` not supported') and the VM gave 5. As a macro, the second case failed expansion. Verifier's notes: Spawning a task inside a macro body is vanishingly rare, so P3. It does break the documented invariant that a fault never leaves the evaluator package (eval_errors.go).
repro: Scratch parity/zz_review4_test.go and zz_review9_test.go.
impact: Only reachable in macro bodies, but the eval_errors.go invariant that a fault never leaves the package is broken, and the task contract is inverted.
fix_proposal: Branch on `f, ok := result.(*fault)`: CompleteTask(handle, nil, errors.New(f.err.Message)) for a fault, and CompleteTask(handle, result, nil) for everything else, including error values. Regression test: Parity cases for spawn of a function that returns error(), and of one that faults, checking both halves of task_wait.

title: Unbounded recursion in a macro body kills the compiler, REPL or web REPL with a fatal Go stack overflow
claim: applyFunction recurses through eval with no depth limit. A recursive function called inside a macro body therefore grows the Go stack to its 1 GB limit, and the runtime ends the process with a fatal error that recover cannot catch. ExpandMacros' doc (macro_expansion.go:54-57) promises to report a bad macro rather than panic. The callers are generator (gen/run), repl --enable-macros and the WASM webrepl. Verifier: The claim is accurate for the CLI compile path. The REPL --enable-macros and webrepl paths call the same ExpandMacros, so they are affected by construction, but I did not run them.
evidence: `let m = macro() { let f = fn(n) { return f(n + 1); }; f(0); quote(1); }; putln(m());` compiled with `mutant.exe run` exited with code 2 after 4.8 s: `runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit ... fatal error: stack overflow`, frames mutant/evaluator.evalIdentifier / eval / evalReturnValues / evalBlockStatement. Verifier: I compiled rp/macrorec.mut (`let m = macro() { let f = fn(n) { return f(n + 1); }; f(0); quote(1); }; putln(m());`) with `mutant.exe run`. It exited with code 2 after 2.3 s and wrote 47 KB of 'runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit ... fatal error: stack overflow' output. applyFunction has no depth counter. The ExpandMacros doc (macro_expansion.go:54-57) says a bad macro is reported rather than panicking. Verifier's notes: Only the script author can trigger it. It is the evaluator counterpart of VM.04, not a duplicate: a different engine and a different fix site.
repro: Compile repro/macrorec.mut with the scratch mutant.exe.
impact: Compiling a program with a runaway macro dumps a multi-megabyte Go stack instead of printing a diagnostic, and ends the REPL session or the web REPL page.
fix_proposal: Carry a call depth through applyFunction, or keep a package counter in the evaluator, and return newError("macro evaluation exceeded N nested calls") past a named limit. A step budget for loops would also bound `while (true) {}` in a macro, which currently hangs compilation. Regression test: An evaluator test where ExpandMacros over the program above returns an error naming the depth limit within a second.

title: Every failed run prints a randomly chosen comfort line on stdout, and some of those lines are untrue
claim: PrintMachineError (and PrintParseErrors and PrintCompilerError) write a line picked by a time-seeded shuffle (cute_machine_errors.go:56-98). cli.go:92-94 sends it to os.Stdout, mixed with the program's own output. So the output of a failing run differs on every invocation. Some lines claim things the tool does not do, for example "The VM tripped over a tiny semicolon and is trying again with confidence." when nothing is retried. Verifier: The comfort lines are a deliberate feature (commit 3af5476 'cute errors'), so their existence and randomness are by design. The defects are these: every diagnostic, not only the comfort line, goes to stdout mixed with program output; that makes a failing run's stdout nondeterministic; and at least one line describes a retry that never happens.
evidence: Three runs of repro/fail.mut (`putln("before"); let x = 1 / 0;`) printed three different lines after `before`: "Tiny bytecode gremlins caused a hiccup...", "The runtime bumped into a snack break..." and "Your program found a spicy edge case...". Verifier: cli/cli.go:92-94 sends PrintMachineTraceback/PrintMachineError to os.Stdout. I ran rp/fail.mu three times with stderr discarded (2>$null). stdout still held the comfort line, the 'vm error:' block and the traceback. The comfort lines differed each run ('The VM did a dramatic faint...', 'A curious opcode took a wrong turn...', 'Oopsie in motion...'). errrs/cute_machine_errors.go includes 'The VM tripped over a tiny semicolon and is trying again with confidence.', and nothing retries. Verifier's notes: Lowered to P3. The run has already failed, so any output a pipeline consumes is incomplete anyway.
repro: Compile repro/fail.mut and run it three times.
impact: Output that pipelines consume (JSON, reports) gets a random sentence injected on failure, expected-failure output cannot be golden-checked, and a user can read "trying again" as a retry that never happens.
fix_proposal: Send diagnostics to stderr. Make the comfort line opt-in or deterministic, and remove the lines that describe behaviour that does not happen. Regression test: A CLI test running a failing program twice that asserts byte-identical stdout, and nothing on stdout except the program's own output.

title: SecureStack and SecureConstantPool have no production caller, SecureGlobal is unreachable, and their clear-String code is a no-op
claim: NewSecureStack is called only by object/classified_test.go. NewSecureConstantPool is called by nothing. NewSecureGlobal is called only when vm.useWrapperGlobals() is true, but resolveVMGlobalMemoryMode (vm/vm.go:143-145) always returns vMMemoryModeRuntime, so wrapper mode exists only in tests. SecureConstantPool.evictOldest and Clear say "Securely clear the object", but for a String they zero `[]byte(v.Value)`, which is a copy. Verifier: The claim is accurate. This was verified statically.
evidence: A grep for NewSecureStack|NewSecureGlobal|NewSecureConstantPool finds object/classified_test.go:43,62 and vm/vm.go:443 only. vm/vm.go:143 is `func resolveVMGlobalMemoryMode() string { return vMMemoryModeRuntime }`. secure_memory.go:418 is `bytes := []byte(v.Value); security.SecureZero(bytes)`. Verifier: git grep finds NewSecureStack only in object/classified_test.go:62. NewSecureConstantPool is referenced only by its definition. NewSecureGlobal is called only at vm/vm.go:443 behind useWrapperGlobals(). vm.memoryMode is assigned only from resolveVMGlobalMemoryMode() (vm.go:230), which always returns vMMemoryModeRuntime (vm.go:143-145). Only tests set wrapper mode. secure_memory.go evictOldest does `bytes := []byte(v.Value); security.SecureZero(bytes)`, which zeroes a copy. Verifier's notes: Related to VM.17: the objectStreamOffset that SECURITY_LLD section 11.3 describes lives only on this unreachable path.
repro: Static only: grep the repository for the constructor names.
impact: About 260 lines of security-looking code that protect nothing and whose semantics have drifted: it returns fresh non-singleton Booleans, supports only four types, and wipes a String's copy. It also costs every reviewer time.
fix_proposal: Delete SecureStack, SecureConstantPool and the wrapper mode, or wire them in with tests, and correct the no-op wipe comments. Regression test: none; removal

title: TestRegisterGobTypesIsRepeatable cannot fail
claim: The test calls RegisterGobTypes twice to guard the sync.Once. But gob.Register of the same type under the same name is idempotent, so the test also passes with the Once removed. Verifier: The claim is accurate: the test cannot detect the sync.Once being removed.
evidence: Scratch serialize/zz_review_test.go called gob.Register for every GobTypes entry twice with no Once, and nothing panicked. Verifier: In my scratch copy I replaced registerOnce.Do(...) in serialize/gobtypes.go with a plain loop calling gob.Register on every type (no Once). `go1.26.2 test ./serialize -run TestRegisterGobTypesIsRepeatable -v` still passed. gob.Register of the same type under the same name is idempotent. I then restored the file from git.
repro: `go1.26.2 test ./serialize -run TestReviewRegisterTwiceWithoutOnce -v`
impact: The test gives false assurance. It is harmless otherwise.
fix_proposal: Delete it, or assert the property that actually matters, such as calling RegisterGobTypes concurrently under -race. Regression test: n/a

title: Lexer stalls forever on common non-ASCII letters (ü, ó, ù, ², Cyrillic в/о...): CLI run/fmt/lint hang, language server wedges
location: lexer/lexer.go:250-260 (dispatch), 456-472 (readNumber), 308 (byte read); parser/parser.go:237-243 (the sync loop that spins)
claim: The lexer reads bytes as runes. The UTF-8 continuation bytes 0xB2 0xB3 0xB9 0xBC 0xBD 0xBE count as numbers for unicode.IsNumber but not as digits for unicode.IsDigit. NextToken therefore emits a zero-width INT "" and returns without advancing, so it produces the same token forever. Verifier: As stated. One addition: the stall is not only a byte-decoding defect. NextToken dispatches on unicode.IsNumber but readNumber scans unicode.IsDigit, and nothing guarantees progress. So a correctly decoded U+00B2 '²' would still stall. The fix needs a progress guarantee (or one predicate) as well as rune decoding.
evidence: lexer.go:308 `l.ch = rune(l.input[l.readPosition])` (one byte, not a decoded rune). lexer.go:250-260 `} else if unicode.IsNumber(l.ch) { val, isFloat := l.readNumber() ... tok.End = l.currentPos(); return tok` returns without l.readRune(). lexer.go:459 readNumber loops only `for unicode.IsDigit(l.ch) || l.ch == '.'`, so it consumes nothing. lexer.go:46-47 says "Zetsu language only supports ascii characters", but nothing rejects non-ASCII input. Verifier: Code: lexer.go:308/539 read one byte as a rune. lexer.go:250 dispatches on unicode.IsNumber, but readNumber (:459) loops on unicode.IsDigit, and the INT branch returns without readRune. So the token is zero-width and repeats forever. The parser's synchronizeToStatementBoundary (parser.go:237-243) then loops for ever waiting for ';' or EOF. My lexer test (lexer/zz_b4_test.go TestB4Stall): 'ü' c3 bc -> IDENT "\xc3" then INT "" @1-1 repeated 49 times. The same for grün, x², ù, в, ó, о and `let grün = 1;`. A scan of U+0080..U+FFFF finds 11,160 BMP code points that stall. CLI (my build): `mutant run r\umlaut.mut` was killed at 15 s with 14.97 CPU-s and 26.5 MB flat. `mutant lint` and `mutant fmt` were killed at 10 s with 10 CPU-s each. The control `let ok = 1;` compiled in 37 ms. LSP (my mlsp.exe over stdio, zz_drive.py): after didOpen of `let grün = 1;` there was no publishDiagnostics and shutdown (id 2) never got a reply. The control got a reply to id 2 and published diagnostics. Verifier's notes: The trigger is ordinary source text: a German, Spanish or French letter, or Cyrillic 'о', in an identifier or outside a string or comment. It is not crafted input, and it wedges every tool path an examiner uses (run, lint, fmt, LSP). S2/P1 kept. It is not P0 because no custody or verification integrity is affected.
repro: Scratch lexer/zz_review_test.go: "ü" (c3 bc) -> IDENT "\xc3" then INT "" at Offset 1, 49 times in a row. The same happens for "grün", "x²", "ù" and "в". CLI: `let grün = 1;` makes `mutant run` still running after 15 s (14.4 CPU-s, flat memory), and `mutant lint` and `mutant fmt` still running after 8 s. LSP: I built mlsp in the scratch copy and drove it over stdio (zz_lsp_drive4.py). After didOpen of `let grün = 1;` it never published diagnostics and never answered shutdown (id 2); the control `let ok = 1;` answered id 2.
impact: One German, Spanish, French or Cyrillic letter typed in code outside a string or comment permanently wedges the language server, whose handlers run on jsonrpc2's single reader goroutine, until it is restarted. Any .mut file of 1 MiB or less in the workspace hangs the background scan goroutine at 100% CPU. The CLI hangs instead of reporting an error.
fix_proposal: Decode runes in readRune/peekRune with utf8.DecodeRuneInString and track the rune width. Use one predicate for both the dispatch and the scan (IsDigit in both). Guarantee progress in NextToken: a non-EOF token with End.Offset == Start.Offset becomes ILLEGAL and consumes one rune. Lex invalid UTF-8 as ILLEGAL. Regression test: Lexer test: for every rune U+0080..U+FFFF and every single byte 0x80..0xFF, lexing it reaches EOF within len(src)+1 tokens and every non-EOF token has End.Offset > Start.Offset. Add the same invariant as a FuzzLexerProgress target.

title: Byte-wise identifier lexing makes distinct names alias one variable, and mutant fmt writes invalid UTF-8 back into the source file
claim: skipWhiteSpace calls unicode.IsSpace on raw bytes, so 0x85 (NEL) and 0xA0 (NBSP), the second bytes of à, Å, Cyrillic х/Р and Š, are skipped as whitespace. readIdentifier stops after the lead byte. Different identifiers therefore collapse into one name that is not valid UTF-8. Verifier: As stated. Aliasing needs a second byte of 0x85 or 0xA0 (for example à Å Š Р х ą), so it is an edge case. The formatter corruption hits any identifier that contains such a character.
evidence: lexer.go:474-477 `func (l *Lexer) skipWhiteSpace() { for unicode.IsSpace(l.ch) { l.readRune() } }`. lexer.go:448-453 readIdentifier `for unicode.IsLetter(l.ch) || unicode.IsDigit(l.ch) || l.ch == '_'` runs on single bytes. lexer.go:262 newToken(ILLEGAL, l.ch) turns byte 0xA9 into the literal "©", a character that is not in the source. Verifier: Lexer test TestB4Alias: 'xà' (78 c3 a0) -> IDENT "x\xc3" (invalid UTF-8), then EOF. 'xÅ' (78 c3 85) -> IDENT "x\xc3". 'xх' (Cyrillic) -> IDENT "x\xd1". 'a é b' -> IDENT \xc3, then ILLEGAL "©", a character that is not in the source. Cause: skipWhiteSpace (lexer.go:474) applies unicode.IsSpace to the raw bytes 0x85 and 0xA0. CLI: r\alias.mut `let xà = 7;\nputln(xÅ);` compiled, and the .mu printed 7. `mutant fmt r\fmtalias.mut` exited 0 ('formatted') and rewrote the file from `78 C3 A0 20 3D` to `78 C3 20 3D`: the A0 bytes were removed from both lines, leaving invalid UTF-8 on disk. Verifier's notes: Same byte-at-a-time lexing as LEX.01, but LEX.01 has an independent second cause (IsNumber vs IsDigit, no progress guarantee), so they are not duplicates. P1 only because the rune-decoding fix for LEX.01 removes this too. On its own it would be P2.
repro: Lexer test: "xà" -> [IDENT:x\xc3], "xÅ" -> [IDENT:x\xc3], "xх" (Cyrillic) -> [IDENT:x\xd1], "a é b" -> IDENT \xc3, ILLEGAL "©". CLI: `let xà = 7;\nputln(xÅ);` compiles and prints 7, although xÅ was never declared. `mutant fmt r\fmtalias.mut` on `let xà = 7;\nputln(xà);` exited 0 and rewrote the file in place to bytes `6c 65 74 20 78 c3 20 3d 20 37 3b ...`: the A0 byte is gone and the source is now invalid UTF-8.
impact: A reference to a name that was never declared silently resolves to a different variable, which gives a wrong answer. The formatter irreversibly corrupts the author's source file. Identifier names can be invalid UTF-8.
fix_proposal: Same root cause as the stall finding: decode runes before classifying them. Then either support Unicode identifiers (IsLetter/IsDigit on decoded runes, NFC-normalised) or reject non-ASCII identifiers with a positioned error. Never split a multi-byte rune across tokens or trivia. Regression test: Lexer test: every IDENT literal equals input[Start.Offset:End.Offset] and is utf8.ValidString. Formatter test: `let xà = 7;` either formats byte-identically or is refused, and is never rewritten.

title: Parser recursion has no depth limit: 1 MB of '(' kills the CLI and the language server with a fatal stack overflow
location: parser/parse_expressions.go:103-105 and the other recursive parse functions
claim: parseGroupedExpression, parsePrefixExpression, parseExpressionList, parseBlockStatement and parseHole recurse through parseExpression with no nesting limit. Go's 1 GB goroutine stack runs out at about 10^6 levels, and that is a fatal error that recover() cannot catch. Verifier: As stated: an uncatchable stack overflow on about 10^6 nesting levels. Only a deliberately built or generated file can trigger it. Real programs never approach this depth (100k levels parse in under 0.1 s).
evidence: parse_expressions.go:103-105 `func (p *Parser) parseGroupedExpression() ast.Expression { p.nextToken(); exp := p.parseExpression(LOWEST)`. The only depth counter in parser/ is blockDepth (parser.go:128), and it is used only to refuse nested imports. There is no debug.SetMaxStack anywhere in the repo. The LSP workspace scan parses every .mut of 1 MiB or less (workspace_scan.go:20 `scanMaxFileBytes = 1 << 20`). Verifier: Parser test TestB4Deep: 100,000 nested parens parse in 85 ms, so the limit is only reached near 10^6 levels. CLI: `mutant run r\deepopen.mut` (1,000,000 bytes of '(') exited 2 after 1.7 s with 'runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit / fatal error: stack overflow'. LSP: didOpen of the same text made mlsp exit rc=2 with the same fatal error. The file is under scanMaxFileBytes (1 MiB, lsp/internal/server/workspace_scan.go:20), and recover() cannot catch a fatal stack overflow. The parser has no depth counter; blockDepth is used only for imports. Verifier's notes: Priority lowered from P1 to P2 because the input is not realistic source. The server can still be made to crash-loop through the workspace scan by a crafted .mut placed in the workspace. This is related to, but distinct from, EVL.12 (macro evaluation recursion) and VM.04 (runtime recursion).
repro: Scratch cmd/zzdeep: 100000 nested parens parse in 177 ms; 700000 unclosed parens parse (700001 errors); 1,000,000 -> 'runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit / fatal error: stack overflow'. CLI: `mutant run r\deepopen.mut` on 1,000,000 bytes of '(' exits 2 with the same fatal error. LSP: didOpen of the same text makes mlsp exit rc=2 with 'fatal error: stack overflow'.
impact: A single file of 1 MB or less crashes the whole language server. Because the background workspace scan parses it, the server crashes again on every start, and the recover at workspace_scan.go:157 cannot catch it. The CLI dies with a runtime dump after committing about 1 GB of stack. The error slice also grows without bound (one error per unclosed paren).
fix_proposal: Add a nesting counter, checked in parseExpression and parseBlockStatement and carried into parseHole's sub-parser. Use a named constant such as 1000 levels. Past the limit, append one positioned error ('expression nested too deeply') and return nil. Also cap the accumulated errors, for example stop after 100. Regression test: In-process parser test: strings.Repeat("(",200000), strings.Repeat("!",200000)+"x" and strings.Repeat("[",200000) each return within 1 s with a 'nested too deeply' error. A stack overflow would kill the test binary, so the test fails loudly.

title: A hash literal whose keys print alike compiles differently on every build: {"k": 1, "k": 2}["k"] is 1 or 2 at random
claim: HashLiteral keeps its pairs in a Go map keyed by node pointer, so source order is lost. The compiler orders the keys with an unstable sort on key.String(). Ties, such as duplicate keys or a string key next to an identifier with the same text, fall back to Go's randomised map iteration.
evidence: ast/hashLiteral.go:12 `Pairs map[Expression]Expression`. parser/parse_literals.go:107 `hash.Pairs[key] = value`. compiler/compiler.go:808-812 `for k := range node.Pairs {...} sort.Slice(keys, func(i, j int) bool { return keys[i].String() < keys[j].String() })`. StringLiteral.String() returns the decoded text without quotes (ast/stringLiteral.go:14), so `"a"` and `a` tie. hashLiteral.go:30-32 already concedes 'Duplicate keys ... no order the compiler defines either'. Verifier: ast/hashLiteral.go:12 `Pairs map[Expression]Expression`. compiler/compiler.go:807-812 ranges the map, then sort.Slice (unstable) by key.String(). StringLiteral.String() is unquoted, so `"a"` and the identifier `a` tie (my TestB4Lossy shows `let s = "a";` and `let s = a;` both rendering `let s = a;`). I compiled r\dup.mut `let h = {"k": 1, "k": 2}; putln(h["k"]);` 16 times and ran each .mu: 2 fourteen times and 1 twice. The language reference does not document duplicate-key behaviour, and the hashLiteral.go:30-32 comment concedes that duplicates have 'no order the compiler defines'. Verifier's notes: Survivor for this root defect. CMP.06 (the compiler view of the same duplicate-key randomness) and the duplicate-key half of EVL.11 are the same defect: HashLiteral stores pairs in a Go map, and the fix is an ordered pair list in the AST. Mark CMP.06 and EVL.11 as duplicate_of LEX.04. EVL.11's evaluator side-effect order and CMP.11's sorted-key evaluation order are fixed by the same change.
repro: `let h = {"k": 1, "k": 2};\nputln(h["k"]);` compiled 16 times with `mutant run` and executed with --dev printed 2,1,2,2,2,2,1,2,1,2,2,2,1,1,2,2.
impact: The same source compiles to different bytecode and gives different answers on different builds, so .mu outputs are not reproducible. Pair expressions are evaluated in key-text order, not source order, so side effects are reordered. Nothing warns about a duplicate key.
fix_proposal: Store pairs as an ordered slice ([]HashPair{Key, Value}) in ast.HashLiteral. The formatter already rebuilds source order from ranges. Compile the pairs in source order. Reject duplicate constant keys in the parser, or at least flag them in the LSP. Regression test: Compile `{"k": 1, "k": 2}` 50 times in-process and assert identical instructions and constants. Add a VM test that `{"b": f(), "a": g()}` calls f before g.

title: Unterminated string literals are accepted silently, and the rest of the file becomes part of the string
claim: End of input ends an ordinary, raw or triple-quoted literal exactly as a closing quote does. The lexer and parser never report it, so a program that loses a quote compiles and runs only its prefix. Verifier: An unterminated string literal of any kind is closed silently at EOF. The program compiles and exits 0, and runs only the code before the stray quote. It is not completely silent: the runner echoes the swallowed tail as the program's last value, and lint and the LSP show a missing-';' warning at EOF. There is still no error and a success exit status.
impact: A script silently runs only the part before the stray quote and reports success. Verification or custody steps near the end of a script can be skipped with no signal.
fix_proposal: When a body scan hits end of input, readStringToken returns an ILLEGAL token carrying the opening quote's position (or sets an error flag the parser reports). Do the same for raw, triple and raw-triple literals. Regression test: Parser test: each of `"abc`, `r"abc`, `"""abc` and `r"""abc` yields a hard parse error naming the line and column of the opening quote.

title: A NUL byte in source is read as end of input, so every statement after it is silently dropped
claim: l.ch == 0 serves both as the end-of-input sentinel and as a real 0x00 byte, so a stray NUL ends the program at that point with no error.
evidence:
lexer.go:305-308 sets `l.ch = 0` at end of input and `l.ch = rune(l.input[l.readPosition])` otherwise, so a 0x00 byte is indistinguishable from the end. lexer.go:222-230 `case 0: tok = newToken(token.EOF, l.ch) ... return tok`. Verifier: Lexer: "a;\x00b;" -> IDENT a, ';', EOF; everything after the NUL is gone. CLI: r
ul.mut (bytes `putln("before");
\x00
putln("after");`) compiled cleanly, and the .mu printed only 'before' and exited 0. r
ul2.mut `let s = "ab<NUL>cd";` fails with 'compiler error: undefined variable: cd'. Cause: lexer.go:305-308 uses l.ch==0 both as the end-of-input sentinel and for a real 0x00 byte, and :222 turns it into EOF. Verifier's notes: Severity lowered from S3 to S4. A raw NUL in a source file is rare: a UTF-16 file does not truncate silently, because its BOM lexes as an identifier and compilation fails. The script author is trusted, but the truncation leaves no signal in run, lint or the LSP.
impact: Code after a stray NUL (from a bad paste or a mixed encoding) is silently not compiled, so what a reviewer reads is not what runs.
fix_proposal: Detect end of input by position (l.position >= len(l.input)), not by l.ch == 0. Lex a real NUL as ILLEGAL, or decide explicitly whether it is allowed inside strings. Regression test: Lexer test: "a;\x00b;" -> IDENT a, SEMICOLON, ILLEGAL, IDENT b, SEMICOLON, EOF. CLI test: the program above fails to compile.

title: A missing ';' between two expressions on one line is accepted, so x--1, 0xFF and 1.5e3 silently split into two statements
claim: consumeStatementTerminator records every missing ';' as a recoverable problem, and only the LSP reads recoverables. The CLI therefore accepts two adjacent expressions with no separator. That contradicts the docs, which say semicolons are required and that 0xFF does not parse. Verifier: A missing ';' is deliberately recoverable, and that includes two expressions on the same line. So `x--1`, `0xFF` and `1.5e3` split into two statements. In most spellings this surfaces as a misleading 'undefined variable' compile error. A silent wrong value needs a contrived spelling (x--1, or xFF being bound). lint and the LSP do warn. The language reference (MUTANT_LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md:613) is inaccurate: `0xFF` does parse, as `0; xFF;`.
evidence: parser.go:319-323 `if stmt == nil || !stmt.RequiresSemicolon() { return }; p.recordMissingSemicolon(p.curToken)`. The comment at parser.go:99-107 says recoverables are kept out of Errors(). The only production reader of Recoverables() is lsp/internal/analyzer/analyzer.go:32. docs/MUTANT_LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md says 'Semicolons are required to terminate statements', and line 613 says 'Mutant has no hex literals, so `0xFF` does not parse.' Verifier: Parser TestB4Semicolon: `let x = 5; let y = x--1;` -> errs=[], 1 recoverable, program `let y = (x--);1`. `let mask = 0xFF;` -> `let mask = 0;xFF`. `1.5e3` -> `1.5;e3`. CLI: r\split.mut printed 4 and 4. r\hex.mut (xFF bound to 9) printed 0. r\hex2.mut failed with 'undefined variable: xFF', and r\exp.mut with 'undefined variable: e3'. Recoverables() has one production reader, lsp/internal/analyzer/analyzer.go:32. BUT `mutant lint r\split.mut` and `mutant lint r\hex.mut` both print 'warning: missing ';' at end of statement', and the LSP shows the same diagnostic. Missing-';'-as-recoverable is deliberate (parser.go:99-107, 306-311; the reference at :941 says the formatter repairs it). Verifier's notes: Severity lowered from S3 to S4. The editor and lint already flag it, and silently wrong values need unusual source. Stage B 2026-09-25: semi2.mut contains `let y = 2` with no ';'. It compiles and runs under --dev (prints 1, 2). `mutant lint` warns 'missing ';' at end of statement [mutant-format]' and exits 0. LANG_REF:941 and TUTORIAL:198 still say semicolons are required.
