repro: `let x = 5; let y = x--1; putln(x); putln(y);` prints 4 and 4 (parsed as `let y = x--; 1;`). `let xFF = 9; let mask = 0xFF; putln(mask);` prints 0. Without xFF bound it fails with 'compiler error: undefined variable: xFF', and `let big = 1.5e3;` fails with 'undefined variable: e3'.
impact: Silent wrong values and hidden side effects: x-- mutates x. Hex and exponent literals produce misleading errors about variables the author never wrote, or wrong values when those names happen to be bound.
fix_proposal: Make a missing ';' a hard error when the next statement starts on the same line as the previous token's End (no newline between them). Keep a line-end omission recoverable so the formatter can still repair it. Alternatively, have the CLI refuse any MissingSemicolon. Regression test: Parser test: `let y = x--1;` and `let m = 0xFF;` produce hard errors, and `let a = 1\nlet b = 2;` stays recoverable only.

title: Integer literals with a leading zero are silently read as octal: 010 is 8
claim: parseIntegerLiteral calls strconv.ParseInt with base 0. The lexer only produces runs of digits, so the only prefix rule that can apply is a leading 0, which ParseInt reads as octal. No document mentions this.
evidence: parse_literals.go:31 `value, err := strconv.ParseInt(p.curToken.Literal, 0, 64)`. The language reference lists 'integers' and says there are no hex literals, and mentions no octal. Verifier: parse_literals.go:31 `strconv.ParseInt(p.curToken.Literal, 0, 64)`. CLI: r\oct.mut `putln(010); putln(0100 + 1);` printed 8 and 65. r\oct8.mut `let month = 08;` fails with 'could not parse "08" as integer', with no position. Parser: a match pattern `010` parses through the same function. No doc mentions octal (a grep of docs/ finds only parse_int's explicit base and CONFIGURATION_POLICY). Verifier's notes: The same base-0 ParseInt appears in builtin/convert_builtins.go:24 (the to_int conversion), which may deserve its own look; that is out of the LEX area.
repro: `putln(010); putln(0100 + 1);` prints 8 and 65. `let month = 08;` fails with 'parser errors: could not parse "08" as integer'.
impact: Zero-padded decimals copied from dates, sector or offset listings, or tool output give wrong values silently. The same applies in match patterns, which use parseIntegerLiteral.
fix_proposal: Use strconv.ParseInt(lit, 10, 64). Optionally reject a leading zero with a message that suggests the intended decimal. Regression test: Parser test: 010 -> 10 (or a positioned error), 08 -> 8, and match pattern 010 behaves the same way.

title: Each interpolation hole is parsed behind padding as long as its line and column, so parse time is quadratic
claim: parseHole builds and lexes a padding string of (Line-1) newlines plus (Column-1) spaces for every hole, so total work grows with the number of holes times their position in the file. Verifier: As stated: parse time grows with holes times position.
evidence: parse_template.go:62-63 `padding := strings.Repeat("\n", part.Start.Line-1) + strings.Repeat(" ", part.Start.Column-1)`; `sub := New(lexer.New(padding + part.Text))`. Verifier: parse_template.go:62-63 builds strings.Repeat("\n", Line-1) plus strings.Repeat(" ", Column-1) padding and re-lexes it for every hole. My parser test TestB4Holes. One line of holes: 5000/10000/20000 -> 0.38 s / 1.69 s / 6.37 s, about 4x per doubling, so quadratic. One hole per line: 5000/10000/20000 lines -> 0.13 s / 0.41 s / 2.01 s. The control without holes (20000 lines) parses in 0.075 s. Verifier's notes: Severity lowered from S3 to S4. It only matters for files with tens of thousands of holes (generated scripts or crafted files). Scripts of ordinary size parse in milliseconds. The LSP re-parses on every change, so a 20k-line template-heavy file costs about 2 s per keystroke.
repro: Scratch cmd/zzdeep holes mode. One line with 5000/10000/20000/40000 `${a}` holes (20-160 KB) parses in 0.53 s / 1.76 s / 5.98 s / 23.4 s. One hole per line for 5000/10000/20000/40000 lines (80-640 KB) parses in 0.15 s / 0.49 s / 1.46 s / 4.97 s.
impact: The LSP re-parses on every change, so a 640 KB generated report script costs about 5 s per keystroke. A 1 MiB single-line template, which is under the workspace-scan cap, would take on the order of 15 minutes.
fix_proposal: Start the sub-lexer at the hole's position (for example lexer.NewAt(text, token.Position)) instead of padding. Alternatively, parse the bare text and shift line, column and offset afterwards. Regression test: Test (or benchmark with a threshold) that parsing 40000 holes on one line finishes in under 1 s and scales linearly.

title: AST String() panics on trees the parser returns with errors, and the language server crashes on `f()[-,] = 1;`
claim: The parser returns nodes with nil children after an error, but PrefixExpression, InfixExpression, IndexExpression, IfExpression, FunctionLiteral and MacroLiteral dereference their children in String() without a nil check. An LSP lint calls String() on such trees, and the publishDiagnostics path has no recover. Verifier: AST String() methods dereference nil children, and the parser returns such nodes after an error. The one production path that reaches them is the LSP assignment-target lint (assignment_target.go:68/76), and it kills the language server process. The trigger is narrower than 'a transient editing state': an index expression has to hold a broken operator followed by one more token before ']' (for example `f()[-,] = 1;` or `[1][1 + ,] = 3;`), and the target has to have no variable root or a non-final index step. Simple mid-edit forms like `a[-] = v;` do not crash.
evidence: prefixExpression.go:20 `out.WriteString(pe.Right.String())`. infixExpression.go:20-22, indexExpression.go:20-22, ifExpression.go:20-22 and functionLiteral.go:34 have the same pattern. parse_expressions.go:72 `expression.Right = p.parseExpression(PREFIX)` returns nil after an error. assignment_target.go:68 calls `assign.Left.String()`. server.go:1317-1318 publishDiagnostics has no recover, and neither glsp v0.2.2 nor jsonrpc2 v0.2.2 contains any recover(). Verifier: Parser test TestB4StringPanic: Program.String() panics with a nil dereference on the parse output of `1 + ;`, `-;`, `!` and `f()[-,] = 1;`. mlsp over stdio, didOpen of `f()[-,] = 1;`: the process exited rc=2. The stack runs PrefixExpression.String (prefixExpression.go:20) <- IndexExpression.String (:22) <- analyzer.lintAssignmentTargets (assignment_target.go:68) <- Diagnostics <- publishDiagnostics (server.go:1318) <- didOpen, on the jsonrpc2 reader goroutine, with no recover. But `a[-] = v;`, `a[-][0] = 1;` and `a[i + ][0] = 3;` did NOT crash: the parser drops the index there because expectPeek(']') fails. The formatter refuses trees with parse errors (formatter.go:45). Verifier's notes: S3 kept: the whole LSP process dies on a keystroke-reachable text, although the inputs are narrow. The LSP half of the fix (recover around Diagnostics) belongs to the LSP area.
repro: Scratch ast/zz_review_test.go: Program.String() on the parse of `1 + ;`, `-;` and `!` panics with 'invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference'. Scratch lsp analyzer test: Diagnostics on `f()[-,] = 1;` and `[1][1 + ,] = 3;` panics. mlsp driven over stdio with didOpen of `f()[-,] = 1;` exited rc=2: 'panic: runtime error ... mutant/ast.(*PrefixExpression).String prefixExpression.go:20'.
impact: A transient editing state kills the language server process. Any tooling that prints a partially parsed tree can panic.
fix_proposal: Nil-guard every String() method, writing a placeholder such as <missing> for a nil child, as AssignExpression and CallExpression already do. Also add a recover around Diagnostics in publishDiagnostics (LSP area). Regression test: Table or fuzz test: for any input, calling String() on the parser's output never panics. Add an LSP test that opens `f()[-,] = 1;`.

title: Program.String() maps different programs to the same text, yet the formatter's structure test compares programs with it
claim: String() is a lossy debug rendering: blocks print without braces and strings print without quotes. The corpus test's check that formatting 'preserves program structure' compares Program.String() renderings, so it cannot see a statement moved out of a block or a string turned into an identifier. For the same reason it cannot serve as the planned print-then-reparse fuzz invariant.
evidence: blockStatement.go:21-23 writes the statements with no braces. stringLiteral.go:14 `func (sl *StringLiteral) String() string { return sl.Token.Literal }` (decoded, unquoted). formatter_corpus_test.go:150-151 `before := canonicalRendering(snapshot.Program.String()); after := canonicalRendering(reparsed.Program.String())`. Verifier: My server-package test TestB4CanonicalBlind puts pairs through the corpus test's own canonicalRendering(Program.String()), and every pair compares EQUAL. `if (a) { b; c; };` and `if (a) { b; }; c;` both give 'ifa bc'. `while (a) { b; a = false; };` and `while (a) { b; }; a = false;` both give 'while (a) b(a = false)'. `let s = "a";` and `let s = a;` both give 'let s = a;'. formatter_corpus_test.go:150-151 compares exactly these renderings, so a formatter that moved a statement out of a block, or unquoted a string, would pass.
repro: Scratch ast test: `if (a) { b; c; }` and `if (a) { b; } c;` both render as "ifa bc". `while (a) { b; c; }` and `while (a) { b; } c;` both render as "while (a) bc". `let s = "a";` and `let s = a;` render the same, as do `f("x, y")` and `f(x, y)`. Reparsing String() output also fails: `let s = "a b";` -> "let s = a b;" -> two statements, and `let f = fn(a) { a; };` -> "let f = fn<f>(a) a;" -> parse error, then a String panic.
impact: A formatter regression that changes program meaning passes the corpus test. A fuzz invariant built on String() would fail on every string literal.
fix_proposal: Add ast.Equal, a structural comparator that compares node kinds, operators, literal kinds and values, and child order, ignoring positions. Use it in the corpus test and in fuzzers. Document String() as a debug rendering. Regression test: canonicalRendering/ast.Equal must report each of the pairs above as different.

title: The Clone and Modify coverage tests use a stale hand-written list: the While, ForIn, Match and Template cases can be deleted and every test still passes
claim: TestCloneCoversEveryNodeType lists 27 of the 31 node types. It omits WhileStatement, ForInStatement, MatchExpression and TemplateLiteral, and the Modify marker tests omit the same types. A dropped case therefore passes the whole suite, although clone.go:346-348 says a coverage-test failure is how a missing case gets noticed.
evidence: clone_test.go:237-265 lists 28 entries (27 node types plus Program). A grep of ast/*.go finds 31 types with expressionNode/statementNode methods. clone.go:346-348: 'a new node type failing the clone coverage test is how this is meant to be noticed'. modify.go:9-10: 'A missing one is silent'. Verifier: The package defines 31 node types with expressionNode/statementNode. The TestCloneCoversEveryNodeType samples (clone_test.go:237-265) list 27 of them plus Program, and omit WhileStatement, ForInStatement, MatchExpression and TemplateLiteral. TestModifyReachesEveryNodeTypeWithChildren also has no While, ForIn, Match or Template cases. Mutation in my scratch copy: I deleted `case *WhileStatement:` from Clone and the WhileStatement and MatchExpression cases from Modify. go vet passed, and `go test ./ast ./evaluator ./parity ./compiler` -> all ok. Both files were then restored from HEAD.
repro: Mutation run in the scratch copy, restored afterwards. Deleting `case *WhileStatement:` from Clone: `go test ./ast` -> ok. Deleting the WhileStatement and MatchExpression cases from Modify: `go test ./ast ./evaluator ./parity ./compiler` -> all ok.
impact: A missing case silently shares subtrees (Clone) or skips them (Modify). Macro expansion inside while or match bodies could regress with no failing test.
fix_proposal: Enumerate the node types automatically, for example by parsing package ast with go/parser in the test and collecting types that have expressionNode/statementNode, and require one sample per type. Add Modify marker cases for the four missing types. Regression test: The enumerating test itself. Re-running the mutation above must then fail.

title: Function and macro parameters accept any token as a name: fn(1, "b", if, [) parses with no error
claim: parseFunctionParameters builds an Identifier from whatever the current token is, without checking that it is an IDENT, for the first parameter and after each comma. Duplicate names are also accepted.
evidence: parser.go:380-384 `p.nextToken(); ... ident := &ast.Identifier{Token: p.curToken, Value: p.curToken.Literal}`, repeated at :388-393 after each COMMA, with no curTokenIs(token.IDENT) check. Verifier: parser.go:380-393 builds an Identifier from the current token without checking curTokenIs(IDENT). Parser test: `let f = fn(1, "two", if, [) { 5 };` -> errs=[], and `let m = macro(1, 2) { 3 };` -> errs=[]. CLI: r\params.mut `fn(1, "b", if) { return 5; }` called with f(7,8,9) printed 5. r\params2.mut `fn(a, a) { return a; }` called with g(1,2) printed 2.
repro: Parser test: `let f = fn(1, "two", if, [) { 5 };` -> errors=[]. CLI: `let f = fn(1, "b", if) { return 5; }; putln(f(7, 8, 9));` prints 5. `let g = fn(a, a) { return a; }; putln(g(1, 2));` prints 2.
impact: Invalid programs are accepted. The formatter prints `fn(1, b, if)`, which re-parses to a different tree. A duplicate parameter silently shadows the first one.
fix_proposal: Require IDENT and report 'expected parameter name, got <type>' at the token. Reject duplicate parameter names with a positioned error. Regression test: Parser test covering a literal, a keyword, a bracket and a duplicate as parameters, each producing an error.

title: Token columns count bytes, the doc says runes, and the LSP sends them as UTF-16 positions
claim: The Position doc promises rune columns, but the lexer computes byte columns, and the LSP passes Column-1 through as the UTF-16 character offset. Every position after non-ASCII text on the same line is off. Verifier: As stated. The doc is wrong, and LSP ranges after any non-ASCII text on the same line are shifted by one or more columns per multi-byte character.
evidence: token.go:7 'Line and Column are 1-based (LSP-friendly) and count runes, not bytes.' lexer.go:280 `Column: l.position - l.lineStart + 1` (byte offsets). lsp/internal/protocol/converters.go:17 `Character: lsp.UInteger(pos.Column - 1)`. Verifier: token.go:7 says Line and Column 'count runes, not bytes'. lexer.go:280 computes `l.position - l.lineStart + 1`, which is bytes. Lexer test: in `"é" b` the IDENT b is at {Column:6 Offset:5}, but its rune and UTF-16 column is 5. protocol/converters.go:17 passes Column-1 as the LSP Character with no conversion. A grep of lsp/ for utf16, positionEncoding and RuneCount finds nothing, and glsp 3.16 means UTF-16 positions. Verifier's notes: Category changed from docs to correctness, because the LSP positions are wrong, not just the comment. Related to, but not a duplicate of, EVL.18 (the runtime caret row uses the same byte column as a rune index). Both come from the unit being ambiguous, and one decision about the unit should settle both.
repro: Lexer test on `a é b`: IDENT b is reported at {Line:1 Column:6 Offset:5}; its rune (and UTF-16) column is 5.
impact: Diagnostics, hovers and semantic tokens after any non-ASCII string or comment on a line are shifted by 1-3 columns per character. No lexer test covers non-ASCII text.
fix_proposal: Pick one unit. Either compute UTF-16 columns in the lexer or convert in protocol/converters.go using the line text. Then correct the doc. Regression test: Position test with "é" and an emoji inside a string before a token, asserting the chosen unit end to end through ToLSPRange.

title: CLI parse errors carry no line or column
claim: appendError stores the bare message in Errors(), which the CLI, module loader, REPL and serve print. The positions exist only in TypedErrors, which only the LSP reads. The single exception is hole errors, which prefix line:col by hand. Verifier: As stated, for every CLI or REPL parse error (entry file and imported modules alike), except hole errors, which prefix line:col themselves. The module path is also dropped (RUN.10), and the comment at module/errors.go:88-89 wrongly says the messages carry file:line:col.
evidence: parser.go:351 `p.errors = append(p.errors, msg)`. module/graph.go:149 `if errs := p.Errors(); len(errs) != 0 { return nil, &ParseError{Path: display, Errors: errs} }`. parse_template.go:84 is the only place that adds 'line %d:%d'. Verifier: parser.go:350-356 appendError stores the bare msg in p.errors, and positions exist only in typedErrors. The entry file is parsed through module.Load -> graph.go:147-150 `ParseError{Path: display, Errors: p.Errors()}` -> generator/generate.go:265 -> cli/cli.go:41 PrintParseErrors. CLI: r\err3.mut (the error is on line 3, `let c 3;`) printed 'parser errors: expected next token to be =, but got INT instead' with no line or column. The typed error has {Line:3 Column:7}. r\oct8.mut printed 'could not parse "08" as integer' with no position. module/errors.go:88-89 claims the messages are 'already carrying their own file:line:col prefixes', which is false. Verifier's notes: Survivor. RUN.10 is the same root defect on the same line (graph.go:149 builds ParseError from p.Errors()), seen through an imported module, and one fix renders both path:line:col from TypedErrors. Mark RUN.10 as duplicate_of LEX.15 and fold in its missing-path point and the false comment in errors.go.
repro: CLI on a 3-line file with an error on line 3 prints 'parser errors:\n\texpected next token to be =, but got ILLEGAL instead'. `let month = 08;` prints 'could not parse "08" as integer'. Neither message says where the error is.
impact: In a script of several hundred lines the author has to search for the error by hand.
fix_proposal: Render the CLI and module errors from TypedErrors as 'path:line:col: msg', or have appendError prefix the token's line:col. Regression test: CLI or module test asserting 'line:col' appears in the parse error output.

title: A backslash is lexed as a division token, so `6 \ 3` parses and only fails in the compiler
claim: The lexer gives '\\' the FSLASH type, so the parser accepts it as infix division. The compiler then rejects the operator '\\'. token.BSLASH is defined but never produced.
evidence: lexer.go:108-109 `case '\\': tok = newToken(token.FSLASH, l.ch)`. token.go:153 `BSLASH = "\\"` is unused; a grep finds no producer. Verifier: lexer.go:108-109 `case '\\': tok = newToken(token.FSLASH, l.ch)`. token.BSLASH (token.go:153) has no producer (grep). Lexer test: `6 \ 3` -> INT, FSLASH "\\", INT. The parser reports no error (program `(6 \ 3)`). CLI: r\bs.mut failed at compile time with 'compiler error: unknown operator \', with no position.
repro: `putln(6 \ 3);` produces no parse error, then 'compiler error: unknown operator \'.
impact: The editor shows no parse diagnostic, and LSP inference treats the expression as division. The error surfaces late, without a position, and with a confusing message.
fix_proposal: Emit ILLEGAL for a backslash outside strings so the parser reports it at its position. Delete BSLASH if it stays unused. Regression test: Lexer or parser test: `6 \ 3` gives a positioned parse error.

title: An unterminated ${ inside a triple-quoted string is silently closed, although the code comment promises an error
claim: scanHole hands the rest of an unterminated hole to the parser as if the brace were present. When that text parses as one expression, the missing '}' is never reported. Verifier: As stated. The ordinary-quote form `"${x"` does report an error, but only when the swallowed tail is not itself a single expression.
evidence: lexer.go:824-826 `if depth > 0 { return body[i+2:], len(body) }`. The comment at :801-803 says 'the resulting error points inside the string, which is where the missing brace is'. Verifier: scanHole (lexer.go:824-826) returns body[i+2:] when depth > 0. Parser: `let s = """b: ${x""";` -> errs=[], and the program renders as `"b: ${x}"`. CLI: r\hole.mut compiled and printed 'b: 5'. The comment at :801-803 promises that 'the resulting error points inside the string'. A related case: `let s = "b: ${x + ";` (ordinary quotes) -> errs=[] too, because skipHole's inner string scan runs to EOF.
repro: `let x = 5;\nlet s = """b: ${x""";\nputln(s);` compiles and prints 'b: 5'.
impact: Malformed source is accepted, and the comment's promise is false.
fix_proposal: Have scanHole return an 'unterminated' flag, and have splitTemplate or parseHole report 'unterminated ${' at the hole's position. Regression test: Parser test: `"""${x"""` and `"${x"` each produce an 'unterminated ${' error.

title: Parse errors from inside a hole carry offsets from the padded sub-parse, not from the file
claim: parseHole shifts nodeRanges into file coordinates but copies the sub-parser's typedErrors and recoverables unshifted. Their Offset fields point into the padding, while the comment says they are already file ranges. Verifier: As stated: latent, because current consumers use line and column.
evidence: parse_template.go:87-88 `p.typedErrors = append(p.typedErrors, sub.typedErrors...)` and `p.recoverables = append(p.recoverables, sub.recoverables...)`. Only nodeRanges get `rng.Shift(0, shift)` (:101-103). The comment at :80-82 says 'their ranges are already file ranges'. Verifier: parse_template.go:87-88 appends sub.typedErrors and sub.recoverables unshifted. Only nodeRanges are shifted (:101-103). Parser test TestB4HoleOffsets: for `${ 1 + }` on line 3, the typed error Start is {Line:3 Column:31 Offset:32}. The offset recomputed from its line and column is 52 (the '}'), while byte 32 of the file is an 'x' inside the literal. The comment at :80-82 says those ranges are already file ranges.
repro: Parser test: `${ 1 + }` on line 3 gives the typed error Start {Line:3 Column:26 Offset:27}. The real offset of that '}' is 104, and byte 27 of the file is the '1' on line 1.
impact: The problem is latent: current LSP consumers use line and column. Any consumer that uses offsets, such as quick-fix edits or a ShiftPositions-style rebase, would point at the wrong bytes.
fix_proposal: Apply the same Shift(0, shift) to sub.typedErrors[i].Range and sub.recoverables[i].Range. Regression test: Assert that a hole error's Range.Start.Offset equals the byte offset recomputed from its line and column.

title: The production parser package imports "testing" through test helpers, and the tracer is dead code
claim: parser_conds.go is a non-test file that holds only test helpers and imports "testing", so the testing package is linked into the mutant binary. parser_tracer.go is referenced only from commented-out lines.
evidence: parser_conds.go:1-7 `import ("fmt"; "mutant/ast"; "testing")`, with helpers such as checkParserErrors and testLetStmt that only _test files call. `go list -deps .` includes testing. evaluator/eval_conds.go follows the same pattern (EVL area). trace/untrace appear only in `// defer untrace(trace(...))` comments (parse_expressions.go:63,79,113,136; parse_literals.go:27). identLevel would panic on a negative Repeat count if untrace ran before trace. Verifier: parser/parser_conds.go:1-7 is a non-_test file that imports "testing" and holds only test helpers (checkParserErrors etc.). In my copy `go1.26.2 list -deps .` prints testing, and `go list -f {{.Imports}} ./parser ./evaluator` shows testing in both packages. parser_tracer.go's trace and untrace are referenced only from commented-out lines (parse_expressions.go:63,79,113,136; parse_literals.go:27). Verifier's notes: EVL.20 is the same root defect in evaluator/eval_conds.go, and its fix text already names parser_conds.go. Both files must move for 'testing' to leave the binary. I kept LEX.19 as the survivor because it also covers the dead tracer. Merging EVL.20 into it (or the reverse) is fine, as long as both files and the tracer end up in the one entry.
repro: `go1.26.2 list -deps .` in the scratch copy prints 'testing'. `go list -f {{.Imports}} ./parser ./evaluator` shows testing in both.
impact: Binary bloat and test-only code in production, including a global mutable traceLevel. No functional impact.
fix_proposal: Rename to parser/parser_helpers_test.go (and evaluator/eval_conds_test.go), and delete parser_tracer.go. Regression test: A policy check that no non-_test.go file in the module imports "testing" (testkit excepted).

title: disclose_verify reported a forged package as verified: the ledger's record of the disclosure was never compared with the package
claim: The ledger check proved only that the manifest's own copy of the Disclosure node's properties (manifest.ledger.record) is in the snapshot. Nothing compared those properties with the package around them: the grant's digest and runs, the record's digest, the view fingerprint, the recipient or the disclosure uid. The manifest signature was checked against the public key the manifest itself carries, and the result never reported that key. So anyone holding one genuine package could relabel it, or put another genuine grant for the same record beside its ledger record, re-sign the manifest with their own key, and get verified: true against the genuine root.
evidence: Stage B: a counsel package with disclosure.recipient set to Mallory and the examiner changed, re-sealed with a fresh Ed25519 key, passed all ten checks with verified true while the ledger record said Counsel; the regulator's grant (runs 3-4) put into counsel's package with counsel's ledger block and proof, re-sealed with a stranger's key, verified while the ledger recorded runs 0-2,5-7 and a different grant digest and uid. Reproduced in Stage C by TestAPackageTheLedgerDoesNotRecordFailsVerification: both forgeries verified. DISCLOSURE_POLICY.md and the metadata promise the ledger holds 'this disclosure property for property'.
repro: builtin/disclose_binding_test.go TestAPackageTheLedgerDoesNotRecordFailsVerification (relabelled and re-signed; another disclosure's grant under this one's ledger record) verified both forgeries before the fix, and the result carried no signing key.
impact: The one check meant to spare a recipient from taking the examiner's word did not tie the grant, recipient, view or record to what the ledger recorded; a recipient, or anyone holding a genuine package of the record, could produce a package that verified while naming a different recipient or granting other segments.
fix_proposal: Add a check requiring the ledger's record to agree with the package, and return the signing keys. Fixed: a new check, ledger_matches_package, compares the ledger record with the manifest's disclosure uid, case, recipient (and recomputes its fingerprint), examiner, method, view label and view fingerprint; with the digests of record.mrec and grant.json computed from the files; with the record's own uid and segment count; and with the grant file's disclosure uid, case, record uid, runs, granted count and descriptors root. Each disagreement is named. verified now needs eleven checks. The result carries manifest_public_key and record_public_key so a recipient can compare the signers with keys they trust. DISCLOSURE_POLICY and the metadata say so; the record_disclosure example reports 11 of 11.

title: disclose_verify panics (index out of range) on a package whose grant names a longer record
claim: checkGrantOpens indexes the packaged record's segment table with every index the opened grant carries, and never bounds them. Grant indices are bounded only by the grant file's own Segments field. The loop also runs after checkGrant has already reported that the grant is for another record. Verifier: Correct. For a grant to reach the indexing, it must open with the passphrase the verifier types, so the input is one the package supplier controls, together with the passphrase they send. Inside a program, containFault (vm/fault.go:47-59) recovers the panic. The run ends with 'vm_runtime_error: recovered panic', which the script cannot catch, and an integrity-failure telemetry event is recorded. The process does not crash.
evidence: disclose.go:1320-1321 `for _, index := range grant.Indices() { segment := v.record.segments[index]`. v.grantFile is set at :1189, before any mismatch is recorded, so checkGrantOpens (:1298) proceeds. record_grant.go:749 bounds runs only by `f.Segments`. Verifier: checkGrantOpens (builtin/disclose.go:1320-1321) indexes v.record.segments[index] for every opened-grant index. Indices are bounded only by the grant file's own Segments (security/record_grant.go:624, 749), and the loop runs even after grant_names_record has failed. TestB4VerifyGrantForLongerRecord put a same-passphrase grant for a 16-segment record into an 8-segment record's package. It panicked with 'runtime error: index out of range [10] with length 8'. Afterwards os.Rename of package/record.mrec failed with 'being used by another process': the Close at disclose.go:1039-1041 is skipped, so the handle leaks. Verifier's notes: Downgraded from S2 to S3 because the VM fault boundary contains the panic. The effect is on availability: the verification run aborts instead of reporting a FAIL check. It produces no false pass. This matches the S3 given to the contained VM panic in VM.06.
repro: TestReviewVerifyPanicsOnGrantForALongerRecord places, in counsel's package for an 8-segment record, a genuine grant with the same passphrase for a 16-segment record of the same case that grants segments 10-15. disclose_verify panics with 'runtime error: index out of range [10] with length 8'. Inside the VM this is recovered at vm/vm.go:764 (containFault) as a fatal 'vm_runtime_error: recovered panic' that aborts the run and records an integrity failure. The record file handle stays open, which is why the test's cleanup failed with 'being used by another process'.
impact: A disclosure package is untrusted input on the recipient's side. A mismatched or crafted package crashes the verification run instead of producing findings, and leaks the open record handle.
fix_proposal: In checkGrantOpens, refuse (as a failed check) when v.grantFile.Segments != len(v.record.segments) or the grant's record uid differs, and bounds-check each index before indexing. Close v.record.file in a defer inside DiscloseVerify. Regression test: A test that swaps in a grant for a longer record of the same case (granting only segments past the packaged record's end) and asserts grant_opens is FAIL and no panic occurs.

title: A withdrawal is bypassed by respelling the recipient
claim: The withdrawn-recipient check keys on a SHA-256 of the exact recipient string after TrimSpace. A later disclosure of the same record to 'counsel for the respondent', 'Counsel  for the respondent' (double space) or an NFD/NFC variant is not refused. Class labels and view names are canonicalised (NFC, case, spacing) precisely to stop this kind of mistake. Verifier: The withdrawn-recipient check matches only the exact asserted spelling after trimming. A case, internal-whitespace or Unicode-normalisation variant is issued a new grant. Class labels and view names are canonicalised, so this is inconsistent with them, and it breaks the metadata's 'refuses to issue this record to this recipient again' for trivially different spellings. The punctuation variant the auditor cites would not be caught by the proposed canonical form either.
evidence: disclose_ledger.go:520-522 `func disclosureRecipientFingerprint(name string) string { return ledgerHash(sha256Of("mutant-recipient-v1|" + name)) }`; disclose.go:331 `recipient := strings.TrimSpace(recipientArg)`; disclose_ledger.go:544 `disclosureWithdrawnFor(g, ..., issue.recipientFP)`. Metadata (metadata.go:1325) and disclose_history.go:16-17 promise that the record is not issued 'to this recipient again'. Verifier: disclosureRecipientFingerprint (builtin/disclose_ledger.go:517-522) hashes the exact recipient string after TrimSpace (disclose.go:331). Its doc comment says so on purpose: 'names a recipient by the exact string the examiner asserted'. TestB4RespelledRecipient disclosed to 'Zoë Counsel' and withdrew it. A re-disclosure with outer spaces was refused as withdrawn. 'zoë counsel', 'Zoë  Counsel' (double space) and the NFD form were each issued new disclosures: f104c9a2..., 195d383e..., 40bd747f.... Verifier's notes: Downgraded from S2/P1. Only the trusted examiner can trigger this, by choosing to disclose again, and they already have a documented deliberate route around a withdrawal: seal a new record, which the refusal message itself suggests. So it is an accident guard that misses an examiner slip, not a withdrawal bypass by an adversary. No embargo needed. The new disclosure is recorded in the ledger, so it is visible in disclose_history.
repro: TestReviewWithdrawalIsBypassedByARespelledRecipient discloses to 'Counsel for the respondent' and withdraws. The same spelling is refused, but 'counsel for the respondent', 'Counsel  for the respondent' and 'Counsel for the respondent.' are each issued new disclosures (uids d25c6be4..., f3a84793..., a6ff5b08...).
impact: The one thing a withdrawal achieves, stopping further grants, fails on a capitalisation or spacing slip. It does so silently, and the ledger then records a fresh disclosure to what is evidently the same party.
fix_proposal: Fingerprint a canonical form: reuse canonicalLabel's rule (NFC, trim, collapse spaces, lower-case, refuse control and format characters) and keep the asserted spelling as a display property. Also consider refusing, or warning, when a recipient canonicalises to one already withdrawn for the record. Regression test: After a withdrawal, disclosure to case, spacing and NFD variants of the recipient must be refused with 'was withdrawn'.

title: A record whose signature no longer verifies is disclosed silently, and the ledger records signed=true
claim: disclose_to_passphrase never looks at record.signatureValid. The Record node writes a single bit, record.signed, which comes from session.signed (the signature is claimed), not from whether it verifies. So a tampered record is disclosed without a word, and the ledger says 'record.signed: true' with no validity property. The two-bit contract (signed and signature_valid) collapses to one bit in the court-facing record. Verifier: Correct. A tampered, signed record is disclosed silently, and the ledger's record.signed means 'carries a signature', not 'the signature verifies'. That disagrees with the manifest's meaning of signed. The recipient's disclose_verify does catch the tampering, so the tampered disclosure cannot pass verification. The harm is a misleading court-facing ledger entry and no warning to the examiner.
evidence: disclose.go:339-345 checks only `record.keys == nil`; disclose_ledger.go:354 `"record.signed": strconv.FormatBool(facts.record.signed)`. The manifest uses `Signed: record.signed && record.signatureValid` (disclose.go:472), so ledger and manifest disagree. Verifier: disclose_to_passphrase (builtin/disclose.go:339-345) checks only record.keys and never record.signatureValid. The Record node writes record.signed from session.signed (disclose_ledger.go:354) and writes no validity property. The manifest uses signed && signatureValid (disclose.go:472). TestB4TamperedRecordDisclosed flipped one byte and reopened the record (signed=true, signature_valid=false). The disclosure was issued with no warning, the result has no signature field, and the ledger Record node has record.signed="true" among 13 properties, none of them validity. A later disclose_bundle and disclose_verify of that package did report record_signature FAIL and grant_opens FAIL, with verified=false. Verifier's notes: Tampering needs write access to the examiner's stored record. Detection downstream is intact.
repro: TestReviewATamperedRecordIsDisclosedAndLedgeredAsSigned flips one byte of a signed record, re-opens it (signed=true, signature_valid=false) and discloses. The disclosure is issued, and the Record node has record.signed="true" and no validity property.
impact: The ledger, which is the document handed to a court, states that a record whose contents changed since signing is signed. The examiner gets no warning at issue time.
fix_proposal: Refuse to disclose (or require an explicit option) when signed && !signatureValid. Write record.signature_valid beside record.signed, and return signed and signature_valid in the result. Regression test: Disclosing a tampered record is refused, or the result and the Record node carry signature_valid=false.

title: record_seal trusts the 'class' tag of a hand-written range and never checks it against a declared class or the range's own label
claim: recordRangesArg copies the hash's 'label' and 'class' fields as given. The tag is then sealed without being resolved against session.classes or against the label. A hand-built or edited range therefore seals bytes under a class the case never declared, or under a tag that disagrees with its label. That is the 'new secret class nobody recognises' failure class_define exists to prevent. Verifier: Correct. record_seal accepts a range whose label disagrees with its tag, and one whose tag belongs to no declared class, and seals by the tag alone. Editing a range's label silently has no effect.
evidence: record.go:499-512 reads `{"label", &entry.label}, {"class", &entry.tag}` directly; the tag becomes the span class (record.go:637 `appendSpan(entry.offset, entry.length, entry.tag)`). The only validation is classTagFromHex in SegmentCount (64 hex characters). Verifier: recordRangesArg (builtin/record.go:499-512) copies 'label' and 'class' as given, and only the tag reaches the span (:637). TestB4SealTrustsHandWrittenTag, case 1: an 'open' range from record_classify_range had its label edited to 'restricted'. It sealed with no error, and its bytes merged into the open span (0-64 restricted tag, then 64-200 open tag). Case 2: a range with a 64-hex tag no class carries (abab...ab) sealed as its own span. Verifier's notes: Downgraded to S4. Only the trusted script author can trigger it, by hand-writing or editing a range hash, and recordRangeShapeError already tells authors to use record_classify_range. The label-edit case can over-disclose: bytes the author believes are restricted are sealed under the open tag. That is a reason not to leave it in the backlog.
repro: TestReviewASealTrustsAHandWrittenRangeTag seals the range {offset:64, length:64, label:'restricted', class:'abab...ab'} (64 hex characters, not declared). The seal succeeds, and the sealed span tags include 'abababab...'.
impact: Classification is enforced only at record_classify_range. Editing a range's label (r["label"] = "pii") silently leaves the old class, and a stray or foreign tag becomes an unnamed class in every later preview and disclosure.
fix_proposal: In recordRangesArg or recordSealImpl, resolve each entry's label with recordLookupClass and require that its Tag equals entry.tag, refusing a mismatch or an undeclared tag. Regression test: A seal with an undeclared tag, and a seal with a label/tag mismatch, are both refused by range number.

title: record_seal_quantised docs say an unnamed class's range is sealed at its boundary; the seal is refused instead
claim: The code comment, the builtin summary and the policy all say a range whose class is not rounds_to is sealed at the boundary it was given. recordAssembleSpans instead refuses the whole seal whenever such a range is not already on a quantum boundary. Verifier: The refusal is the tested, intended behaviour, and the three documents describe behaviour that does not exist. A range of any class other than rounds_to must already be quantum-aligned, or the seal is refused.
evidence: record.go:582-583 '// a span of any other class is sealed at the boundary they gave it', but :585-594 `if sorted[i].tag != roundsTo.Tag { return nil, 0, newError(...would widen...)`. metadata.go:1231: 'a range whose class is not the one named is sealed at the boundary it was given rather than rounded'. DISCLOSURE_POLICY.md:213 says the same. Verifier: The code comment at builtin/record.go:582-583, metadata.go:1231 and DISCLOSURE_POLICY.md:212-214 all say a range of another class 'is sealed at the boundary it was given'. The code at :585-594 refuses the whole seal instead. TestB4QuantisedOtherClass: restricted 34+4 with pii 100+4, quantum 16 and rounds_to restricted, was refused with 'rounding to 16 bytes would widen the range at 100+4, which carries "pii"'. With pii at an aligned 96+16 the seal succeeds. Existing tests (record_test.go:348, :563) pin the refusal. Verifier's notes: This is a documentation defect. The code and the tests agree with each other.
repro: TestReviewAnUnnamedClassRangeIsNotSealedAtItsBoundary: ranges restricted 34+4 and pii 100+4, quantum 16, rounds_to restricted. The seal is refused: 'rounding to 16 bytes would widen the range at 100+4, which carries "pii"...'. The existing tests (record_test.go:333, :530) also assert the refusal.
impact: An examiner who follows the documentation cannot seal mixed ranges and gets a refusal the documents say will not happen. There is no way to have only rounds_to ranges rounded when another class is unaligned.
fix_proposal: Either implement 'leave other classes at their boundary' (skip widening for tag != roundsTo) or rewrite the three documents to say the seal is refused unless every other class's range is already aligned. Regression test: Pin whichever behaviour is chosen with a test mixing a rounds_to range and an unaligned other-class range.

title: A second reclassification of the same record makes every later disclosure of it fail with a false 'ledger tampered' error
claim: reclassWrite checks uniqueness only per old>new pair, so reclassifying record A a second time (with C after B) writes a second ReclassEvent with the same reclass.superseded_uid. disclosureFind on that key then errors, as if on foreign writes. Verifier: Correct. Refusing is right, since A is superseded, but the stated reason falsely accuses a ledger that only disclose_* wrote of foreign writes.
evidence: disclose_reclassify.go:269-270 `pair := oldUID + ">" + newUID; ... disclosureFind(g, disclosureNodeReclass, "reclass.pair", pair)`. disclose_ledger.go:536 looks up reclass.superseded_uid, and :202-204 reports '...this family writes each one once; the ledger has been written to by something other than disclose_*'. Verifier: reclassWrite (builtin/disclose_reclassify.go:269-277) deduplicates only on reclass.pair. TestB4SecondReclassification: disclose_reclassified(B, A) and then (C, A) both succeeded. disclose_to_passphrase(A) was then refused with 'the ledger holds 2 ReclassEvent nodes for reclass.superseded_uid = ..., and this family writes each one once; the ledger has been written to by something other than disclose_*'. The only reader of superseded_uid is disclose_ledger.go:536, and disclose_history still works on that ledger.
repro: TestReviewASecondReclassificationReadsAsTampering: disclose_reclassified(B, A) and then disclose_reclassified(C, A) both succeed. disclose_to_passphrase(A) then fails with 'the ledger holds 2 ReclassEvent nodes for reclass.superseded_uid = ... the ledger has been written to by something other than disclose_*'.
impact: A forensic tool accuses a clean ledger of tampering. The refusal itself is correct, since A is superseded, but the stated reason is false.
fix_proposal: Either refuse a second reclassification of an already-superseded record (naming the first) or look up superseded_uid with a query that tolerates many events and names the newest. Regression test: After two reclassifications of A, disclosing A is refused with 'was reclassified by', not with a tampering message.

title: record_seal's 4096-range argument limit admits range lists the header cannot carry
claim: recordRangesArg allows up to MaxRecordSpans (4096) ranges. Each non-adjacent range also adds a default-class gap span, and SegmentCount caps spans at 4096, so about 2047 separated ranges is the real limit. The seal is refused later with a span count the program never wrote. Verifier: Correct. The real limit for separated ranges is about 2047, and the refusal names a span count that does not appear in the program.
evidence: record.go:131 `recordMaxRangesInArg = security.MaxRecordSpans`; :471 `if len(array.Elements) > recordMaxRangesInArg`. security/record_file.go:322 refuses more than MaxRecordSpans spans after gaps are added (record.go:634-641). Verifier: recordRangesArg bounds the argument at recordMaxRangesInArg = MaxRecordSpans = 4096 (record.go:131, :471). Gap spans are added later (:634-641). TestB4RangeLimit: 2100 separated one-byte ranges, well under 4096, passed the argument check. The seal was then refused with 'a record carries at most 4096 classification spans, this one declares 4201'. Verifier's notes: The seal is refused either way, so this is only a matter of the message and where the limit is checked.
repro: TestReviewTheRangeLimitIsNotTheSpanLimit: 3000 one-byte ranges pass the argument check, and the seal is refused: 'a record carries at most 4096 classification spans, this one declares 6001'.
impact: The limit named at the argument is wrong, and the refusal names a count (6001) that appears nowhere in the program.
fix_proposal: Check the assembled span count against MaxRecordSpans in recordAssembleSpans with a message in terms of ranges and gaps, or bound the argument at (MaxRecordSpans-1)/2 for the worst case. Regression test: 3000 separated ranges are refused at the argument (or assembly) with a message naming ranges.

title: Every record_read walks the whole segment table
claim: recordReadSpan iterates all segments on each call and skips the non-overlapping ones, so sequentially reading a record is quadratic in its segment count. Verifier: Correct. The cost is bounded by MaxRecordSegments (1,048,576).
evidence: record_read.go:58-62 `for _, segment := range session.segments { segmentEnd := ...; if segmentEnd <= offset || segment.Offset >= end { continue }`. Segments are sorted by offset, so a sort.Search would find the first overlap. Verifier: recordReadSpan (builtin/record_read.go:58-62) walks every segment on each call. TestB4ReadScaling, 1000 one-byte reads at the front of the record: 16,384 segments took 165 µs per read and 262,144 segments took 2.22 ms per read. That is about 13x for 16x the segments, so a read is linear in the segment count and a sequential read of the whole record is quadratic. Verifier's notes: It bites only on records with very many small segments read in small chunks.
repro: TestReviewAReadWalksEverySegment: on a 1,048,576-segment record, 2000 one-byte record_read calls averaged 13.9 ms each. Reading the record in segment-sized pieces would take about 4 h of table walking.
impact: Chunked reads of large records with small segments slow down severely. The effect is bounded by MaxRecordSegments.
fix_proposal: Binary-search the first overlapping segment (sort.Search on Offset+Length > offset) and stop once segment.Offset >= end. Regression test: A benchmark or timing test: 10,000 one-byte reads on a 1M-segment record stay near the cost of the decrypts.

title: The end-to-end example test's 'no plaintext printed' assertion cannot catch the form a leak takes
claim: The test checks the printed output only for the literal strings 'finance@example.org' and 'TVqQ'. A classified buffer that leaks through any Inspect path prints as hex, and the runner's own stdout echo is not captured at all, so the assertion passes while plaintext is printed. Verifier: Correct. The one end-to-end mark test cannot detect a leak rendered as hex, and it does not see the runner's stdout echo.
evidence: example_record_disclosure_test.go:133-136 `for _, plaintext := range []string{"finance@example.org", "TVqQ"} { if strings.Contains(printed, plaintext) {`. printed is only builtin.SetOutput (:91-94); runner.go:521 writes to os.Stdout. Verifier: example_record_disclosure_test.go:133-136 searches the output only for the literal strings 'finance@example.org' and 'TVqQ', and captures only builtin.SetOutput, not the runner's os.Stdout. In my scratch copy, record_disclosure.mut gained line 211 `putln("B4-LEAK", error("wrapped", "b4", {"k": address}));`, which leaks through REC.03. TestTheRecordDisclosureExampleRunsEndToEnd still PASSED while its captured output contained 'related={k=66696e616e6365406578616d706c652e6f7267}', which is finance@example.org in hex. Verifier's notes: I reproduced this through REC.03's error-related route, not through bytes_write (REC.07, refuted as a documented limit). The test gap stands on its own either way.
repro: Scratch copy: record_disclosure.mut gains `putln("REVIEW-LEAK", bytes_write_u16_le(address, 0, 26214));`. TestTheRecordDisclosureExampleRunsEndToEnd still PASSES while its output contains 'REVIEW-LEAK 66666e616e6365406578616d706c652e6f7267', the victim address in hex.
impact: The one test that takes the mark through the real VM would not notice a regression that leaks plaintext.
fix_proposal: Also search for hex.EncodeToString and base64 of each secret, and capture os.Stdout as well as builtin output. Regression test: This change to the test is itself the regression test. The scratch leak line must make it fail.

title: An empty or comment-only program compiles, then panics the runner
location: runner/runner.go:517-521 (vm/vm.go LastPoppedStackElement returns the nil slot)
claim: runvm prints last.Inspect() without checking for nil. When a program never pushed a value, LastPoppedStackElement returns a nil stack slot, and the run dies with a Go nil-pointer panic (exit 2, full goroutine dump) instead of exiting 0 with no output. Verifier: An empty or comment-only program compiles, and the runner then dies with a Go nil-pointer panic (exit 2) instead of exiting 0 silently. Only the script author can trigger it, with trivial input. No evidence or security impact, so S4. It is cheap to fix and highly visible (a new file run from the editor), so P1.
evidence: runner.go:517-521: `last := machine.LastPoppedStackElement()` / `if multi, ok := last.(*object.MultiValue); ok && multi.IsVoid() {` / `io.WriteString(os.Stdout, last.Inspect())`. vm.go:1704-1708 returns `vm.decryptForUse(vm.stack[vm.stackPointer])` whenever stackPointer is in range, and that slot is nil for a program that pushed nothing. Verifier: runner.go:517-521 calls last.Inspect() with no nil check. In my scratch build, `mutant gen empty.mut` (0-byte file) and `gen comment.mut` (`// only a comment`) both exit 0. Running either .mu with --compat prints `panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference ... mutant/runner.runvm ... runner/runner.go:521`, exit=2, 19 lines of goroutine dump. A program holding only `let x = 1;` prints `1` (stale slot, as the auditor noted). Verifier's notes: REC.02 is a separate defect on the same line: runner.go:521 prints classified values without checking the mark. The fixes will touch the same line, so coordinate them.
repro: `: > empty.mut; mutant gen empty.mut --dev` prints `Compiled in: 48ms`. Then `mutant empty.mu --dev` gives `panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference ... mutant/runner.runvm ... runner/runner.go:521` with exit=2. A file holding only `// only a comment` fails the same way. The standalone path uses the same runvm.
impact: The simplest valid program crashes with a stack trace. A new file run from the editor, or a module stub, shows a Go panic instead of nothing.
fix_proposal: In runvm, treat a nil `last` (and global.Null from an empty program) as void and return nil. Optionally make LastPoppedStackElement return global.Null for a nil slot. Regression test: runner: compile "" with generator.CompileForDebug, runvm(bytecode, "pw", false) returns (nil, "") without panicking. Same for a comment-only source.

title: A standalone binary's case manifest names the .exe but records the digest of the embedded payload
claim: The reproducibility record pairs a path with a digest of different bytes. For a release binary the path is the executable, but the hash is sha256 of the extracted payload, so re-hashing the named file never matches. The runtime that actually executed is covered by no digest. Verifier: For a standalone release, the manifest's program record names the executable but hashes only the embedded payload (the signed bytecode). Re-hashing the named file never matches, and the runtime that actually executed is not identified by any digest. The payload hash is, strictly, the digest of 'the .mu that produced it', so the language-reference promise is half kept. The path/hash pairing is what is wrong.
evidence: runner.go:82-99: `signedCode, err := os.ReadFile(srcpath)` / `signedCode, err = extractStandaloneSignedCode(signedCode)` / `builtin.SetProgramIdentity(srcpath, signedCode)`. For standalone, srcpath is the executable (main.go:145 `runtimeDeps.runCode(executablePath, opts)`). custody_seal.go:61-70 hashes the bytes it is given and stores Path unchanged. The docs promise the opposite: MUTANT_LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md:2320-2321 says 'the path and digest of the exact `.mu` that produced the document'. The tool record (custody.go:1148-1153) has only version, go_version, os and arch, and no executable digest. Verifier: runner.go:82-99 reads srcpath (the .exe for standalone runs, main.go:145), replaces signedCode with the extracted payload, then calls SetProgramIdentity(srcpath, signedCode). custody_seal.go:61-70 stores that path next to sha256 of the payload. My repro, ident.mut (case_open, case_close, print manifest.program): as ident.mu the manifest hash equals Get-FileHash ident.mu (018ec81c...ad07). I then built `mutant release --src ident.mut --os windows --arch amd64` and ran ident.exe. It gave path=...\ident.exe and hash=1ea5ad8a...797e, but Get-FileHash ident.exe=5d2337ba...667a, which does not match. The tool record carries no digest of the runtime. Verifier's notes: Priority is P2, not P1. Manifest signature verification is unaffected. The misleading part is the reproducibility section of standalone manifests.
repro: ident.mut does case_open, then case_close, then prints manifest.program. As a .mu: `hash: e743cdf6...94c2` and `file sha256: e743cdf6...94c2`, which match. As `mutant release --src ident.mut --os windows --arch amd64`, running ident.exe gives `path: ...\\ident.exe`, `hash: 941edcaf...22fb`, while `exe sha256: d59dd5ae...4542`, which does not match.
impact: Verifying the signed manifest's program record against the file it names fails for every standalone release, which looks like tampering. Meanwhile a modified runtime carrying the original payload yields an identical record.
fix_proposal: For a standalone run, record both the container (path plus sha256 of the whole executable) and the payload digest, under distinct keys. Or record the payload under a name that does not claim to be the file at `path`. Update the language reference. Regression test: runner: Run on a makeStandaloneBinaryBlob file records a program identity whose hash equals sha256(file) for the path key, and whose payload hash equals sha256(payload).

title: mutant release has no darwin/arm64 or windows/arm64 runtime; the default target fails on two shipped hosts
claim: The embedded runtime table covers 7 targets, missing darwin/arm64 and windows/arm64. The build scripts ship CLIs for exactly those hosts, and --os/--arch default to the host, so `mutant release --src x.mut` fails there by default. The help advertises the full OS x arch cross product, and the error's remedy cannot fix it. Verifier: As stated. On Apple Silicon and Windows-on-ARM hosts, `mutant release` with default target fails loudly, and the suggested remedy cannot work because regeneration never builds those targets.
evidence: release_assets.go:21-29 releaseTargets = darwin/amd64, linux/amd64, linux/386, linux/arm64, linux/arm, windows/amd64, windows/386. scripts/build.ps1:19-24 and build.sh:77-83 build darwin/arm64 and windows/arm64. main.go:1111-1112 default `runtime.GOOS` / `runtime.GOARCH`. main.go:887-891 help: `Supported OS values: darwin, linux, windows` / `Supported architecture values: amd64, arm64, arm, 386, x86`. assets_runtime.go:25: `embedded runtime asset missing for %s (run 'mutant gen --release-assets' and rebuild mutant)`, but regenerating never produces these targets. Verifier: generator/release_assets.go:21-29 lists 7 targets, none of them darwin/arm64 or windows/arm64. scripts/build.sh:77-83 and build.ps1:19-24 ship CLIs for both. The --os/--arch defaults are runtime.GOOS/GOARCH (main.go:1111-1112), and the help lists `arm64` for all three OSes. In my scratch build, `mutant release --src hello.mut --os darwin --arch arm64 --password-file pw.txt` gave `embedded runtime asset missing for darwin/arm64 (run 'mutant gen --release-assets' and rebuild mutant)`, exit 1. windows/arm64 failed the same way. git log -L shows the table has not changed since it was added in 0df6b36, and I found no documented reason for the gap. Verifier's notes: It fails loudly rather than producing a wrong result, so P2. Before adding darwin/arm64, check that appending a payload to an ad-hoc-signed arm64 Mach-O still launches.
repro: Scratch build with the local assets copied in: `mutant release --src hello.mut --os darwin --arch arm64 --password-file pw.txt` gives `unable to generate release mode builds: embedded runtime asset missing for darwin/arm64 (run 'mutant gen --release-assets' and rebuild mutant)` with exit=1. windows/arm64 fails the same way. darwin/amd64 and windows/amd64 succeed.
impact: Apple Silicon and Windows-on-ARM users of the shipped CLI cannot build a release for their own machine, and the error sends them on a fix that cannot work.
fix_proposal: Add darwin/arm64 and windows/arm64 to releaseTargets. List the exact supported os/arch pairs in help and docs (not a cross product). Make the missing-asset error say the pair is unsupported rather than suggesting a regeneration. Regression test: generator: a test that every GOOS/GOARCH in the build scripts' target lists appears in releaseTargets. main: help text lists the pairs in releaseTargets.

title: gen assets builds the release runtimes with whatever 'go' is on PATH, in the current directory
claim: The runtime embedded in every standalone release is built by exec.Command("go", ... ".") with no cmd.Dir, so it uses the PATH toolchain (not the pinned go1.26.2) and builds whatever package is in the working directory. The embedded assets on this tree are go1.27.0, and standalone manifests report it. Verifier: gen assets always uses the `go` on PATH and builds '.' in the current directory, so it only works from the module root. Its runtimes can differ from the toolchain that built the CLI when the CLI was built with a non-PATH go. The claim that shipped runtimes escape the 1.26.2 pin is overstated: build.sh does not enforce the pin for any of its binaries (it uses PATH go throughout). That is a build-script gap broader than this command. Only the release gate checks the toolchain.
evidence: release_assets.go:111-128: `cmd := exec.Command("go", "build", "-trimpath", ... "-o", outPath, ".")` with `cmd.Env = append(os.Environ(), ...)` and no cmd.Dir. printAssetsHelp (main.go:841-858) states neither requirement. The ledger's M26-TEST-006 fixed the same class for the gate and sweep, not for this command. Verifier: release_assets.go:111-128 runs exec.Command("go", "build", ..., ".") with no cmd.Dir. In my repro, `mutant gen assets --out <scratch>/assets_out` from a non-module directory printed `failed to generate release runtime asset for darwin/amd64: go: go.mod file not found ...`, exited 1, and left data/placeholder.bin behind. The standalone ident.exe manifest reports tool go_version go1.27.0 (the PATH go, N:\tools\scoop\shims\go.exe) while the go1.26.2 CLI reports go1.26.2. However, scripts/build.sh:154 resolves GO_BIN from PATH and uses it for the bootstrap build, the asset generation (after `cd "$REPO_ROOT"`) and the final binaries. It also prunes releaseassets/data to placeholder.bin first. So in the documented release flow the CLI and the embedded runtimes share one toolchain and are built in the module root. The go1.27 assets in this tree are gitignored local artifacts from 2026-09-17, not shipped files. Verifier's notes: The same class as M26-TEST-006 (sweep used PATH go) at a different call site, so not a duplicate. Downgraded to S4: the documented flow is internally consistent, and the non-module failure is loud.
repro: (1) Dumped the seven embedded runtimes via releaseassets.Get in a scratch test and ran `go1.26.2 version` on each: every one reports `go1.27.0`. (2) Standalone ident.exe manifest `tool go_version: go1.27.0`, while the same program as .mu run by the go1.26.2 CLI reports `go1.26.2`. (3) Running `mutant gen assets --out <dir>` from a non-module dir gives `failed to generate release runtime asset for darwin/amd64: go: go.mod file not found in current directory` with exit 1, and leaves <dir>/data/placeholder.bin behind.
impact: The owner's Go 1.26.2 pin does not reach the code that actually runs standalone artifacts. Shipped runtimes are built by an unpinned toolchain the gate never checked, and the command only works from the source root.
fix_proposal: Build with the toolchain that built this binary (filepath.Join(runtime.GOROOT(), "bin", "go"), or an explicit --go flag), set cmd.Dir to the module root (or refuse when CWD is not the mutant module), and verify each produced asset's buildinfo GoVersion against go.mod before writing. Write into a temp dir and rename on success. Regression test: generator: build one asset for the host target and assert debug/buildinfo GoVersion == "go"+go.mod version. A test that GenerateReleaseAssets from a non-module CWD fails before writing anything.

title: A password file written by Windows PowerShell (BOM or UTF-16) silently changes the password
claim: readFile uses the file bytes verbatim apart from one trailing newline. A UTF-8 BOM or a UTF-16LE file, which is what Windows PowerShell 5.1 writes with `>` or `Set-Content -Encoding UTF8`, becomes part of the password. On compile the artifact is encrypted under bytes the examiner never typed. Verifier: As stated. A BOM or UTF-16 password file becomes part of the password. On run this is a loud decryption failure. On gen it yields an artifact that opens only with that exact file, which a prompt cannot reproduce.
evidence: credential.go:252-257 `data, err := os.ReadFile(path)` ... `return trimOneNewline(data), nil`. trimOneNewline (307-310) strips only `\n` then `\r`. There is no BOM or NUL check. Verifier: credential.go:252-257 returns the file bytes with only one trailing \n and \r stripped (trimOneNewline, :307-310). Windows PowerShell 5.1.26100 `'reviewpass' > f` wrote FF FE 72 00 ... 0D 00 0A 00. With hello.mu compiled from the plain password, both that file and a UTF-8-BOM file gave `decryption failed: cipher: message authentication failed`, exit 1. A plain CRLF file worked. Compile side: `gen h16.mut --password-file <UTF-16 file>` exited 0. The result then fails with the typed password and opens only with the same file. No doc mentions encoding. Verifier's notes: S4, not S3: nothing is lost while the file exists, and every failure is loud.
repro: In Windows PowerShell 5.1: `'reviewpass' > pw16.txt` (bytes `FF FE 72 00 65 00 ...`) and `'reviewpass' | Set-Content -Encoding UTF8 pw8bom.txt` (bytes `EF BB BF 72 65 ...`). With hello.mu compiled from a file holding plain `reviewpass`, both `mutant hello.mu --compat --password-file pw16.txt` and `--password-file pw8bom.txt` give `decryption failed: cipher: message authentication failed` with exit=1.
impact: On the Windows hosts this DFIR tool targets, the usual way to write a key file produces an opaque decryption failure. Used at compile time, it produces an artifact that opens only with that exact file, never with the typed password.
fix_proposal: Strip a leading UTF-8 BOM. Refuse a file with a UTF-16 BOM or embedded NUL bytes, with a message naming the encoding and how to rewrite it. Regression test: credential: TestPasswordFileTrimsExactlyOneLineTerminator gains cases "\xEF\xBB\xBFsecret\r\n" -> "secret" and a UTF-16LE file -> an error that names UTF-16.

title: --password-stdin takes all of stdin as the password, so it cannot coexist with gets()
claim: readAllLine reads stdin to EOF and trims one newline, so the password is everything piped in. A pipeline that sends the password then data gets a wrong password, and a program using gets() then sees EOF. The help presents the flag as 'for CI and pipelines', and the function name says 'line'. Verifier: --password-stdin consumes all of stdin, consistent with --password-file and the common convention. A program that reads stdin with gets() therefore cannot take its password from stdin. The limitation and the multi-line behaviour are undocumented, and the helper's name (readAllLine) suggests a single line. This is a documentation and enhancement item, not a defect.
evidence: credential.go:174-176 `secret, err := readAllLine(r.stdin())`; 312-318 `data, err := io.ReadAll(r)` / `return trimOneNewline(data), nil`. builtin/gets.go:14 reads the same os.Stdin. Verifier: credential.go:174-176 and 312-318 read stdin to EOF with io.ReadAll. In my repro, readin.mut (gets) run with `--password-stdin < stdin_both.txt` (pw\nline) gave `decryption failed: cipher: message authentication failed`, exit 1. With only the password piped it gave `got: ERROR:gets: EOF`. However, this is the conventional --password-stdin semantics (docker login reads to EOF), and it matches --password-file, which also takes the whole file minus one newline. README.md:124 documents the use as `--password-stdin < secret`. Verifier's notes: Downgraded to S5/P3 because the behaviour is by convention. Document it, or offer a one-line mode.
repro: readin.mut = `let line = gets(); putln("got: " + to_string(line));`. `mutant readin.mu --compat --password-stdin < stdin_both.txt` (reviewpass\nevidence-line-1\n) gives `decryption failed: cipher: message authentication failed`. With only the password on stdin: `got: ERROR:gets: EOF`.
impact: Scripts that read stdin cannot use the recommended non-interactive password source. On `gen`, extra piped lines silently become part of the encryption password.
fix_proposal:
Read exactly one line (bufio.Reader up to the first 
, with a length cap) and leave the rest of stdin for the program. Rename the function and document the behaviour. Regression test: credential: Resolve(Request{Stdin:true}) with Stdin "pw
rest
" returns "pw", and the reader still yields "rest
".

title: The same import spelling resolves on Windows and fails on Linux (backslash, trailing space)
claim: Resolve validates the trimmed spelling but joins the untrimmed one, and it converts only '/' via FromSlash. ast.ImportStatement.Namespace deliberately treats '\\' as a separator on every host. So `import "lib\\util.mut"` and `import "util.mut "` compile on Windows (Win32 path rules) and are 'cannot find module' on Linux. The trailing-space form also binds the namespace `util.mut ` and gets a distinct module key. Verifier: As stated. Import spellings with a backslash or trailing whitespace compile on Windows and fail (loudly) on Linux, while the namespace derivation treats both separators alike.
evidence: resolve.go:69-73 `validateSpelling(spelling)` checks `strings.TrimSpace(spelling)` (109-122), then `local := filepath.FromSlash(spelling)`. ast/importStatement.go:64-69 says 'a Windows author may well type a backslash, and the namespace should not depend on which'. Verifier: resolve.go:69-73 validates strings.TrimSpace(spelling) but joins filepath.FromSlash(spelling), which leaves backslashes alone on Linux. My own module/zz_b4_test.go: on Windows, `lib\\util.mut` resolved to ...\\lib\\util.mut and `util.mut ` resolved to `...\\util.mut ` (Win32 strips the trailing space). The same test cross-compiled for linux/amd64 and run in WSL Ubuntu gave `cannot find module "lib\\util.mut"; searched: /tmp/.../lib\util.mut` and `cannot find module "util.mut "`. ast/importStatement.go:64-69 deliberately treats backslash as a separator for the namespace.
repro: Scratch module/zz_review_backslash_test.go. On Windows both tests pass: `resolved ...\\lib\\util.mut, namespace "util"`, and `namespace "util.mut " key "...\\util.mut "`. The linux/amd64 test binary run in WSL Ubuntu fails with `cannot find module "lib\\util.mut"; searched: /tmp/.../lib\util.mut` and `cannot find module "util.mut "`.
impact: A multi-file program written on a Windows workstation fails to compile on the Linux analysis box, and the language server (which uses its own resolver in sema) may disagree with both.
fix_proposal: Normalise the spelling once: reject leading/trailing whitespace in validateSpelling, and either convert '\\' to '/' before FromSlash on every host (matching Namespace) or reject backslashes with a message. Regression test: module: the two scratch tests above, run on both hosts, assert identical outcomes.

title: --password-stdin=true and --dev=true are accepted by gen's FlagSet but ignored
claim: registerPasswordFlags declares password-stdin and dev as bool flags, so the flag package accepts `--password-stdin=true` and `--dev=true`. The raw-argv extractors match only the bare spelling, so the flag is ignored, and the error then tells the user to pass the flag they passed. Verifier: As stated. The `=true` spellings are accepted by the FlagSet and then ignored, and the error message names the flag the user just passed.
evidence: main.go:1075-1082 hasBoolFlag: `if arg == "-"+name || arg == "--"+name`. main.go:308-315 hasDevModeArg is exact-match. main.go:1098-1099 `fs.BoolVar(&discardBool, "password-stdin", ...)` / `fs.BoolVar(&discardBool, "dev", ...)`. Verifier: hasBoolFlag (main.go:1075-1082) and hasDevModeArg (:308-315) match exact spellings only, while registerPasswordFlags (:1098-1099) declares both as bool flags, so the FlagSet accepts `=true`. In my repro, `gen h2.mut --password-stdin=true < pw` and `gen h2.mut --dev=true` both gave `gen: no password given and stdin is not a terminal ... Use --password-file <path> or --password-stdin ...`, exit 1. The bare `--password-stdin` form succeeded. The file-run path behaves the same (`h2.mu --compat --password-stdin=true` exit 1). Verifier's notes: P3: a rare spelling, and it fails loudly.
repro: `Get-Content pw.txt | mutant gen hello.mut --password-stdin=true` gives `gen: no password given and stdin is not a terminal ... Use --password-file <path> or --password-stdin ...` with exit=1. `mutant gen hello.mut --dev=true` gives the same message, exit=1.
impact: A standard Go flag spelling that the subcommand itself accepts is silently dropped, and the error message is self-contradictory.
fix_proposal: Read the password and dev switches from the parsed FlagSet values (or make hasBoolFlag/hasDevModeArg accept =true/=false), and keep one parser as the source of truth. Regression test: main: extractPasswordRequest([... "--password-stdin=true"]) has Stdin true, and hasDevModeArg([... "--dev=true"]) is true.

title: The release target OS is lowercased for asset lookup but not for the .exe suffix
claim: releaseassets.Get lowercases goos, so `--os Windows` builds a Windows PE, but Generate adds .exe only when `goos == "windows"` exactly. The output is an extensionless Windows executable.
evidence: generate.go:70-72 `if goos == global.WINDOWS { dstpath += global.WindowsPE32ExecutableExtension }`. assets_runtime.go:22 `strings.ToLower(goos)`. Verifier: generate.go:70-72 appends .exe only when goos == "windows", while releaseassets.Get lowercases (assets_runtime.go:22). Repro: `mutant release --src hello.mut --os Windows --arch amd64 --password-file pw.txt` compiled in 525 ms, exit 0, and wrote `hello` (49,519,149 bytes) with no .exe.
repro: `mutant release --src hello.mut --os Windows --arch amd64 --password-file pw.txt` gives `Compiled in: 537ms`, exit=0. The directory listing shows `hello  49519149` and no hello.exe.
impact: The shipped binary cannot be launched by double-click or by name on Windows until renamed.
fix_proposal: Normalise goos/goarch once in prepareRelease (lowercase, x86 to 386) and use the normalised values everywhere. Regression test: generator: Generate(..., goos "Windows", release=true) writes dst+".exe".

title: BINARY_ARTIFACT_SECURITY_DEEP_DIVE describes the pre-M-4 verification matrix and overstates the trailer
claim: §4 says secure mode without signer-auth 'Skips signature verification path', and §2 says VerifyCode is 'Used in compatibility mode'. Since M-4, runner.go:122-144 self-verifies in every mode. §6 claims 'Security value' from a provenance hash that is an unkeyed sha256 anyone can recompute, and the runner discards the profile code and still accepts V1/V2 trailers. Verifier: As stated. The deep dive's §2/§4 describe the pre-M-4 matrix, and §6 presents a recomputable, unkeyed trailer digest as protection against payload replay, when it only detects corruption.
evidence: Deep dive §4 item 2: `secureMode=true, enforceSignerAuth=false - Skips signature verification path.` Code: runner.go:122-144 else-branch runs security.VerifyCode for both modes. profile.go:66-71 DeriveStandaloneProvenance = sha256(payload||checksum||profile). runner.go:470 `if _, ok := security.ProtectionProfileFromCode(profileCode); !ok` discards the profile. runner.go:412-416 falls back to V2/V1. Verifier: The deep dive §4 item 2 says secure mode without signer-auth 'Skips signature verification path', and §2 says VerifyCode is 'Used in compatibility mode'. runner.go:122-144 runs VerifyCode in every mode (M-4). Repro: `mutant hello.mu --password-file pw.txt` on a copy with one byte flipped printed `event=signature_failed stage=secure-mode-self-verify action=terminate`, exit 1. §6 claims 'Security value' from provenance, but DeriveStandaloneProvenance (security/profile.go:66-71) is an unkeyed sha256(payload||checksum||profile) anyone can recompute. runner.go:470 only range-checks the profile code, and V1/V2 trailers are still accepted (:412-416). Stage B DOC3.09 (CONFIRMED): Three more documents say secure mode without --signer-auth skips signature verification; the runner self-verifies in every mode
repro: `mutant hello.mu --trusted-key wrong.hex --password-file pw.txt` (secure, no signer-auth) prints `[security] self-verification only; ...`, which shows the branch the doc says is skipped does run.
impact: Reviewers and operators reason about the wrong trust model: the doc understates what default mode checks and overstates what the trailer protects.
fix_proposal: Regenerate §2/§4 from EXECUTION_MODES.md's table. State that the trailer checksum, canary and provenance detect corruption only, and that authenticity comes from AES-GCM under the password plus --signer-auth. Regression test: none (docs); optionally a doc-lint that the deep dive's matrix matches the runner branches.

title: Every REPL start or command-less invocation reads the whole executable into memory
claim: shouldAttemptEmbeddedRun is true for bare `mutant` and any unrecognised flag, and HasStandalonePayload then does os.ReadFile on the entire executable just to inspect its last 90 bytes.
evidence: main.go:195-198 `if len(args) == 1 { return true }`. runner.go:393-399 `binaryData, err := os.ReadFile(srcpath)` then `validateStandalonePayload(binaryData)`. Verifier: shouldAttemptEmbeddedRun (main.go:195-198) is true for bare `mutant` and for unknown args, and HasStandalonePayload (runner.go:393-399) calls os.ReadFile on the whole executable. On the 174 MB scratch dev build, five runs of `mutant --notaflag` took 96-121 ms against 35-48 ms for `mutant help`.
repro: Dev build (174 MB). `mutant --notaflag` takes 105-122 ms against 35-48 ms for `mutant help`, and allocates the whole binary.
impact: Startup latency and a large transient allocation on every REPL launch (smaller on stripped release builds).
fix_proposal: Open the file, Seek to size-StandaloneTailV3Size, read the trailer, and read the payload only when a trailer is found. Regression test: runner: HasStandalonePayload on a 64 MiB file without a trailer allocates under 1 MiB.

title: Dead and duplicated code in the run path
claim: Several pieces never run or are duplicated. (a) runner.go:291-292 computes `cfg := security.ResolveRemoteScanConfig()` and immediately overwrites it with `cfg = resolveRemoteScanCfg()`. (b) generate.go:50-58, `if privateKey == nil { keyPair, err := security.GenerateKeyPair() ...`, is unreachable because EnsureLocalSigningKeyPair never returns a nil key without an error, and its comment 'Local keypair bootstrap provides deterministic signer identity per host' describes an ephemeral key. (c) main.go:1005 newFlagSet has no callers. (d) module/resolve.go:55 Resolver.SearchPaths has no callers, not even tests. (e) deriveStandaloneTailCanary is copied verbatim in runner.go:488 and generator/writebinary.go:47.
evidence: `git grep -n newFlagSet` finds only its definition at main.go:1005. `git grep SearchPaths()` finds only resolve.go:55. security/key_bootstrap.go:37-70 returns a non-nil key on every nil-error path. Verifier: (a) runner.go:291-292 assigns ResolveRemoteScanConfig() and immediately overwrites it. (b) EnsureLocalSigningKeyPair (key_bootstrap.go:37-70) returns a non-nil key on every nil-error path, so generate.go:50-58 is unreachable and its comment is wrong. (c) `git grep newFlagSet` finds only main.go:1005. (d) `git grep SearchPaths()` and `.SearchPaths` find only resolve.go:55. (e) deriveStandaloneTailCanary is identical at runner.go:488 and generator/writebinary.go:47.
repro: git grep for each symbol, and reading key_bootstrap.go.
impact: Misleading comments, and a trailer derivation that can drift between writer and reader.
fix_proposal: Delete (a)-(d). Move the canary derivation into security (next to DeriveStandaloneProvenance) and call it from both sides. Regression test: none needed; staticcheck U1000/SA4006 would catch (a),(c),(d).

title: Local signing-key bootstrap can destroy the private key or leave a mismatched pair; after that, every newly signed record reports a failed signature
claim: EnsureLocalSigningKeyPair has three defects. (1) If only the public-key file is missing, the load returns IsNotExist and a new pair is generated. That overwrites the existing private key with os.WriteFile, so the organisation's signing key is lost silently. (2) loadLocalSigningKeyPair never checks that the public file matches the private key, so a mismatched pair loads without error. (3) Creation is neither exclusive nor atomic: no O_EXCL, no lock, and two separate WriteFile calls. First-use bootstraps running concurrently can therefore interleave and leave the private key from one run and the public key from another. SignRecordFooter, SealCaseKeyFile and ledger_open all publish the public key from the file beside a signature made with the private key. Once the pair is mismatched, every record sealed afterwards verifies as "the signature does not cover this header and these segments", and so do every case-key file and ledger signed afterwards. Verifier: Confirmed: the private key is overwritten when only the public file is missing; a mismatched pair loads unchecked; after that every newly signed record, case-key file and ledger reports a failed signature; and concurrent first-use bootstraps in one process can leave a mismatched pair. Two refinements. (a) 'Silently' is overstated.
