No depth check exists anywhere in vm/, evaluator/ or compiler/ (grep for depth/overflow finds only a comment in resource.go:51 that assumes 'a stack overflow' is an error the VM reports). traceback.go:27 also speaks of 'A runaway recursion produces a thousand identical frames', which assumes a runaway recursion ends in an error. Verifier: pushFrame/ensureFrameCapacity (vm/vm.go:369-378, 2403-2410) grow without bound. global.MaxFrames is documented in global/const.go:3 as an initial capacity. git grep finds no depth limit or SetMaxStack in production code. TestB4Recursion: `let f = fn(n) { return f(n + 1); }; f(0);` was still running after 5 s with no error, heap at only 25 MiB, so the quadratic integrity sweep (VM.10) makes it crawl rather than quickly run out of memory. TestB4RecursionThroughMap with debug.SetMaxStack(64 MiB): `f` recursing through map() killed the test binary with 'runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 67108864-byte limit / fatal error: stack overflow'. My deferred recover never ran, so the crash cannot be contained and deferred cleanup is skipped. The comments at vm/resource.go:49-51 ('a stack overflow') and vm/traceback.go:27 assume the VM reports runaway recursion as an error. Verifier's notes: Not a duplicate of LEX.03 (parser recursion) or EVL.12 (macro-evaluator recursion): each needs its own limit in a different package.
repro: vm/zz_review_b1b_test.go TestReviewB1UnboundedRecursion: `let f = fn(n) { return f(n + 1); }; f(0);` was still running after 4 s with 44,308 frames and no error. vm/zz_review_b1e_test.go: `let f = fn(n) { return map([1], fn(x) { return f(n + 1); }); }; f(0);` with debug.SetMaxStack(32 MiB) killed the test binary with `runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 33554432-byte limit / fatal error: stack overflow`. With the real CLI and the default 1 GB stack, rrec/rec.mu was still running after 180 s.
impact: A recursive-descent parser in a script walking nested evidence, or any recursion bug, hangs the run or kills the process. A kill skips CleanupSensitiveData and WaitForTasks.
fix_proposal: Add a named frame-depth limit (for example 10,000, budgeted in policy/limit_budget.go). pushFrame returns `call depth exceeded %d` through callClosure's error path. Count CallClosureSync re-entries toward the same limit so the Go stack cannot be exhausted first. Rename MaxFrames to InitialFrameCapacity. Regression test: vm: TestRunawayRecursionIsAnError and TestRecursionThroughMapIsAnError. Both must return an error naming the limit within a bounded time.

title: `!x` is not the negation of truthiness (`!0`, `!""`, `!0.0` are false), and the two engines disagree on `!""` and `!"false"`
claim: execBangOperation only special-cases the True, False and Null singletons and returns False for everything else. isTruthy, which `if`, `&&`, `||` and filter use, treats 0, 0.0, "" and empty bytes as falsy. So both `if (x)` and `if (!x)` skip their branch when x is 0 or "". The evaluator's version compares Inspect strings, so it answers `!""` = true (Null renders as "") and `!"false"` = true, where the VM answers false for both.
evidence: `switch operand { case global.True: ... case global.False: ... case global.Null: return vm.push(global.True); default: return vm.push(global.False) }`, while isTruthy says `case *object.String: return len(o.Value) != 0 ... case *object.Integer: return o.Value != 0`. docs/WASM_REPL_REFERENCE.md 3.3 lists integer 0 and the empty string as falsy. Verifier: execBangOperation (vm/vm.go:2115-2128) switches on pointer identity with True/False/Null and returns False for everything else. isTruthy (vm.go:2655) treats 0, 0.0, "" and empty bytes as falsy. The language reference (MUTANT_LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md:548) says && and || use 'the same truthiness rules as if'. I ran TestB4Bang: `!0`, `!""` and `!0.0` all give false, and `if (0)`, `if ("")` and `if (!0)` are all not taken. Both `x` and `!x` are therefore falsy for 0 and "". Parity (parity/zz_b4_test.go): `!""` evaluator=true vm=false; `!"false"` evaluator=true vm=false. The evaluator compares Inspect text (eval_expressions.go:39-49). No test pins `!0`; only `!5` is pinned. Verifier's notes: EVL.07 is the same root defect, the bang operator in both engines. I keep VM.05 as the survivor because it names the concrete values and both disagreements. Also, docs/WASM_REPL_REFERENCE.md 3.3 lists 'whitespace-only string' as falsy, which neither isTruthy implements, so fix the truthiness table in one place.
repro: vm/zz_review_b1_test.go TestReviewB1BangDisagreesWithTruthiness: `!0` => false, `!""` => false, `!0.0` => false, while `if (0)` is not taken. parity/zz_review_b1_test.go: `!""` evaluator=BOOLEAN(true) vm=BOOLEAN(false); `!"false"` evaluator=BOOLEAN(true) vm=BOOLEAN(false).
impact: `if (!count) { putln("no hits"); }` never fires for zero hits, and `if (!name)` never fires for an empty string. The program takes the wrong branch silently. Macro-time evaluation (the evaluator) and run time also disagree.
fix_proposal: Implement OpBang as `push(nativeBoolToBooleanObject(!isTruthy(operand)))`, and make evaluator.evalBangOperatorExpression call its isTruthy too. Pin the truthiness table in one shared place. Regression test: parity: TestBangIsTheNegationOfTruthiness over 0, 0.0, "", empty bytes, "false", "0", [], {}, null. Both engines must equal !isTruthy.

title: A negative index past the start of an array or string panics, and the panic is logged as a security integrity failure
claim: execArrayIndex and execStringIndex compute `max+i+1` for a negative i with no lower bound, unlike execBytesIndex (vm.go:2078-2081), which returns null. The Go index panic is contained by containFault. containFault calls `security.RecordIntegrityFailure("vm-panic")`, which appends an `integrity_failed` event to the process audit chain whose head is sealed into case manifests. Negative indexing is also VM-only: the evaluator returns NULL for every negative array index.
evidence: `} else if i < 0 { return vm.push(arrayObj.Elements[max+i+1]) }` and `strObj := &object.String{Value: string(strVal[max+i+1])}` have no check that max+i+1 >= 0. Verifier: execArrayIndex (vm.go:2094) and execStringIndex (vm.go:2057) index `max+i+1` with no lower bound. execBytesIndex (vm.go:2078-2081) does check it (my hex_decode probe returned a STRING, so the bytes arm is not affected). TestB4NegIndex: `[1, 2][-3]`, `[1, 2][-5]` and `"ab"[-5]` give 'vm_runtime_error: recovered panic: runtime error: index out of range'. containFault (vm/fault.go:58) calls security.RecordIntegrityFailure("vm-panic"), which appends an integrity_failed audit event and bumps the telemetry counter that custody.go:1132-1137 writes into every case manifest. CLI rb4/neg.mut: audit_head entries went from 2 to 3 after a task evaluated xs[-5], and top-level `putln(xs[-4])` ended the run with exit 1 and a 'recovered panic' traceback. Parity: `[1, 2, 3][-1]` evaluator=NULL vm=INTEGER(3); `[1, 2, 3][-4]` evaluator=NULL vm=panic. Negative indexing is not documented in the language reference. Verifier's notes: EVL.08 is the same root defect (negative array index: evaluator null, VM counts from the end, panic past -len). I keep VM.06 as the survivor because it also records the false integrity_failed counter in manifests.
repro: vm/zz_review_b1_test.go TestReviewB1NegativeIndexPanics: `[1, 2][-5];` and `"ab"[-5];` give `vm_runtime_error: recovered panic: runtime error: index out of range [-3]`. CLI rneg/neg.mut: audit_head().entries is 1 at start, still 1 after a task divides by zero, and 2 after a task evaluates `xs[-5]`. Parity: `[1, 2, 3][-1]` evaluator=NULL vm=INTEGER(3); `[1, 2, 3][-4]` evaluator=NULL vm=panic.
impact: An ordinary off-by-one ends the run, or fails a task, with a message about a recovered panic. It also records a false tamper indication in the audit chain and the case manifest counters. The engines disagree on what negative indexes mean at all.
fix_proposal: Bound the negative path the way execBytesIndex does: `if max+i+1 < 0 { return vm.push(global.Null) }`. Decide once whether negative indexing is language (then implement it in the evaluator and document it) or not (then return null in the VM). Regression test: vm: TestNegativeIndexPastTheStartIsNull for arrays and strings, asserting that the audit chain does not grow. parity: add the negative-index rows to TestIndexParity.

title: String indexing turns a byte into a rune, returning a character the string does not contain
claim: `s[i]` indexes the UTF-8 bytes and then converts the byte with `string(strVal[i])`. That treats the byte as a code point, so any byte >= 0x80 becomes an unrelated Latin-1 character. The result is neither byte semantics nor rune semantics. `for (i, c in s)` iterates runes (object/iterator.go:86-93), so `s[i]` and the loop's c disagree for any non-ASCII string. The evaluator does not support string indexing at all and returns ERROR.
evidence: `strObj := &object.String{Value: string(strVal[i])}`, where strVal[i] is a byte. Verifier: vm.go:2057 and 2060 do `string(strVal[i])` on a byte, which converts the byte value to a code point. TestB4StringIndex: `"héllo"[1]` = "Ã" (U+00C3) and `[2]` = "©" (U+00A9). Neither character is in the string. str_char_at(s, 1) = "é". TestB4ForInIndexVsStringIndex: `for (i, c in s)` yields 1:é while s[1] is Ã, and 4:o while s[4] is l. So the loop index and s[i] disagree for any non-ASCII string. The evaluator returns ERROR for string indexing. The language reference does not define s[i] for strings. It says str_char_at indexes by rune. Verifier's notes: The engine silently fabricates characters on non-ASCII data such as file names and user names, and the fix is small.
repro: parity/zz_review_b1b_test.go: `"héllo"[1]` gives vm=STRING("Ã") (U+00C3, a character not in the string) and evaluator=ERROR. `"héllo"[-4]` gives vm=STRING("©").
impact: Scripts that index file names, registry values or user names containing non-ASCII characters get fabricated characters with no error.
fix_proposal: Index by rune, as the for-in iterator and str_char_at do: `runes := []rune(s); ... string(runes[i])`, with the same null/negative rules as arrays. Implement the same in the evaluator. Regression test: parity: TestStringIndexIsByRune. `"héllo"[1] == "é"` in both engines, and `s[i]` equals the for-in value at i for a non-ASCII s.

title: Equality falls back to comparing rendered text, so null == "", "0" == 0 and "true" == true
claim: Any pair that is not int/float, bytes, error or enum is compared with `right.Inspect() == left.Inspect()`. The code already carves out bytes, errors and enums because rendered-form equality made unequal values equal (comments at 2178-2198). The same collision remains for string vs integer, boolean, null and array.
evidence: `case code.OpEqual: return vm.push(nativeBoolToBooleanObject(right.Inspect() == left.Inspect()))`. docs/MUTANT_LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md says nothing about cross-type equality except for bytes (line 757). Verifier: execComparison falls back to `right.Inspect() == left.Inspect()` (vm.go:2202) after carving out numbers, bytes, errors and enums, and the comments for those carve-outs describe the same collision. TestB4Equality gives true for `f() == ""` (null vs empty string), `"0" == 0`, `"true" == true` and `[1] == "[1]"`. `"1.5" == 1.5` is false, because the float renders differently. Parity shows the evaluator gives the same true answers (eval_expressions.go:93). The language reference defines cross-type equality only for bytes (line 757) and errors (line 148). No test pins this behaviour. Verifier's notes: This is related to EVL.04 (float Inspect rounding) and EVL.02 (struct Inspect order), which are other defects in the 'Inspect is the equality' family, but it is not a duplicate of either.
repro: vm/zz_review_b1g_test.go TestReviewB1CrossTypeEquality: `let f = fn() { }; f() == "";` => true, `"0" == 0;` => true, `"true" == true;` => true. The parity probe shows `[1] == "[1]"` is true in both engines.
impact: A value parsed from evidence as the string "0" or "true" compares equal to the number or the boolean. A missing (null) value compares equal to an empty string. Filters built on == then report wrong matches with no error.
fix_proposal: Make values of different types unequal, except integer vs float, which is already numeric. Keep Inspect comparison only within one type, for arrays, hashes and structs. Change the evaluator the same way and record the rule in the language reference. Regression test: parity: TestCrossTypeEqualityIsFalse over (null, ""), ("0", 0), ("true", true), ([1], "[1]"), and TestIntFloatEqualityStillNumeric.

title: The integrity sweep re-verifies every active frame, making deep recursion quadratic
claim: About every 251-333 steps the sweep runs verifyFrameControlFlow and a SHA-256 of fn.Instructions for every frame on the stack. It does not deduplicate frames that run the same function, so the cost of each sweep grows with recursion depth.
evidence: `for i := 0; i < vm.frameIndex; i++ { ... verifyFrameIntegrity(vm.frames[i], "vm-frame-sweep") }`, and verifyFrameIntegrity does `actual := sha256.Sum256(fn.Instructions)` on every call. Verifier: verifyActiveFramesIntegrity (vm.go:2566-2577) runs verifyFrameControlFlow plus a SHA-256 of the instructions for every active frame, every 251 + jitter%83 steps, with no deduplication. TestB4SweepQuadratic, `sum(n) = n + sum(n - 1)`. Probes on: 63 ms at 2k, 140 ms at 4k, 407 ms at 8k, 1.36 s at 16k. integrityEvery = 0: 35, 62, 127 and 274 ms, which is linear. Verifier's notes: Lowered to P3. At realistic recursion depths in forensic walkers (hundreds) the overhead is negligible. It matters mainly because it turns runaway recursion (VM.04) into a crawl.
repro: vm/zz_review_b1i_test.go: `sum(n) = n + sum(n - 1)` took 38 ms, 90 ms, 278 ms and 934 ms at depths 2k, 4k, 8k and 16k. With integrityEvery = 0 (probes off) the same runs took 23, 43, 97 and 179 ms, which is linear.
impact: Recursive walkers over deep evidence structures (directory trees, nested containers) slow quadratically: 5x at depth 16k, and worse beyond.
fix_proposal: In the sweep, hash each distinct *CompiledFunction once (a per-sweep set), or check a bounded, randomly chosen sample of frames. Regression test: vm benchmark BenchmarkDeepRecursionSweep, asserting that time at depth 16k is under 3x the time at depth 8k.

title: Every builtin error decrypts and fully renders every argument of every frame on the stack
claim: stampError calls Traceback() for each error a builtin returns. That runs frameArguments over every frame, and for a non-bytes value it calls `strings.Join(strings.Fields(obj.Inspect()), " ")` on the whole value before cutting it to 48 characters. err.Stack has no cap on frames and no collapsing, unlike renderFrames. The whole Error, Stack included, is then gob-encoded on every push (mutil/util.go:273-287).
evidence: `text := strings.Join(strings.Fields(obj.Inspect()), " "); if len(text) > maxRenderedArgValue { text = text[:maxRenderedArgValue-3] + "..." }` and `err.Stack = make([]string, 0, len(frames))` with every frame appended. Verifier: stampError (traceback.go:594-625) runs on every builtin error with Line==0. It calls Traceback(), whose frameArguments runs decryptForUse and a full Inspect() + strings.Fields on every argument of every frame before truncating to 48 characters. err.Stack is uncapped. TestB4ErrorStampCost, 200 failing parse_int calls: 75 ms with a small argument, 54 ms with a 4 MiB string argument and 0 errors, 3.62 s with the 4 MiB argument and 200 errors, and 3.16 s with the 4 MiB argument one frame further up. That is about 17 ms per error. Verifier's notes: This is related to M26-VM-001 (a decrypt cost that scales with size), but the trigger is the error path, not variable loads, so it is a separate fix.
repro: vm/zz_review_b1f_test.go TestReviewB1ErrorStampRendersLargeArgumentsPerError: 200 failing parse_int calls inside `scan(blob, n)` took 48 ms with a small blob and 2.53 s with a 4 MiB string blob. With 0 errors the 4 MiB blob run took 34 ms.
impact: Scripts that probe many candidates and expect most to fail (paths, offsets, parse attempts) pay O(size of every argument on the stack) per failure.
fix_proposal: Render arguments with a bounded renderer that never materialises more than the cap: a string prefix, and a container summary such as 'array(20000)'. Collapse and cap err.Stack the same way renderFrames does. Regression test: vm: TestErrorStampCostIndependentOfArgumentSize. Error cost with a 4 MiB argument must stay within 2x of the cost with a small one.

title: Each pmap worker and each spawned task allocates 2 MiB of globals regardless of the program
claim: snapshotGlobals copies the full 65,536-slot globals slice (1 MiB). NewWithGlobalStoreAndPassword first runs New, which allocates another 65,536-slot slice (1 MiB), and then replaces it with the snapshot. So a worker costs 2 MiB before it runs anything, even for a program with three globals.
evidence: `globals := make([]object.Object, len(vm.globals)); copy(globals, vm.globals)` and `globals: make([]object.Object, initialGlobalsCapacity)` in New, followed by `if globals != nil { vm.globals = globals }`. Verifier: New (vm.go:216) allocates make([]object.Object, 65536) for globals. NewWithGlobalStoreMode then replaces it with the caller's slice. snapshotGlobals (parallel.go:47-51) copies all 65,536 slots. TestB4WorkerAlloc: 100 calls to newWorkerVM on a three-global program cost 2.05 MiB per worker, with len(globals) = 65536. Verifier's notes: Lowered to P3. The default worker count is NumCPU (tens of MiB total), and the 2 GiB case needs an explicit 1,024-worker request. Churn per net_serve connection is garbage collector work, not a leak.
repro: vm/zz_review_b1h_test.go: pmap over 1,024 elements. TotalAlloc was 1,072 MiB with 1 worker (mostly the array build, see VM-001), 1,202 MiB with 64 workers and 3,174 MiB with 1,024 workers, about 2 MiB per worker.
impact: pmap at its 1,024-worker cap allocates about 2 GiB. A net_serve handler that spawns per connection churns 2 MiB per connection.
fix_proposal: Snapshot only as many slots as the program's highest global index (the compiler knows it, since GlobalNames has that length). Skip New's globals allocation when the caller supplies a store. Regression test: vm: TestWorkerAllocationIsBoundedByProgramGlobals, asserting per-worker allocation under 64 KiB for a three-global program.

title: Line coverage misses every line that runs only on a pmap/peach/spawn worker
claim: Only the main VM has `cover` set. Worker VMs are built without it, so lines executed only inside parallel callbacks are reported as missed. docs/DEBUGGING.md explains the equivalent limit for the debugger. Nothing explains it for `mutant test --cover`.
evidence: newWorkerVMWithGlobals copies serveContext, secureMode and enforceSecurityCheckOpcodes, but not cover. Verifier: Real CLI: `mutant test --cover rb4\t`. lib.mut's `double` body (lines 2-3) runs only through `pmap(xs, double)` in a passing test. It was reported as 'missing 2-3' at 60.0%. TestB4CoverageWorkers: pmap gives map[1:true 2:false 3:false 5:true], and the same program with map gives all true. newWorkerVMWithGlobals does not copy cover. docs/TESTING.md does not mention the limit, while docs/DEBUGGING.md:142 documents the equivalent limit for the debugger.
impact: Coverage understates tests of parallel code and points reviewers at lines that are in fact covered.
fix_proposal: Give each worker its own coverage recorder and merge its marks into the parent under a mutex when the worker finishes, or share a recorder guarded by a mutex. Regression test: vm: TestCoverageCountsLinesRunOnWorkers, with the repro above expecting lines 2 and 3 as hit.

title: assert_eq on two errors compares their positions, while == deliberately does not
claim: testValuesEqual falls back to `a.Inspect() == b.Inspect()`, and Error.Inspect includes 'at file:line:col'. So two identical errors raised on different lines fail assert_eq. `==` uses Error.Equals, which object/errorObj.go documents as excluding position on purpose.
evidence: `default: return a.Inspect() == b.Inspect()`, and errorObj.go:283-294: 'Position is deliberately excluded ... Comparing what went wrong rather than where settles both at once'. Verifier: testValuesEqual's default arm (vm/testing.go:655-656) is `a.Inspect() == b.Inspect()`, and Error.Inspect includes the position. object/errorObj.go:285-291 says position is 'deliberately excluded' from == for exactly this reason. Real CLI: `let a = error("boom"); let b = error("boom"); assert(a == b); assert_eq(a, b);` failed with 'assert_eq: got ERROR:boom at ...:6:31 ..., want ERROR:boom at ...:6:54'. The assert passed. Two errors built on the same line (mk() twice) compare equal, which confirms that position is the cause. Verifier's notes: The metadata documents rendered-form comparison only for arrays, hashes and structs, so errors falling through to it is a gap, not a documented choice.
repro: vm/zz_review_b1b_test.go TestReviewB1AssertEqOnErrorsDisagreesWithEquals: `let a = error("boom"); let b = error("boom"); assert(a == b); assert_eq(a, b);` passes the assert and fails assert_eq with 'got ERROR:boom at 3:10 context=user, want ERROR:boom at 4:10 context=user'.
impact: Tests comparing an expected error with the one a function returned fail spuriously, which pushes authors toward comparing message strings.
fix_proposal: In testValuesEqual, add `case *object.Error: return left.Equals(b.(*object.Error))`. Consider reusing the VM's comparison for bytes and enums as well. Regression test: vm: TestAssertEqComparesErrorsLikeEquals.

title: Debugger Evaluate answers a closure's captured variable with a global of the same name
claim: Evaluate searches the frame's local slots and then the globals. It never looks at the closure's free variables (frame.cl.Free), so a captured name resolves to an unrelated global and shows the wrong value. Scopes does not list captured variables either. docs/DEBUGGING.md says 'A debugger that answered anyway would be guessing'.
evidence: `for slot := fn.NumLocals - 1; slot >= 0; slot-- {...}` is followed by `for slot, global := range d.vm.bytecode.GlobalNames { if global != name ... return d.variable(name, d.vm.getGlobal(slot)) }`. Verifier: Debugger.Evaluate (vm/debugger.go:898-937) searches frame locals, then GlobalNames, and never frame.cl.Free. TestB4DebuggerFreeVar: at a breakpoint on `return x;` in inner, where the program reads the captured x = 2, Evaluate(0, "x") returned {Type:INTEGER Value:1}, the global. Scopes(0) listed only Globals (x = 1). With no same-named global, Evaluate on a captured y answers 'no variable called "y" is in scope here', which is also false but at least not a wrong value.
repro: vm/zz_review_b1c_test.go TestReviewB1DebuggerEvaluateFreeVariableShowsGlobal: `let x = 1; let outer = fn() { let x = 2; let inner = fn() { return x; }; return inner(); }; outer();` with a breakpoint on `return x;`. Evaluate(0, "x") returns {Type:INTEGER Value:1}, while the program reads 2.
impact: The watch window shows a confident wrong value inside closures, which are the language's callbacks for map, filter and with_resource.
fix_proposal: Have the compiler record FreeNames on CompiledFunction (debug info, stripped with the other names). Search free variables between locals and globals, and add a 'Captured' scope. Until then, refuse to answer when the frame has free variables and the name is not a local. Regression test: vm: TestEvaluateResolvesCapturedVariables with the repro above expecting 2.

title: The VM copies containers on every load, so aliasing differs from the evaluator
claim: Every load decrypts to a fresh deep copy of an array, hash or struct, so `let b = a; b[0] = 9;` leaves `a` unchanged in the VM. The evaluator shares the container and changes `a`. The language reference states neither rule. parallel.go:72-74 also says 'a captured array is still the same array in both', which is not true in the VM.
evidence: DecryptObject ARRAY_OBJ: `elements := make([]object.Object, len(arrayObj.Elements)) ... return &object.Array{Elements: elements}`. Verifier: DecryptObject's ARRAY/HASH arms rebuild fresh containers on every load (mutil/util.go:450-476). Parity (parity/zz_b4_test.go): `let a = [1, 2]; let b = a; b[0] = 9; a[0]` gives evaluator=INTEGER(9) vm=INTEGER(1). `let h = {"k": [1]}; let x = h["k"]; x[0] = 5; h["k"][0]` gives evaluator=5 vm=1. MUTANT_LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md ('Assigning through a container', lines 640-680) states neither aliasing rule. Verifier's notes: Lowered to P3. The evaluator runs only at macro-expansion time, so the divergence reaches users only through macro bodies that mutate through an alias, and the runtime behaviour (value semantics) is consistent. EVL.16 is the same root defect; I keep VM.18 as the survivor because it also flags the wrong parallel.go:72-74 comment. Severity/priority raised from S4/P3 by duplicate EVL.16.
repro: parity/zz_review_b1b_test.go: `let a = [1, 2]; let b = a; b[0] = 9; a[0]` gives evaluator=INTEGER(9) vm=INTEGER(1). `let h = {"k": [1]}; let x = h["k"]; x[0] = 5; h["k"][0]` gives evaluator=5 vm=1.
impact: Macro-time evaluation (evaluator) and run time disagree on programs that mutate through an alias. Authors cannot tell from the docs which behaviour is intended.
fix_proposal: Decide the rule (value semantics fits the VM's storage model), document it in the language reference, make the evaluator copy on binding, and add parity rows. Fix the parallel.go comment. Regression test: parity: TestAliasedContainerMutation with the two rows above.

title: Dead and duplicated code in vm.go
claim: StackTop and NewWithPasswordAndGlobalStore have no callers in the repository. NewWithPassword and SecureMode are called only from tests. execBinaryOperation checks `rtype == INTEGER && ltype == INTEGER` twice, so the first `case` of the switch below it can never run.
evidence: A repo-wide grep finds 0 callers of `.StackTop(` and `NewWithPasswordAndGlobalStore(`. `if rtype == object.INTEGER_OBJ && ltype == object.INTEGER_OBJ { return ... }` is followed by `switch { case rtype == object.INTEGER_OBJ && ltype == object.INTEGER_OBJ:`. NewWithGlobalStoreAndPassword and NewWithPasswordAndGlobalStore take the same arguments in a different order and apply different security posture (enforceSecurityCheckOpcodes), which invites the wrong choice. Verifier: git grep: StackTop (vm.go:1686) has no callers. NewWithPasswordAndGlobalStore (vm.go:557) has no callers. NewWithPassword is called only from vm/vm_security_policy_test.go:63,73, and SecureMode() only from dap/session_test.go:331. vm.go:1829-1835 checks `rtype == INTEGER && ltype == INTEGER` and returns, and the first `case` of the switch after it repeats the same test, so that case is unreachable. NewWithPasswordMode sets enforceSecurityCheckOpcodes = true (vm.go:542), while NewWithGlobalStoreAndPassword goes through New with it false. So the two same-argument constructors really do differ in security posture. Verifier's notes: Related, outside this finding: serve/serve.go:114 builds net_serve handler VMs with NewWithGlobalStoreAndPassword, which leaves enforceSecurityCheckOpcodes false. Stage B should check whether that is intended.
repro: grep -rn '\.StackTop(\|NewWithPasswordAndGlobalStore(' --include=*.go .
impact: Nine near-identical constructors make it easy to pick the one that skips security-opcode enforcement.
fix_proposal: Delete StackTop and NewWithPasswordAndGlobalStore, and the unreachable switch case. Collapse the constructors into one taking an options struct. Regression test: none needed beyond compilation.

title: global/ mixes VM sizing, CLI constants and the release version, and MaxFrames is not a maximum
claim: StackSize, GlobalSize and MaxFrames are VM initial capacities, used as such only by the VM, yet MaxFrames reads as a limit (see the recursion finding). GlobalSize is also required by runner, serve, repl, test_runner and dap only to allocate the slice the VM would allocate itself. The package also holds file extensions, GOOS names and Version. global.True, False and Null are the VM's singletons, while the evaluator keeps its own (errorObj.go: 'the two engines hold different null singletons').
evidence: `// Initial capacities for VM storage. The VM grows these slices dynamically at runtime. const ( StackSize = 2048 GlobalSize = 65536 MaxFrames = 2048 ...` Verifier: global/const.go:3-7: 'Initial capacities for VM storage. The VM grows these slices dynamically', yet MaxFrames = 2048. vm.go:132-134 uses them only as initial* capacities. global.GlobalSize is also used by dap/session.go:267, repl/repl.go:387, runner/runner.go:503, serve/serve.go:112, test_runner.go:294 and webrepl/repl.go:71. The package also holds Version, the file extensions and the GOOS names.
repro: grep -rn 'global\.GlobalSize' --include=*.go . lists callers in runner, serve, repl, test_runner and dap.
impact: Readers take MaxFrames for a recursion limit that does not exist. The 65,536-slot globals size is copied per worker (see the 2 MiB finding).
fix_proposal: Move the capacities into vm as unexported initial* constants and let the VM allocate its own globals when nil is passed. Keep global/ for cross-package identity constants (Version, extensions). Regression test: none.

title: SECURITY_LLD section 10.3 describes a probe schedule the VM does not run
claim: The doc says probes run 'every integrityEvery steps', 'jittered: when stepCount % 97 == integrityJitter % 97', and 'sweep: every 251 steps'. The code runs a probe at integrityEvery + jitter%31 steps and a sweep at 251 + jitter%83 steps. There is no modulo-97 test anywhere.
evidence: `integritySweepBase = uint64(251); integritySweepSpread = uint64(83); integrityProbeSpread = uint64(31)` and `return vm.integrityEvery + (vm.integrityJitter % integrityProbeSpread)`. Verifier: docs/SECURITY_LLD.md 10.3 lists three triggers: every integrityEvery steps, a jittered `stepCount % 97 == integrityJitter % 97`, and a sweep every 251 steps. The code (vm.go:135-137, 173-187, 1632-1663) has two: a probe at integrityEvery(64) + jitter%31, and a sweep at 251 + jitter%83. git grep finds no '% 97' anywhere in the Go source. Verifier's notes: Checked by reading code against doc; there is no runtime behaviour to reproduce. Stage B DOC3.10 (CONFIRMED): SECURITY_DIAGRAMS section 5 repeats the modulo-97 jitter probe schedule that the VM does not run
repro: Read docs/SECURITY_LLD.md section 10.3 against vm.go:173-187.
impact: The security design document misstates when tamper checks fire.
fix_proposal: Rewrite section 10.3 from the constants, and note that the sweep's cost grows with call depth. Regression test: none.

title: The release gate accepts a log directory inside the repository, then fails its own test step on the Go files it writes there
claim: Both gate scripts promise that nothing is written into the working tree, but they create whatever -LogDir / --log-dir they are given, and the gofmt step writes an LF copy of every Go file under it. When that directory is inside the repository -- even a gitignored one -- the copies are packages of the module: go test ./... compiles them beside the real ones, and every guard that walks the tree reads them too.
evidence: Windows gate 2026-09-25 with -LogDir set to a gitignored directory inside the repository: go test ./... FAILed with 'setup failed' for every package under <logdir>/gofmt-lf, TestTheRecordDisclosureExampleRunsEndToEnd failed inside the copy (its fixture path resolved into gofmt-lf), and the real cmd/gendocs TestLimitsReferenceIsUpToDate failed because the limits scan counted the copies' constants. None of it is a defect in the code under test.
repro: policy/gate_guard_test.go TestGateRefusesALogDirInsideTheRepository before the fix: pwsh scripts/release_gate.ps1 -Go <anything> -Quick -LogDir <repo>/policy/gate-logdir-probe-<pid> ran every step and exited 1 instead of refusing with 2.
impact: A contributor who keeps gate logs beside the code gets a red gate whose failures point nowhere near their cause, and a green run no longer means the tree was checked alone.
fix_proposal: Both scripts resolve the log directory (the bash twin through its deepest existing ancestor with pwd -P, so symlinks resolve as the root does) and exit 2 with the reason when it is the repository root or inside it, before creating anything. The CHANGELOG gate entry says so.
reporter: Stage B Windows gate re-run, go1.26.2, 2026-09-25

title: DestList v3/v4 entries read the path size from the access-count field, so every Win8+ jump list gets garbage paths and misaligned entries
claim: parseDestList reads the v3/v4 path size at entry offset 0x74 (116). Per libyal dtformats and JLECmd (DestListEntry.cs: `BitConverter.ToInt16(rawBytes, 128)` for version > 1) it is at 128 (0x80); 116 is the access/interaction count. The path, and every later entry (off = pathEnd + trailer), is decoded from the wrong bytes. Verifier: As stated, and worse: on real Win10/11 DestLists (v4-v6) the loop breaks after the first misread entry, so jumplist_parse loses almost all DestList metadata (hostname, last_access, pinned, dest_path), not only the paths.
evidence: jumplist_builtins.go:178-183 `pathSizeOff := 0x70 ... if version >= 3 { pathSizeOff = 0x74; trailer = 4 }`; :196 `pathChars := int(binary.LittleEndian.Uint16(buf[off+pathSizeOff : ...]))`. The owned test builtin/jumplist_builtins_test.go:72 writes the path size at `base+0x74` too, so it can only prove the bug is self-consistent. Repro output: `v3 DestList laid out per libyal/JLECmd (path size @128): parsed 2 of 2 entries  [0] stream=1 host="WKSTN01" path="\x00\x00\x00"  [1] stream=0 host="" path=""` (paths C:\Users\x\Desktop\secret.docx and C:\Tools\mimikatz.exe written). Verifier: jumplist_builtins.go:178-183 uses path size @0x74 for v>=3. Re-ran TestZZ_DestListV3Layout: garbage paths. My own TestZZ_RealDestList read the DestList of all 115 real Win11 AutomaticDestinations files on this host (all version 6). Current parser: 1 entry, 0 plausible paths. Path size @0x80 (libyal/JLECmd layout): 409 entries, 409 plausible paths. The owned TestParseDestList writes @0x74, so it only proves the code agrees with itself. Verifier's notes: Proved against real host artifacts. Only aggregate counts were printed.
repro: scratch tree builtin/zz_art_test.go TestZZ_DestListV3Layout (CGO_ENABLED=0 go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZ_DestListV3Layout)
impact: jumplist_parse on any Windows 8/10/11 automaticDestinations-ms returns wrong dest_path values, wrong stream_id and hostname for the second and later entries, and so merges DestList metadata (last_access, pinned) onto the wrong LNK target. The error is silent.
fix_proposal: For version >= 2 read the path size at 0x80 and the path at 0x82; keep 0x70 for v1. Optionally expose the interaction count at 0x74. Fix TestParseDestList to use a real layout (ideally a real Win10 DestList fixture). Regression test: Build a v3 DestList with two entries laid out per libyal (path size @128, 4-byte trailer). Assert both paths, stream IDs and hostnames round-trip.

title: prefetch_parse reports run_count 0 (or an unrelated field) for Windows 10/11 v30 'variant 2' prefetch files
claim: For v30/31 the run count is always read at 0xD0 (file-info offset 124). Newer Windows 10/11 files use the 212-byte file-information variant (metrics offset 0x128). There the run count is at file-info offset 116 (absolute 0xC8), per libscca and PECmd Version30or31.cs (reads 124-8 when the value at 120 is non-zero). Verifier: As stated. The variant-2 layout is taken from libscca/PECmd; the repro is synthetic, not a real Win11 .pf.
evidence: prefetch_builtins.go:81-82 `case 30, 31: // Windows 10 / 11\n runTimesOff, runTimesCount, runCountOff = 0x80, 8, 0xD0`. No check of the metrics-array offset (0x54) or of the value at 0xCC. Repro: a v30 buffer with metrics offset 0x128 and run count 7 at 0xC8 gives `run_count reported = 0`. Verifier: prefetch_builtins.go:81-82 always reads the v30/31 run count at 0xD0, with no branch on the metrics offset at 0x54. Re-ran the synthetic variant-2 buffer (metrics 0x128, count 7 @0xC8): run_count=0. I could not check a real .pf because C:\Windows\Prefetch denies access without admin. The owned MAM vector is synthetic and writes 0xD0.
repro: zz_art_test.go TestZZ_PrefetchV30Variant2RunCount
impact: Run count is core program-execution evidence. On current Windows 10/11 prefetch it comes back as 0 or as an unrelated field, with no error.
fix_proposal: Branch on the file-metrics offset (0x130 means variant 1, run count at 0xD0; 0x128 means variant 2, run count at 0xC8), or follow PECmd's test on the value at 0xCC. Add a real compressed Win11 .pf fixture. Regression test: Synthetic v30 buffers for both variants (metrics offset 0x130/0x128). Assert run_count equals the value at 0xD0 and at 0xC8 respectively.

title: Prefetch volume entries use the wrong stride for v17 (XP) and v26 (Win8.1), so every volume after the first is misread
claim: The volume-information entry size is 40 bytes for v17, 104 for v23 and v26, and 96 for v30 (libscca; PECmd Version17.cs `j*40`, Version26.cs `j*104`, Version30or31.cs `j*96`). The code uses 104 for everything below 26 and 96 for 26 and above.
evidence: prefetch_builtins.go:140-143 `stride := 104 // v23\n if version >= 26 { stride = 96 // v26/v30/v31 }`. Repro (serials 11111111, 22222222 written at the spec stride): `v17 (spec stride 40): parsed [11111111 00000000]`, `v26 (spec stride 104): parsed [11111111 00000000]`; v23 and v30 are correct. Verifier: prefetch_builtins.go:140-143 uses stride 104 below v26 and 96 from v26 up. Re-ran: v17 [11111111 00000000], v26 [11111111 00000000]; v23 and v30 are correct. Per libscca the strides are 40/104/104/96.
repro: zz_art_test.go TestZZ_PrefetchVolumeStride
impact: On XP and Win8.1 prefetch with more than one volume (for example a USB stick), the second and later volumes report the wrong serial, creation time and device path. That breaks linking an execution to removable media.
fix_proposal: switch version { case 17: 40; case 23, 26: 104; default (30/31): 96 } Regression test: Table test over versions 17/23/26/30 with two volumes at the spec stride. Assert both serials.

title: Registry 'ri' subkey lists are followed with no visited set: a 4 KB hive makes hive_list_keys hang, and legal-depth DAGs multiply results exponentially
claim: collectSubkeyList recurses into each ri entry with only a depth cap of 32. It records no visited cells, so a self-referencing ri (fan-out 2) costs 2^33 calls, and a chain of k ri cells with two entries each returns 2^k duplicate subkey offsets. Every hive-backed reader goes through it: hive_*, reg_* on a regf file, amcache_parse, and shimcache_parse's key walk. Verifier: As stated. The self-loop costs about 2^33 calls, so it ends eventually but is a practical hang.
evidence: hive_builtins.go:123 `if depth > 32 { return nil }`; :150-157 `case "ri": ... out = append(out, h.collectSubkeyList(binary.LittleEndian.Uint32(c[base:base+4]), depth+1)...)`. Repro: ri chain k=12, a 4512-byte file, gives 4096 names; k=16 (4576 bytes) gives 65536; k=20 (4640 bytes) gives 1,048,576 names, all the same one subkey. Self-loop ri (4232-byte hive): `hive_list_keys ... did not return within 15s`. Verifier: collectSubkeyList recurses through ri cells with only a depth>32 cap and no visited set. Re-ran: ri chain k=12/16/20 in 4512-4640-byte hives gives 4096/65536/1048576 names for one subkey. Self-referencing ri (4232 bytes): hive_list_keys did not return within 15 s.
repro: zz_art_test.go TestZZ_HiveRiFanout (k=12/16/20) and the self-loop case (now split as TestZZH_HiveRiSelf)
impact: A crafted or corrupted hive hangs the analysis (goroutine CPU burn with no timeout), or returns millions of duplicate keys, with memory growing as 2^depth. That is a hang on crafted evidence in every registry parser.
fix_proposal: Keep a visited set of list cells across the recursion, and bound total offsets by the number of cells or by the nk's subkeyCount. Only lf/lh/li may appear under ri (ri may not nest), so recurse at most one level. Regression test: Self-referencing ri hive: hive_list_keys must return promptly with an error or an empty list. ri-chain k=20 must return exactly one name.

title: Header counts size allocations before any bounds check (hive valueCount, hive big-data size, DestList total, bplist numObjects/array count): a few-byte field can kill the process with a fatal out-of-memory
claim: Several parsers pre-size a slice from a count read out of the file. The loop that follows is bounded by the real buffer, but the allocation is not. A Go allocation that exceeds commit is a fatal runtime error that recover() cannot catch. Sizes: hive valueCount (uint32, 8 bytes each, up to 32 GiB); readBigData size (dataSize & 0x7FFFFFFF, up to 2 GiB); DestList total (uint32, 56-byte structs, up to 240 GB); bplist numObjects (uint64 as int, 8 bytes each); bplist array count (16 bytes each), repeated at every nesting level (depth cap 100) when an array references itself. Verifier: As stated. The fatal-OOM sizes are extrapolated from linear growth, not run.
evidence: hive_builtins.go:170 `out := make([]*vkValue, 0, nk.valueCount)`; :218 `out := make([]byte, 0, size)`; jumplist_builtins.go:176 `entries := make([]destEntry, 0, total)`; plist_builtins.go:216 `offsets := make([]int, numObjects)`; :289 `elems := make([]object.Object, 0, count)`. Measured (TotalAlloc, file size fixed): hive valueCount 2^22 -> 33 MiB, 2^24 -> 132 MiB (4256-byte hive); big-data declared 64 MiB -> 65 MiB, 256 MiB -> 262 MiB (24 KB hive, 20 KB actually returned); DestList total 2^20 -> 57 MiB, 2^22 -> 230 MiB (32-byte stream); bplist numObjects 2^22 -> 32 MiB, 2^24 -> 128 MiB (48-byte file); bplist array count 2^20 -> 16 MiB, 2^22 -> 64 MiB (55-byte file); a self-referencing array with count 2^14 -> 25 MiB, 2^16 -> 101 MiB. A first run of the self-referencing array at count 2^22 tripped the 1 GiB heap watchdog. Verifier: Re-ran all five allocation repros under the 1 GiB watchdog. The file size stayed fixed while allocation grew linearly with the header field: hive valueCount 2^22/2^24 -> 32/128 MiB (4256 B); big-data declared 64/256 MiB -> 64/256 MiB; DestList total 2^20/2^22 -> 56/224 MiB (32 B); bplist numObjects -> 32/128 MiB (48 B); array count -> 16/64 MiB; self-referencing array 2^14/2^16 -> 25/101 MiB. Verifier's notes: Same class as FS2.03 and NET.09 but separate code, so not a duplicate.
repro: zz_art_test.go TestZZ_HiveValueCountAlloc, TestZZ_HiveBigDataAlloc, TestZZ_DestListTotalAlloc, TestZZ_PlistNumObjectsAlloc, TestZZ_PlistArrayCountAlloc (all under a 1 GiB heap watchdog; the fatal sizes were extrapolated, not run)
impact: hive_open/hive_list_values/reg_*/amcache_parse/shimcache_parse, jumplist_parse and plist_parse can each be killed outright by one small crafted artifact. Allocation grows linearly with a field the attacker sets, not with the file size. The earlier Stage B attempt showed this class exhausts the shared host.
fix_proposal: Cap every pre-size at what the buffer can hold: min(valueCount, len(cell)/4); min(size, numSegs*16344, len(file)); min(total, len(buf)/130); min(numObjects, (len(data)-offsetTableOffset)/offsetIntSize) and validate it before make; min(count, (len(data)-dataStart)/refSize). Better, drop the pre-size and append. Regression test: For each parser, craft a header-only input with the count at 2^24 and assert TotalAlloc stays under a few MiB and an error or empty result comes back.

title: evtx_parse: a chunk whose first record has size 0 loops LastEventRecNumber-FirstEventRecNumber times, appending the same record each time (hang plus unbounded memory)
claim: evtx_parse hands every chunk to Velocidex Chunk.Parse. That loops `for i := First; i <= Last; i++` over attacker-controlled uint64s and re-seats to `start_of_record + int(record.Header.Size)`. A zero Size never advances, and NewEventRecord keeps finding the '**' magic at the same offset. Mutant validates neither the chunk header nor the record count before calling it. Verifier: As stated. I did not re-run the 2^64-2 case; linear growth is proven.
evidence: evtx_builtins.go:91 `parsed, err := chunk.Parse(0)`; library evtx.go:139 `for i := self.Header.FirstEventRecNumber; i <= self.Header.LastEventRecNumber; i++ {` ... :153 `ctx.SetOffset(start_of_record + int(record.Header.Size))`. Repro on Velocidex's own Security_1_record.evtx (1 record) with record size set to 0: Last=first+1000 gives count=1001 in 14 ms, 9 MiB; Last=first+4000 gives count=4001 in 45 ms, 37 MiB (linear). With Last=2^64-2 the test binary died within 10 s with `fatal error: runtime: cannot allocate memory` inside Velocidex TemplateNode.Expand. Verifier: Velocidex evtx@v0.2.0 evtx.go:139-154 loops First..Last and re-seats by record.Header.Size. Mutant (evtx_builtins.go:83-96) passes chunks through without validating them. Re-ran on Security_1_record.evtx with record size 0: Last=first+1000 -> count 1001 (9 MiB), +4000 -> 4001 (37 MiB), linear growth.
repro: zz_art_test.go TestZZ_EvtxZeroSizeRecord with ZZ_EVTX1=<GOMODCACHE>/www.velocidex.com/golang/evtx@v0.2.0/testdata/Security_1_record.evtx (the unbounded case is now gated behind ZZ_EVTX_INF)
impact: An 8-byte edit to any .evtx makes evtx_parse/evtx_parse_bytes never finish and exhaust memory, which kills the Mutant process. parseEvtxChunk's recover cannot stop it.
fix_proposal: Before Parse, reject chunks where LastEventRecNumber < FirstEventRecNumber or where the span exceeds (65536-512)/24. Or walk records yourself and stop when Size < 24, when the offset does not advance, or when it leaves the chunk. Cap records per chunk. Regression test: Mutate Security_1_record.evtx (record size 0, Last=2^64-2). evtx_parse must return within 1 s with at most one record per chunk.

title: evtx_parse silently drops whole chunks: 2 changed bytes remove 76 of 739 events with no error and no skipped count
claim: parseEvtxChunk turns a panic or an error into nil records, and Velocidex's Parse returns the partial result (nil error) when a record header fails. The result carries chunk_count and count but no field reporting chunks or records that failed. That contradicts the project's own mft_parse rationale for a 'skipped' field.
evidence: evtx_builtins.go:86-94 `defer func() { if r := recover(); r != nil { recs = nil } }() ... if err != nil { return nil }`. Repro on Velocidex testdata Security.evtx: original `chunk_count=10 count=739`. After overwriting 2 bytes of chunk 2's first record magic: `err=<nil> chunk_count=10 count=663 keys=source,chunk_count,count,records`. Verifier: Re-ran on Velocidex Security.evtx: 739 events became 663 after a 2-byte magic edit in chunk 2, with err nil and no skipped or expected field. The metadata says it 'Walks every chunk and decodes each record'.
repro: zz_art_test.go TestZZ_EvtxCorruptChunkSilent (ZZ_EVTXN=.../testdata/Security.evtx)
impact: Corrupting or tampering one record header hides a chunk of events (up to ~64 KB of logs) from the examiner, and the output looks complete. That is anti-forensic and silent.
fix_proposal: Count chunks that panic, error or yield fewer records than FirstEventRecNumber..Last implies, and return skipped_chunks / expected_records next to count, as mft_parse does with skipped. Regression test: Corrupt one record magic in chunk 2 and assert skipped_chunks == 1 or expected-minus-count > 0.

title: Binary plist object references are expanded with no memoisation: a 134-byte DAG doubles time and memory per level (depth cap 100 means 2^100)
claim: parseObject re-parses every referenced object each time it is referenced. The only guard is depth > 100, so an array of two refs to the next array, repeated, expands to 2^depth leaves.
evidence: plist_builtins.go:237 `if depth > 100 {`; :290-297 `for i := 0; i < count; i++ { ref := ...; v, err := p.parseObject(ref, depth+1) ... elems = append(elems, v) }`. Repro: depth 12 (104-byte file) 8 ms / 0 MiB; 14 (114 B) 9 ms / 1 MiB; 16 (124 B) 14 ms / 4 MiB; 18 (134 B) 37 ms / 16 MiB, so memory x4 per 2 levels. Depth 40 would be about 2^40 objects. Verifier: Re-ran TestZZ_PlistDAG: depth 12/14/16/18 (104-134 byte files) -> 0/1/4/16 MiB, x4 per two levels. parseObject has no memoisation, only depth>100. Verifier's notes: Raised from P2 to P1 to match the other S2 crafted-evidence hangs (ART.04, ART.06).
repro: zz_art_test.go TestZZ_PlistDAG
impact: A plist of a few hundred bytes (a common artifact inside macOS/iOS triage images) hangs plist_parse and exhausts memory. That kills the process, and recover cannot catch it.
fix_proposal: Memoise parsed objects by index (bplist objects are immutable) and reject cycles with an in-progress set. Also cap total objects produced at a multiple of numObjects. Regression test: zzBplistDAG(60) must parse in well under 1 s with memory O(depth).

title: XML plist parsing recurses with no depth limit: nested <array> kills the process with a fatal stack overflow
claim: parseXMLPlistValue and parseXMLPlistArray/Dict recurse once per nesting level. Unlike the binary path (depth > 100) there is no cap, and encoding/xml's Decoder.Token has no depth limit. Stack overflow is fatal and bypasses PlistParse's recover. Verifier: As stated. At the default 1 GB stack the input must be multi-MB.
evidence: plist_builtins.go:93-94 `case "array": return parseXMLPlistArray(dec)` and :158-159 `case xml.StartElement: v, verr := parseXMLPlistValue(dec, t)`. Repro with debug.SetMaxStack(16 MiB): depth 20,000 (140 KB) returns; depth 100,000 (700 KB) gives `runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 16777216-byte limit / fatal error: stack overflow`, with frames alternating parseXMLPlistValue/parseXMLPlistArray. That is 168-839 bytes of stack per level, so the default 1 GB limit is reached at about 1.3M-6.4M levels, a 9-45 MB file of '<array>'. Verifier: With SetMaxStack 16 MiB, depth 100000 (700 KB) -> 'fatal error: stack overflow' with parseXMLPlistArray/parseXMLPlistValue frames; depth 20000 returns. The XML path has no depth counter. Verifier's notes: Same class as DAT.04 and M26-LEX-003, but a distinct parser that needs its own fix.
repro: zz_art3_test.go TestZZX_PlistXMLDeep (ZZ_DEPTH=100000 ZZ_MAXSTACK=16777216; run alone)
impact: A crafted .plist of tens of MB terminates Mutant (and the LSP or REPL host if evaluated there) with an uncatchable crash. The same class as M26-LEX-003, but a separate parser needing its own fix.
fix_proposal: Thread a depth counter through the XML path and refuse past the same 100 levels as the binary path. Regression test: XML plist with 1000 nested arrays gives an error mentioning nesting depth; no crash with a small SetMaxStack.

title: hive_get_value / hive_list_values / reg_* return the 'db' big-data header instead of values larger than 16 KB
claim: valueData, which every hive_* and hive-backed reg_* reader uses, treats the data-offset cell as the value. It does not follow a big-data ('db') record the way rawValueBytes (used only by shimcache) does, so any value over 16344 bytes comes back as the 8-12 byte db header.
evidence: hive_builtins.go:314-323 `c, err := h.cell(vk.dataOff) ... if int(size) <= len(c) { raw = c[:size] } else { raw = c }`, with no 'db' branch; rawValueBytes:199-200 has one. Repro with a 20000-byte REG_BINARY stored as db: rawValueBytes gives 20000 bytes equal to the payload, but `hive_get_value: type=REG_BINARY data=64620200504e000000000000 data_bytes len=12 equal=false`. Verifier: valueData (hive_builtins.go:302-324) has no 'db' branch, unlike rawValueBytes. Re-ran: for a 20000-byte REG_BINARY, hive_get_value data_bytes is 12 bytes ('db' header) while rawValueBytes returns 20000 correct bytes.
repro: zz_art_test.go TestZZ_HiveBigDataValue
impact: Large binary values (for example AppCompatCache, UserAssist/ShellBags blobs, certificates) read through hive_get_value/reg_get_value are silently wrong: the hex and data_bytes are 'db...' header bytes.
fix_proposal: Have valueData call rawValueBytes. Also recognise db only when size > 16344 on hive version >= 1.4, so a small value whose data starts with 'db' is not misparsed. Regression test: Hive with a 20000-byte db value: hive_get_value data_bytes equals the payload.

title: A shell link whose LinkInfo header is cut short reads past the slice length; with an exact-capacity buffer it panics, and jumplist_parse then loses the whole file
claim: parseLnkLinkInfo checks start+16 <= len but then reads data[start+16:start+20], which Go allows up to cap, not len. With spare capacity it reads bytes that are not part of the link (a bogus local_base_path). With exact capacity (jumplist automatic streams use make([]byte, f.Size); os.ReadFile of a file of 511 bytes or more has cap len+1) it panics. The recover in JumplistParse then discards every entry of the jump list. Verifier: As stated. The panic is recovered (no crash); the cost is losing the whole result.
evidence: lnk_builtins.go:161 `if start+16 > len(data) {`; :172 `lbpOffset := int(binary.LittleEndian.Uint32(data[start+16 : start+20]))`; jumplist_builtins.go:88 `buf := make([]byte, f.Size)`. Repro: 600-byte .lnk gives `lnk_parse: panic during parse: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:604] with capacity 601`; 200-byte variant gives local_base_path="<" (read from spare capacity); automaticDestinations with DestList + good link + truncated link gives `jumplist_parse: panic during parse: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:4100] with capacity 4096`, while the control without the bad stream returns 2 entries. The random-mutation pass also hit it (`slice bounds out of range [:96] with capacity 92`). Verifier: parseLnkLinkInfo checks start+16 but reads data[start+16:start+20]. Re-ran: 600-byte lnk -> 'panic during parse ... [:604] with capacity 601'; 200-byte lnk -> local_base_path '<' read from spare capacity; jumplist with one truncated link stream -> whole-file error, while the control returns 2 entries. The mutation pass also hit '[:96] with capacity 92'.
repro: zz_art_test.go TestZZ_LnkTruncatedLinkInfo; zz_art4_test.go TestZZ_MutationPanics
impact: One damaged or partially recovered LNK stream makes jumplist_parse return an error instead of the DestList and other entries, and lnk_parse loses the header timestamps it had already parsed.
fix_proposal: Require start+20 <= len(data) (and start+0x1C for the header fields) before reading, and slice data[:len(data):len(data)] before parsing. Treat a failing link stream as skipped, not as a whole-file error. Regression test: A 600-byte link with LinkInfo 16 bytes from the end: lnk_parse returns the header fields with an empty local_base_path, and jumplist_parse still returns the other entries.

title: LNK LinkFlags names are shifted one bit for 0x1000-0x8000 (HasDarwinID missing, RunAsUser reported as HasDarwinID, etc.)
claim: MS-SHLLINK 2.1.1 defines HasDarwinID=0x1000, RunAsUser=0x2000, HasExpIcon=0x4000, NoPidlAlias=0x8000. The table maps 0x2000, 0x4000 and 0x8000 to HasDarwinID, RunAsUser and HasExpIcon, and nothing to 0x1000.
evidence: lnk_builtins.go:29-31 `{0x00002000, "HasDarwinID"}, {0x00004000, "RunAsUser"}, {0x00008000, "HasExpIcon"}`. Repro: `LinkFlags 0x1000 -> []`, `0x2000 -> [HasDarwinID]`, `0x4000 -> [RunAsUser]`, `0x8000 -> [HasExpIcon]`. The owned test (lnk_builtins_test.go:77) only asserts `len(decoded.Elements) < 4`. Verifier: lnk_builtins.go:29-31 maps 0x2000/0x4000/0x8000 to HasDarwinID/RunAsUser/HasExpIcon. MS-SHLLINK 2.1.1 has HasDarwinID=0x1000, RunAsUser=0x2000, HasExpIcon=0x4000, NoPidlAlias=0x8000. Re-ran: 0x1000->[], 0x2000->[HasDarwinID], 0x4000->[RunAsUser], 0x8000->[HasExpIcon].
repro: zz_art_test.go TestZZ_LnkFlagBits
impact: link_flags_decoded says a link runs as a different user (or not) and hides Darwin (MSI advertised shortcut) links. These are indicators examiners use for persistence and LNK-based attacks.
fix_proposal: Correct the bit values and add the remaining flags (0x10000-0x4000000). Regression test: Table test: each single flag bit decodes to exactly its MS-SHLLINK name.

title: email_parse / email_attachments / email_urls ignore nested multipart parts: the common mixed>alternative email yields no body, no attachment, no URL
claim: parseMultipartEmail walks only the top-level parts. A part whose type is multipart/* is neither an attachment nor text/plain or text/html, so it is dropped with its bodies, links and attachments. Most real mail (including phishing) is multipart/mixed containing multipart/alternative and sometimes multipart/related.
evidence: email_forensics.go:250-267: attachment only when `strings.Contains(contentDisposition, "attachment") || filename != ""`, else text/plain or text/html. There is no recursion on `multipart/`. Repro (mixed > alternative(text, html) + related(payload.exe)): `email_parse: text= html= attachments=[]`, `email_attachments: []`, `email_urls: []`. Verifier: parseMultipartEmail walks only the top-level parts and never recurses into multipart/*. Re-ran mixed>alternative+related(payload.exe): text='' html='' attachments=[], email_attachments [], email_urls [].
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_EmailNestedMultipart
impact: Phishing triage reports 'no attachments, no links' for an email that carries payload.exe and a malicious URL: a wrong forensic answer reported as right.
fix_proposal: Recurse into multipart/* parts (bounded depth, e.g. 16) using the part's own boundary. Also handle message/rfc822 attachments as parts. Regression test: The nested fixture above: attachments == [payload.exe with sha256], text and html non-empty, email_urls contains both evil.example URLs.

title: email_urls silently stops at the first body line longer than 64 KB (bufio.Scanner default), losing every URL in the message
claim: collectURLs scans the body with a default bufio.Scanner (64 KiB token limit) and never checks scanner.Err(). A long line, such as minified HTML or an inline data: image, ends the scan silently.
evidence: email_forensics.go:319-321 `scanner := bufio.NewScanner(strings.NewReader(body)); for scanner.Scan() {` with no Buffer() and no Err(). Repro: HTML body whose first line has a 70 KB data: URI followed by `<a href=https://first.example/x>` and a second short line `<a href=https://second.example/y>` gives `email_urls ... : [] ... err=<nil>`. Verifier: collectURLs uses a default bufio.Scanner and never checks Err(). Re-ran: a 70 KB first HTML line -> email_urls [] with err nil; both URLs are lost.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_EmailLongLineURLs
impact: HTML phishing mail commonly has very long lines, so email_urls returns an empty or partial URL list with no error.
fix_proposal: Run the regexp over the whole body (it is already in memory), or set scanner.Buffer to the body length and check Err(). Regression test: The 70 KB-line fixture returns both URLs.

title: extract_iocs refangs ordinary prose (' at ' becomes '@', ' dot ' becomes '.'), fabricating email and domain IOCs
claim: The refang replacer includes the bare-word rules " at " -> "@" and " dot " -> ".", and ExtractIOCs applies it to all input text before matching.
evidence: ioc_builtins.go:30 `... " dot ", ".",` and :32 `... " at ", "@",`; :225 `text := refangReplacer.Replace(s)`. Repro: "The operator logged in at example.com and clicked the red dot on the map." gives `emails=[in@example.com] domains=[example.com, red.on]`; "The implant beacons at evil.com every hour." gives `emails=[beacons@evil.com]`. Verifier: Re-ran: 'logged in at example.com ... red dot on the map' -> emails [in@example.com], domains [example.com, red.on]; 'beacons at evil.com' -> [beacons@evil.com]. The metadata says only 'refanged first' and does not disclose the bare-word rules.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_ExtractIOCsProse
impact: Report text or email bodies run through extract_iocs produce email addresses and domains that do not exist in the evidence. They can end up in blocklists or case reports.
fix_proposal: Drop the bare-word ' at ' / ' dot ' rules from the implicit refang (keep the bracketed forms), or require brackets such as [at] and (dot). Regression test: The two sentences above yield no emails and only example.com/evil.com domains.

title: sigma windash expands only '-' and only uniformly, so mixed-dash or '/'-written values evade the rule
claim: pySigma's SigmaWindowsDashModifier replaces every `\B[-/]\b` occurrence with a placeholder and expands each one independently over {-, /, en dash, em dash, horizontal bar}. Mutant replaces only '-' after start or whitespace, and all occurrences with the same dash, so it produces 5 uniform variants and never expands a '/' written in the rule. The comment claims '-enc' and '/enc' are treated as the same switch.
evidence: sigma_engine.go:542-551 `for _, dash := range []string{"/", "–", "—", "―"} { ... if r == '-' && (i == 0 || runes[i-1] == ' ' || runes[i-1] == '\t') { sb.WriteString(dash)`. Repro: `windash|contains ' -nop -enc '` vs `powershell.exe -nop /enc SQBFAFgA` gives matched=false; `' /c '` vs `cmd.exe -c whoami` gives matched=false (both match under pySigma). Verifier: sigmaWindash replaces only '-' after start or whitespace, and replaces every occurrence with the same dash. Re-ran: ' -nop -enc ' vs '-nop /enc' -> false; ' /c ' vs 'cmd.exe -c' -> false. docs/DETECTION_RULES.md promises that -enc and /enc are the same switch and that a rule is never a silent non-match.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_SigmaWindash
impact: Attackers routinely mix -/ switches. SigmaHQ rules written with windash give false negatives in sigma_match/sigma_scan.
fix_proposal: Match `\B[-/]\b` positions and emit the cartesian product (bounded, e.g. at most 5^4 variants, else a compile error), or compile to one regexp with a [-/–—―] class at each position. Regression test: Mixed '-nop /enc' and '/c' vs '-c' cases match.

title: sigma `1 of them` / `all of them` include underscore-prefixed search identifiers, contrary to the Sigma spec
claim: Sigma rules spec v2.1: `1 of them`/`all of them` are 'across all defined search identifiers not starting with an underscore _'. resolve() returns p.names unfiltered.
evidence: sigma_engine.go:781-785 `if strings.EqualFold(target, "them") { ... return p.names, nil }`. Repro: selection (Image endswith \evil.exe) plus _helper (User SYSTEM), condition `1 of them`, on {Image good.exe, User SYSTEM} gives matched=true (spec: false). `all of them` on {Image evil.exe, User alice} gives matched=false (spec: true). Verifier: resolve() returns p.names unfiltered for 'them'. Re-ran: '1 of them' with only _helper true -> matched=true; 'all of them' with _helper false -> false. The Sigma spec excludes identifiers that start with '_'.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_SigmaUnderscoreThem
impact: False positives and false negatives on rules that use the underscore helper convention.
fix_proposal: Filter names with a '_' prefix when resolving `them`. If none remain, refuse at compile time. Regression test: The two cases above.

title: sigma accepts vacuous searches that match every event (empty mapping, `|all: []`) and silently re-means `null` inside a list
claim: The engine promises that a construct with no defined meaning is a compile error (it refuses an empty list search). But `selection: {}` compiles to a group with no fields, and evalGroup returns true. `Field|all: []` has zero matchers, and `hits == len(field.matchers)` is 0 == 0, true even when the field is missing. `null` inside a list (disallowed by the spec) becomes the pattern for the empty string. Verifier: As stated. Also, 'Field: []' compiles and silently never matches.
evidence: evalGroup :851-857 `all := true; for ... ` (no fields means true); :889-890 `if field.all { return hits == len(field.matchers) }`; sigmaValueStrings :1151 `return []string{sigmaScalarString(value)}` (nil becomes ""). Repro on {Image: good.exe}: `empty mapping -> matched=true`, `empty all list -> matched=true`; `null in list` matches {ParentImage: ""} but not a missing ParentImage; `selection: []` is correctly refused. Verifier: Re-ran: 'selection: {}' -> true and '|contains|all: []' -> true on an unrelated event; [null,'x'] matches ParentImage '' but not a missing field; 'selection: []' is refused. Verifier's notes: The rule author, not the evidence, triggers this.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_SigmaVacuous
impact: A malformed or templated rule fires on every event in sigma_scan and floods hits. This inverts the engine's stated 'never silently wrong' contract.
fix_proposal: Refuse empty mappings and empty value lists at compile time, and refuse null inside a value list. Regression test: Each of the three rules fails to compile with a named reason.

title: browser_downloads reports the initiating tab's URL as the download 'url' and maps Chromium state 4 (INTERRUPTED) to 'unknown'
claim: The Chromium downloads query reads tab_url (the page the user was on) and ignores downloads_url_chains, where the file's actual source URL is stored. The state map uses 3 for 'interrupted', but Chromium's DownloadState is INTERRUPTED=4 (3 is the legacy BUG_140687).
evidence: :162 `chromeDownloadStates = map[int64]string{0: "in_progress", 1: "complete", 2: "cancelled", 3: "interrupted"}`; :187 `SELECT tab_url, target_path, ...`; :197 `"url": stringObj(rowStr(r, "tab_url"))`. Repro: invoice.exe downloaded from https://cdn.evil.example/payload.exe while on https://mail.example/inbox, state 4, gives `url=https://mail.example/inbox state=unknown`. Verifier: The query reads tab_url as 'url' and ignores downloads_url_chains. The state map has 3 as interrupted, but Chromium DownloadState is INTERRUPTED=4 (3 is BUG_140687). Re-ran: url=https://mail.example/inbox, state=unknown for state 4.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_BrowserDownloads
impact: The download's origin, the key IOC, is reported as the webmail or tab page, and interrupted downloads show state 'unknown'.
fix_proposal: Join downloads_url_chains (the last chain_index is the final URL; also return the full chain) and report tab_url, referrer and site_url separately. Map 4 to interrupted (and 3 to interrupted/legacy). Regression test: The fixture above gives url=https://cdn.evil.example/payload.exe and state=interrupted.

title: bodyfile_parse splits on every '|' with fixed indices: a filename containing '|' injects its own MAC times
claim: Only the name field can contain '|' (legal on ext4/HFS+/NTFS alternate streams), and the last nine fields are fixed. The parser reads fields[2..10] from the left, so a crafted filename sets the inode and all four timestamps.
evidence: :41 `fields := strings.Split(line, "|")`; :47-56 fixed indices 1..10. Repro: file named `x|0|0|0|0|0|999|999|999|999` whose real times are 1600000000..3 gives `name=/tmp/x inode=0 atime=999 mtime=999 ctime=999 crtime=999`. Verifier: strings.Split on '|' with fixed indices. Re-ran: the name 'x|0|0|0|0|0|999|999|999|999' gives name=/tmp/x, inode 0, and all times 999.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_BodyfilePipeInName
impact: An attacker-chosen filename poisons the super-timeline (mactime/timeline_merge) and hides the file's real times.
fix_proposal: Take md5 = first field, the last nine fields from the right, and join the middle as the name. Reject rows with fewer than 11 fields. Regression test: The row above gives name `/tmp/x|0|0|0|0|0|999|999|999|999` and atime 1600000000.

title: go_symbols classifies any module path without a dot in its first segment as stdlib, so 'user' mode drops the malware's own code
claim: isStdlibPackage treats a first path segment without a '.' as standard library. `go mod init agent` (a dotless module, very common in malware and small tools) makes every one of the program's own packages 'stdlib'.
evidence: :379 `return !strings.Contains(first, ".")`. Repro: probe built with module `agent` and package agent/agent/core (StealCredentials, go:noinline). `go_symbols(probe, "user"): user_function_count=1; [main.main stdlib=false]`; in all mode, `agent/agent/core.StealCredentials stdlib=true`. Verifier: I built my own probe (module 'agent', package agent/core, StealCredentials noinline) with go1.26.2. go_symbols user mode lists only main.main; all mode shows agent/core.StealCredentials stdlib=true. The heuristic is admitted only in a code comment, not in the metadata.
repro: scratch probe/ (module agent) + zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_GoSymbolsDotlessModule (ZZ_GOPROBE=probe.exe)
impact: Triage with mode 'user' (the point of the filter) shows only main.main for such binaries and hides the capability functions.
fix_proposal: Classify against the real stdlib package list for the binary's Go version (GoReSym and go/build carry one), or use buildinfo's main module path: packages under bi.Main.Path are user code. Regression test: The dotless-module probe: StealCredentials is in user mode, stdlib=false.

title: shimcache_parse refuses Windows 8 / 8.1 AppCompatCache (header 0x80) although the doc and the error message say both are supported
claim: Win8 and Win8.1 caches have a 0x80-byte header (Mandiant ShimCacheParser WIN8_STATS_SIZE) and a different entry layout (package data, flags). The decoder accepts only 0x30/0x34 (Win10), yet the metadata summary says 'Supports Win8/Win8.1/Win10 (10ts/00ts)' and the refusal message itself says 'only Win8/Win8.1/Win10 are supported'.
evidence: :108 `if headerSize != 0x30 && headerSize != 0x34 {`; metadata.go:1504 `Supports Win8/Win8.1/Win10 (10ts/00ts)`. Repro: `decodeShimcache(Win8 header 0x80 + 00ts entry): err=unsupported AppCompatCache header 0x80 (only Win8/Win8.1/Win10 are supported)`, same for 10ts. Verifier: decodeShimcache accepts only header 0x30/0x34. Re-ran: a 0x80 header with 00ts or 10ts -> 'unsupported AppCompatCache header 0x80 (only Win8/Win8.1/Win10 are supported)'. metadata.go:1504 claims Win8/Win8.1 support.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_ShimcacheWin8Header
impact: The doc promise is broken and the error is self-contradictory. Win8/8.1 SYSTEM hives always fail.
fix_proposal: Implement the 0x80 Win8/8.1 layout (skip the package, read flags and the FILETIME after it), or change the doc and error to 'Win10/11 only'. Regression test: A synthetic Win8.1 blob parses, or the error and doc name Win10 only.

title: mft_parse attributes deleted files to whatever directory now occupies their parent's MFT slot (the parent sequence number is discarded)
claim: The $FILE_NAME parent reference's sequence number is masked off and never compared with the parent record's current sequence, so a reused slot is treated as the original parent.
evidence: :192 `row.parent = fn.ParentDirectory & 0x0000FFFFFFFFFFFF // strip sequence bits`; reconstructMFTPaths uses byRecord[rec] with no sequence check. Repro: record 6 is now 'NewDir' seq 3; deleted evil.exe's parent ref is record 6 seq 2. Result: `in_use=false path=\NewDir\evil.exe parent_record=6`. Verifier: The parent reference sequence is masked off at mft_builtins.go:192. Re-ran: deleted evil.exe (parent record 6 seq 2, slot now 'NewDir' seq 3) -> path \NewDir\evil.exe. Verifier's notes: Shares walkMFT with FS2.02 but is a different defect.
repro: zz_art_test.go TestZZ_MftStaleParent
impact: Deleted-file paths in the MFT timeline are confidently wrong: a file is placed in a directory it never lived in. That matters for fs_deleted too, which shares walkMFT.
fix_proposal: Keep the parent sequence and compare it with the parent row's sequence (allowing seq+1 for a deleted parent). On mismatch prefix the path with a marker such as '?\[orphan]' and expose parent_sequence. Regression test: The fixture above gives a path that is not \NewDir\evil.exe plus a parent-reused flag.

title: mem_read / mem_read_bytes: offset+size overflows to a negative slice bound and the unrecovered panic aborts the whole script
claim: end := start + int(size) wraps for large sizes, the `end > len(data)` clamp misses a negative end, and data[start:end] panics. memRead has no recover, so the VM contains it as vm_runtime_error and records a vm-panic integrity failure. Verifier: As stated. Downgraded to S4 because the VM contains the panic and it needs a size near MaxInt64.
evidence: :103-107 `end := start + int(lengthObj.Value); if end > len(data) { end = len(data) }; slice := data[start:end]`. Go repro: `builtin panicked out (no recover in memRead): runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:-9223372036854775808]` for both mem_read and mem_read_bytes. CLI repro (`let chunk, err = mem_read("mem.bin", 1, n);` with n = MaxInt64) gives `vm error: vm_runtime_error: recovered panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:-9223372036854775808]` at memovf.mut:3; the err binding is never reached. Verifier: end := start+int(size) wraps to negative. Go repro: MemRead and MemReadBytes panic out with 'slice bounds out of range [:-9223372036854775808]'. CLI (my own build, memovf.mut compiled and then run --dev): 'vm_runtime_error: recovered panic: ...'; the err binding is never reached.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_MemReadOverflow; scratch tree memovf.mut run via mutant.exe run / mutant.exe memovf.mu --dev
impact: A size read from evidence (for example a length field in a dump) ends the whole analysis run instead of returning an error, and pollutes the integrity log.
fix_proposal: Compute in int64 with an overflow check: if size > int64(len(data)-start) { end = len(data) }. Regression test: mem_read(path, 1, MaxInt64) returns the tail with no error or panic.

title: Every mem_* builtin (and detect_injection) loads the whole memory image into RAM, even to read 16 bytes
claim: mem_map, mem_read, mem_read_bytes, mem_scan, mem_strings, mem_find_pe, mem_find_shellcode and detect_injection all call os.ReadFile on the image. mem_read allocates the entire file per call to return a range, which its own comment (:110-111) acknowledges can be 'a multi-gigabyte dump'. mem_map additionally builds one hash per 4 KiB page.
evidence: memory_forensics.go:94 `data, err := os.ReadFile(pathObj.Value)` followed by `slice := data[start:end]`. Repro: mem_read_bytes of 16 bytes from a 16 MiB image allocates 16 MiB; from a 64 MiB image, 64 MiB. Verifier: Each mem_* builtin calls os.ReadFile on the whole image. Re-ran: mem_read_bytes of 16 bytes from a 16/64 MiB image allocates 16/64 MiB. The metadata does not disclose this.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_MemReadWholeFile
impact: On realistic memory dumps (8-64 GB) these builtins either exhaust memory and crash or cost O(image) per call. A script that loops mem_read over offsets is quadratic.
fix_proposal: Use os.Open + ReadAt for mem_read/mem_read_bytes, and stream in chunks with overlap for scan/strings/find_*. Cap mem_map output or page it. Regression test: mem_read_bytes from a 64 MiB image allocates under 1 MiB.

title: detect_injection reports 'detected' (score 60) on random bytes: any two 'MZ' byte pairs count as multiple PE headers
claim: The 40-point multiple_pe_headers signal counts raw 0x4D5A occurrences without validating e_lfanew (mem_find_pe does validate). Random data has about 1 per 64 KiB, and 'fc e8' (+20) is equally common, so the score reaches the 60 threshold.
evidence: :72-76 `mzOffsets := carveOffsets(data, []byte{0x4d, 0x5a}); if len(mzOffsets) > 1 { score += 40 ...`; :120 `"detected": boolObj(score >= 60)`. Repro, seeded random data: 1 MiB gives `detected=true score=60 pe_headers=9` and mem_find_pe confirms 0 of 9; 4 MiB gives `detected=true score=60 pe_headers=84`, 0 confirmed. The owned test only checks a positive fixture. Verifier: Re-ran on seeded random data: 1 MiB -> detected=true score 60 pe_headers 9, mem_find_pe confirmed 0; 4 MiB -> 84 headers, 0 confirmed.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_DetectInjectionOnRandom
impact: Any compressed or encrypted memory region or file is reported as code injection, a false-positive verdict presented as a detection.
fix_proposal: Count only PE headers validated as in validatePEAt, and weight the 2-byte signatures by density rather than presence. Regression test: 4 MiB of seeded random bytes gives detected=false.

title: bin_yara_scan with caseInsensitive=true reports offsets into a lower-cased re-encoding, not into the file
claim: strings.ToLower on binary data replaces each invalid UTF-8 byte with U+FFFD (3 bytes) and can change rune widths, so the offsets returned no longer match file positions. Patterns containing non-UTF-8 bytes can never match.
evidence: :273-276 `haystack := string(data); if caseInsensitive { haystack = strings.ToLower(haystack) }`. Repro, data FF FE 00 'ABC' 80 'abc': case-sensitive gives offsets [7] (correct); case-insensitive gives `offsets: [7, 13]` where the true offsets are ABC=3 and abc=7. The owned CI test uses ASCII-only data and asserts only the count. Verifier: strings.ToLower on binary data. Re-ran: for FF FE 00 ABC 80 abc, CI offsets are [7,13] where the true offsets are 3 and 7.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_BinYaraScanCaseInsensitiveOffsets
impact: Offsets reported for binaries or dumps are wrong, so carving or reading at a reported offset lands elsewhere.
fix_proposal: Fold ASCII case byte-wise (bytes.ToLower is also Unicode-aware, so use a custom ASCII fold over []byte) or use a (?i) regexp over bytes. Regression test: The fixture above gives CI offsets [3, 7].

title: Xpress-Huffman decoder never detects the end of input: a truncated MAM prefetch decodes to garbage with no error
claim: xhU16 returns 0 past the end of src, and the decode loop runs until outSize bytes are produced, so a stream cut mid-block yields a full-length buffer of symbols decoded from zero bits. Only a missing 256-byte table at a block boundary is detected.
evidence: :343-346 `if i < 0 || i+2 > len(src) { return 0 }`; loop :206 `for len(dst) < blockEnd {` with no input-exhausted check. Repro with the owned MAM vector (382 compressed bytes to 768): cut to 264 bytes gives `err=<nil>, output 768 bytes, first 16 bytes match`; cut to 319 gives 296 matching; cut to 366 gives 626 matching. Verifier: Re-ran TestZZ_XpressTruncated: the owned MAM vector cut to 366/319/264 of 382 bytes gives err nil and 768 bytes out, with only 626/296/16 bytes correct.
repro: zz_art4_test.go TestZZ_XpressTruncated
impact: A carved or partially recovered Win10 prefetch can yield fabricated files_loaded/volume strings instead of an error.
fix_proposal: Track consumed input and fail when a refill or byteAt passes len(src) before outSize is reached. Also verify that bs.index <= len(src) at the end. Regression test: A truncated vector returns 'truncated' errors.

title: hive_list_values / reg_enum_values name the unnamed value '(default)', but hive_get_value / reg_get_value cannot find '(default)'
claim: The enumerators rename the empty value name to '(default)', while the getters compare vk.name ('') against the requested name, so a name taken from a listing cannot be read back.
evidence: hive_builtins.go:527-529 `if name == "" { name = "(default)" }` versus :557 `if strings.EqualFold(vk.name, valueName)`. Repro: `hive_list_values: [{data: 7, name: (default), type: REG_DWORD}]`; `hive_get_value("(default)")` gives `value "(default)" not found`; `hive_get_value("")` succeeds. Verifier: Re-ran: hive_list_values names the value '(default)'; hive_get_value('(default)') -> not found; hive_get_value('') works.
repro: zz_art_test.go TestZZ_HiveDefaultName
impact: Scripts that enumerate then fetch values fail on every key's default value (for example Run keys and class registrations).
fix_proposal: Accept '(default)' as an alias for '' in the getters (unless a value literally named '(default)' exists). Regression test: get_value("(default)") returns the unnamed value.

title: syslog_parse assumes UTC and the analysis year: a 'Feb 29' line becomes 1 March, and the result depends on the day the script runs
