claim: RFC 3164 timestamps have no year or zone. The code uses time.Now().Year() (disclosed) and UTC (not disclosed). time.Date normalises Feb 29 in a non-leap current year to Mar 1, and no field marks ts as inferred. Verifier: As stated. Only the undisclosed consequences count as the defect.
evidence: :47 `year := time.Now().Year()`; :148 `time.Date(year, t.Month(), t.Day(), ..., time.UTC)`. Repro (run in 2026): `line stamped Feb 29 12:00:00 -> 2026-03-01T12:00:00Z`; `Dec 31 23:59:59 -> 2026-12-31` (in the future relative to the run date); entry keys carry no inferred flag. Verifier: Re-ran in 2026: 'Feb 29 12:00:00' -> 2026-03-01T12:00:00Z; Dec 31 -> future date; no inferred flag. The current-year assumption is disclosed in the metadata; UTC and the date normalisation are not.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_SyslogYear
impact: The same evidence yields different timelines depending on the analysis date, and events land in the wrong day or year.
fix_proposal: Take the year and timezone as optional arguments (or derive the year from a reference time and roll back when the result is in the future), refuse invalid dates, and add ts_year_inferred=true. Regression test: A fixed reference year makes Feb 29 either valid (leap) or an error.

title: timeline_sort/timeline_merge compare int64 timestamps as float64, misordering nanosecond timestamps
claim: eventTimestamp converts Integer to float64. Unix-nanosecond values (about 1.7e18) have a 256 ns float spacing, so close events compare equal and keep input order. Verifier: As stated. Most Mutant 'ts' fields are unix seconds, so only nanosecond-scale ts is affected.
evidence: :223 `return float64(n.Value), true`. Repro: ts 1700000000000000100 ('later') then ...000 ('earlier') sorts as `[later earlier]`. Verifier: Re-ran: ts ...100 then ...000 sorts [later earlier], because float64 comparison ties.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_TimelineSortNanoseconds
impact: Nanosecond super-timelines (mft *_ns-derived, evtx SystemTime) come out misordered.
fix_proposal: Compare Integer with Integer exactly, and fall back to float only when one side is a Float. Regression test: The two events above sort earlier then later.

title: timestamp_normalize: sub-second pre-1970 FILETIME/webkit values get an iso one second early and a unix that disagrees with unix_ms
claim: The iso is built as time.Unix(unixSec, (unixMs%1000)*ms). For negative times unixSec is floored (-2) but unixMs%1000 is negative (-500), which gives -2.5 s. The same instant given as unix_ms yields unix -1 (truncated).
evidence: :38 `time.Unix(unixSec, (unixMs%1000)*int64(time.Millisecond))`. Repro: FILETIME for 1969-12-31T23:59:58.5Z gives `{iso: 1969-12-31T23:59:57.5Z, unix: -2, unix_ms: -1500}`; unix_ms -1500 gives `{iso: ...58.5Z, unix: -1}`. Verifier: Re-ran: the FILETIME for 23:59:58.5Z -> iso 23:59:57.5Z, unix -2; unix_ms -1500 -> iso 58.5Z, unix -1.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_TimestampNormalizePre1970
impact: Wrong iso for pre-epoch timestamps with fractions (rare, but a silent wrong time), and an inconsistent 'unix' rounding direction across formats.
fix_proposal: Build iso with time.UnixMilli(unixMs), and floor unixSec from unixMs consistently for every format. Regression test: Both inputs above give iso ...58.5Z and unix -2.

title: Doc and comment claims that the code contradicts: mft_parse 'streams' a $MFT that it io.ReadAll's; the JSON registry backend 'never yields REG_BINARY' but does
claim: MftParse's comment says a standalone $MFT 'is streamed record-by-record', but walkMFT reads the whole file into memory (multi-GB $MFT files are common). The regEntry.raw comment says registryTypeName 'has no case that yields REG_BINARY', but a JSON object value is typed REG_BINARY, which reg_get_value returns with no data_bytes.
evidence: mft_builtins.go:96 `data, rerr := io.ReadAll(f)`; registry_forensics.go:545-546 `case map[string]any: return "REG_BINARY"`. Repro: reg_get_value on JSON {"Blob":{"a":1}} gives `{data: {a: 1}, name: Blob, type: REG_BINARY}` (no data_bytes). Verifier: mft_builtins.go:18-21 says the $MFT is 'streamed record-by-record', but :96 calls io.ReadAll. registry_forensics.go:28-31 says there is 'no case that yields REG_BINARY', but :545 maps map[string]any to REG_BINARY. Re-ran: reg_get_value on a JSON object -> type REG_BINARY with no data_bytes.
repro: zz_art2_test.go TestZZ_RegJSONBinaryType
impact: Misleading maintenance comments. The $MFT path has an unstated memory cost of the file size plus all rows.
fix_proposal: Fix the comments, or read the $MFT record-by-record with a bufio.Reader. Decide whether JSON objects should be REG_BINARY at all. Regression test: n/a (comment and doc fix)

title: time_parse gives an instant that depends on the host's time zone: a zone abbreviation the host does not use is silently read as UTC
claim: time_parse passes value and layout straight to Go's time.Parse. For a zone abbreviation (layout 'MST'), Go uses the offset only when the abbreviation belongs to the host's local zone. Otherwise it builds a fabricated zone with offset 0. So '10:00 PDT' parses correctly on a Los Angeles host and 7 hours wrong on a UTC or IST host, with no error either way. The metadata (metadata.go:824-829, 'Parses value with a Go reference layout; returns (unixSeconds, err)') mentions none of this. Verifier: As stated. This is Go's documented time.Parse rule for zone abbreviations, but Mutant does not mention it, and the result depends on the examiner's host zone. I kept S2 because the output is a silently shifted timestamp that cannot be reproduced across hosts. It only affects layouts that contain a zone abbreviation.
evidence: time_builtins.go:60 `t, err := time.Parse(layout, value)` then `return resultAndError(intObj(t.Unix()), nil)`. TestZZTimeParseHostZone set time.Local and parsed "2024-07-01 10:00 PDT" with layout "2006-01-02 15:04 MST": host UTC gave 1719828000, host America/Los_Angeles 1719853200 (correct), host Asia/Kolkata 1719828000. No error in any case. Verifier: time_builtins.go:60 `t, err := time.Parse(layout, value)`, then `t.Unix()`. TestZZTimeParse (tree/builtin/zz_verify_test.go) set time.Local and parsed "2024-07-01 10:00 PDT" with layout "2006-01-02 15:04 MST". Host UTC gave 1719828000, America/Los_Angeles gave 1719853200 (the correct value), Asia/Kolkata gave 1719828000. None of the three returned an error. The metadata and CAPABILITY_REFERENCE say only 'Parses value with a Go reference layout'. Verifier's notes: Numeric-offset layouts (-0700, Z07:00) are unaffected.
repro: builtin/zz_blt3_test.go TestZZTimeParseHostZone (scratch copy): `go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZTimeParseHostZone -v` FAILS with 'the same timestamp parses to 2 different instants depending on the host zone'.
impact: Log and e-mail timestamps carrying PDT/EST/CET-style abbreviations enter a timeline shifted by the zone offset, and the result looks valid. The same script on two examiners' machines gives different instants, so the result cannot be reproduced.
fix_proposal: Parse with time.ParseInLocation(layout, value, time.UTC). Refuse (return an error) when the layout contains a zone abbreviation and the parsed zone offset is 0 but the name is not UTC/GMT/Z, or resolve abbreviations through an explicit table. Document the rule in the metadata summary. Regression test: A builtin test that sets time.Local to two different zones and asserts time_parse("2024-07-01 10:00 PDT", "2006-01-02 15:04 MST") gives the same answer: 1719853200, or an error, on both.

title: Integer math and sort go through float64: sum, clamp, floor/ceil/round, min, max and sort corrupt integers above 2^53, and overflow or NaN becomes MinInt64
claim: requireNumericArg turns every INTEGER into float64. sum and clamp then convert the float back with int64(). floor/ceil/round do the same even for an INTEGER argument. min/max compare the floats, and sort's numericValue compares them too. Integers more than 2^53 apart by less than one ulp therefore compare equal or change value. An out-of-range float (1e19, NaN) is converted with int64(), which gives MinInt64 silently. sum([MaxInt64, 1]) also gives MinInt64. NTFS FILETIMEs (~1.3e17), Unix-nanosecond times (~1.7e18) and 64-bit file reference numbers all lie in this range. Verifier: As stated. abs(MinInt64) also returns MinInt64 silently.
evidence: math_builtins.go:171 `return intObj(int64(total))`; :82 `return intObj(int64(r))`; :147 `return intObj(int64(fn(x)))`; :54 compares `f < bestF` on float64; collections_builtins.go:76 `numericValue(out[i]) < numericValue(out[j])`; convert_builtins.go:17 `intObj(int64(v.Value))`. TestZZIntegersThroughFloat gave: sum([9007199254740993]) = 9007199254740992; sum([133700000000000001, 1]) = 133700000000000000; sum([MaxInt64, 1]) = -9223372036854775808; clamp(2^53+1, 0, 2^53+1) = 9007199254740992; floor(2^53+1) = 9007199254740992; round(133700000000000001) = 133700000000000000; min(FT+1, FT) = FT+1; max(FT, FT+1) = FT; sort([FT+1, FT]) unchanged; floor(1e19), round(NaN) and to_int(1e19) = -9223372036854775808. CLI rp/misc.mut printed `sum of FILETIME and 1 =133700000000000000` and `min =133700000000000002`. Verifier: TestZZIntFloat results: sum([2^53+1]) = 9007199254740992. sum([MaxInt64,1]) = MinInt64. clamp(2^53+1,0,2^53+1) = 9007199254740992. floor(2^53+1) = 9007199254740992. min(FT+1,FT) returns FT+1. max(FT,FT+1) returns FT. sort([FT+1,FT]) is unchanged. floor(1e19), round(NaN), to_int(1e19) and abs(MinInt64) all return MinInt64. In the CLI, rp/misc.mut printed `sum of FILETIME and 1 =133700000000000000` and `min =133700000000000002`. Verifier's notes: ART.32 (timeline_sort compares int64 as float64) is the same pattern at a different site. It is not a duplicate.
repro: builtin/zz_blt3_test.go TestZZIntegersThroughFloat: FAIL, 12 of 12 results wrong. rp/misc.mut through mutant.exe run + --dev printed the two wrong CLI values above.
impact: The minimum or maximum of two timestamps 1 us apart comes back as the wrong one. A sorted timeline misorders sub-microsecond events. floor/round of an integer timestamp change it. An overflowing sum reports a large negative number. None of these raises an error.
fix_proposal: Keep an integer path wherever every operand is an INTEGER: int64 compare in min/max/clamp/sort, int64 accumulation in sum with an overflow check that returns an error, and floor/ceil/round returning the INTEGER unchanged. For FLOAT to INTEGER (floor/round/to_int), refuse NaN, Inf and values outside [MinInt64, MaxInt64]. abs(MinInt64) (returns MinInt64) needs the same overflow error. Regression test: Table test over sum/clamp/min/max/sort/floor/round/to_int with 2^53+1, 133700000000000001, MaxInt64, NaN and 1e19, asserting exact integers or an error.

title: Script arguments panic three builtins (str_substr, rand_int, str_repeat); the panic aborts the program and is recorded as a security integrity failure
claim: str_substr computes `end := start + length` with no overflow check, so a large length (the natural 'rest of the string' idiom) wraps negative and runes[start:end] panics. rand_int calls mrand.Int63n(hi-lo), and hi-lo overflows to a non-positive number when the range exceeds MaxInt64, so Int63n panics. str_repeat passes a count whose byte length overflows to strings.Repeat, which panics. The VM contains the panic as `vm_runtime_error: recovered panic`, stops the main program, and containFault calls security.RecordIntegrityFailure("vm-panic"), which appends an event to the audit chain sealed into case manifests.
evidence: TestZZPanics: str_substr("abc", 1, MaxInt64) panicked `runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:-9223372036854775808]`; rand_int(-5e18, 5e18) panicked `invalid argument to Int63n`; str_repeat("ab", MaxInt64/2+1) panicked `strings: Repeat output length overflow`. CLI rp/panics.mut: audit_head() entries went from 1 to 2 after a spawned task called str_substr("abc", 1, 9223372036854775807). The task error was `task failed: vm_runtime_error: recovered panic: ...`. The same call at top level ended the run with 'vm error: vm_runtime_error: recovered panic' and exit=1. Verifier: TestZZPanics produced three panics. str_substr("abc",1,MaxInt64) panicked with 'slice bounds out of range [:-9223372036854775808]'. rand_int(-5e18,5e18) panicked with 'invalid argument to Int63n'. str_repeat("ab",MaxInt64/2+1) panicked with 'strings: Repeat output length overflow'. CLI rp/panics.mut printed 'audit entries before: 1', then the task error 'recovered panic', then 'audit entries after: 2'. The top-level call ended the run with a vm error and exit=1. Verifier's notes: The audit-chain side effect goes through the same containFault path as M26-VM-008, but each fix belongs in its own builtin, so this is not a duplicate.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZPanics -v (3 DEFECT lines). Compile and run rp/panics.mut with mutant.exe: 'audit entries before: 1', 'audit entries after: 2', then vm error with exit 1.
impact: An ordinary call ends the whole run instead of returning an error value. Every occurrence adds a false integrity failure to the audit chain, and case manifests seal that chain.
fix_proposal: str_substr: clamp with `if length > int64(len(runes))-start { end = len(runes) }` before adding. rand_int: when hi-lo overflows, draw from uint64 (or math/rand/v2 Int64N on a shifted range). str_repeat and str_pad: check len(s)*n against a cap before allocating (see the allocation finding). VM-008 is a sibling (the VM's index panic); its fix is in the VM, and these need their own guards. Regression test: Builtin tests that call each of the three with the overflowing arguments under a recover and require an *object.Error, not a panic. A VM test that asserts audit_head entries do not change.

title: keys()/values()/entries() order is random for keys that render alike, differs from for-in and print order, and two calls on the same hash can mis-pair
claim: hashSortedPairs collects pairs from the Go map and sorts them with sort.SliceStable on Key.Inspect() alone. Keys of different types that render the same (1 and "1", true and "true") tie, and the tie keeps the random map order. Separate keys(h) and values(h) calls can therefore disagree about which key comes first. Even without ties, the order (string order: [10, 2]) differs from the order that for-in and printing use (object.hashKeyLess: [2, 10]). The metadata promises 'sorted for determinism'.
evidence: collections_builtins.go:306 `sort.SliceStable(pairs, func(i, j int) bool { return pairs[i].Key.Inspect() < pairs[j].Key.Inspect() })`, while object/iterator.go:77 and hashObj.go:70 sort with hashKeyLess. TestZZKeysOrder: keys({2,10}) = [10, 2] while for-in gave [2 10]. On {1: "int", "1": "str"}, 400 calls produced 4 distinct keys()/values() combinations, and keys()[0] and values()[0] from separate calls mis-paired 92 times. CLI rp/keys.mut printed 'keys(h)[0] and values(h)[0] mis-paired 95 of 200 times' and 'keys({2: a, 10: b}) =[10, 2]'. Verifier: collections_builtins.go:306 sorts by Key.Inspect() alone. TestZZKeys on {1:"int","1":"str"} found keys()[0] and values()[0] from separate calls mispaired 100 times in 400. keys({2,10}) returned [10, 2], while Hash.Inspect prints {2: x, 10: x}. Verifier's notes: Related to M26-EVL-006 (float keys in hashKeyLess), which covers the object package's order. This finding is about the builtins not using hashKeyLess at all.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZKeysOrder -v (FAIL). Compile and run rp/keys.mut with mutant.exe.
impact: zip(keys(h), values(h)), or indexing keys(h)[i] and values(h)[i] together, attaches values to the wrong keys when keys mix types. Output order from keys() differs from printing and looping, so the same program's output changes from run to run.
fix_proposal: Export the object package's hashKeyLess (or an object.SortedPairs helper) and use it in hashSortedPairs, so keys/values/entries, printing and for-in share one total order. Break any remaining ties by type name. Regression test: Builtin test: for {1: a, "1": b} and {2: x, 10: y}, run keys/values 500 times, assert a single order, and assert it equals the object.NewIterator key order.

title: to_int auto-detects the base: to_int("010") is 8, to_int("0755") is 493, and to_int("08")/("09") fail
claim: to_int on a STRING calls strconv.ParseInt(v.Value, 0, 64). Base 0 reads a leading 0 as octal and also accepts 0x/0b/0o prefixes and '_' separators. The metadata (metadata.go:770-773) says it converts 'numeric strings'. parse_int is the builtin documented as auto-detecting with base 0. Zero-padded decimal fields in evidence, such as dates, times, permissions and fixed-width IDs, silently become different numbers or errors.
evidence: convert_builtins.go:24 `n, err := strconv.ParseInt(v.Value, 0, 64)`. TestZZToIntBase: "010" -> 8, "0755" -> 493, "08" and "09" -> error 'cannot parse', "0x1F" -> 31, "0b101" -> 5, "1_000" -> 1000. CLI rp/misc.mut printed `to_int of 010 =8` and `to_int of 08 error =ERROR:to_int: cannot parse "08" as integer`. The LEX-008 verifier pointed at this exact line as out of the LEX area. Verifier: convert_builtins.go:24 calls `strconv.ParseInt(v.Value, 0, 64)`. TestZZToInt: "010" gives 8, "0755" gives 493, "08" is an error, "0x1F" gives 31, "1_000" gives 1000. In the CLI, misc.mut printed `to_int of 010 =8` and the error for "08". Verifier's notes: This is the same base-0 call as M26-LEX-008, but at a different site with its own fix, so it is not a duplicate.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZToIntBase -v (FAIL). Compile and run rp/misc.mut with mutant.exe.
impact: to_int(fields[1]) on '09' (September) fails, and on '010' returns 8, silently. Timeline and report fields end up wrong.
fix_proposal: Use strconv.ParseInt(strings.TrimSpace(v.Value), 10, 64) in to_int. Leave base auto-detection to parse_int(s, 0). State 'decimal' in the metadata summary. This is related to M26-LEX-008 (same base-0 call in the parser), but the fix location differs. Regression test: to_int("010") == 10, to_int("08") == 8, to_int("0x1F") is an error, parse_int("0x1F", 0) == 31.

title: task_wait(h, 0) on a task that has already finished reports 'still running' about half the time
claim: For timeoutMs >= 0, TaskWait creates time.NewTimer(timeoutMs) and selects between task.done and timer.C. With timeout 0 the timer is due at once. When the task is already done, both cases are ready and Go's select picks one at random, so a finished task is reported as 'task is still running after 0ms'. The zero timeout is the polling idiom, and chan_recv handles its own 0 correctly: it checks without waiting first (channels.go:301-315). Verifier: As stated. The task_wait metadata does not define 0, but chan_recv documents 0 as 'give up immediately', so a caller will reasonably treat 0 as a poll.
evidence: tasks.go:194-199 `timer := time.NewTimer(time.Duration(timeoutMs) * time.Millisecond) ... select { case <-task.done: case <-timer.C: return resultAndError(nil, newError("task_wait: task is still running after %dms", timeoutMs)) }`. TestZZTaskWaitZeroOnFinished (RegisterTask, CompleteTask, then TaskWait(h, 0)) got the error 1037 of 2000 times. CLI rp/taskwait.mut (spawn, spin on task_done until true, then task_wait(h, 0)) printed 'task_wait(h, 0) on a finished task returned an error 89 of 200 times'. The earlier attempt's CLI '0 of 200' came from a script that compared type_of(err) with "ERROR" when the type is ERROR_OBJ. Verifier: tasks.go:193-200 creates a NewTimer(0) and then selects over task.done and timer.C. In TestZZTaskWait0, 501 of 1000 task_wait(h,0) calls on an already-completed task returned 'task is still running after 0ms'.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZTaskWaitZeroOnFinished -v (FAIL 1037/2000). Compile and run rp/taskwait.mut with mutant.exe.
impact: A poll loop that uses task_wait(h, 0) treats finished work as still running, retries or times out wrongly, and at random.
fix_proposal: Check task.done without blocking before creating the timer: `select { case <-task.done: goto collected; default: }`, then create the timer only when timeoutMs > 0, and treat 0 as 'do not wait'. Regression test: tasks_test: complete a task, then assert task_wait(h, 0) returns its value, 1000 times in a loop.

title: Cache round trip changes values: INTEGER comes back as FLOAT (losing precision above 2^53) and BYTES comes back as a hex STRING
claim: cache_put encodes the value to JSON and crankdb stores it after json.Unmarshal into interface{}. cache_get re-marshals it and json.Unmarshals into `any` without UseNumber, so every number becomes float64 and then an object.Float. BYTES is encoded through Inspect() as hex and comes back as a STRING. The metadata (metadata.go:1747-1764) says the value may be 'any type' and that cache_get returns 'the stored value'. Verifier: As stated. cache_get returns a {found, value} hash, and the value inside it is the one that changes.
evidence: cache.go:431-436 `var raw any; json.Unmarshal(packet.GetJsonVal(), &raw); obj, err := jsonValueToObject(raw)`; json.go:121-122 `case float64: return &object.Float{Value: v}`; json.go:64-65 `case *object.Bytes: return v.Inspect(), nil`. TestZZCache: INTEGER 42 -> FLOAT 42.000000; INTEGER 9007199254740993 -> FLOAT 9007199254740992; BYTES dead -> STRING dead. CLI rp/cache.mut printed `FLOAT 133700000000000000.000000` for a cached 133700000000000001. Verifier: TestZZCache: after cache_put of INTEGER 9007199254740993, cache_get returned value FLOAT 9007199254740992.000000. A put of BYTES de ad came back as the STRING "dead". In the CLI, cache.mut printed `FLOAT 133700000000000000.000000`.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZCache -v. Compile and run rp/cache.mut with mutant.exe.
impact: Offsets, inode numbers and timestamps cached between stages come back as different numbers of a different type. Buffers come back as text, so bytes_* builtins then read the hex digits instead of the data.
fix_proposal: Store the object itself (see the logging finding). If JSON must stay, decode with json.Decoder.UseNumber, which jsonValueToObject already handles as INTEGER, and refuse BYTES/STRUCT/functions with an error, or tag them. Regression test: cache_test: put INTEGER 9007199254740993, BYTES, FLOAT and HASH values; assert cache_get returns an equal value of the same type.

title: The cache backend never frees deleted or expired entries, so a TTL or rotating-key cache grows for the life of the process
location: builtin/cache.go:183-211 (cache_delete writes null), 358-365 (expiry only touches store.entries); crankdb server/database.go (no delete)
claim: crankdb's Database has Add and Retrieve only. cache_delete removes the key from mutant's entries map and then writes JSON null into crankdb, so the key stays. TTL expiry (cacheCleanupExpiredLocked, and the check in cache_get) deletes only from store.entries, so the expired value stays in crankdb's map. Only cache_clear or cache_close release anything, and cache_stats reports items=0 while every value is still held. Verifier: As stated. I confirmed the delete path by running it and the TTL path by reading the code.
evidence: TestZZCacheBackendNeverFrees read the crankdb store length through reflect. After put+delete of 1000 distinct keys, cache_stats said items=0 and the backend held 1000 entries; with 2000 keys it held 2000. 500 keys put with ttl=1s, checked after 1.1 s, gave cache_stats expires=500 items=0 and a backend holding 500 entries, each still carrying the value "secret". Verifier: TestZZCache: after 1000 cache_put and cache_delete pairs on distinct keys, reflecting into the crankdb Database showed 1000 entries in store, while cache_stats reported items 0 and deletes 1000. crankdb database.go has only Add and Retrieve. cacheCleanupExpiredLocked and the expiry check in cache_get delete only from store.entries (cache.go:143, 165, 361).
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZCacheBackendNeverFrees -v: the backend entry count grows linearly (1000 -> 1000, 2000 -> 2000) while items stays 0.
impact: A net_serve handler or long-running script that caches per-connection or per-file keys with a TTL leaks memory without bound. Values that were deleted or expired, including sensitive ones, stay resident.
fix_proposal: Keep the values in the cacheStore map itself and delete them on delete and on expiry. Alternatively rebuild the crankdb Database without the key, or drop crankdb. Regression test: cache_test: put and delete 1000 distinct keys, and put 100 keys with a TTL then let them expire; assert the backend holds 0 entries (through an internal size accessor).

title: text_index and len count bytes while str_substr, str_char_at and str_pad count runes, so composing them cuts non-ASCII text at the wrong place
claim: text_index returns strings.Index, a byte offset, and len(s) returns the byte count. The str_* builtins convert to []rune and take rune offsets. Neither text_index's nor len's metadata states the unit. The language reference warns only that str_substr disagrees with bytes_get, not with the text_* family.
evidence: text_matching.go:42 `return intObj(int64(strings.Index(haystack.Value, needle.Value)))`; strings_builtins.go:164 `runes := []rune(s)`. TestZZTextIndexUnits: for "José: admin", text_index(s, ":") = 5, and str_substr(s, 5, 1) = " " instead of ":". CLI rp/units.mut printed `text_index =5 len =12`, `str_substr(s, 0, i): José:` (the colon is included), and `str_char_at(s, len(s)-1)` -> `ERROR: ... index 11 out of range (len=11)`. Verifier: TestZZTextIndex with s="José: admin": text_index returns 5 (a byte offset), len returns 12, and str_substr(s,5,1) returns " " instead of ":". The language reference (line 733) notes the rune/byte disagreement only against bytes_get, not against text_index or len.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZTextIndexUnits -v (FAIL). Compile and run rp/units.mut with mutant.exe.
impact: Splitting a user name, path or header at a delimiter found with text_index returns the wrong field for any non-ASCII input. Loops bounded by len(s) over str_char_at fail on non-ASCII strings.
fix_proposal: Pick one unit for the string family. At minimum, make text_index (and text_count docs) return a rune index to match str_*, state 'bytes' in len's summary for STRING, and document the rule next to the existing bytes_get note in MUTANT_LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md. Regression test: For s = "José: admin": str_substr(s, text_index(s, ":"), 1) == ":".

title: str_pad_left/right, str_repeat and rand_bytes allocate whatever size the script asks for, with no cap
claim: The width or count goes straight into an allocation. range caps at 10M elements (collections_builtins.go:256), chan_new at 1<<20 and net reads have caps, but these three have none. A width taken from evidence (a length field, a column width) makes the runtime attempt the full allocation. Past the commit limit, Go aborts with 'fatal error: out of memory', which neither the VM's recover nor the (value, err) convention can catch. Verifier: As stated. I did not repeat the full-size fatal OOM, because it would endanger the shared host.
evidence: Small-scale growth (TestZZUnboundedAllocSmallScale, heap watchdog on): n=1,048,576 -> str_pad_left allocated 6,299,712 B, str_repeat 1,048,624 B, rand_bytes 2,097,416 B. n=4,194,304 -> 25,174,720 B, 4,194,352 B and 8,388,752 B. That is exactly linear: 6 B per requested rune for pad, 1 B for repeat, 2 B for rand_bytes, with no ceiling. The earlier attempt's CLI log shows str_pad_left("x", 1099511627776, " ") ending with `runtime: VirtualAlloc of 4398046511104 bytes failed ... fatal error: out of memory` (exit 2). My own 1 TiB CLI attempt took the PowerShell host down with 'Out of memory', so I did not repeat it. Verifier: TestZZAlloc, run under a 1 GiB watchdog, measured TotalAlloc deltas. At n=2^20: pad 6,351,992, repeat 1,048,640, rand_bytes 2,097,432. At n=2^22: 25,174,080, 4,194,352 and 8,388,640. Growth is exactly linear with no cap, and none of the three code paths has a size check. Stage B 2026-09-25: builtin/hash_builtins.go:164 random_hex does `make([]byte, n)` and refuses only n<0. :184-188 nanoid allocates two n-byte buffers and refuses only n<1. Nothing caps n from above, the same cause as the row's existing sites.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZUnboundedAllocSmallScale -v: allocation grows linearly with the argument at 2^20 and 2^22.
impact: One call with a large argument kills the whole mutant process, including an open case, with no error value and no custody close. On a shared host it first drives the machine into memory pressure.
fix_proposal: Cap the output size (for example the 64 MiB-class limit other readers use) and return an error above it. Compute len(pad)*needed and len(s)*n with overflow checks before allocating. Add the limits to policy/limit_budget.go under a name. Regression test: str_pad_left("x", 1<<40, " "), str_repeat("a", 1<<40) and rand_bytes(1<<40) each return an *object.Error without allocating (TotalAlloc delta under 1 MiB).

title: The frozen legacy ordinal table misbinds v2.3.0 artifacts: their help() call now runs pmap
location: builtin/legacy_ordinals.go:3-12, 411-422; builtin/builtin.go:748-757 (and the ABI note at 366-371)
claim: help is appended to Builtins in init(), after every literal entry, so each release that added builtins moved help's ordinal: 211 in v2.2.0, 398 in v2.3.0, 408 in v2.4.0. legacyBuiltinOrdinals is a v2.4.0 snapshot, and bytecode from v2.3.0 and v2.4.0 carries the same (absent) version, so a v2.3.0 OpGetBuiltin 398 (help) resolves to pmap. The table's comment says 'A .mu built by any earlier release resolves its OpGetBuiltin operands through this slice', and builtin.go:750-751 says 'Appending keeps every existing builtin's slice index stable, so previously compiled bytecode stays valid'. Both are false for help. TestLegacyBuiltinOrdinalsAreFrozen pins the table against its own digest, so it cannot detect this. Verifier: As stated. The table is a correct snapshot of v2.4.0 only. The header comment ('any earlier release') and builtin.go:750-751 ('Appending keeps every existing builtin's slice index stable') are false for help. I did not check the v2.2.0 divergence myself.
evidence: A script over `git show <tag>:builtin/builtin.go` found v2.3.0 differs from the legacy table in exactly one slot, (398, 'help' vs 'pmap'), and v2.4.0 in none. End to end: a v2.3.0 CLI built in scratch compiled `let h = help("len"); putln(type_of(h)); putln(h);`. v2.3.0 ran it and printed `STRING` / `builtin len(value)`. The HEAD runtime (Version 2.5.0) ran the same .mu and printed `ERROR_OBJ` / `ERROR:pmap: want 2 or 3 arguments (array, function[, workers]), got 1`. Verifier: A v2.3.0 archive plus a test showed Builtins[398] = help (399 entries). legacy_ordinals.go:412 maps 398 to pmap. End to end: I compiled help23.mut (`let h = help("len")...`) with a v2.3.0 CLI I built. The v2.3.0 runtime printed STRING and the help text. The HEAD runtime printed `ERROR_OBJ` and `ERROR:pmap: want 2 or 3 arguments (array, function[, workers]), got 1`.
repro: Build old_v2.3.0/mutant23.exe (git archive v2.3.0), `mutant23 gen help23.mut --password reviewpass`, then run help23.mu with both binaries (--dev).
impact: Every v2.3.x artifact that calls help() breaks on 2.5+, with a message that names an unrelated builtin. The ABI note gives false confidence that old artifacts are safe.
fix_proposal: v2.3 and v2.4 artifacts cannot be told apart by version, so the table cannot serve both. Correct both comments to 'v2.4.x', and add a CHANGELOG/compat note that v2.3.x artifacts calling help must be recompiled. Optionally add a test that diffs legacyBuiltinOrdinals against each tag's registry and lists known divergences explicitly. Regression test: A resolve_test that embeds the v2.3.0 and v2.2.0 registry name lists and asserts the only divergences from legacyBuiltinOrdinals are the documented ones.

title: has_key/get/set/delete accept BYTES keys, but their metadata forbids them; the editor flags working code, and its suggested fix changes the answer
claim: hashableKinds is documented as 'the set of kinds that implement object.Hashable' but omits BYTES, and object.Bytes does implement HashKey (object/bytesObj.go:115). The hash builtins accept a BYTES key (hashableKey only asserts Hashable). The language reference lists buffers as valid hash keys 'in a keyspace disjoint from strings'. The LSP builtinArgType rule reads the metadata and reports an error on set/has_key with a BYTES key, then suggests bytes_to_string(value, "utf8"). Because the keyspaces are disjoint, that conversion makes has_key return false. hashableKey's own error text also lists STRING/INTEGER/FLOAT/BOOLEAN.
evidence: TestZZHashKeyBytes: the key param kinds of has_key, get, set and delete are [STRING INTEGER FLOAT BOOLEAN] (Accepts(BYTES)=false), yet has_key(h, bytes) is true and get(h, bytes, d) returns the value. The analyzer (lsp zz_blt3_test.go) reports on `let h = set({}, b, 1); putln(has_key(h, b));` the messages "argument 2 to `set` must be STRING, INTEGER, FLOAT, or BOOLEAN, got BYTES; convert it with bytes_to_string(value, \"utf8\")" and the same for has_key. CLI rp/byteskey.mut printed `has_key(h, b) =true get =1` and, after the suggested conversion, `has_key(h, s) =false`. Verifier: hashableKinds (metadata.go:338) omits BYTES. TestZZBytesKey: has_key(h, bytes) is true, has_key(h, "ab") is false, and the key kinds of has_key, get, set and delete are all [STRING INTEGER FLOAT BOOLEAN]. The analyzer test TestZZVerifyBytesKey emits `argument 2 to `set` must be STRING, INTEGER, FLOAT, or BOOLEAN, got BYTES; convert it with bytes_to_string(value, "utf8")` and the same message for has_key.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZHashKeyBytes -v (FAIL); go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/analyzer -run TestZZHashKeyBytesFlagged -v; compile and run rp/byteskey.mut with mutant.exe.
impact: The editor reports an error on correct code that keys by hash or byte signature. Following its advice silently breaks lookups.
fix_proposal: Add ParamBytes to hashableKinds, fix its param doc text and hashableKey's message, and drop the bytes_to_string hint for hash-key positions. Regression test: A metadata test asserting that every kind implementing object.Hashable (checked by type switch over sample objects) is in hashableKinds, plus the analyzer test above expecting no diagnostic.

title: The parameter-kind conformance test silently passes 404 positions it never reached, so undeclared kinds after argument 1 go unchecked
claim: For builtins outside pureProbeCategories, every position other than the probed one is filled with NULL. A builtin that checks argument 1 first rejects the NULL, so position 2+ is recorded as 'unreached' and nothing fails. The unreached list is logged only when it has 40 entries or fewer, and at HEAD it has 404, so it is not printed at all. Every hash builtin (has_key, get, set, delete, category 'standard library') falls in this hole, which is how the BYTES-key mismatch above got through. Verifier: Partly. The comment at lines 27-33 documents treating an unreached position as not-a-failure as a deliberate safety choice. The gap is that there is no pinned budget, the list is hidden, and pure collection builtins in 'standard library' never have their later positions probed.
evidence: Test log at HEAD: 'parameter-kind conformance: 677 declared positions confirmed ..., 404 not reached (an earlier argument was rejected first), 25 builtins skipped'. That is 37% of probed positions, all passing. TestZZCategoryOfHashOps: CapabilityCategory of has_key/get/set/delete/keys/contains/sort is "standard library", which is not in pureProbeCategories. Verifier: Running TestDeclaredParamKindsMatchImplementation logs '677 declared positions confirmed ..., 404 not reached ..., 25 builtins skipped' and does not print the list, because it only prints lists of 40 or fewer (param_kind_conformance_test.go:187). pureProbeCategories does not include 'standard library', so has_key#2 is filled after a NULL hash and is never reached. Verifier's notes: Lowered to P3 because it is a test gap. The BLT.13 fix brings its own regression test.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run 'TestDeclaredParamKindsMatchImplementation$' -v, then read the logged counts.
impact: The test is presented as the guarantee that argument-type diagnostics are false-positive-free, but for most multi-argument builtins it proves nothing about positions after the first.
fix_proposal: Add 'standard library' collection/convert/math builtins to the pure set, or fill the other positions with valid samples for any builtin not on arityProbeSkip. Fail, or at least always log, when unreached positions exceed a pinned budget. Regression test: Pin the unreached count: the test fails if it rises above the recorded value, and has_key#2 must be confirmed.

title: err.context names the wrong builtin for at least 23 builtins (uuid_v7 -> builtin.uui_dv7, reverse -> builtin.reverse_array, spawn limit -> builtin.register_task)
claim: newError derives Error.Context by walking the Go call stack to the first exported mutant/builtin function and snake-casing its Go name, which also strips a 'Bin' prefix. Wherever the Go name does not snake-case to the builtin's name, the context names something no program can call. The language reference documents context as 'which builtin, e.g. builtin.fs_read', and programs are told to read err.context. Verifier: As stated. I did not re-count all 23 mismatches, but two independently confirmed cases show the mechanism.
evidence: TestZZContextNames (each non-executor builtin called with 9 array arguments) found 23 mismatches, among them uuid_v4 -> builtin.uui_dv4, uuid_v7 -> builtin.uui_dv7, bin_pe_parse -> builtin.pe_parse, bin_is_go -> builtin.is_go, bin_macho_parse -> builtin.mach_o_parse, email_urls -> builtin.email_ur_ls, extract_iocs -> builtin.extract_io_cs, bytes_cstr_at -> builtin.bytes_c_str_at, nanoid -> builtin.nano_id, base64url_encode -> builtin.base64_url_encode, reverse -> builtin.reverse_array, go_buildinfo -> builtin.go_build_info, net_syn_scan -> builtin.net_connect_scan, ext_journal_inode_versions -> builtin.ext_inode_versions. TestZZRegisterTaskLimitContext: the spawn ceiling error has context "builtin.register_task". CLI rp/misc.mut printed `reverse(1) error context: builtin.reverse_array`. Verifier: newError (builtin.go:790-835) derives the context from the Go function name. TestZZContext: reverse(1) gives context builtin.reverse_array, and uuid_v7 with bad arguments gives builtin.uui_dv7. The CLI misc.mut printed `reverse(1) error context: builtin.reverse_array`. The language reference documents err.context as naming the builtin.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run 'TestZZContextNames|TestZZRegisterTaskLimitContext' -v; compile and run rp/misc.mut with mutant.exe.
impact: Scripts and reports that dispatch on err.context ("builtin.uuid_v7") never match. The names shown to examiners are garbled.
fix_proposal: Stamp the context from the registry name at dispatch (the VM knows which builtin it called) instead of reverse-engineering Go function names. Or build a map from Go function pointer to registered name once from Builtins. resourceError already works around this for with_resource. Regression test: For every registered builtin with a wrong-arity call that returns an error, assert Context == "builtin." + name.

title: putln drops the separating space before any value that starts with . , ; : ) ] } and after one ending in = ( [ {, although documented as space-separated
claim: shouldInsertSpaceBefore decides spacing from the rendered text of the values themselves, not from separators the programmer wrote. Data that starts with punctuation, such as a file extension, a dotfile, an NTFS stream name (':Zone.Identifier') or an IPv6 '::1', gets glued to the preceding label. The metadata says 'Prints values separated by spaces'. Verifier: The compaction is deliberate and tested, but no user documentation mentions it. The defect is the documentation contract, plus a heuristic that also fires on data values that begin with '.' or ':'.
evidence:
TestZZPutlnGlue printed `extension.exe`, `user:root`, `sum =5`, `deleted:.bash_history` for putln("extension", ".exe"), putln("user", ":root"), putln("sum =", 5) and putln("deleted:", ".bash_history"). CLI rp/misc.mut printed `extension.exe` and `sum =5`. putln_test.go pins the compaction on purpose (TestPutlnCompactsDelimiterSpacing), but no user doc describes it. Verifier: TestZZPutln output was "extension.exe
deleted:.bash_history
sum =5
stream:Zone.Identifier". CAPABILITY_REFERENCE.md:73 and metadata.go:399 say 'separated by spaces'. putln_test.go TestPutlnCompactsDelimiterSpacing pins the compaction as intended. Verifier's notes: Lowered to P3.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZPutlnGlue -v; compile and run rp/misc.mut with mutant.exe.
impact: Printed findings read as different artefacts: 'deleted.bash_history' looks like a file name, and a label and its value merge.
fix_proposal: Apply the compaction only to string literals the programmer passed as separators (for example a compile-time flag), or document the rule in the metadata and language reference and exempt values that begin with '.' or ':'. Regression test: putln("ext", ".exe") prints "ext .exe".

title: range overflows near the int64 limits: range(MaxInt64-1, MaxInt64, 2) builds 10M elements, then errors instead of returning one element
claim: The loop `for i := start; i < end; i += step` wraps when i+step overflows, so i goes negative and the loop keeps appending until the 10,000,000 cap. Also, because the length is never computed before the loop, any range longer than the cap allocates 10M objects first and only then reports the error.
evidence: TestZZRangeOverflow: range(MaxInt64-1, MaxInt64, 2) returned `ERROR:range: exceeds maximum length 10000000` after 424 ms; range(MinInt64+1, MinInt64, -2) returned the same. Verifier: TestZZRange (under the watchdog): range(MaxInt64-1, MaxInt64, 2) returned 'range: exceeds maximum length 10000000' after 481 ms. The loop at collections_builtins.go:256-272 wraps on i += step.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZRangeOverflow -v (FAIL, under the 1 GiB heap watchdog).
impact: Wrong result at the edges, and a large transient allocation for any oversized range.
fix_proposal: Compute the element count up front with overflow-safe arithmetic ((end-start-1)/step+1 using uint64). Refuse above the cap before allocating, then fill a make([]object.Object, n). Regression test: range(MaxInt64-1, MaxInt64, 2) == [9223372036854775806]; range(0, 20000000) errors with TotalAlloc under 1 MiB.

title: pop([]) and rest([]) return null while their contracts declare ARRAY
claim: Both return Go nil (NULL) for an empty array. core_builtins_test.go:70-79 pins that behaviour for pop. The metadata declares ret(..., ParamArray) 'a new array without the ...', so hover and type inference promise an ARRAY, and len(pop(x)) fails at runtime for x = [].
evidence: TestZZEmptyArrayReturns: `rest([]) = <Go nil> ; declared ARRAY` and `pop([]) = <Go nil> ; declared ARRAY`. CLI rp/misc.mut printed `pop([]) type: NULL`. Verifier: TestZZPopRest: pop([]) and rest([]) both return Go nil, and ReturnSpec(pop).Kinds is [ARRAY]. The CLI printed `pop([]) type: NULL`.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZEmptyArrayReturns -v; compile and run rp/misc.mut with mutant.exe.
impact: The editor's contract is wrong for the empty case, and code written to it fails on empty input.
fix_proposal: Return an empty array (preferred, matching rest([x]) and pop([x])), or declare ParamArray|ParamNull and say 'null when the array is empty' as first/last do. Regression test: type_of(pop([])) and type_of(rest([])) match their ReturnSpec kinds.

title: text_levenshtein, text_similarity and text_fuzzy_find are O(n*m) with no input cap
claim: levenshteinDistance fills a full n*m dynamic-programming table over rune slices with no length limit. text_fuzzy_find repeats that for every candidate. Two strings read from evidence (file contents, log lines) of 1M runes each mean about 1e12 cell updates. Verifier: As stated. Memory use is O(m) (two rows); only time is quadratic.
evidence: TestZZLevenshteinQuadratic: n=3000 took 14.2 ms, n=6000 took 57.4 ms, a ratio of 4.04 (quadratic). Extrapolated at ~1.6 ns/cell, 100k runes take about 16 s and 1M runes about 27 min, with no error and no way to interrupt. Verifier: levenshteinDistance (fuzzy_matching.go:146) has no length cap. TestZZLev took 7.0 ms at n=2000 and 25.4 ms at n=4000, a ratio of 3.6, which is quadratic.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZLevenshteinQuadratic -v (two sizes, watchdog on).
impact: A script that compares file contents effectively hangs.
fix_proposal: Cap rune lengths (for example 64k) and return an error beyond the cap. Optionally add a banded or threshold variant for fuzzy_find using maxDistance. Regression test: text_levenshtein on two 1M-rune strings returns an error in under 100 ms.

title: Timeouts of more than ~292 years overflow time.Duration and fire at once (task_wait, chan_send, chan_recv, sleep_ms)
claim: time.Duration(ms) * time.Millisecond wraps for ms > ~9.2e12. MaxInt64 wraps to -1 ms, so a caller asking to wait as long as possible gets an immediate timeout, and sleep_ms returns at once.
evidence: TestZZTimeoutOverflow: task_wait(running, MaxInt64) returned after 0s with 'task is still running after 9223372036854775807ms'; chan_recv(empty, MaxInt64) returned after 0s with timeout: true. Verifier: In TestZZTimeout, task_wait(running, MaxInt64) returned after 0s with 'still running after 9223372036854775807ms'. chan_recv(empty, MaxInt64) returned after 0s with timeout true. sleep_ms(MaxInt64) also returned after 0s. timeoutArg (channels.go:157) does not clamp the value.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZTimeoutOverflow -v.
impact: Small. A wait-forever idiom based on a huge timeout silently turns into a poll.
fix_proposal: Clamp ms to math.MaxInt64/int64(time.Millisecond) before multiplying, or treat values above the clamp as 'wait indefinitely'. Regression test: task_wait(running, MaxInt64) is still blocked after 50 ms.

title: help("bytes") and help("policy") point at example files that do not exist, and the struct/enum snippets can never be shown
claim: replExamples points 'bytes' at examples/bytes/bytes_parser_example.mut and 'policy' at examples/policy/policy_eval_example.mut; neither file exists. The bytes snippet `let value = bytes_read_u32_le(blob, 0);` binds a (value, err) pair to one name, the pattern the language reference calls a mistake. RenderReplHelp checks replKeywordDocs before the examples, so help("struct") and help("enum") always return the keyword blurb, and those two snippets are unreachable.
evidence: `ls examples/bytes/bytes_parser_example.mut examples/policy/policy_eval_example.mut` -> No such file or directory; the directories hold bytes_cursor_*_demo.mut and policy_engine_example.mut / policy_inline_allow_deny.mut. repl_help.go:118 `if doc, ok := replKeywordDocs[normalizedTopic]; ok { return ... }` runs before renderExamplesHelp at :136, and replKeywordDocs has "struct" and "enum". Verifier: examples/bytes holds only bytes_cursor_*_demo.mut, and examples/policy holds policy_engine_example.mut and policy_inline_allow_deny.mut. The files the help examples name do not exist. RenderReplHelp checks replKeywordDocs (repl_help.go:48-49 has struct and enum) before renderExamplesHelp, so the struct and enum examples are never shown. bytes_read_u32_le is declared pairRet, and the bytes snippet binds its result to a single name.
repro: ls of the two paths in the scratch copy fails. Reading the RenderReplHelp control flow shows the struct/enum snippets are unreachable (not executed).
impact: The REPL sends learners to missing files and teaches a binding the editor warns about.
fix_proposal: Point at bytes_cursor_sample_demo.mut and policy_engine_example.mut, use `let value, err = ...` in the snippet, and check examples before keyword docs, or rename the topics. Regression test: repl_help test: every replExamples location exists on disk, and every topic returns its snippet from RenderReplHelp.

title: Comments that say something the code does not do
claim: metadata.go:335 says hashableKinds is 'the set of kinds that implement object.Hashable', but BYTES implements it and is missing. metadata.go:594-598 says every digest builtin 'funnels through hashOneString -> requireStringArg ... Byte buffers are STRING values in Mutant, so hashing bytes needs no separate kind', yet the entries right below declare ParamString, ParamBytes and BYTES is a distinct type. error_builtin.go:74 says 'Mutant hash keys may be STRING, INTEGER or BOOLEAN', but FLOAT and BYTES keys exist.
evidence: object/bytesObj.go:115 `func (b *Bytes) HashKey() HashKey`; metadata.go:599-601 `param("s", "Text or buffer to digest.", ParamString, ParamBytes)`. Verifier: metadata.go:335 says hashableKinds are 'the kinds that implement object.Hashable', but object/bytesObj.go:115 gives Bytes a HashKey. The comment at metadata.go:594-596 says 'exactly one STRING ... Byte buffers are STRING values', yet the declarations right below it accept ParamBytes. error_builtin.go:74 says hash keys may be 'STRING, INTEGER or BOOLEAN'. Verifier's notes: The hashableKinds half overlaps BLT.13, whose fix should also correct this comment.
repro: Code reading against object/bytesObj.go and the adjacent declarations (no runtime repro needed).
impact: The stale hashableKinds comment is what let the BYTES-key contract bug look correct.
fix_proposal: Fix the three comments. The hashableKinds list itself is fixed in the BYTES-key finding. Regression test: None beyond the hashableKinds test in that finding.

title: sqlite_query was not read-only: ATTACH reached files outside its temp copy, so a SELECT could modify evidence and a bound buffer could be written anywhere
claim: sqlite_query and sqlite_query_bytes copy the database they are given and promise the original is never modified, but ran the script's SQL, several statements at a time, on a read-write connection to the copy with no limit on ATTACH. ATTACH opened the original of any path read-write. A SELECT through an attached WAL-mode database checkpointed its WAL into it and deleted the -wal file, destroying uncheckpointed and deleted records. DELETE through an attachment emptied the original. INSERT into an attached new file wrote any bound parameter, a classified buffer included, to a path of the script's choosing, and VACUUM INTO wrote a whole copy anywhere. classified.go exempts sqlite_query from the classified sinks on the grounds that a bound buffer goes nowhere.
evidence: Reproduced at 7aeee5a and again at the fix's parent: over a WAL-mode evidence.db with two uncheckpointed rows, 'ATTACH ?1 AS o; SELECT count(*) AS n FROM o.t' with ?1 = evidence.db returned no error and changed evidence.db's SHA-256 and deleted evidence.db-wal and -shm; 'ATTACH ?1 AS o; DELETE FROM o.t; SELECT 1' deleted every row of the original; 'ATTACH ?1 AS o; CREATE TABLE o.leak (x); INSERT INTO o.leak VALUES (?2); SELECT 1' created leak.db holding the classified buffer; 'VACUUM INTO ?1' created a new file. Only SQL the script writes can do this, not evidence content, but ATTACHing a second evidence database to join it is the natural idiom with a one-path builtin, and it silently checkpointed and deleted that database's WAL.
repro: builtin/sqlite_readonly_test.go TestSqliteQueryCannotReachAnyFileButItsCopy: before the fix, eight statements ran that must be refused, evidence.db, -wal and -shm changed or vanished, and leak.db and vacuumed.db were created, for both builtins.
impact: A query the documentation calls read-only modified evidence and destroyed the write-ahead log that holds uncheckpointed and deleted records, with no warning; and classified plaintext could be written to disk past the classified mark.
fix_proposal: Open the copy read-only, refuse ATTACH and VACUUM INTO, and keep a bound buffer off the disk. Fixed: withSQLiteCopy folds the copy's WAL into the copy (PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE on the temp file, the only SQL run on a writable connection), then reopens it as file:...?mode=ro -- an open flag SQL cannot undo, unlike PRAGMA query_only -- on one *sql.Conn whose sqlite3_limit(SQLITE_LIMIT_ATTACHED) is 0, verified after it is set; VACUUM INTO attaches its output the same way, so it is refused too. temp_store is MEMORY. The browser_* parsers read through the same confined connection. A refusal names why (ATTACH/VACUUM INTO refused; the query is read-only). The committed rows still in the WAL are read, as before.

title: report_table and report_list turned a classified buffer into hex as it was added, so report_render and report_write, named classified sinks, emitted the plaintext
claim: The report builders render each cell or item to a string with csvFieldText when it is added, and csvFieldText renders a buffer as its hex. The document the sinks receive therefore holds no marked buffer, so refuseClassified in report_render and report_write walked the report and found nothing, and the builders themselves never checked. The script never asked for a conversion: it put a buffer in a report and called a named sink, which is exactly the accident the mark exists to catch. The editor did not warn either, because the builders were not listed sinks.
evidence: Stage B: report_render of {x: secret} directly was refused, but report_table(r, [["content", secret]]) followed by report_render(r, "html") contained 5345435245542d504c41494e54455854 ('SECRET-PLAINTEXT'), and report_write wrote 'content,5345...54' to disk. Reproduced in Stage C by TestAReportBuilderRefusesAClassifiedBuffer: report_table accepted the buffer and the plaintext was both rendered and written to disk; report_list accepted it and rendered it.
repro: builtin/report_classified_test.go TestAReportBuilderRefusesAClassifiedBuffer accepted a classified buffer in both builders before the fix and showed where the plaintext went.
impact: Classified plaintext left the process through the sinks documented to stop it, by the ordinary route of putting a buffer in a report table, and the editor gave no warning.
fix_proposal: Refuse in the builders and list them as sinks, or keep buffers as objects until render. Fixed: report_table and report_list call refuseClassified over their whole argument list before anything else, and ClassifiedSinks lists them, so TestClassifiedSinksAreTheBuiltinsThatRefuse holds the list to the code and the editor's classifiedPlaintext rule, which reads the list, warns at those calls too. The refusal names the record, the classes and the length, not the bytes. report_new, report_section and report_text take strings only and cannot be handed a buffer. DISCLOSURE_POLICY section 10 and MUTANT_LANGUAGE_REFERENCE list the two builders among the sinks and say why.

title: toml_parse and msgpack_parse have no nesting limit: deep input crashes the process with a fatal Go stack overflow
claim: Both libraries decode recursively with no depth bound. The maxNativeDepth backstop only runs on the tree they return, after the recursion has already happened. The comment claims it is the backstop for libraries that do not bound depth. A stack overflow is fatal and cannot be caught by any recover. Verifier: As stated. At the default 1 GB stack the crash needs input on the order of tens of MB, which is linear extrapolation from the 64 MiB result plus the auditor's trail of 8M '[' crashing. I did not re-run that at 1 GB to spare the shared host.
evidence: format_native.go:36-38: "a few hundred bytes of input can describe a hundred thousand levels ... this is the backstop for the ones that do not". convertNative is called only after `toml.Decode(...)` / `decoder.DecodeInterface()` return. Verifier: TomlParse calls toml.Decode and MsgpackParse calls decoder.DecodeInterface before convertNative applies maxNativeDepth=256, so the depth check comes after the recursion has already happened. Ran each case in its own process from a compiled test binary with debug.SetMaxStack(64 MiB): toml 'a = '+100000x'[' returned an error in 146 ms, and 2,000,000 levels gave 'goroutine stack exceeds 67108864-byte limit / fatal error: stack overflow'. msgpack 100000x0x91 returned 'nests deeper than 256 levels' in 75 ms, and 2,000,000 levels gave a fatal stack overflow. There is no SetMaxStack in production code. Verifier's notes: Same class as ART.09 (plist) and LEX.03 (parser), but a different root defect in different libraries.
repro: zz_dat2_test.go TestZZ2_DeepNesting, one process per case, debug.SetMaxStack(64 MiB). toml "a = "+100000x'[' returns in 169 ms (100k library levels). toml with 2,000,000x'[' gives "runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 67108864-byte limit / fatal error: stack overflow". msgpack 100000x0x91 gives "document nests deeper than 256 levels", but only after the library had recursed 100k deep. msgpack at 2,000,000 gives fatal stack overflow. yaml control: "exceeded max depth of 10000" at both sizes. Attempt-1 trail: at the default 1 GB stack, 8M '[' in toml crashed with "goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit".
impact: An evidence file of a few MB (a TOML config or a msgpack blob) kills the whole run, the REPL, or any host process using the package.
fix_proposal: Pre-scan depth before decoding. For TOML, count unclosed [ and { outside strings and comments. For msgpack, walk container headers iteratively. Refuse input past maxNativeDepth. Alternatively decode msgpack with a depth-limited custom walker. Regression test: toml_parse("a = "+1e6x'[') and msgpack_parse(1e6x0x91+0xc0) return an error naming the depth limit, under a reduced SetMaxStack so a regression fails rather than crashes the suite.

title: tar on .tar.zst never closes its zstd decoders: reads intermittently fail and decoder goroutines outlive tar_close
claim: Every tarStream call builds a zstd.Decoder (dec.IOReadCloser()) and returns it as a plain io.Reader, and nothing ever closes it. When a read stops before EOF (any member other than the last), the abandoned decoder's async goroutines keep reading the shared *os.File. They race the next call's Seek(0) and new decoder.
evidence: archive.go:502-506 `dec, err := zstd.NewReader(r) ... return dec.IOReadCloser(), nil`; :567 `func tarStream(state tarHandleState) (io.Reader, error)`. No Close anywhere on the result. Verifier: The zstd wrap returns dec.IOReadCloser(), tarStream returns it as an io.Reader, and nothing closes it. Re-ran TestZZ3 with GOMAXPROCS=16: with a 2 MiB random member, 2/20 alternating tar_read_bytes calls failed with 'invalid input: magic number mismatch' and 27 goroutines were still running after tar_close. With a 64 KiB member there were 0 failures and 0 leaked.
repro: zz_dat3_test.go TestZZ3_TarZstdReadsFail: a .tar.zst with a.txt plus a 2 MiB random big.bin; tar_open, then 20 alternating tar_read_bytes calls; GOMAXPROCS=16. Three runs: 1/20, 2/20 and 1/20 reads failed with "archive/tar: invalid tar header" (an earlier run failed with "invalid input: magic number mismatch"), and 30 goroutines were still running after tar_close each time. With GOMAXPROCS=1: 0 failures, 0 leaked. With a 64 KiB member: 0 failures.
impact: Reading members of a valid zstd-compressed collection fails at random, depending on core count, and every early-member read leaks decoder goroutines and window buffers for the rest of the process.
fix_proposal: Make tarStream return an io.ReadCloser that closes the zstd decoder (and the gzip reader), and defer Close in scanTarHeaders and tarRead. Optionally use zstd.WithDecoderConcurrency(1), since reads are sequential. Regression test: On a multi-core host, 50 alternating reads of the first and last member of a .tar.zst all succeed with the right bytes, and runtime.NumGoroutine after tar_close returns to its value before tar_open.

title: tar_open refuses any archive whose stream expands past 1000x its size, and nothing can raise that cap (tar_read's max_bytes cannot)
claim: tarStream wraps every compressed stream in a cappedReader of state.Size*1000 regardless of any caller limit, and tar_open has no parameter. A highly compressible collection cannot even be opened. This contradicts the file's promise that 'the caller can name its own limit when it knows better' and the max_bytes doc 'replaces the default limit'.
evidence: archive.go:582 `stream = newCappedReader(wrapped, state.Size*maxDecompressionRatio)`; archive.go:47-49 names the case: "a sparse disk image or a repetitive log compresses far past any ratio". Verifier: tarStream wraps every compressed stream in newCappedReader(wrapped, state.Size*maxDecompressionRatio), and TarOpen accepts exactly one argument. Re-ran it: a 65,349-byte .tar.gz holding notes.txt plus 64 MiB of zeros gives 'tar_open: decompression limit exceeded: stream expands past 65349000 bytes'. The file's own comment (archive.go:47-56) says a sparse disk image compresses past any ratio and that the caller can name its own limit.
repro: zz_dat2_test.go TestZZ2_TarCompressibleRefused: a 65,349-byte .tar.gz holding notes.txt and 64 MiB of zeros gives "tar_open: decompression limit exceeded: stream expands past 65349000 bytes". The later attempt's trail shows the same refusal for zstd.
impact: Real triage tarballs that contain sparse or zero-filled files (lastlog, swap, VM disks, preallocated logs) cannot be opened at all, and the error gives no way forward.
fix_proposal: Give tar_open an optional max_bytes/options argument, store it in tarHandleState, and use it for the walk cap. Let tar_read's explicit max_bytes lift the stream cap for that call. Regression test: tar_open(path, {max_bytes: 128 MiB}) on the 64 MiB-zeros .tar.gz succeeds and tar_read_bytes of notes.txt returns 'hello'.

title: unsafe_path judges tar symlink targets from the archive root (false positives) and never checks zip symlinks
claim: A symlink's Linkname is relative to the link's own directory, but unsafeArchivePath(header.Linkname) cleans it in isolation, so ordinary rootfs links such as usr/lib/x -> ../lib64/y are flagged. Zip entries carry symlinks as mode bits plus a body naming the target, and only the entry name is checked. That is the half the file's own comment says 'gets forgotten'. Verifier: As stated. The severity is lowered because unsafe_path is an advisory flag: nothing extracts, as archive.go:31-35 says.
evidence: archive.go:701 `return unsafeArchivePath(header.Name) || unsafeArchivePath(header.Linkname)`; ZipOpen:248 `if unsafeArchivePath(entry.Name)` only. Verifier: unsafeTarHeader checks unsafeArchivePath(header.Linkname) from the archive root, and ZipOpen checks only entry.Name. Re-ran it: the tar symlink usr/lib/libfoo.so -> ../lib64/libfoo.so.1 gives unsafe_path_count=1. A zip with a symlink entry 'link' (body /etc) plus link/cron.d/evil gives 0.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_UnsafePathLinkTargets: tar symlink usr/lib/libfoo.so -> ../lib64/libfoo.so.1 (resolves to usr/lib64/libfoo.so.1) gives unsafe_path_count=1. A zip holding 'link' (symlink mode, body '/etc') and 'link/cron.d/evil' gives unsafe_path_count=0.
impact: The count that 'is itself a finding' is inflated on every Linux rootfs tarball, and a zip symlink-escape archive reports clean.
fix_proposal: For TypeSymlink, test path.Join(path.Dir(name), linkname), keeping absolute targets unsafe; hardlinks stay root-relative. For zip entries with Mode()&os.ModeSymlink, read the capped body as the target and apply the same rule. Regression test: The two archives above yield 0 and 1 respectively. Keep a tar symlink a/b -> ../../etc flagged.

title: tar_open misreads a plain tar whose first member name starts with a compression magic (e.g. 'BZh') and refuses it
claim: Detection compares the file's first bytes, which in a plain tar are the first member's name, against the gzip, bzip2 and zstd magics, before checking for a ustar header. Verifier: As stated. It needs a first member name that starts with 'BZh' (the gzip and zstd magics are not plausible names), so it is rare.
evidence: archive.go:534 `if bytes.HasPrefix(head, archiveCompressions[i].magic)`; bzip2 magic is []byte("BZh"). Verifier: detectArchiveCompression matches the first 8 bytes against the magics without first checking for ustar at offset 257. Re-ran it: a plain tar whose first member is BZhistory.txt gives 'tar_open: bzip2 data invalid: invalid compression level'.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_TarBZhMagic: a plain tar whose first member is BZhistory.txt gives "tar_open: bzip2 data invalid: invalid compression level".
impact: A valid archive cannot be opened, and the error blames bzip2.
fix_proposal: First check for 'ustar' at offset 257 (or a valid tar header checksum) and treat the file as plain; only then sniff compression magics. Alternatively fall back to plain when the decompressor fails on the first read. Regression test: A plain tar with first member BZhistory.txt opens with compression 'none'.

title: tar_read of a hardlink or symlink member returns an empty buffer and no error
claim: tarRead matches the member by name and reads its body. A TypeLink or TypeSymlink member has no body, so the result is empty with no error and no mention of the link. Verifier: As stated. Raised to S3 because the wrong answer is silent: hashing every member reports the empty-file digest for hardlinked binaries, which are common in rootfs tarballs.
evidence: archive.go:822 checks only `header.Typeflag == tar.TypeDir`, then `data, err := readLimited(reader, limit)`. Verifier: tarRead refuses only TypeDir, then readLimited reads the body of whatever matched. Re-ran it: tar_read_bytes of bin/tool2 (TypeLink -> bin/tool 'payload') returns empty BYTES with err nil.
repro: zz_dat2_test.go TestZZ2_TarHardlinkRead: bin/tool2 (TypeLink -> bin/tool, which holds 'payload') makes tar_read_bytes return an empty BYTES with err nil.
impact: A script hashing every member reports the empty-file digest for hardlinked binaries, which is a wrong answer about their content.
fix_proposal: Follow a hardlink to its target member (a second walk), and refuse a symlink with an error naming the target. Regression test: tar_read_bytes(bin/tool2) returns 'payload', or an error that names bin/tool.

title: tar_open holds every header in memory: a 44 KB .tar.gz retained 40 MiB (944x), contrary to 'the cost is time rather than memory'
claim: Every *tar.Header, including PAX records and names of up to about 1 MiB each, is retained for the life of the handle. The only bounds are 1<<20 entries and the 1000x stream ratio, so held memory scales with 1000x the compressed size.
evidence: archive.go:692 `headers = append(headers, header)`; :594 "Bodies are skipped rather than held, so the cost is time rather than memory." Verifier: scanTarHeaders appends every *tar.Header to headers, kept for the life of the handle. Re-ran it: a 44,456-byte .tar.gz with 40 PAX members with ~1 MiB names held 40 MiB of heap after GC (945x). The TarOpen comment says 'the cost is time rather than memory'.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_TarHeaderMemoryAmplification: 40 PAX members with ~1 MiB names in a 44,456-byte .tar.gz; tar_open held 40 MiB of heap after GC (944x the file).
impact: A 1 MB crafted .tar.gz pins about 1 GB for as long as the handle is open.
fix_proposal: Keep only the listed fields and cap the total header bytes (for example the sum of name, linkname and PAX sizes) with a named limit. Regression test: Opening the crafted archive either fails with the named limit or holds less than a small multiple of its size.

title: protobuf_parse refuses every message that contains a group (wire type 3)
claim: ConsumeGroup is called with field number 0, and protowire checks that the end-group marker carries the same number. Real groups (field number >= 1) therefore always fail with 'mismatching end group marker', and the whole parse fails. Verifier: As stated. Lowered to S4 because the failure is loud (an error, not a wrong answer) and groups exist only in proto2 and are deprecated.
evidence: format_binary.go:344 `payload, n := protowire.ConsumeGroup(protowire.Number(0), data)`; protowire consumeFieldValueD: `if typ2 == EndGroupType { if num != num2 { return errCodeEndGroup } ...}`. Verifier: format_binary.go:344 calls protowire.ConsumeGroup(protowire.Number(0), data). Re-ran it: 0b 10 01 0c gives 'protobuf_parse: field 1 at offset 0: proto: mismatching end group marker'.
repro: zz_dat2_test.go TestZZ2_ProtobufGroup: bytes 0b 10 01 0c (group 1 containing field 2 = 1) give "protobuf_parse: field 1 at offset 0: proto: mismatching end group marker".
impact: Any proto2 capture using groups cannot be read at all, although the doc promises a schemaless walk of whatever is there. No test covers groups.
fix_proposal: Pass the tag's number into decodeProtobufValue and call protowire.ConsumeGroup(number, data). Regression test: protobuf_parse(0b 10 01 0c) returns one field (field 1, wire_type 'group') whose message holds field 2 = 1.

title: protobuf_parse has no total node budget: nesting sidesteps the per-message cap and retained heap is ~353x the input
claim: maxProtobufFields bounds one message only, and every length-delimited payload is re-walked as a nested message. Unlike der_parse (maxDERNodes) and the native bridge (maxNativeNodes), no budget is shared across the tree.
evidence: format_binary.go:245 `if len(fields) >= maxProtobufFields` is per call; walkProtobuf(payload, depth+1) starts a fresh `fields` slice. Verifier: maxProtobufFields is checked per walkProtobuf call, and each nested payload starts a fresh fields slice with no shared budget. Re-ran it: 600,012 bytes retains 202 MiB and 1,200,024 bytes retains 404 MiB (353x, linear).
repro: zz_dat2_test.go TestZZ2_ProtobufHeap: 600,012 bytes retains 202 MiB; 1,200,024 bytes retains 404 MiB (353x at both sizes).
impact: A 12 MB gRPC blob needs about 4 GB of heap. Memory is exhausted from evidence of ordinary size.
fix_proposal: Thread a shared budget pointer (as walkDER does) and fail with a named limit. Regression test: A nested message exceeding the budget returns the named error instead of allocating.

title: der_parse decodes UTCTime years 50-68 as 2050-2068; RFC 5280 says 1950-1968
claim: UTCTime is parsed with Go's '06' layout, which maps 00-68 to 20xx. X.509 (RFC 5280 4.1.2.5.1) maps YY >= 50 to 19YY. Verifier: As stated. Only years 50-68 are wrong; Go already maps 69-99 to 19xx.
evidence: format_binary.go:613 `return derTime(content, []string{"060102150405Z0700", "0601021504Z0700"})`. Verifier: UTCTime is parsed with Go's '06' layouts. Re-ran it: 170d3530303130313030303030305a gives der_parse 2050-01-01T00:00:00Z, while encoding/asn1 gives 1950-01-01T00:00:00Z.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_DerUTCTimeCentury: 170d3530303130313030303030305a gives der_parse 2050-01-01T00:00:00Z, while encoding/asn1 gives 1950-01-01T00:00:00Z.
impact: A certificate or ticket time from 1950-1968, typical of forged or odd certificates, is reported 100 years later as if it were fact.
fix_proposal: Parse YY by hand: YY >= 50 gives 1900+YY, else 2000+YY. Regression test: UTCTime 500101000000Z decodes to 1950-01-01T00:00:00Z, and 491231235959Z to 2049-12-31T23:59:59Z.

title: cbor_encode and msgpack_encode stringify integer map keys: COSE does not round-trip and {1:v} collides with {"1":v}
claim: objectToNative always builds map[string]any using nativeKeyText, even for CBOR and MessagePack, which support integer keys. This contradicts cbor_parse's 'integer map keys are supported' and cbor_encode's 'hash_sha256(cbor_encode(v)) is a stable identifier for v'.
evidence: format_native.go:298 `out := make(map[string]any, len(v.Pairs))` ... `key, err := nativeKeyText(pair.Key)`; nativeKeyToObject:190-191 itself warns that "a key quietly turned into text collides with a real key of that spelling". Verifier: objectToNative builds map[string]any through nativeKeyText for every format. Re-ran it: cbor_parse(a10126) gives {1: -7}, and cbor_encode of that gives a1613126. {1:"v"} and {"1":"v"} both encode to a161316176 in CBOR, and both give 81a131a176 in msgpack. This contradicts cbor_encode's 'stable identifier for v' and cbor_parse's integer-key support. Verifier's notes: Priority lowered to P2: the wrong output is re-encoded data, not an evidence reading.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_CborEncodeRewritesIntegerKeys: cbor_parse(a10126) = {1: -7}, and cbor_encode of that is a1613126. {1:"v"} and {"1":"v"} both encode to a161316176. msgpack_encode gives 81a131a176 for both.
impact: Re-encoded COSE headers carry the wrong labels (a verifier finds no alg), and the documented stable identifier collides across different values.
fix_proposal: When rawBytes is true, build map[any]any, keeping INTEGER and BOOLEAN keys typed. Regression test: cbor_encode(cbor_parse(x)) == x for a10126, and {1:"v"} and {"1":"v"} produce different bytes.

title: toml_parse shifts local datetimes, dates and times by the host's UTC offset and labels them Z
claim: TOML local date-times carry no zone. The library tags them with the host's offset, and convertNative converts them to UTC and appends Z. The same file gives different, wrong times on different hosts. Verifier: As stated. The output depends on the host and is wrong everywhere except UTC hosts.
evidence: format_native.go:126 `return stringObj(v.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339Nano)), nil`; metadata toml_parse: "TOML datetimes become RFC 3339 strings, so they sort against every other timestamp". Verifier: format_native.go:126 formats time.Time as v.UTC().Format(RFC3339Nano). Re-ran it on this UTC+05:30 host: when = 1979-05-27T07:32:00 gives 1979-05-27T02:02:00Z, day = 1979-05-27 gives 1979-05-26T18:30:00Z, and at = 07:32:00 gives 0000-01-01T02:02:00Z.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_TomlLocalDatetime on this host (UTC+05:30): when = 1979-05-27T07:32:00 gives "1979-05-27T02:02:00Z"; day = 1979-05-27 gives "1979-05-26T18:30:00Z"; at = 07:32:00 gives "0000-01-01T02:02:00Z".
impact: Timestamps from tool and cloud configs are reported as specific UTC instants that are wrong by the examiner's own offset, and the date can even change.
fix_proposal: Recognise the datetime-local, date-local and time-local locations (by Location().String()) and render them without a zone designator and without conversion. Regression test: Under TZ set to +05:30 and to UTC, the three values render as 1979-05-27T07:32:00, 1979-05-27 and 07:32:00.

title: toml_parse refuses any document with an array of tables ([[x]])
claim: BurntSushi decodes [[x]] into []map[string]interface{}, which convertNative does not handle.
evidence: format_native.go:175 `return nil, fmt.Errorf("unsupported decoded value of Go type %T", value)`. Verifier: convertNative has no []map[string]any case. Re-ran it: '[[bin]] name=a [[bin]] name=b' gives 'toml_parse: unsupported decoded value of Go type []map[string]interface {}'.
repro:
zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_TomlLocalDatetime: "[[bin]]
name = "a"
[[bin]]
name = "b"
" gives "toml_parse: unsupported decoded value of Go type []map[string]interface {}".
impact: Common TOML files (Cargo.toml [[bin]], many tool configs) cannot be read.
fix_proposal: Add `case []map[string]any:` that converts each element as a table. Regression test: The document above parses to {bin: [{name: a}, {name: b}]}.

title: json_parse accepts trailing data: concatenated documents silently yield only the first, and ndjson_parse accepts a stray '}' or ']'
claim: JsonParse decodes one value and never checks for EOF. ndjson_parse's decoder.More() returns false before a '}' or ']', so a trailing closer passes. yaml_parse_all's comment names this exact failure ('returns only the first -- silently') as the bug to remove.
evidence: json.go:43 `if err := decoder.Decode(&raw); err != nil {` with no follow-up; format_text.go:780 `if decoder.More() {`. Verifier: JsonParse decodes once and never checks for EOF. Re-ran it: '{"a":1} {"b":2}' gives {a: 1} with no error, and '{"a":1} trailing garbage' gives {a: 1}. ndjson_parse of "{\"a\":1}}\n{\"b\":2}]\n" gives [{a:1},{b:2}], although its doc says a malformed line fails with its line number.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_JsonParseLossy: `{"a":1} {"b":2}` gives {a: 1} with no error; `{"a":1} trailing garbage` gives {a: 1}; ndjson "{\"a\":1}}\n{\"b\":2}]\n" gives [{a: 1}, {b: 2}].
impact: A log file of concatenated JSON objects is read as one record with no warning, and malformed evidence passes as valid.
fix_proposal: After Decode, require EOF (`if _, err := decoder.Token(); err != io.EOF { refuse }`) in json_parse and in each ndjson line. Regression test: All three inputs return errors.

title: json_parse turns integers above MaxInt64 into a lossy FLOAT, while every other decoder returns decimal STRING
claim: When Int64 overflows, jsonValueToObject falls back to Float64 and loses precision. The shared bridge deliberately renders such values as exact decimal text.
evidence: json.go:133-138 `i, err := v.Int64(); if err != nil { f, fErr := v.Float64() ... return &object.Float{Value: f}, nil }`. Verifier: json.go:132-139 falls back to Float64 when Int64 overflows. Re-ran it: json_parse gives FLOAT 18446744073709551616.000000, while msgpack_parse, yaml_parse and cbor_parse give STRING 18446744073709551615. Verifier's notes: Distinct from BLT.08 (the cache round trip).
repro: zz_dat2_test.go TestZZ2_UintDrift: json_parse gives FLOAT 18446744073709551616.000000; msgpack_parse and yaml_parse give STRING 18446744073709551615.
impact: 64-bit unsigned identifiers above 2^63 read from JSON become a different number, and one value gets different types depending on the format it came in.
fix_proposal: For an integer literal (no . e E) that overflows int64, return stringObj(raw) as uintToObject does. Regression test: json_parse("18446744073709551615") returns STRING "18446744073709551615".

title: xml_find returns one element several times and not in document order; repeated ** multiplies results
claim: '**' matches the current node against the rest of the path and then recurses into every child with '**' still in front. Paths such as **/dir/**/file therefore reach the same node through several ancestors, and nothing deduplicates. Direct children are matched before deeper descendants, which breaks document order.
evidence: format_text.go:676-682 `if err := xmlWalk(node, segments[1:], out) ... for _, child := range children { xmlWalk(child, segments, out) }`. Verifier: The xmlWalk '**' branch matches the rest of the path at the current node, then recurses into the children with '**' still in front, and nothing deduplicates. Re-ran it: with '**/x' gives [2 1], although metadata promises 'in document order'. '**/dir/**/file' returns one twice. A depth-60 chain with '**/**/**/**/a' gives 595,665 results in 117 ms.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_XmlFindDuplicatesAndOrder: with "**/x" gives ids [2 1]. with "**/dir/**/file" gives 2 matches for one element. TestZZ_XmlFindStarStarBlowup: a depth-60 chain with "**/**/**/**/a" gives 595,665 results for 60 distinct elements.
impact: Counts of matching elements (for example scheduled-task actions) are wrong, and a short path over a 256-deep document can explode.
fix_proposal: Collect matches in a set keyed by node pointer and emit in a pre-order walk, or collapse consecutive ** and memoise (node, segment index). Regression test: The two documents give [1 2] and exactly 1 match. The depth-60 case gives 60.

title: events_from drops sub-second precision from every timestamp not given as unix seconds with an ns field (fs_report ISO, unix_ms, filetime, webkit)
claim: normalizeTimestamp returns (unix, ms, format, err), and entryTimestamps discards ms.
