Nanoseconds come only from an explicit nsField. fs_report rows carry RFC3339Nano strings (filesystem_parsers.go:2786-2791), so ECS, OCSF and Timesketch output is truncated to whole seconds, contradicting 'Normalization is additive, never lossy'. Verifier: The normalized timestamp fields and the ECS, OCSF and Timesketch emitters lose sub-second precision for sources that have no ns companion field. The source value itself survives verbatim in `extra`, which is what 'additive, never lossy' refers to, so that part of the claim is overstated.
evidence: schema_events.go:566 `unix, _, _, err := normalizeTimestamp(value, format)`; :570 `{unix: unix, ns: entryNanos(entry, spec.nsField)}`. Verifier: entryTimestamps discards the ms that normalizeTimestamp returns, and ns comes only from spec.nsField. fs_report has no ns field, and formatTime emits RFC3339Nano. Re-ran it: created 2024-01-02T03:04:05.678901234Z gives iso ...05Z, ts_ms 1704164645000, Timesketch 1704164645000000 and OCSF time 1704164645000. Verifier's notes: Priority lowered to P2 because extra keeps the original.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_EventsFromDropsSubSecond: an fs_report row with created 2024-01-02T03:04:05.678901234Z gives iso 2024-01-02T03:04:05Z, ts_ms 1704164645000, Timesketch timestamp 1704164645000000, and OCSF time 1704164645000.
impact: Supertimelines lose ordering within a second, and the sub-second fraction (a timestomping tell) disappears in export.
fix_proposal: Derive ns from the parsed time (for ISO keep t.Nanosecond(); for numeric formats use ms%1000*1e6 or finer) when no nsField is given. Regression test: The same row gives ts_ms ...678 and iso ...05.678901234Z. A unix_ms custom mapping keeps its milliseconds.

title: ocsf_event files a deletion under activity_id 99 (Other) instead of 4 (Delete)
claim: For File System Activity (class 1001), 'Deletion Time' and action 'delete' fall through to 99 with the name 'delete', giving type_uid 100199. OCSF defines activity 4 = Delete (type_uid 100104).
evidence: schema_emitters.go:579-591 cover Creation, Content Modification, Last Access, Metadata Modification and 'open' only; :597-598 `if action != "" { return 99, action }`. Verifier: ocsfActivity has no Deletion Time or delete case for class 1001, so it falls to 99. Re-ran it: an fs_report row with deleted_at gives activity_id=99, activity_name=delete, type_uid=100199. ECS for the same event gives [deletion]. OCSF 1001 defines 4 = Delete.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_OcsfDeletionActivity: an fs_report row with deleted_at gives OCSF activity_id=99, activity_name=delete, type_uid=100199. ECS for the same event gives event.type [deletion].
impact: OCSF consumers and detections keyed on File Delete (100104) never see deletions from ext dtime, and the output does not conform to the class's activity enum.
fix_proposal: Add `case "Deletion Time": return 4, "Delete"` and `if action == "delete" { return 4, "Delete" }` for class 1001. Regression test: The deleted_at event gives activity_id 4, activity_name "Delete" and type_uid 100104.

title: evtx Level 5 (Verbose) is mapped to severity 'low', ranking above Level 4 (Information)
claim: Windows levels run 1 Critical, 2 Error, 3 Warning, 4 Information, 5 Verbose. Mapping 5 to 'low' makes verbose debug records more severe than informational ones in the ECS and OCSF output.
evidence: schema_events.go:251-254 `case 4: return "informational"  case 5: return "low"`. Verifier: evtxLevelSeverity maps 4 to informational and 5 to low. Re-ran it: OCSF severity_id is 1 for Level 4 and 2 for Level 5, and ECS log.level for Level 5 is 'low'.
repro: zz_dat2_test.go TestZZ2_EvtxVerboseSeverity: OCSF severity_id is 1 for Level 4 and 2 for Level 5; ECS log.level for Level 5 is "low".
impact: Severity filters and sorting in a SIEM surface verbose noise above informational events.
fix_proposal: Map 5 to 'informational' (or to nothing). Regression test: Level 5 severity_id <= Level 4 severity_id.

title: sqlite_query binds a BYTES parameter as its hex text, so it never matches a BLOB
claim: objToSQLParam has no *object.Bytes case, so a buffer falls into the default arm and is bound as o.Inspect(), which is lowercase hex TEXT. Verifier: As stated. The lookup silently returns 'not present'.
evidence: sqlite_builtins.go:276-277 `default: return o.Inspect()`. Verifier: objToSQLParam has no *object.Bytes case, so the default arm returns o.Inspect(). Re-ran it: WHERE k = ?1 with BYTES deadbeef against X'DEADBEEF' gives row_count 0, and typeof(?1)=text, value deadbeef.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_SqliteBytesParamNeverMatchesBlob: a table with k = X'DEADBEEF'; sqlite_query_bytes(db, "... WHERE k = ?1", [BYTES de ad be ef]) gives row_count 0; typeof(?1) = text with value deadbeef.
impact: Looking up evidence by a binary key (a GUID, hash or blob id) silently returns no rows, which reads as 'not present'.
fix_proposal: Add `case *object.Bytes: return v.Value`. Regression test: The query above returns 1 row, and typeof(?1) = blob.

title: sqlite_query rewrites DATETIME/DATE/TIMESTAMP column text: fractions and the stored offset are lost
claim: modernc returns time.Time for columns declared DATE, DATETIME or TIMESTAMP. The converter formats them as UTC RFC3339 with whole seconds, so the value reported differs from what is stored.
evidence: sqlite_builtins.go:258 `return stringObj(x.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339))`. Verifier: sqlite_builtins.go:257-258 formats time.Time as x.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339). Re-ran it: the stored text '2024-01-02 03:04:05.678+05:30' in a DATETIME column is reported as '2024-01-01T21:34:05Z'. Verifier's notes: Priority lowered to P2: most forensic SQLite stores integer epochs, and only declared DATE, DATETIME and TIMESTAMP columns holding text are affected.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_SqliteDatetimeRewritten: stored '2024-01-02 03:04:05.678+05:30' (typeof text) is reported as ts="2024-01-01T21:34:05Z".
impact: Application-database timestamps lose sub-second precision and the recorded offset, and the reported text is not what the evidence contains.
fix_proposal: Use RFC3339Nano at minimum. Better, return the stored text unchanged, for example by scanning such columns as their raw value (CAST(col AS TEXT)) or keeping the original offset. Regression test: The stored value round-trips unchanged (or at least keeps .678 and +05:30).

title: policy_allow and policy_rules document 'or the module source itself' for a STRING, but a STRING is only ever looked up as a policy name
claim: The param doc says the policy argument may be 'the module source itself'. In the code, a STRING is only looked up in policyStore, and only a HASH with a 'module' key is parsed inline.
evidence: policy_engine.go:252-254 `program, ok := policyStore.defs[p.Value]; if !ok { return ..., newError("policy `%s` not found", p.Value) }`. Verifier: resolvePolicyProgram looks up a STRING only in policyStore.defs. metadata.go policy_allow and policy_rules say 'or the module source itself'. Re-ran it: policy_allow(module source, {user: alice}) gives 'policy `package demo ...` not found'.
repro:
zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_PolicyAllowModuleSourceString: policy_allow("package demo
default allow = false
allow { input.user == "alice" }
", {user: "alice"}) gives "policy `package demo ...` not found".
impact: Following the documented form fails, and the LSP and capability reference repeat the wrong contract.
fix_proposal: Either parse a STRING that contains a package clause as an inline module, or change the two param docs to 'policy name, or a {module: ...} hash'. Regression test: The call above returns true, or the metadata test asserts the corrected doc text.

title: Markdown report rendering leaves a line-leading '~~~' fence unescaped, turning the rest of the report into a code block
claim: The block-start escape set is "#>-+=|". A tilde fence is not in it (backtick fences are safe only because ` is escaped inline), so evidence text starting with ~~~ opens a code block that swallows the following headings and findings.
evidence: report.go:945 `const markdownBlockStarters = "#>-+=|"`. Verifier: markdownBlockStarters = "#>-+=|" has no '~'. Re-ran it: report_text('~~~') renders an unescaped '~~~' line, followed by the '## Conclusion' section, which then falls inside a fence.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_MarkdownTildeFence: report_text("~~~") renders the line '~~~' unescaped. The following '## Conclusion' heading and its paragraph render inside the fence.
impact: The report reads wrong and nothing says so, which is the failure the markdown escaping exists to prevent.
fix_proposal: Add '~' to markdownBlockStarters, and escape a leading 4-space indent, which starts an indented code block. Regression test: No rendered line starts with an unescaped ~~~, and the Conclusion heading renders as a heading.

title: fs_exists reports true whenever stat fails for a reason other than not-exist (invalid name, permission, ENOTDIR)
claim: The result is !os.IsNotExist(err), so any other stat error counts as 'exists'.
evidence: fs.go:141 `return resultAndError(boolObj(!os.IsNotExist(err)), nil)`. Verifier: fs.go:141 returns !os.IsNotExist(err). Re-ran it on Windows: fs_exists('...\\no<such>file?.txt') gives true, while os.Stat reports an invalid-name error.
repro: zz_dat2_test.go TestZZ2_FsExistsInvalidName (Windows): fs_exists("...\\no<such>file?.txt") gives true, while os.Stat reports "The filename, directory name, or volume label syntax is incorrect."
impact: A script branches as if a file is present when it is not; for example, on Linux 'file.txt/x' returns ENOTDIR and reads as present.
fix_proposal: Return true only when err == nil, and return (false, err) for errors other than not-exist. Regression test: The invalid name gives false (or an error).

title: bytes_cursor_* copies the whole buffer twice per read and bytes_read_* once, so walking a buffer is quadratic
claim: Each call converts the BYTES payload to a string (a copy), and each cursor step builds a new cursor with another full copy, so the cost per read is O(len) instead of O(1).
evidence: bytes.go:454 `return string(v.Value), nil`; :556 `dataObj = &object.Bytes{Value: []byte(data)}`. Verifier: requireBytesStringArg returns string(v.Value), which copies, and makeBytesCursor does []byte(data), which copies again. Re-ran it at the Go level: 4096 bytes_cursor_read_u8 calls took 93 ms on a 64 KiB buffer and 355 ms on 256 KiB; 4096 bytes_read_u32_le calls took 44 ms and 176 ms. Per-call cost is linear in buffer size. Verifier's notes: Related to M26-VM-001 (the VM-side copy of each variable read) but a separate root cause. Fixing either one alone leaves scripts O(n) per read.
repro: zz_dat_test.go TestZZ_BytesCursorQuadratic (Go-level, no VM): 4096 bytes_cursor_read_u8 took 157.7 ms on a 64 KiB buffer and 570.5 ms on 256 KiB; 4096 bytes_read_u32_le took 84.7 ms and 219.6 ms. Time per call grows linearly with buffer size.
impact: Parsing a multi-MB structure with the cursor API is O(n^2) and impractical. This is separate from M26-VM-001, since the builtin copies even when the VM does not.
fix_proposal: Use requireBinaryArg (which aliases BYTES) and let the cursor share the backing slice; the cursor never mutates it. Regression test: Per-call time of bytes_cursor_read_u8 is flat across 64 KiB and 1 MiB buffers (within 2x).

title: der_parse renders a huge INTEGER to decimal in superlinear time
claim: Every non-int64 INTEGER is converted with big.Int.String(), which is superlinear, and no size bound applies to one element.
evidence: format_binary.go:640 `return stringObj(value.String()), true`. Verifier: derInteger renders every non-int64 INTEGER with big.Int.String(). Re-ran it: a 128 KiB INTEGER took 44 ms and a 512 KiB one 550 ms (12.5x for 4x the size).
repro: zz_dat2_test.go TestZZ2_DerHugeInteger: a 128 KiB INTEGER took 37.9 ms and a 512 KiB one 365.8 ms (9.7x for 4x the size).
impact: A crafted multi-MB DER blob costs minutes of CPU. It is minor because the input size is bounded by memory.
fix_proposal: Render decimal only up to a bound (for example 4 KiB of content) and hex beyond it. Regression test: A 1 MiB INTEGER parses in well under a second.

title: ext_open at any non-zero offset fails with 'invalid ext superblock': libext reads relative to the reader and ignores BaseOffset
claim: The partition-offset feature does not work for ext. Mutant gives libext a reader that starts at image byte 0 (the file itself, or io.NewSectionReader(img, 0, end)) and sets Options.BaseOffset. libext adds BaseOffset only to the offsets it reports. Its reads stay relative to the reader, so it looks for the superblock at image byte 1024 rather than offset+1024. Every ext partition inside a disk image fails to open (bounded or unbounded), and the error says a healthy volume has a corrupt superblock. Every ext_* builtin that needs a handle from ext_open inherits this. Verifier: As stated. The documented partition-offset form of ext_open never works on a real ext volume, and the refusal falsely says the superblock is invalid. The unit tests miss it because ext offsets are tested only through a fake backend.
evidence: filesystem_parsers.go:1852 `fs, err := libext.OpenWithOptions(reader, libext.Options{ ImageSize: uint64(size), BaseOffset: region.Offset,})` where reader comes from filesystem_region.go:217 `io.NewSectionReader(img, 0, region.end())` or the file itself. libext v0.3.0 options.go:22 says 'BaseOffset is added to every absolute disk offset the library reports. Set it to the partition start when the reader is volume-relative'. ext.go:110-111 calls loadSuperblock and superblock.go:7 calls `fs.readAt(superblockOffset, buf)` with superblockOffset=1024 (types.go:6). fs.go readAt calls `fs.r.ReadAt(buf, int64(off))` without adding the base. The memory note partition-offset-opening.md lists libext as 'verified in source', but filesystem_region_test.go:33-34 covers ext only through a fake backend that records the region. The only real-volume offset test is FAT. Repro output: `ext4.img at offset 1 MiB (args=3): open refused: ext_open: invalid ext superblock` (args=2 gives the same), and the same for ext2.img. HFS+, XFS v4 and NTFS open at the same offset. Through the CLI (zzfs1.mut), the carved image lists 5 root entries, but `ext_open(disk-ext4.img, 1048576, 16777216) error: ERROR:ext_open: invalid ext superblock`. Verifier: libext v0.3.0 fs.go:148-155 readAt calls fs.r.ReadAt(buf, int64(off)) with no base; options.go:22-25 says BaseOffset is only added to reported offsets 'when the reader is volume-relative'. filesystem_region.go openVolumeRegion returns the whole file or io.NewSectionReader(img, 0, end), and realEXTBackend.Open passes BaseOffset=region.Offset. The auditor's TestZZEveryFamilyOpensAtAnOffset, re-run in my tree: ext4.img and ext2.img open when carved, but embedded at 1 MiB they give 'ext_open: invalid ext superblock' for both the bounded and unbounded forms. CHANGELOG:101 publishes ext_open's offset argument. Verifier's notes: Loud failure, so no silent wrong content. S2 because the refusal is a false corruption claim about healthy evidence and a published feature is dead for ext.
repro: scratch tree builtin/zz_fs1_offset_test.go TestZZEveryFamilyOpensAtAnOffset: a real mkfs.ext4 or mkfs.ext2 image (WSL, mkimg.sh) streamed 1 MiB into 0xA5 filler, then ExtOpen(path, 1048576, len) and ExtOpen(path, 1048576). The same via mutant.exe with zzfs1.mut.
impact: An ext partition cannot be examined in place. The examiner has to carve it to a file first, which is the step this feature was built to remove. Worse, the message says the evidence is corrupt ('invalid ext superblock'), which is false.
fix_proposal: In realEXTBackend.Open, give libext a volume-relative reader: io.NewSectionReader(img, region.Offset, lengthOrRest), with ImageSize = volume length, and keep BaseOffset = region.Offset so reported offsets stay image-absolute. Correct the libext row in the design note. Report libext's README wording at 379-381 upstream. Regression test: A real ext2 image (hand-built superblock and GDT, or a small checked-in fixture) embedded 1 MiB into non-zero filler: ext_open(path, 1048576[, len]) lists the same root as the carved image, and ext_report fragment offsets equal the carved offsets + 1048576.

title: GPT start/length byte offsets wrap in uint64: a crafted entry is reported at another partition's start_byte and fat_open on it opens that partition
claim: tablePartitionFrom takes libtable's Table.ByteOffset/ByteSize. These are unchecked `t.Offset + p.StartLBA*uint64(t.BlockSize)` and `p.LengthLBA*uint64(BlockSize)`, and table_parsers.go:548-549 casts them to int64. A GPT entry with StartLBA = 2^55+2048 reports start_byte 1048576, which is the byte offset of the real partition. Passed to fat_open, that hash opens the real partition's volume. The custody record and the open result then describe the crafted entry. Another row in the same listing reports a negative length_byte. Verifier: Mechanism as stated. Impact is narrower than claimed: the crafted row can only alias bytes the table already exposes through another partition (it hides nothing), its start_lba is visibly absurd, and the table raises out_of_bounds. The real defects are a wrong start_byte/length_byte in the listing and fsRegionFromPartition accepting that row. This is a correctness defect on untrusted input, not an embargo-worthy verification bypass.
evidence: libtable partition/types.go:182 `return t.Offset + p.StartLBA*uint64(t.BlockSize)`. Repro output: `row: name=crafted start_lba=36028797018966016 start_byte=1048576 length_byte=2621440 allocated=true`, the same start_byte as `name=real start_lba=2048 start_byte=1048576`. Then `fat_open(crafted partition hash) = {bounded: true, ... volume_length: 2621440, volume_offset: 1048576}`, and fat_list_files lists the real volume's /SUBDIR. The gap row is `start_lba=16384 start_byte=8388608 length_byte=-7340032`. libtable raised only warning_codes=[out_of_bounds], which Mutant surfaces and then ignores when it builds the byte fields. Verifier: libtable partition/types.go:181-188 ByteOffset/ByteSize are unchecked uint64 arithmetic, and table_parsers.go:548-549 casts them with int64(). Re-run TestZZTableGPTStartByteWraps: the 'crafted' row has start_lba=36028797018966016 and start_byte=1048576, the same as 'real'. fat_open(crafted row) returns bounded:true, volume_offset 1048576 and lists /SUBDIR of the real volume. A gap row has length_byte=-7340032. table warning_codes=[out_of_bounds]. Verifier's notes: Downgraded from S2 security. Kept P1 because the trigger is untrusted evidence and the fix (bits.Mul64/Add64, refuse the row's byte fields) is small.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_test.go TestZZTableGPTStartByteWraps: buildTestGPTImage with entries 'real' at LBA 2048 and 'crafted' at LBA 2^55+2048, a FAT16 volume at LBA 2048, then TableOpen, table_list_partitions, and FatOpen(path, craftedHash).
impact: A partition table written by an adversary can alias a partition to another's bytes. The examiner analyses the 'crafted' partition, gets the other volume's content, and the manifest records the wrong partition as opened. Negative or wrapped lengths also corrupt any sum over the listing.
fix_proposal: Compute start and length with overflow checks (math/bits.Mul64/Add64). When a result overflows or exceeds MaxInt64, report start_byte/length_byte as -1 with a per-row `byte_range_valid:false`, or refuse the row's byte fields. In fsRegionFromPartition, reject a hash whose byte range is invalid. Regression test: GPT with an entry at StartLBA 2^55+2048: the row's start_byte != the real partition's, and fat_open(path, row) is refused. No row has a negative length_byte.

title: Streaming extract/hash report truncated=false when the image ends inside a file; read_file_at returns 0 bytes with no error
claim: fsStreamSection bounds the copy at Located, and `truncated` is computed only from Located < Size. When the image, or a bounded partition, ends inside a file's clusters, the underlying ReadAt returns io.EOF. io.Copy treats that as a clean end. fat_extract_file then writes a prefix under the file's name with truncated=false and a digest of the prefix, and fat_hash_file does the same. fsReadWindow accepts a short read with io.EOF and returns a 0-byte buffer for an offset inside located_bytes. Its own comment (228-230) and the metadata say that case must be an error. The whole-file read on the same file refuses correctly. Verifier: As stated. bytes_written/bytes_hashed do expose the shortfall, but the documented gate (read `truncated` before trusting `digest`) reads false.
evidence: filesystem_stream.go:132 `"truncated": boolObj(reader.truncated())` and :35 `func (r fsFileReader) truncated() bool { return r.Located < r.Size }`. :242 `if err != nil && err != io.EOF {`. fsWriteEvidenceFile never compares `written` with the expected length. Repro output: `truncated image, unbounded open: extract size=65536 located=65536 bytes_written=32112 truncated=false on_disk=32112 digest_is_full_file=false`. `hash bytes_hashed=32112 located=65536 truncated=false`. `fat_read_file_at(40000, 4096) returned 0 bytes and no error`. The case bounded to a partition shorter than the volume gives identical numbers. Meanwhile `fat_read_file_bytes ... refuses: cluster chain shorter than entry size: 32112 of 65536 bytes`. The metadata for fat_extract_file says 'read `truncated` before treating `digest` as the file's digest'. Existing tests (TestATruncatedChainExtractsItsPrefixAndSaysSo) cover only Located<Size, and TestAnExtractionThatFailsPartWay... covers only a reader that errors. Verifier: filesystem_stream.go:35 truncated() is Located<Size only. :94-97 SectionReader bounded at Located. io.Copy treats the EOF from a short underlying read as success. :242 accepts io.EOF with a short read. Re-run TestZZStreamShortReadReportedComplete (FAT16 cut to 70000 bytes, and bounded to 70000): fat_extract_file bytes_written=32112 located=65536 truncated=false. fat_hash_file bytes_hashed=32112 truncated=false. fat_read_file_at(40000,4096) returns 0 bytes and no error. fat_read_file_bytes on the same file refuses. fsReadWindow's own comment (228-230) says a short buffer here would hide the finding. Verifier's notes: Could argue P0 (it breaks a documented integrity gate), but the shortfall is visible in bytes_written, so I kept P1.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_test.go TestZZStreamShortReadReportedComplete: a FAT16 volume (buildFAT16Image plus writeFATFileEntry, 65536-byte file) cut to 70000 bytes, and also opened fat_open(p, 0, 70000); then FatExtractFile, FatHashFile, FatReadFileAt(40000, 4096).
impact: A truncated acquisition yields extracted evidence files and hashes that claim to be complete. A script that follows the docs quotes the digest of a prefix as the file's digest, and the prefix sits on disk under the file's name. This applies to all six families, since NTFS, ext, HFS and XFS set Located = Size.
fix_proposal: In fsExtractFile and fsHashFile, compare the bytes copied with reader.Located. On a shortfall, either error out (removing the partial output) or set truncated=true with a `short_read` reason and the true byte count. In fsReadWindow, treat read < length inside Located as an error that names both numbers. Regression test: FAT16 volume cut inside a file: extract and hash must return an error or truncated=true when bytes_written < located_bytes; read_file_at(offset inside located, n) must error rather than return a short or empty buffer.

title: *_verify reports verified=true on HFS+, XFS v4 and ext2, formats the family says carry nothing to verify; a check that examined 0 things counts as passed
claim: The file header, the metadata ('a volume with nothing checkable is never verified'; for HFS, 'an integrity claim about an HFS+ volume has to rest on the image's own digests ... rather than on the filesystem') and the design note ('A format with no checksums reports verified: false, checks_run: 0') all promise that a no-checksum format is not verified. The code instead adds structural or flag 'checks' with Checked:true, so verified() returns true. On HFS, parser_anomalies is Checked:true, Passed:true with Examined:0, and its own detail says it is 'not about the volume'. Verifier: Partly right. HFS+ reporting verified=true contradicts the published CHANGELOG promise, the file's own design comment and the test's motivating case. parser_anomalies counts as a run check with examined 0 ('not about the volume'), and btree_headers is structural. The XFS v4 part is by design (pinned by a test comment). The ext2 part is consistent with the reference doc, which counts superblock_plausibility as a run check. The defect is that structural/flag observations can carry `verified` on a format with no integrity mechanism, most clearly HFS+.
evidence: filesystem_verify.go:747-756 `Name: "parser_anomalies", Checked: true, Passed: true, Examined: 0`. :808-810 `Name: "clean_state", Checked: true, Passed: !needsRepair` (its detail says 'not a check of the bytes'). :312-314 `superblock_plausibility ... Checked: true`. Repro output on mkfs-made images: `hfs_verify(hfsplus.img): verified=true checks_run=2 ... parser_anomalies(checked=true passed=true examined=0)`. `xfs_verify(xfs4.img): verified=true checks_run=1 checks=superblock_crc(checked=false ...) clean_state(checked=true passed=true examined=1)`. `ext_verify(ext2.img): verified=true checks_run=1 ... metadata_checksums(checked=false ...)`. The CLI prints `hfs_verify(hfsplus.img): verified =true checks_run =2`. The only real-volume verify tests are FAT (filesystem_verify_test.go:544-619). Verifier: Re-run TestZZVerifyNoChecksumFormats: hfs_verify(hfsplus.img) gives verified=true checks_run=2, with parser_anomalies checked=true passed=true examined=0. xfs_verify(xfs4.img) gives verified=true via clean_state. ext_verify(ext2.img) gives verified=true via superblock_plausibility. CHANGELOG 2.6.0 says 'one boolean would have an HFS+ volume assert a check its format does not contain'. filesystem_verify.go:3-35 says HFS+ 'carries nothing at all', and verified()'s doc says a no-checksum format 'reports false with checks_run zero'. TestVerifiedNeedsACheckToHaveRun names HFS+ as 'the case that motivates the rule'. However, the same test says 'An unavailable check must not drag down a real pass, or a v4 XFS volume whose other checks all held could never be verified', so XFS v4 verified via clean_state is deliberate. CAPABILITY_REFERENCE for ext_verify/hfs_verify also describes the structural checks as checks that run. Verifier's notes: Downgraded to S3: the checks array plainly shows metadata_checksums unchecked, and the reference doc describes the structural checks. It is still a broken published promise for HFS+.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_test.go TestZZVerifyNoChecksumFormats on hfsplus.img, xfs4.img (mkfs.xfs -m crc=0) and ext2.img (-O ^metadata_csum), built with WSL mkimg.sh; plus zzfs1.mut run through mutant.exe.
impact: A report template that reads `verified` states that an HFS+, XFS v4 or ext2 volume was integrity-verified when the format has no integrity mechanism. The family was designed to prevent exactly this failure (EVIDENCE_HANDLING_POLICY: 'looks like verification').
fix_proposal: Separate integrity checks from structural observations. Either give fsVerifyCheck a kind (`integrity` vs `structural`/`flag`) and have verified() count only integrity checks, or set Checked:false for structural and flag checks. Never count a check with Examined==0 as run. Update the three metadata summaries to match. Regression test: Real HFS+, XFS v4 and ext2 (no metadata_csum) images: verified=false, the checksum check unavailable, and no passing check with examined 0.

title: ntfs_verify treats MFT records it cannot read (I/O errors) as unallocated, so a truncated MFT verifies
claim: The `default:` branch is documented as 'ErrInvalidMFTEntry covers a never-written record ...' but it swallows every error, including libntfs I/O errors for records that lie past the end of the image. When half the MFT is missing, examined drops from 8 to 4, no finding is raised, and verified=true. Verifier: As stated. Unreadable MFT records (I/O/EOF) are silently dropped from the denominator, so a truncated MFT verifies with no finding.
evidence: filesystem_verify.go:621-627 `default: // ErrInvalidMFTEntry covers ...` (no errors.Is check). libntfs returns `I/O read at offset 0x5000 (size 1024): EOF` with errors.Is(err, ErrInvalidMFTEntry)=false for entries 4-7 (TestZZNTFSSkippedErrorKinds). Repro output: `whole image: verified=true checks=mft_update_sequence(checked=true passed=true examined=8)` and `image cut inside the MFT: verified=true ... examined=4 findings=0`. In the crafted-run case, 262,144 claimed records with 262,136 unreadable still give verified=true, examined=8. Verifier: filesystem_verify.go:621-627 `default:` has no errors.Is(ErrInvalidMFTEntry) test. TestZZNTFSSkippedErrorKinds: entries 4-7 of an image cut at 20480 bytes return 'I/O read at offset 0x5000 (size 1024): EOF', and errors.Is(ErrInvalidMFTEntry)=false. TestZZNTFSVerifyTruncatedMFT: whole image examined=8 verified=true; cut image examined=4, findings=0, verified=true. The CAPABILITY_REFERENCE says only records that are 'unallocated or that the volume marked bad are skipped'. Verifier's notes: Not a fixup-tamper bypass: a torn record is still caught. Truncation would also show in image digests, so this is P1, not P0.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_test.go TestZZNTFSVerifyTruncatedMFT: ntfs.img dumped from libntfs's own buildTestNTFSImage (scratch copy libcopy/libntfs) cut to 20480 bytes, then NtfsOpen and NtfsVerify.
impact: An NTFS volume whose MFT is truncated or unreadable is reported as verified with no finding. The volume is at its least verifiable, and the report says the opposite.
fix_proposal: Handle errors.Is(err, libntfs.ErrInvalidMFTEntry) as the skip case. Count every other error as an unreadable record, add a finding, and fail the check (or add an `mft_readable` check). Report unreadable count beside examined. Regression test: NTFS fixture cut inside the MFT: ntfs_verify has verified=false, or a failed check with a finding that names the unreadable records.

title: ntfs_verify and ntfs_report iterate an MFT record count taken from $MFT's own data run, unbounded by the image and uncancellable
claim: libntfs MFTEntryCount is sum(run.LengthClusters*bytesPerCluster)/recordSize, taken straight from the image. ntfs_verify loops that many times calling GetMFTEntry, and ntfs_report calls Report() (not ReportContext), which does the same. A 64 KiB crafted image can claim billions of records. Time grows linearly with the claimed count, and nothing cancels it. Verifier: As stated. A crafted 64 KiB NTFS image makes ntfs_verify/ntfs_report run for hours, and nothing cancels them.
evidence: libntfs file.go:231-242 maxMFTEntries has no image bound. filesystem_verify.go:601 `for entryNum := uint64(0); entryNum < count; entryNum++`. Repro on a 64 KiB image: `clusters=0x4000 MFTEntryCount=65536: ntfs_verify took 409.8ms`, `clusters=0x10000 MFTEntryCount=262144: ntfs_verify took 1.658s`, `ratio for 4x the claimed clusters: 4.0x`. ntfs_report goes 316ms to 1.250s (3.95x) and returns complete=true. At 0x0FFFFFFF clusters (1,073,741,820 records) that extrapolates to about 1.9 h per call. With an 8-byte run length the count is effectively unbounded. Verifier: libntfs v0.3.3 file.go maxMFTEntries = sum(run.LengthClusters*bytesPerCluster)/recordSize, with no image bound. filesystem_verify.go:601 loops count times. filesystem_report.go:640 calls s.volume.Report(), which is ReportContext(context.Background()). My re-run on a 64 KiB image: ntfs_verify took 333ms at 0x4000 clusters and 1.24s at 0x10000 (3.7x). ntfs_report took 312ms and then 1.28s, and reports complete=true with file_count=0. Time grows linearly with a count the evidence declares. Verifier's notes: Same untrusted MFTEntryCount as FS2.03 (ntfs_deleted OOM), but a different sink and failure mode (time, not allocation), so I did not mark it a duplicate. One bounded-count helper should fix all three call sites.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_test.go TestZZNTFSVerifyUnboundedMFTCount and zz_fs1_ntfsreport_test.go: patch the $MFT data run in record 0 to lengthSize 4 (0x14, clusters LE, 0x04) and time NtfsVerify and NtfsReport at two sizes, under a 1 GiB heap watchdog.
impact: A crafted NTFS image hangs a verification or report run for hours, a denial of service against a triage pipeline. The report also claims complete=true over records it never read.
fix_proposal: Cap count at (volume length or image size) / recordSize before looping, and raise a finding when the $MFT run claims more than the image holds. Call ReportContext with a context the builtin can cancel. Consider sharing the context/deadline mechanism other long builtins use. Regression test: 64 KiB NTFS with a $MFT run claiming 0x0FFFFFFF clusters: ntfs_verify and ntfs_report return in < 1 s, with a finding or warning that the MFT claims more records than the image can hold.

title: exFAT path lookup returns the first same-named entry, deleted or not: the listed live file cannot be read and xfat_metadata describes the deleted one
claim: libxfat's ReadRootDir and ReadDir return deleted (0x05) entry sets beside live ones. xfatFindEntryByName returns the first case-insensitive name match without checking IsDeleted, and findEntryByPath caches it. When a directory holds a deleted 'a.txt' ahead of a live 'a.txt' (a file deleted and re-created, which is how many editors save), xfat_read_file, xfat_hash_file and xfat_extract_file on the listed live path fail, and xfat_metadata reports the deleted entry's size and cluster as the live file's.
evidence: filesystem_parsers.go:2738-2742 `for _, entry := range entries { entryName := strings.TrimSpace(entry.Name()); if strings.EqualFold(entryName, name) { return entry, true } }`. Repro output: `listed path=/a.txt deleted=true size=20`, `listed path=/a.txt deleted=false size=17`, `xfat_read_file_bytes(/a.txt) of the live, listed file failed: xfat_read_file_bytes: unable to read deleted entry`, `xfat_hash_file(/a.txt) failed: ... unable to read deleted entry`, `xfat_metadata(/a.txt): deleted=true size=20 entry_cluster=4`. The only unit test, TestXFATFindEntryByNameHelper (filesystem_parsers_test.go:1054-1059), checks an empty slice. Verifier: filesystem_parsers.go:2737-2745 xfatFindEntryByName returns the first EqualFold match without checking IsDeleted, and findEntryByPath caches it (2716). Re-run TestZZXFATPathResolvesToDeletedEntry: the listing shows /a.txt twice (deleted size 20, live size 17). xfat_read_file_bytes and xfat_hash_file on /a.txt fail with 'unable to read deleted entry'. xfat_metadata(/a.txt) reports deleted=true size=20 entry_cluster=4. Verifier's notes: A deleted set ahead of a live same-named set is routine on exFAT media, and an adversary can also plant one.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_test.go TestZZXFATPathResolvesToDeletedEntry: a hand-built exFAT volume (strict mode, valid set checksums) whose root holds a deleted a.txt set (cluster 4) and then a live a.txt set (cluster 3).
impact: On exFAT media (SD cards, USB sticks) the live file at a path cannot be extracted or hashed. Its metadata (size, cluster, times) is silently replaced by a deleted predecessor's, which is a wrong forensic answer.
fix_proposal: In xfatFindEntryByName, prefer a non-deleted match and skip deleted entries entirely for path resolution (deleted entries are reachable through xfat_deleted and xfat_recover_file). Key the cache on the resolved entry. Regression test: The same fixture: xfat_read_file_bytes('/a.txt') returns 'LIVE FILE CONTENT', and xfat_metadata reports deleted=false size=17.

title: normalizeFSPath rewrites '\' to '/', so a listed name containing a backslash reads a different file or cannot be read
claim: Listings build paths with joinFSPath, which keeps a backslash in an entry name. Every read and metadata builtin passes the path through normalizeFSPath, which replaces '\' with '/' (and trims whitespace). On ext, XFS and HFS+ a backslash is a legal name character. So reading the path a listing returned resolves a different path: another file's content, or 'not found'. systemd writes such names on every Linux host (for example `mnt-data\x2dbackup.mount`). Verifier: As stated. The common case (systemd-escaped unit names) fails loudly. A crafted 'x\y' beside a directory 'x' silently returns decoy content under the listed name.
evidence: filesystem_parsers.go:2758 `v = strings.ReplaceAll(v, "\\", "/")`. Repro on a mkfs.ext4 -d image: `ext_read_file_bytes("/a\\b") = "CONTENT-OF-A-SLASH-B\n"`, which is the content of /a/b, not of the 26-byte file named 'a\b'. Also `listed path "/etc/systemd/system/mnt-data\\x2dbackup.mount" (size 31) cannot be read back: ext_read_file_bytes: path not found: /etc/systemd/system/mnt-data/x2dbackup.mount`. TestNormalizeFSPathCannotEscapeVolumeRoot asserts the rewrite as intended behaviour. Verifier: filesystem_parsers.go:2758 normalizeFSPath does strings.ReplaceAll(v, "\\", "/") and TrimSpace, while joinFSPath keeps the raw name. Re-run TestZZExtBackslashNames on a mkfs.ext4 image: ext_read_file_bytes("/a\\b") returns "CONTENT-OF-A-SLASH-B\n" (the content of /a/b). The listed /etc/systemd/system/mnt-data\\x2dbackup.mount gives 'path not found: .../mnt-data/x2dbackup.mount'. The rewrite was added deliberately to stop '\..' escapes, but its effect on ext/XFS/HFS+ names that legally contain a backslash is not documented. Verifier's notes: S2 rests on the silent decoy case from untrusted evidence.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_test.go TestZZExtBackslashNames on ext4.img from WSL mkimg.sh (files 'a/b', 'a\b', 'etc/systemd/system/mnt-data\x2dbackup.mount').
impact: Real systemd unit files, which are routine persistence evidence, are unreadable by the path the listing gives. An adversary who names a file 'x\y' beside a directory 'x' makes the examiner read decoy content under the listed name.
fix_proposal: Stop translating backslashes for filesystems where they are legal name bytes (ext, XFS, HFS+), or translate only for NTFS/FAT/exFAT. Stop TrimSpace-ing path components. Alternatively, accept a path array or an inode/identity form so a listed entry can be addressed exactly. Regression test: ext image with 'a\b' and 'a/b': ext_read_file(path from ext_list_files) returns the listed file's own bytes, and its length equals the listed size.

title: ewf_open_partial reports partial=false for an explicit segment list with a hole and for a set whose last segment has no done-section
claim: `partial` is derived only from filename discovery, which is skipped for arrays of two or more paths and cannot see a set truncated at its end. libewf is opened with AllowIncompleteSegmentSet and accepts both incomplete cases, and the reader's own metadata shows it (has_done_section=false, observed_chunk_count < number_of_chunks). The field that the docs say 'carr[ies] the caveat into whatever report is built' reads false. Verifier: As stated for the flag. Impact is smaller than claimed: the caller explicitly used ewf_open_partial, the docs forbid hashing/carving its output, and custody records the op name. The defect is a broken doc promise on the report field.
evidence: Repro output: `ewf_open_partial(end-truncated set): partial=false missing=[] segments=[img.E01 img.E02] ... has_done=false total=24 observed_chunks=2 declared_chunks=3` (ewf_open on the same set refuses: 'highest segment 2 has no done section'). `ewf_open_partial(list with hole): partial=false missing=[] segments=[img.E01 img.E03] ... observed_chunks=2 declared_chunks=3` (ewf_open refuses: 'segment 2 is missing'). The ewf_open_partial metadata lists 'one whose final segment carries no done-section' as a case it opens and says partial carries the caveat. TestEWFOpenPartialProceedsPastAHoleAndSaysSo uses only a fake Discover. Verifier: disk_image_parsers.go:582 partial = len(discovered.MissingNumbers) > 0, and discovery runs only when len(segmentPaths)==1. Re-run TestZZEWFPartialFlag: ewf_open_partial on the end-truncated {E01,E02} gives partial=false has_done=false observed_chunks=2 declared=3. [E01,E03] gives partial=false missing=[]. ewf_open refuses both. CAPABILITY_REFERENCE:865 says partial/missing_segments 'carry the caveat into whatever report is built'. Verifier's notes: Downgraded from S2.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_ewf_test.go TestZZEWFPartialFlag: EWF v1 segments built with a copy of libewf's own test writer (3 segments, one 8-byte chunk each), opening {E01,E02} by path and [E01,E03] as an array.
impact: A report built from the open result states that a partial image is whole. Hashes and carves over it describe something other than the acquired media, and nothing in the returned hash says so.
fix_proposal: Set partial = allowIncomplete && (discovered missing || !reader.Metadata().HasDoneSection || ObservedChunkCount < Media.NumberOfChunks || the first segment != 1), computed after Open. Fill missing_segments from the reader's segment numbers when discovery was skipped. Regression test: ewf_open_partial on {E01,E02} of a 3-segment set, and on [E01,E03], both return partial=true, and the second has missing_segments=[2].

title: ewf_open_partial on one path of a holed set opens only that file, dropping the segments that are present
claim: On a hole, realEWFBackend.Discover returns MissingNumbers but no Paths, so ewfOpen falls back to opening only the path it was given. ewf_open_partial(E01) of set {1,3} decodes E01 alone and never opens the present E03. Named by E03, it opens E03 alone, which has no volume section, and every read fails. The docs say the set is discovered from any member, and libewf's OpenPathWithOptions with AllowIncompleteSegmentSet would open the present members.
evidence: disk_image_parsers.go:1091-1099 returns `ewfSegmentSet{Contiguous: false, PresentCount: ..., MissingNumbers: numbers, MissingFiles: ...}` with Paths nil. Repro output: `ewf_open_partial(img.E01, set 1+3): partial=true missing=[2] segments=[img.E01] device="AAAAAAAA" ... observed_chunks=1` and `ewf_open_partial(img.E03, set 1+3): partial=true missing=[2] segments=[img.E03] device="<read error: ewf_read_at: reader: no usable media geometry: libewf: corrupt image>" total=0`. The unit test TestEWFOpenPartialProceedsPastAHoleAndSaysSo passes only because its fake Discover returns Paths [E01, E03], which the real backend never does. Verifier: disk_image_parsers.go:1091-1099 returns an ewfSegmentSet with Paths nil on MissingSegmentsError, so ewfOpen opens only the named path. Re-run TestZZEWFPartialDiscoveryDropsPresentSegments: E01 of set {1,3} gives segments=[img.E01] device='AAAAAAAA'. E03 gives segments=[img.E03] and a read error 'no usable media geometry'. The unit test's fake Discover returns Paths, which the real backend never does.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_ewf_test.go TestZZEWFPartialDiscoveryDropsPresentSegments.
impact: Triage of damaged EWF evidence decodes less than is available, and the result depends on which member the script names. The segments list and custody record omit files that were present.
fix_proposal: On MissingSegmentsError, build the present paths (a directory scan with libewf's family rules, or libewf.OpenPathWithOptions(path, AllowIncompleteSegmentSet()), recording which files that reader opened). Make the fake Discover in the tests match the real backend. Regression test: Set {1,3}: ewf_open_partial(E01) and ewf_open_partial(E03) both give segments=[E01,E03] and the same device bytes.

title: hfs_verify reports a critical failure on every classic HFS volume for an attributes b-tree the format does not have
claim: hfs_verify always reads the catalog, extents and attributes b-tree headers and counts any error as a failed check. Classic HFS (and HFS+ without an attributes file) has no attributes b-tree. libhfs returns ErrMissingExtent, IsCorrupt() is true, and a freshly formatted volume gets checks_failed=1 and a 'critical' finding. Verifier: As stated for classic HFS. The HFS+-without-attributes-file case is plausible but was not reproduced.
evidence: filesystem_verify.go:682 `{"attributes", s.volume.AttributesBTreeHeader}` and :686-697 `failed++ ... if libhfs.IsCorrupt(err) { severity = "critical" }`. Repro on mkfs.hfs output: `hfs_verify(hfs.img): verified=false checks_run=2 checks_failed=1 ... btree_headers(checked=true passed=false examined=3) ... findings=[critical/attributes b-tree header/header could not be read]`. Verifier: filesystem_verify.go:676-711 always reads the attributes b-tree header and scores an IsCorrupt error as critical. Re-run on hfs.img (mkfs.hfs -h, classic HFS): verified=false checks_failed=1, finding critical/'attributes b-tree header'/'header could not be read'. HFS+ from mkfs.hfsplus passes 3/3.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_test.go TestZZVerifyNoChecksumFormats (hfs.img from `mkfs.hfs -h`).
impact: A pristine legacy HFS volume is reported as structurally damaged with a critical finding, a false corruption claim in an examiner's report.
fix_proposal: Skip the attributes tree when the volume has none (libhfs Capabilities().ExtendedAttributes false, or header.AttributesFile.TotalBlocks == 0) and report it as absent by format, not failed. Regression test: Classic HFS image: hfs_verify has checks_failed=0 and no critical finding.

title: ext_report fragments: length off by one per fragment (libext EndOffset is inclusive) and file_offset ignores holes
claim: libext's FileFragment.EndOffset is inclusive and holes are omitted. Mutant passes length 0, so fsLocatedFragment derives `end - start` (one byte short per run), and file_offset is set to the running sum of those lengths (which ignores holes and inherits the off-by-one). ext is also the only report whose end_offset is inclusive, while ntfs and fat use exclusive, so the 'one shape' is not one shape.
evidence: libext report.go:122 'Offsets are inclusive of EndOffset'; report.go:176 `end := (e.PhysicalBlock+e.Blocks)*blockSize - 1`. Mutant :837-838 `fsLocatedFragment(fragment.StartOffset, fragment.EndOffset, file.Layout.BytesCovered, 0, ...)`. Repro on /sparse.bin (debugfs EXTENTS: (0):1298, (256):1299): `fragment 0: {end_offset: 5320703, file_offset: 0, length: 4095, ...}`, `fragment 1: {end_offset: 5324799, file_offset: 4095, length: 4095, ...}`, `layout={... bytes_covered: 8190 ...}`. The expected values are length 4096, fragment 1 file_offset 1048576, and bytes_covered 8192. The unit test TestALocatedFragmentKeepsItsOffsetsAndDerivesItsLength asserts exclusive-end derivation, but ext, its only caller, passes an inclusive end. Verifier: libext report.go:122 'Offsets are inclusive of EndOffset'. filesystem_report.go:831-843 passes length 0, so fsLocatedFragment (587-589) derives end-start, and file_offset is the running BytesCovered. The code comment assumes 'the runs tile the file in order'. Re-run TestZZExtReportSparseFragments: both fragments length 4095, fragment 1 file_offset 4095 (debugfs says logical block 256 = 1048576), bytes_covered 8190.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_test.go TestZZExtReportSparseFragments on ext4.img (mkfs.ext4 -d with a 2-extent sparse file).
impact: A carve or timeline driven by ext_report fragments drops the last byte of every run and places the data of sparse files at the wrong file offsets.
fix_proposal: For ext, pass length = end - start + 1 and render end_offset as end+1 (exclusive, matching the other five). Take file_offset from the extent's logical block (libext Extent.LogicalBlock via the extent map) rather than a running sum. Do the same for the volume-level end_offset. Regression test: ext image with extents (0):A and (256):B: fragments have length 4096, file_offsets 0 and 1048576, and bytes_covered 8192.

title: ext_report ignores libext's warnings: a file whose block map could not be read is reported with no fragments and complete=true
claim: realEXTSession.Report never reads s.fs.Warnings(). libext records WarnDegradedRead when an inode's extent tree is unreadable and emits the row with no fragments. ext_report sets Complete:true and raises no layout warning, unlike the FAT and exFAT reports, which count a failed layout.
evidence: There is no s.fs.Warnings() call between 763 and 859. The report is initialised `Complete: true, WarningsAvailable: true`, and failedRows passed to fsReportFragmentWarnings is 0. Repro output: `/a/b row: size=21 fragments=[] layout={... derived: extent_map, error: , ...}`, `report: complete=true warning_codes=[listing_not_reconciled]`, while the same handle's libext warnings (via ext_metadata) are `[degraded_read: inode 13 block map is unreadable (... bad extent node magic 0x0000); reported without fragments]`. Verifier: filesystem_report.go:763-859 never reads s.fs.Warnings(), and fsReportFragmentWarnings gets failedRows 0. Re-run TestZZExtReportDropsLibextWarnings: /a/b size=21 fragments=[] with an empty layout.error, report complete=true with only listing_not_reconciled, while libext holds degraded_read for inode 13. Verifier's notes: Distinct from FS2.08 (the libext warning cap in ext_deleted/ext_xattrs).
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_test.go TestZZExtReportDropsLibextWarnings: zero the extent-header magic of /a/b's inode in ext4.img, then ExtReport.
impact: A damaged inode reads like a file with no data, in a document that claims to be complete.
fix_proposal: Fold s.fs.Warnings() into the report (degraded_read to layout_not_resolved on the row, and to incomplete). Set layout.error for rows with size>0 and no fragments. Regression test: Same corrupted fixture: ext_report has complete=false, and the /a/b row has layout.error set with a layout warning code.

title: A region whose offset+length overflows int64 passes the image-size check and is opened 'bounded' with an unbounded reader
claim: end() = Offset+Length overflows to a negative number for a non-zero offset with a huge length. The check `region.end() > size` then passes. io.NewSectionReader(img, 0, negative) overflows its own arithmetic and sets remaining=MaxInt64, so the open succeeds with bounded:true and volume_length MaxInt64 while reads are not bounded. A crafted partition hash (length_byte just under 2^63) reaches this. Verifier: As stated. Reachable from a crafted partition hash via FS1.02-style lengths.
evidence: filesystem_region.go:67 `return r.Offset + r.Length`. Repro: `FatOpen(path, 4096, 1<<63-1)` succeeded, and the test aborted with 'fat_open accepted a region that runs past the image' (the handle stayed open, as the TempDir cleanup error shows). With offset 0 the same length is refused as 'runs to byte ...'. Verifier: filesystem_region.go:63-68 end() = Offset+Length with no overflow check, and openVolumeRegion's `region.end() > size` passes on a negative end. Re-run TestZZRegionEndOverflow: FatOpen(path, 4096, MaxInt64) succeeded (the handle stayed open and blocked TempDir cleanup). With offset 0 the same length is refused.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_test.go TestZZRegionEndOverflow (embedVolume FAT16 at 4096).
impact: The truncated-image refusal and the bounded guarantee (no reading into the neighbouring partition) are both bypassed by an over-long length.
fix_proposal: In validateFSRegion, reject Length > math.MaxInt64 - Offset. Regression test: fat_open(path, 4096, MaxInt64) is refused with 'runs to byte'/overflow.

title: xfs_report start_offset and end_offset are always 0
claim: The XFS report never sets StartOffset or EndOffset (libxfs's XFSReport carries no volume range), so the shared fields read 0/0 for every XFS volume, including one opened at an offset. The other five fill them in.
evidence: The fsReport literal at 1328 omits StartOffset/EndOffset. Repro output: `xfs_report start_offset=0 end_offset=0 blocks=81920 block_size=4096` on a 335,544,320-byte volume. Verifier: The fsReport literal at filesystem_report.go:1328-1339 sets no StartOffset/EndOffset. Re-run TestZZXFSReportOffsets: start_offset=0 end_offset=0 for a 335544320-byte volume.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_test.go TestZZXFSReportOffsets on xfs4.img.
impact: A consumer that intersects report ranges across volumes (the purpose of the image-absolute convention) treats every XFS volume as an empty range at byte 0.
fix_proposal: Set StartOffset = region offset (pass it to the session) and EndOffset = offset + NumberOfBlocks*BlockSize. Regression test: xfs_report on xfs4.img: end_offset == blocks*block_size; opened at 1 MiB, start_offset == 1048576.

title: vhdi_discover emits duplicate-identity warnings in map iteration order
claim: The duplicate_link_identity warnings come from `for identity, paths := range byIdentity`, so the same directory produces its warnings in a different order from call to call.
evidence: disk_image_extents.go:1179 `for identity, paths := range byIdentity {`. Repro: `distinct duplicate-warning orders over 40 calls on one directory: map[a1.vhd,b1.vhd,c1.vhd:27 b1.vhd,c1.vhd,a1.vhd:7 c1.vhd,a1.vhd,b1.vhd:6]`. Verifier: disk_image_extents.go:1179 `for identity, paths := range byIdentity` emits the warnings in map order. Re-run: 3 distinct orders over 40 calls on one directory (29/3/8).

title: *_hash_file labels its digest with the raw argument: algorithm "" (the documented default) or "SHA256"
claim: fsHashAlgorithm accepts "" and any case, but the result echoes the argument instead of the canonical algorithm name, so a sha256 digest can be labelled "" or "SHA256".
evidence: Repro output: `fat_hash_file(algorithm="") -> algorithm="" digest=9af4c73b...` and `fat_hash_file(algorithm="SHA256") -> algorithm="SHA256"` (same digest). The metadata says 'An empty string means sha256'. Verifier: filesystem_stream.go:171 renders stringObj(algorithm), the raw argument. Re-run TestZZHashFileAlgorithmLabel: algorithm "" and "SHA256" are echoed verbatim, with the same sha256 digest.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_misc_test.go TestZZHashFileAlgorithmLabel.
impact: A hash-set lookup or report keyed on the algorithm field misfiles or omits the digest.
fix_proposal: Return the canonical name ("md5"/"sha1"/"sha256") from fsHashAlgorithm and render that. Regression test: algorithm "" and "SHA256" both return algorithm "sha256".

title: ewf_open expands a one-element array by discovery, contradicting 'an array of paths (taken as given)'
claim: The code discovers whenever len(segmentPaths)==1, whatever the argument's form. The docs say an array is taken as given and nothing is discovered. Verifier: As stated. The code comment and the public doc disagree.
evidence: disk_image_parsers.go:533 `if len(segmentPaths) == 1 {`. Repro: `ewf_open([img.E01]): ... segments=[img.E01 img.E02 img.E03]`. Verifier: disk_image_parsers.go:533 discovers whenever len(segmentPaths)==1, and its own comment says 'two or more paths is taken as given'. CAPABILITY_REFERENCE:864 says 'Given an array of paths, those files are taken as given and nothing is discovered'. Re-run: ewf_open([img.E01]) gives segments=[E01,E02,E03].
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs1_misc_test.go TestZZEWFOneElementArrayIsDiscovered.
impact: A script cannot open one segment deliberately. The documented escape hatch does not work for a single file.
fix_proposal: Discover only when argument 1 was a STRING, or change the docs to say 'two or more paths'. Regression test: ewf_open([E01]) opens segments=[E01] only (or the docs state otherwise).

title: Stale comments: maxInMemoryReadBytes says xfat stages through a temp file; ntfs_verify's default branch claims it is ErrInvalidMFTEntry
claim: disk_image_parsers.go:20-22 says xfat_read_file 'has to stage its content through a temp file', but filesystem_parsers.go:2176-2179 says that route was removed. filesystem_verify.go:622 says the default case is ErrInvalidMFTEntry, but it catches every error (see the ntfs_verify finding).
evidence: `// Shared by the *_read_at builtins and by xfat_read_file, which has to stage its content through a temp file.` versus `libxfat v1.3.0 added a reading API, so this no longer round-trips the content through a temp file.` Verifier: disk_image_parsers.go:20-22 says xfat_read_file 'has to stage its content through a temp file', while filesystem_parsers.go:2176-2179 says that route was removed. filesystem_verify.go:622 comment claims the default branch is ErrInvalidMFTEntry, but it catches every error (FS1.05). Verified by code reading. Verifier's notes: The second half is fixed with FS1.05.

title: A FAT orphan record whose first cluster is now a live file's is reported as preserved, checked and free, and fat_recover_file writes the live file's bytes under its name with no caveat
claim: The orphan sweep reports records that were never marked 0xE5 (they sit in a deleted directory's freed cluster). For those, libfat's FragmentOffsetsWithOptions walks the current FAT from the record's first cluster, because the entry is not Deleted. If that cluster now belongs to a live file, the walk returns the live file's chain. Mutant then reports content_state preserved, allocation_checked=true (FirstCluster != 0) and reallocated=false. libfat sets FirstClusterReallocated only for deleted entries (fragment.go:97-100, 220), so nothing ever checks ownership. The recovery writes the live file's content under the orphan's name with an empty caveats list. Verifier: As stated, with the severity recalibrated. The orphan sweep reports a non-0xE5 record found in a freed directory cluster. For such a record libfat walks the current FAT, so fat_deleted and fat_recover_file return a live file's chain as preserved, allocation_checked=true, reallocated=false, and recovery adds no caveat. That breaks the published fat_deleted promise that content is located for one cluster only. I rate it S2 (a wrong forensic answer reported as right; untrusted evidence or ordinary directory reuse can trigger it), not S1. It is P0 because it breaks a published promise of the deleted-recovery contract.
evidence: filesystem_deleted.go:887-900: `entry.ContentState = fsDeletedContentFirstOnly; if result.ChainWalked { entry.ContentState = fsDeletedContentPreserved } ... entry.AllocationChecked = dirEntry.FirstCluster != 0; entry.Reallocated = result.FirstClusterReallocated`. Repro TestZZFatOrphanFollowsLiveChain, image: live NEW.TXT owns clusters 8-9; deleted dir OLDDIR at free cluster 7 holds non-deleted STALE.TXT -> cluster 8. Output: `entry 4: name="STALE.TXT" path="/$OrphanFiles/STALE.TXT" source=orphan_scan state=preserved realloc=false checked=true runs=[{Offset:40448 Length:1024}]`; recovery: `state=preserved len=1024 realloc=false checked=true caveats=[] first="NNNNNNNN"` (all 1024 bytes are live NEW.TXT's 'N'). libfat IsClusterAllocated(8)=true. Verifier: Re-ran the auditor's TestZZFatOrphanFollowsLiveChain in my own tree. Output: `entry 4: name="STALE.TXT" path="/$OrphanFiles/STALE.TXT" source=orphan_scan state=preserved realloc=false checked=true runs=[{Offset:40448 Length:1024}]`. Recovery: `state=preserved len=1024 realloc=false checked=true caveats=[] first="NNNNNNNN"`, and those bytes are the live NEW.TXT's. libfat IsClusterAllocated(8)=true. Code: filesystem_deleted.go:880-900 marks the result preserved whenever ChainWalked, sets AllocationChecked = FirstCluster != 0, and takes Reallocated from FirstClusterReallocated. libfat sets that flag only for deleted entries (fragment.go:97-100, 220). The fat_deleted metadata (metadata.go:2752) and fatDeletedScope (filesystem_deleted.go:809-813) both promise 'Content is located for one cluster and no further'. This orphan returns a two-cluster live chain. Verifier's notes: The auditor rated it S1. It does not silently break custody or ledger integrity, so S2. The published scope contradiction is what justifies P0.
repro: scratch tree builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZFatOrphanFollowsLiveChain (builds on buildFAT16DeletedImage): CGO_ENABLED=0 go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZFatOrphanFollowsLiveChain -count=1 -v
impact: The examiner gets a live file's content, written as a recovered deleted file, labelled 'preserved' (the filesystem's own map survived), 'allocation_checked true, reallocated false' and no caveat. It is attributed to the wrong file and presented as certain. This is custody-grade misattribution.
fix_proposal: For dirEntry.Orphaned, do not trust a chain walk. Treat the record like a deleted one: first cluster only, or AssumeContiguous only through the explicit builtin. Set Reallocated from volume.IsClusterAllocated(first cluster), because an orphan found in freed clusters that points at an allocated cluster points at someone else's data. Report AllocationChecked=true only when that call succeeded. Apply the same rule in RecoverDeleted. Regression test: FAT16 image with a live file on clusters 8-9 and a freed directory holding a non-deleted record pointing at cluster 8. Assert that fat_deleted reports the orphan with reallocated=true (or content_state first_cluster_only), and that fat_recover_file carries the reallocation caveat or refuses. Fixed: realFATSession.freedRecordFragments, used by fat_deleted and fat_recover_file alike, treats an orphan-sweep record as deleted before asking libfat for runs, so it is located for its first cluster alone (or the contiguity hypothesis a script names), and reads reallocation from IsClusterAllocated itself: allocation_checked is true only when that read succeeded. Over the auditor's image STALE.TXT now reports first_cluster_only, reallocated true, and its recovery carries the live-file caveat; a free-cluster orphan reports reallocated false, checked true. exFAT is not affected: its carve parses deleted (0x05) entry sets only, which libxfat never walks.

title: ntfs_recover_file truncates to the $FILE_NAME size, which NTFS does not keep current, and reports size_matched true
claim: For NTFS the deleted entry's Size is the $FILE_NAME RealSize, not the $DATA attribute's size. NTFS updates the $FN size fields lazily, and they are routinely stale or zero. recoveryFromRuns caps the output at entry.Size, so a recovery whose $DATA runs are fully located is silently cut to the stale $FN figure. size_matched then compares against that same wrong number, reports true, and adds no truncation caveat. fs_deleted's size field has the same source. Verifier: As stated. There is a second problem: when $FN RealSize is 0, which is common, the cap does not apply and the output is padded to the whole allocated clusters (covered length). The recovered length is therefore wrong in both directions, depending on a field NTFS does not keep current.
evidence: filesystem_recover.go:340-343: `length := covered; if entry.Size > 0 && entry.Size < length { length = entry.Size }`. Repro on a synthetic NTFS image (record 6 deleted, $FN RealSize 100, non-resident $DATA of 1 cluster = 4096 bytes of 'D'): scan `size=100 located=4096 state=preserved runs=[{FileOffset:0 Offset:40960 Length:4096}]`; recovery `written=100 size_matched=true caveats=[nothing cross-referenced ...]` -> DEFECT: 4096 located bytes, 100 written. Verifier: TestZZNtfsRecoveryTruncatedToFileNameSize on a synthetic image: scan `size=100 located=4096 state=preserved`, recovery `written=100 size_matched=true` with only the 'nothing cross-referenced' caveat. Code: mft_builtins.go:193 row.size = fn.RealSize; filesystem_deleted.go ntfsDeletedEntry Size: int64(row.size); filesystem_recover.go:340-343 caps length at entry.Size.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZNtfsRecoveryTruncatedToFileNameSize (zzNTFSImage builder using exported libntfs helpers): go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestZZNtfsRecoveryTruncatedToFileNameSize -count=1 -v
impact: Recovered NTFS files come out short. The result says the size matched and gives no warning, so a truncated file is hashed and attached as complete. When $FN is 0 the cap does not apply, which makes the behaviour depend on an unreliable field.
fix_proposal: For NTFS deleted entries, take Size from the primary $DATA attribute: NonResident.RealSize (DataSize) or the resident value length. Report the $FN size as a separate field (fn_size), and have the recovery cap at the $DATA size. Apply the same change to fs_deleted's size. Regression test: A deleted MFT record whose $FN RealSize is smaller than its $DATA RealSize. Assert size == $DATA size and bytes_written == located bytes.

title: ntfs_deleted allocates rows by the $MFT's self-declared run length: a 128 KB crafted image kills the process with 'fatal error: out of memory'
claim: MFTEntryCount is sum(run.LengthClusters*bytesPerCluster)/recordSize from $MFT record 0's own data runs (libntfs file.go:231-241). Nothing bounds it by the image or volume size (volume.go:459-488 stores the runs unchecked). ScanDeleted preallocates `make([]mftRow, 0, count)` and then loops count times. A crafted run length makes the allocation arbitrarily large. Past the commit limit the Go runtime aborts with a fatal error, which no recover() can catch, and the whole mutant process dies. Smaller values still turn into proportional allocation plus a loop of count iterations. Verifier: As stated. A crafted $MFT run length drives an allocation and a loop proportional to the declared record count, not the image size. At large counts the make() is an uncatchable fatal out-of-memory.
evidence: Repro: a 131072-byte image declaring 16384 MFT clusters -> `examined=65536 unreadable=65533 allocated=72 MiB`. 65536 clusters -> `examined=262144 allocated=288 MiB`, `ratio 4.00 for 4x the declared length`. Declaring 0xFFFFFFFF clusters -> `declared count=17179869180 -> make([]mftRow,0,...) = 1374389534400 bytes`, `runtime: VirtualAlloc of 1374389534720 bytes failed with errno=1455 / fatal error: out of memory`, stack at `mutant/builtin.(*realNTFSSession).ScanDeleted ... filesystem_deleted.go:555`. The commit failed immediately, so no real memory was consumed. sizeof(mftRow)=80. Verifier: TestZZNtfsDeletedPreallocatesByDeclaredMFTLength (1 GiB heap watchdog), on a 131072-byte image: 16384 declared clusters gave `examined=65536 allocated=72 MiB`; 65536 clusters gave `examined=262144 allocated=288 MiB`, `ratio 4.00`. Code filesystem_deleted.go:547-558: `rows := make([]mftRow, 0, count)`, with count from MFTEntryCount, which is unbounded (sizeof mftRow = 80). I did not re-run the fatal 0xFFFFFFFF case, per the no-runaway rule. Linear growth plus the unbounded make() are enough for a crafted count of ~1.7e10 to abort in make. Verifier's notes: Same untrusted libntfs MFTEntryCount as FS1.06 (ntfs_verify / ntfs_report iterate it). The site and failure mode differ: this one is a fatal preallocation, that one is an uncancellable loop. One shared clamp helper would fix both, so fix them together. Plain DoS, not an embargo item.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZNtfsDeletedPreallocatesByDeclaredMFTLength (two sizes under a 1 GiB heap watchdog; the fatal case was run once, then removed)
impact: Code-path denial of service from evidence input. One crafted NTFS image (or partition) opened with ntfs_open and passed to ntfs_deleted terminates the interpreter unrecoverably, losing the run and any unsaved custody state. fs_deleted on a volume image goes through EachMFTEntry with the same count and loops without preallocating, so it hangs rather than crashing (mft_builtins.go:132, not owned).
fix_proposal: Bound count by what the image can hold: min(count, (imageSize - mftOffset)/recordSize), or the volume's total clusters * clusterSize / recordSize. Do not preallocate by the declared count; append instead. Stop after a run of unreadable records past the end of the reader, and report incomplete with the declared vs examined counts. Regression test: A synthetic NTFS image whose $MFT $DATA run declares 2^32 clusters. Assert ntfs_deleted returns in bounded time and memory with complete=false and a warning about the declared length.

title: fat_recover_file_assuming_contiguous reports allocation_checked true / reallocated false for assumed clusters nothing checked, one of which is allocated
claim: When AssumeContiguous synthesises ceil(size/cluster) clusters, only the first cluster's allocation was known (libfat sets FirstClusterReallocated = entry.ClusterAllocated, fragment.go:220). Mutant still sets AllocationChecked = native.FirstCluster != 0 and Reallocated = FirstClusterReallocated for the whole run. The result therefore claims the assumed ranges were cross-referenced and found free. The caveat vocabulary (filesystem_recover.go:548-551) defines allocation_checked as 'cross-referenced these ranges against the allocation map'. Verifier: As stated. With AssumeContiguous, allocation_checked/reallocated describe only the first cluster but are reported for the whole assumed run, which here includes a live file's cluster. The hypothesis caveat is present, which lowers the impact to S3. The two-bit contract is still false.
evidence: Repro on buildFAT16RecoverableImage (ONE.TXT deleted, first cluster 3, size 2048; cluster 4 allocated to another file): `cluster 3 allocated=false, cluster 4 allocated=true ...`; recovery `runs=[{Offset:37888 Length:2048}] assumed=true checked=true realloc=false` -> DEFECT. The output contains cluster 4's bytes from another file. Verifier: TestZZFatAssumedRunClaimsCheckedAndFree: cluster 3 allocated=false, cluster 4 allocated=true. Recovery `runs=[{Offset:37888 Length:2048}] assumed=true checked=true realloc=false`. The caveats include the 'assumed contiguous ... hypothesis' text. Code filesystem_recover.go:842-845 (FAT) and 921-923 (exFAT twin); libfat fragment.go:220 checks only the entry's first cluster. Verifier's notes: The same collapse applies to exFAT declared_contiguous runs: libxfat checks only the first cluster.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZFatAssumedRunClaimsCheckedAndFree
impact: The hypothesis caveat is present, but the two allocation bits state a fact that is false: 'checked, not reallocated' for a range that includes another live file's cluster. A report filtered on reallocated=false keeps it.
fix_proposal: When result.Assumed, call volume.IsClusterAllocated (libfat volume.go:774; libxfat IsClusterAllocated fragment.go:526) for every assumed cluster. Set Reallocated when any is allocated, and add a caveat naming them. Otherwise report AllocationChecked=false for the assumed part. Regression test: The existing FAT16 recoverable image with cluster 4 allocated. Assert that the assuming recovery reports reallocated=true or allocation_checked=false.

title: A run past the end of the image reads as zeros and is counted as located_bytes (io.EOF swallowed in fsRunReader)
claim: fsRunReader zero-fills p and then ignores io.EOF from image.ReadAt, so a run that lies wholly or partly beyond the image (a truncated acquisition, or a crafted offset) returns zeros with no error. recoveryFromRuns counts every byte of a run with Offset >= 0 as LocatedBytes, which is documented as 'read from the image at a run's offset', and computes UnlocatedBytes as the remainder. The output is zeros labelled as located content.
evidence: filesystem_recover.go:308: `if _, err := r.image.ReadAt(p[lo-off:hi-off], at); err != nil && err != io.EOF {`. Repro: FAT16 image cut at 37888 (start of cluster 3). The recovery of ONE.TXT gives `run=[{Offset:37888 Length:512}] len=512 located=512 unlocated=0`, the written bytes are all zero, and no caveat mentions it. Verifier: TestZZFatRunPastImageEndCountedAsLocated, with the image cut at 37888: `run=[{Offset:37888 Length:512}] len=512 located=512 unlocated=0`. The written bytes are all zero, and no caveat mentions the image end. Code filesystem_recover.go:308 swallows io.EOF, and recoveryFromRuns counts every run with Offset>=0 as located. Verifier's notes: Sibling of FS1.03, the same swallowed-EOF pattern in the streaming extract/hash reader (filesystem_stream.go). The code and fix site are different, so this is not a duplicate. Fix both together.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZFatRunPastImageEndCountedAsLocated
impact: On a short or partial image, recovered files are silently zero-filled and reported as fully located evidence. The 'three kinds of zero' contract, the reason this family exists, is broken for the most common acquisition defect.
fix_proposal: Have fsRunReader track the byte count ReadAt actually returned, and treat a short read inside a run as unlocated. The simplest version is to return an error from the recovery naming the offset past the image end. Check run.Offset+Length against the reader size in recoveryFromRuns and count the overflow as unlocated_bytes, with a caveat. Regression test: Truncate a FAT/ext image mid-file. Assert located_bytes excludes the missing part and a caveat names it, or that the recovery refuses.

title: An ext inode on the orphan list (unlinked while open) is reported reallocated=true, with a caveat that its own bytes are 'most likely another file's'
claim: libext's judgeRecovery grades Partial whenever any block is allocated. An orphan-list inode is still allocated, so its blocks are allocated to itself and it always grades Partial. Mutant maps Partial to Reallocated=true for every source and ignores libext's DeletedEntry.Allocated (the inode-bitmap answer). xfs_unlinked handles the same situation correctly, with AllocationChecked=true and Reallocated=false. Verifier: As stated. The error is a false alarm (reallocated=true on the inode's own blocks), not a false assurance. The ext_deleted doc already warns that reallocated may mean 'nobody could check', so I lower it to S3 P2.
evidence: filesystem_deleted.go:794: `entry.Reallocated = deleted.Recoverable == libext.RecoveryPartial`. Repro on ext4 image (mkfs.ext4 -d; /a.txt of 20000 'Q' made an orphan via debugfs: links 0, last_orphan 12): `entry 0: inode=12 source=orphan_list conf=partial state=preserved realloc=true checked=true size=20000 located=20000`; recovery `recovered len=20000 allQ=true realloc=true caveats=["libext graded this entry partial ..." "the entry's blocks are allocated to a live file, so what was read is most likely that file's content and not this one's"]`. Verifier: TestZZExtOrphanReportedReallocated on ext_orphan.img: `inode=12 source=orphan_list conf=partial state=preserved realloc=true checked=true size=20000 located=20000`. Recovery: all 20000 bytes are the file's own 'Q', but realloc=true, with the caveat 'the entry's blocks are allocated to a live file, so what was read is most likely that file's content'. Code filesystem_deleted.go:793-794 maps Partial to Reallocated. libext DeletedEntry.Allocated (deleted.go:104-106) is unused.
repro: WSL mkall.sh builds img/ext_orphan.img; scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZExtOrphanReportedReallocated
impact: The strongest ext deletion evidence (a file deleted while held open) is recovered intact, and the result tells the examiner it is probably someone else's data. A report that drops reallocated=true rows discards it.
fix_proposal: For Source orphan_list/orphan_file, or whenever deleted.Allocated is true, the blocks belong to the inode itself: set Reallocated=false and AllocationChecked=true, and skip the 'partial' caveat. Map Partial to Reallocated only for inodes the bitmap says are free. Regression test: An ext4 image with an orphan-chain inode (debugfs as in mkall.sh). Assert reallocated=false and no 'allocated to a live file' caveat.

title: ext_journal_inode_versions and ext_recover_journalled_file narrow the inode number to uint32: inode 4294967308 returns and recovers inode 12
claim: The builtins accept any positive int64 and pass uint32(inode) to libext. 2^32+12 wraps to 12, so the result is inode 12's journalled versions echoed under extra.inode = 4294967308, and the recovery writes inode 12's bytes. Verifier: As stated. The inode number comes from the script author (trusted), so the only triggers are a typo or a computed value; I rate it S3 P2, not S2 P1.
evidence: Repro on ext_jnl.img (the inode-table block of inode 2..16 journalled via debugfs jw): `asked=4294967308 extra.inode=4294967308 entry_count=1` -> DEFECT; `RecoverJournalledFile(4294967308, 0) recovered 20000 bytes of inode 12`. Verifier: TestZZExtJournalInodeNarrowed: `asked=4294967308 extra.inode=4294967308 entry_count=1`, and `RecoverJournalledFile(4294967308, 0) recovered 20000 bytes of inode 12`. Code filesystem_journal.go:1320 and 1431 `uint32(inode)`; the argument checks at 488/528 reject only <=0.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZExtJournalInodeNarrowed
impact: A typo or computed value yields another inode's history and content, labelled with the number the script asked for. That is misattributed evidence.
fix_proposal: Reject inode > math.MaxUint32, or better > Superblock().InodesCount, with a clear error in both builtins and both session methods. Regression test: ext_journal_inode_versions(h, 4294967308) must return an error.

title: Once libext's 256-warning cap is reached, every later ext_deleted / ext_xattrs on the handle reports complete=true with no warnings; ext_journal labels the saturation as journal_superblock_unreadable
claim: ext_deleted and ext_xattrs take the delta of s.fs.Warnings() before and after the call. libext keeps at most 256 warnings per FS for its lifetime (libext fs.go:106, 121-136) and drops the rest. After saturation the delta is always empty, so a scan that hit the same damage reports complete=true and warnings=[]. collectEXTWarnings in the journal family does detect the cap, but reports it under fsJournalWarnSuperblock = "journal_superblock_unreadable", a code with a different meaning. It also dumps every volume warning, not only this call's, which is inconsistent with the delta rule the other two use.
evidence: Repro on ext_orphan_broken.img (orphan chain broken with dtime 999999): `scan 1: complete=false reason="the scan recorded warnings; see warning_codes" warnings=1`; `scan 300: complete=true reason="" warnings=0` -> DEFECT. filesystem_journal.go:1070: `scan.warn(fsJournalWarnSuperblock, "", "libext's warnings channel is full ...")`. Verifier: TestZZExtWarningsSaturation on ext_orphan_broken.img: `scan 1: complete=false warnings=1`; `scan 300: complete=true reason="" warnings=0`. libext fs.go:106 caps warnings at 256 for the FS lifetime. filesystem_journal.go:1070 reports the cap under fsJournalWarnSuperblock, i.e. journal_superblock_unreadable. Verifier's notes: P1 because a later call on the same handle claims complete=true, silently.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZExtWarningsSaturation (300 scans, 3.3 s)
impact: On a damaged volume, or after many calls on one handle (a script looping over files calling ext_xattrs), later results silently claim completeness. A script matching journal_superblock_unreadable misreads saturation as a missing journal superblock.
fix_proposal: Add a helper extWarningsSince(before) that also returns saturated = len(Warnings()) >= extWarningCap. When saturated, mark the result incomplete with a dedicated code (warnings_saturated). Use that code in collectEXTWarnings, and give the journal the same delta semantics. Regression test: Call ext_deleted 300 times on an image with a broken orphan chain. The last result must be complete=false with warning code warnings_saturated.

title: fs_hash, fs_entropy, fs_diff, fs_carve and fs_extract_strings read the whole file into memory
claim: Every one of these does os.ReadFile with no bound. They are forensic primitives routinely pointed at disk images and memory dumps, and each allocates the file's full size (fs_diff allocates two). fs_carve and fs_extract_strings also build unbounded result arrays: a 2-byte signature such as pe/bmp can yield one hash object per occurrence. fs_magic already reads a 512-byte prefix for exactly this reason (lines 175-183).
evidence: `data, err := os.ReadFile(pathObj.Value)` at each site.
