Repro: `fs_hash over 32 MiB allocated 32 MiB`, `fs_entropy over 32 MiB allocated 32 MiB`, `fs_hash over 128 MiB allocated 128 MiB`, `fs_entropy over 128 MiB allocated 128 MiB` (4x input -> 4x allocation, under a 1 GiB watchdog). Verifier: TestZZFsHashReadsWholeFile under the watchdog: fs_hash and fs_entropy allocated 32 MiB for a 32 MiB file and 128 MiB for a 128 MiB file. Code: os.ReadFile at fs_forensics.go:39, 221, 248-252, 304, 337. fs_hash is the only host-file hasher in CAPABILITY_REFERENCE; the per-filesystem *_hash_file builtins stream, but only inside images. Verifier's notes: Not a duplicate of M26-BLT-002 (the error text for fs_hash on a directory).
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZFsHashReadsWholeFile
impact: fs_hash of a multi-GB evidence image, the COOKBOOK's own pattern, exhausts memory or fails where a streaming digest would succeed. On a shared analysis host this is resource exhaustion from input size.
fix_proposal: Stream: io.CopyBuffer into the hash; count entropy per chunk; compare fs_diff in fixed-size chunks while hashing both; carve with a sliding window of len(sig)-1 overlap. Cap carve hits and extracted strings with a truncated flag and a true count, as the *_deleted family does. Regression test: Hash a 256 MiB sparse file and assert TotalAlloc stays below a small multiple of the buffer size.

title: fs_carve reports the signature's position, not the artifact's start, for signatures at a non-zero offset (mp4 +4, tar +257)
claim: The metadata promises 'returns the byte offsets where it starts'. fileSignatures records mp4's 'ftyp' at offset 4 and tar's 'ustar' at 257, but carveSignature returns only the bytes, so the reported offset is where the magic string sits. The start is 4 or 257 bytes earlier.
evidence: Repro: an ISO-BMFF box starting at 100 -> `fs_carve(mp4) offset=104, artifact starts at 100`. A USTAR archive starting at 512 -> `fs_carve(tar) offset=769, artifact starts at 512`. Verifier: TestZZCarveReportsSignatureOffset: `fs_carve(mp4) offset=104, artifact starts at 100`; `fs_carve(tar) offset=769, artifact starts at 512`. The fileSignatures table records offsets 4 (mp4, fs_forensics.go:425) and 257 (tar, :409), and carveSignature returns only def.sig. The fs_carve metadata says 'returns the byte offsets where it starts'.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZCarveReportsSignatureOffset
impact: A script that extracts from the reported offset gets a corrupt artifact (tar header misaligned by 257 bytes, mp4 box missing its size field).
fix_proposal: Return def.offset from carveSignature and report hit-def.offset, dropping hits where that is negative. Alternatively add a signature_offset field and document it. Regression test: Embed a tar and an mp4 at known offsets and assert fs_carve returns those offsets.

title: fs_walk depth is counted from separators in the root's spelling, so '.' walks one level deeper than the same directory's absolute path
claim: baseDepth counts separators in filepath.Clean(root), and depth counts separators in each path. For '.', Clean gives '.' (0 separators) and its child 'a' also has 0, so direct children get depth 0, the same as the root. With maxDepth=1 the walk from '.' returns a grandchild that the absolute-path walk excludes. A volume root such as 'C:\' behaves the same way.
evidence: Repro: `fs_walk(abs,1): 2: ...\001@0 ...\001\a@1`; `fs_walk(".",1): 3: .@0 a@0 a\b@1` -> DEFECT. Verifier: TestZZWalkDepthDependsOnRootSpelling: fs_walk(abs,1) returns 2 entries (root@0, a@1); fs_walk(".",1) returns 3 (.@0 a@0 a\b@1). Code fs_forensics.go:81, 89 count separators in the root's spelling.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZWalkDepthDependsOnRootSpelling
impact: The same tree yields different entries and depths depending on how the root was typed, which is non-reproducible collection scope.
fix_proposal: Compute depth as the number of components in filepath.Rel(root, path), with 0 for the root itself. Regression test: Assert that fs_walk('.', 1) and fs_walk(abs, 1) return the same relative set and depths.

title: fs_walk: one unreadable subdirectory aborts the whole walk and returns no entries
claim: The WalkDir callback returns walkErr as-is, so a single permission-denied directory ends the walk. The builtin returns only an error, discarding every readable entry already collected.
evidence: Repro (Windows, icacls deny RX on walkroot\locked): `result=` (null), `err=ERROR:fs_walk: open ...\walkroot\locked: Access is denied.`, while walkroot\ok\file.txt is readable. Verifier: Denied RX with icacls on my own scratch walkroot\locked. TestZZWalkDeniedDirectory: `err=ERROR:fs_walk: open ...\walkroot\locked: Access is denied.` and the result is null, although ok\file.txt is readable. Code fs_forensics.go:84-87 returns walkErr unchanged.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZWalkDeniedDirectory on scratch walkroot
impact: Walking a live system or mounted evidence with any protected directory yields nothing. The examples' baseline and triage scripts built on fs_walk fail outright.
fix_proposal: On walkErr for a non-root path, record {path, error} in an errors list and return filepath.SkipDir (dir) or nil. Return the entries plus the errors, with complete=false. Regression test: A tree with one unreadable dir. Assert the other entries are returned and the error is listed.

title: xfs_unlinked reports complete=true when an unlinked inode was unreadable (warnings added after the completeness check)
claim: UnlinkedInodes marks the scan incomplete only for anomalies known before the entry loop. xfsUnlinkedEntry then adds inode_unreadable / data_runs_unavailable warnings and increments Unreadable, but nothing re-checks, so the result says complete=true beside a warning and unreadable>0.
evidence: Repro on xfs_v4_bogus.img (AGI unlinked[12]=140, a free inode): `entry_count=2 complete=true unreadable=1 warnings=[{Code:inode_unreadable Detail:inode not found Location:inode 140}]`. Verifier: TestZZXfsUnlinked on xfs_v4_bogus.img: `entry_count=2 complete=true unreadable=1 warnings=[{Code:inode_unreadable Detail:inode not found Location:inode 140}]`. Code filesystem_deleted.go:1297-1307: the completeness check runs before the loop, and the warn/Unreadable++ calls inside xfsUnlinkedEntry come after it.
repro: WSL xfs_db -x 'agi 0' 'write unlinked[12] 140'; scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZXfsUnlinked
impact: A script gating on complete accepts a scan that could not read one of the filesystem-asserted deletions.
fix_proposal: Move the `if len(scan.Warnings) > 0 { scan.incomplete(...) }` after the loop, or call scan.incomplete inside xfsUnlinkedEntry on each failure. Regression test: An XFS image with a bucket pointing at a free inode. Assert complete=false.

title: xfs_unlinked reports created_at (and any zero time) as 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z instead of empty
claim: formatTime blanks only t.IsZero(), but time.Unix(0, 0) is the Unix epoch, not Go's zero time. A v4 XFS inode has no creation-time field (CreationTimeNS 0), so created_at reads as a real 1970 timestamp. libxfs's own Inode.CreationTime() accessor returns time.Time{} for 0 (types.go:551-556) and is bypassed. Verifier: As stated for created_at. Correction to the fix: libxfs Inode.CreationTime() maps 0 to the zero time, but AccessTime() and ModificationTime() (types.go:539-545) do not. Switching to the accessors fixes only created_at. The accessed_at of 1970 in the same repro needs an explicit NS==0 check.
evidence: `entry.CreatedAt = formatTime(time.Unix(0, inode.CreationTimeNS).UTC())`. Repro on a mkfs.xfs -m crc=0 image with inode 131 on AGI unlinked[3]: `created="1970-01-01T00:00:00Z" modified="2026-09-25T12:03:53.056272Z" accessed="1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"`. Verifier: TestZZXfsUnlinked on xfs_v4_unlinked.img: inode 131 `created="1970-01-01T00:00:00Z" accessed="1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"`. Code filesystem_deleted.go:1339-1341 uses time.Unix(0, ns), and formatTime blanks only IsZero.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZXfsUnlinked (xfs_v4_unlinked.img)
impact: A timeline shows a fabricated 1970 creation time for the one filesystem-asserted deletion source.
fix_proposal: Use inode.CreationTime(), ModificationTime() and AccessTime() (the libxfs accessors), or check NS == 0 before converting. Regression test: A v4 XFS unlinked inode. Assert created_at == "".

title: fat_deleted reports one deleted record twice (descent into the deleted directory and the orphan sweep), and entry_count counts both
claim: With both options, libfat reports a child of a deleted directory once under the deleted parent's path and again under $OrphanFiles. Both rows carry the same EntryAbsoluteOffset. The scan adds both and entry_count counts the one on-disk record twice, and neither the scope nor the entries say so. libxfat documents the same double report for exFAT (walk.go, DescendDeletedDirectories doc).
evidence: Repro: `entry 3: name="_ONE2.TXT" path="/_LDDIR/_ONE2.TXT" source=directory entry_offset=40032` and `entry 5: name="_ONE2.TXT" path="/$OrphanFiles/_ONE2.TXT" source=orphan_scan entry_offset=40032`; `one on-disk record GONE2.TXT appears 2 times; entry_count=6`. Verifier: TestZZFatOrphanFollowsLiveChain: `entry 3: _ONE2.TXT path=/_LDDIR/_ONE2.TXT source=directory entry_offset=40032` and `entry 5: _ONE2.TXT path=/$OrphanFiles/_ONE2.TXT source=orphan_scan entry_offset=40032`, entry_count=6. Neither fatDeletedScope nor the metadata mentions double reporting.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_fs2_test.go TestZZFatOrphanFollowsLiveChain (dup assertion)
impact: Deleted-file counts in reports are inflated, and a recovery loop writes the same file twice under two paths.
fix_proposal: Deduplicate on EntryAbsoluteOffset (FAT) and EntrySetOffset (exFAT). Keep the directory-sourced row and note the orphan-sweep sighting in reasons, or report a duplicates count. Regression test: A deleted directory holding a deleted child. Assert that one row per entry_offset and entry_count equals the number of distinct records.

title: hfs_deleted reports allocation_checked=true unconditionally, including when libhfs's allocation check failed or an extent was out of bounds
claim: libhfs gradeRecovered (deleted.go ~620-653) sets inBounds=false and leaves overwritten=false when an extent lies past TotalBlocks or BlockAllocated returns an error. Mutant hard-codes AllocationChecked: true and Reallocated: record.Overwritten, so a record whose check never ran reads as 'checked, not reallocated'. This is the two-bit collapse the file comment forbids. Verifier: The mechanism is real, but only in one case: when libhfs cannot read the allocation-file bitmap for an in-bounds extent, the entry reports allocation_checked=true and reallocated=false with runs present. The out-of-bounds case the auditor cites produces no runs, so its wrong bits carry no content. The trigger is narrow (a damaged or truncated allocation file), and confidence then reads Low/Medium rather than High, hence S4.
evidence: `AllocationChecked: true, Reallocated: record.Overwritten,`. libhfs: `inUse, err := v.BlockAllocated(b); if err != nil { inBounds = false; break }` ... `return conf, overwritten`. Verifier: Code reading only; I had no HFS+ image or builder. filesystem_deleted.go:1130-1134 hard-codes AllocationChecked: true. In libhfs v0.3.2 gradeRecovered (deleted.go:611-654), a BlockAllocated error sets inBounds=false with overwritten=false, and BlockAllocated can error on a bitmap read (alloc.go:28). For out-of-bounds extents, ExtentRanges fails in hfsDeletedEntry, so content_state is none and no runs are reported. The practical exposure is therefore only an unreadable allocation file, where confidence is also below High.
impact: Recovered HFS+ records whose blocks may belong to live files are presented as free.
fix_proposal: Re-run the allocation test in Mutant with volume.BlockAllocated over the extents, or set AllocationChecked=false when Confidence is below High and Overwritten is false. Better, ask libhfs to expose the checked bit. Regression test: An HFS+ image whose allocation file is truncated. Assert allocation_checked=false for recovered records.

title: exFAT allocation_checked is AllocationPossible(), a record-field flag, not whether the bitmap check ran
claim: The code's own comment says libxfat leaves FirstClusterReallocated false when the bitmap could not be read. Mutant still sets AllocationChecked = xfatEntry.AllocationPossible(), which says whether the record's cluster fields are meaningful, not whether the cross-reference ran. An unreadable bitmap therefore yields checked=true, reallocated=false. Verifier: As stated, and the published xfat_deleted doc makes a promise the code does not keep. When the bitmap is unreadable, entries report allocation_checked=true and reallocated=false.
evidence: filesystem_deleted.go:1035-1041 comment: "...and it leaves the flag false in the second case. AllocationPossible is what says the record's cluster fields mean anything at all." followed by `entry.AllocationChecked = xfatEntry.AllocationPossible()`. Verifier: Code reading only; I had no exFAT image. filesystem_deleted.go:1041 and filesystem_recover.go:923 set AllocationChecked = AllocationPossible(), a record flag (libxfat struct.go:382), not a record of whether the check ran. libxfat fragment.go:490-494 (deletedResult) leaves FirstClusterReallocated false when IsClusterAllocated errors. The xfat_deleted metadata (metadata.go:2765) claims this libxfat behaviour 'is what makes allocation_checked meaningful here', but the code never records whether the bitmap read succeeded.
impact: Same as the HFS case: the forbidden collapse, on exFAT.
fix_proposal: Call fs.IsClusterAllocated(first cluster) directly, and set AllocationChecked only when it returns without error. Regression test: An exFAT image with a damaged bitmap stream. Assert allocation_checked=false.

title: ext_deleted 'examined' equals entry_count: it counts entries returned, not inodes examined
claim: The fsDeletedScan doc says Examined is 'how many records, inodes or clusters the scan looked at', a denominator. For ext it is incremented once per DeletedEntry returned, so examined == entry_count always and gives no denominator.
evidence: `for _, deleted := range entries { scan.Examined++; scan.add(...) }` Verifier: New repro TestZZExtExamined on ext_orphan.img (8 MiB ext4): `examined=1 entry_count=1`. Code filesystem_deleted.go:727-730 increments Examined once per returned entry. The Examined doc comment (line 233) calls it the number of records the scan looked at.
repro: code reading; not separately asserted
impact: 'Examined 3, found 3' on a volume with a million inodes misstates coverage.
fix_proposal: Report the inode count scanned (the sum of usable inodes in the initialised groups, which libext exposes via GroupDescriptors and Superblock), or name the field differently for ext. Regression test: On an ext image, assert examined >= number of initialised inodes.

title: Only FAT has real-library tests: every ext/NTFS/HFS/XFS/exFAT deleted, recover, slack, journal and xattr path is tested only against fakes
claim: The owned tests build real sessions only for FAT (openRealFATDeletedSession). slack, journal and xattr tests use no real session at all. Every non-FAT defect above (NTFS $FN truncation, NTFS count allocation, ext orphan reallocated, uint32 narrowing, warnings saturation, XFS complete/1970) lives in code no test executes.
evidence: grep counts: filesystem_deleted_test.go `6 openRealFATDeletedSession 2 realFATSession`; filesystem_recover_test.go `6 openRealFATDeletedSession`; filesystem_slack_test.go, filesystem_journal_test.go, filesystem_xattr_test.go: no real* session. Verifier: grep: filesystem_deleted_test.go and filesystem_recover_test.go build only openRealFATDeletedSession / realFATSession. filesystem_slack_test.go, filesystem_journal_test.go and filesystem_xattr_test.go build no real session; the journal tests feed hand-built libntfs/libext structs to converters. No test anywhere references realEXTBackend, realXFSBackend, realNTFSSession, realHFS* or realXFAT*. The only image under git is examples/data/usb_stick.img (FAT).
repro: grep -o 'real[A-Z]*Session|openRealFAT[A-Za-z]*' over the five test files
impact: The library-trap contract (the two bits, three kinds of zero) is asserted only against hand-written fakes that encode the author's model of each library.
fix_proposal: Add small real fixtures: a synthetic NTFS image (the libntfs-helper builder in zz_fs2_test.go), the debugfs/xfs_db recipes above checked in as generated testdata, and exercise each real session once. Regression test: n/a (this is the test gap)

title: xfs_slack reports a leaf-format directory's live leaf block, at file offset 32 GiB, as file slack and gives allocated_bytes as 32 GiB + 4 KiB
claim: XFS keeps a directory's leaf and free-index blocks in the data fork at logical offsets XFS_DIR2_LEAF_OFFSET (32 GiB) and XFS_DIR2_FREE_OFFSET (64 GiB). di_size covers only the data section. realXFSSession.Slack does not treat directories differently. It takes allocated = max(fileOffset+length) over DataRuns and then reports everything in the spans between Size and allocated as file_slack. Every leaf- or node-format directory therefore has its live index blocks reported as slack, with complete=true and no warning. allocated_bytes becomes about 34 GB. Verifier: As stated. On a leaf- or node-format XFS directory, xfs_slack reports the live leaf block (and, for node format, the free-index block) as file_slack, reports allocated_bytes as about 32 GiB, and sets complete=true with no warning. I lowered the severity to S3 because xfs_slack takes a single path and only goes wrong when that path is a directory. Its param doc says 'Path of the file', and nothing in Mutant calls Slack across a whole tree.
evidence: filesystem_slack.go:1147 `scan.Size = int64(inode.Size)`; 1182 `if end := fileOffset + length; end > allocated { allocated = end }`; 1198 `for _, r := range spansWithin(spans, scan.Size, allocated, fsSlackClassFileSlack) { scan.add(r) }`. IsDirectory is set at 1146 and never consulted. HFS (1078-1084) returns early for directories. XFS does not. xfs_db on the repro image: /big has core.size=24576, and bmap shows 'data offset 8388608 startblock 32782 count 1' (the leaf block at 32 GiB). Verifier: I ran TestZZXFSDirSlack in my scratch copy against the auditor's mkfs.xfs -p image. Output: dir=true size=24576 allocated=34359742464 file_slack_bytes=4096 ranges=[{file_slack FileOffset:34359738368 Offset:83943424 Length:4096}] complete=true. In filesystem_slack.go:1146-1202, realXFSSession.Slack sets IsDirectory and never reads it again. It takes allocated as max(FileOffset+Length) over DataRuns, and those runs include the directory's leaf block at XFS_DIR2_LEAF_OFFSET. HFS returns early for a folder at 1078-1084. Verifier's notes: Fix: cap a directory inode's runs below 32 GiB, or report 'not applicable' as HFS does. Regular files are not affected.
repro: WSL mkfs.xfs -p proto (img/mkxfs.sh) creates /big with 400 long-named entries, a leaf-format directory. The test is scratch tree/builtin/zz_fs2t_test.go TestZZXFSDirSlack: realXFSBackend{}.Open(xfs_dir.img).Slack("/big"). Output: dir=true size=24576 allocated=34359742464 file_slack_bytes=4096 ranges=[{Class:file_slack FileOffset:34359738368 Offset:83943424 Length:4096}] complete=true. It failed as predicted.
impact: An examiner who carves 'file slack' from a directory gets the directory's own live hash/leaf index, labelled as residue from a previous occupant. allocated_bytes of about 34 GB for a 24 KiB directory is also quoted as a measurement. The same happens for the free-index block of any node-format directory.
fix_proposal: For a directory inode, cap the spans at the data section: ignore runs whose FileOffset >= XFS_DIR2_LEAF_OFFSET (32 GiB) when computing allocated and file slack. Alternatively report directory slack as not applicable, with a warning naming the leaf and free sections, as HFS does. Also set scan.AllocatedBytes from the data section only. Regression test: A real-image test with a leaf-format XFS directory (mkfs.xfs -p fixture) asserting file_slack_bytes == 0 and allocated_bytes == size for /big. Keep a regular-file case with a real EOF tail to show slack is still found.

title: hfs_xattrs (and hfs_deleted) lose library anomalies after the first file: libhfs dedups anomalies volume-wide, so the before/after slice diff finds nothing new
claim: Mutant finds 'this call's' anomalies by slicing s.volume.Anomalies()[before:]. libhfs noteAnomaly (cache.go:142-158) deduplicates on (Op, Detail) for the life of the volume, and its detail strings are constants ('inline attribute declares more data than its record holds'). The second and later files on a handle with the same defect therefore add nothing, and hfs_xattrs reports their attributes with no warning. The clamped length becomes the attribute's size, so value_truncated is false as well. Even for the first file, an anomaly only becomes a warning: complete stays true. The 1000-entry cap (maxTrackedAnomalies) makes it permanent once reached. This is the same class as FS2.08 (the libext warning cap), but a different library and a different mechanism: a dedup on (op, detail), not a count cap. The fix is also different: use AnomalyCount() deltas plus a per-CNID check, not a slice index. Verifier: As stated, and stronger than stated: even re-querying the file that carries the anomaly loses the warning once any earlier call on the handle recorded the same (op, detail). complete is never set to false for an HFS xattr anomaly. For hfs_deleted the blind spot hits a second walk on the same handle, or a walk after another call that raised the same anomaly.
evidence: xattr.go:1356 `before := len(s.volume.Anomalies())` ... 1402 `anomalies := s.volume.Anomalies()` ... 1406 `for _, anomaly := range anomalies[before:] { scan.warn(...) }`. libhfs cache.go:149-156: `if len(v.anomalies) >= maxTrackedAnomalies { return }; for _, a := range v.anomalies { if a.Op == op && a.Detail == detail { return } }`. libhfs xattr.go:107-110 clamps `size = uint32(len(payload) - attrInlineHeaderSize)` after noting the anomaly. Verifier: I ran the auditor's test and my own reverse-order test on one session. /many.txt, then /inline.txt, then /many.txt again: only the first call gets the xattr_inline warning. The second file, and the same file queried a second time, both return warnings=[] with complete=true and the clamped size. libhfs v0.3.2 cache.go:142-158 noteAnomaly deduplicates on (Op, Detail) and the detail text is constant. xattr.go:1356/1402-1408 reads anomalies with a slice diff. filesystem_deleted.go:1080/1104 (hfs_deleted) uses the same pattern. Mutant never calls AnomalyCount(). Verifier's notes: Same class as FS2.08 (a volume-wide library warning state defeats per-call attribution), but a different library, mechanism and fix. Kept separate. Not security: the attribute bytes themselves are correct and only the damage warning is lost.
repro: I built an HFS+ image with libhfs's own xattr fixture helpers (a scratch copy of libhfs, zz_dump_test.go): /inline.txt and /many.txt each carry one inline attribute that declares more bytes than its record holds (200 and 300). Test TestZZHFSXattrAnomalyDedup calls Xattrs on both through one realHFSBackend session. Output: /inline.txt warnings=[{Code:xattr_inline ...}] complete=true; /many.txt size=11 value="second-file" complete=true warnings=[]. It failed as predicted.
impact: A damaged or tampered attribute record on the second file examined reads as a clean, complete, correctly sized attribute. The order of calls decides whether the damage is reported. hfs_deleted's anomaly accounting has the same blind spot.
fix_proposal: Compare s.volume.AnomalyCount() before and after the call (it counts repeats), and when it moved without a new list entry, warn with a generic 'library anomaly (deduplicated)' code. Mark scan incomplete whenever any anomaly fired during the call. Long term, ask libhfs for per-call anomaly reporting, such as ListXAttrsWithReport. Regression test: The two-file fixture above: assert that both files get an xattr_inline warning and complete=false, and that the result is the same with the call order reversed.

title: hfs_xattrs gives a fork-backed value's offset as its first extent only; the scope's promise that the value 'stays reachable with raw_read_at_bytes' reads other data for a fragmented value
claim: For a fork-backed attribute, Offset = ranges[0].DiskOffset, and the extent list is thrown away. A value over the 4096-byte render cap is not read. The warning says 'its length and position are reported and the bytes stay readable from the image'. The scope says a fork-backed value 'is still reachable with raw_read_at_bytes'. When the attribute fork has more than one extent, reading size bytes at that offset returns the first extent followed by unrelated blocks. Nothing in the result says the value is fragmented. Verifier: As stated. For a fragmented fork-backed attribute, the one offset reported plus the size does not locate the value, and nothing in the result says the value is fragmented. That makes the documented promise wrong.
evidence: xattr.go:1373 `if ranges, rangeErr := s.volume.XAttrRanges(record.CNID, attr.Name); rangeErr == nil && len(ranges) > 0 { entry.Offset = ranges[0].DiskOffset }`. libhfs's own fixture (xattr_test.go:31-41) deliberately uses 9 non-contiguous extents 'so a reader that assumes adjacency produces wrong bytes'. Verifier: I ran TestZZHFSXattrForkOffset. user.big is 35630 bytes, fork-backed, in 9 non-contiguous extents. The result reports offset=40960 and the value_longer_than_render_cap warning, which says the bytes 'stay readable from the image'. Image byte at offset+4096 is 0x00, while the value's second extent holds 0xA1. xattr.go:1373 keeps only ranges[0].DiskOffset. The scope text at 1324-1326 promises the value 'is still reachable with raw_read_at_bytes'. Verifier's notes: The auditor's image was built from libhfs's own 9-extent fixture helpers. How common fragmented attribute forks are on real volumes is unknown, but the doc promise fails regardless.
repro: TestZZHFSXattrForkOffset on the same crafted image: user.big is 35630 bytes in 9 one-block extents at blocks 10, 12, ..., 26. Output: offset=40960, and the byte at offset+4096 is 0x0 where the value's second extent holds 0xA1. It failed as predicted.
impact: An examiner who follows the documented route to read a large attribute, such as a resource-fork-as-xattr or a large quarantine or metadata blob, gets wrong bytes. They hash or carve the wrong content, and nothing in the result flags it.
fix_proposal: Return the attribute's ranges (fork_offset, offset, length), as hfs_resource_fork already does, or at least an extent_count plus a fragmented warning. Change the scope and warning text to say one offset is enough only when there is a single range. Regression test: On the fragmented fixture: assert that the result lists 9 ranges (or fragmented=true), and that reading every range and concatenating the reads gives the value ReadXAttr returns.

title: ntfs_log_transactions groups $LogFile records in physical page order, so a transaction that straddles the wrap seam is split into two: an 'open' head and a clipped tail with start_present false
claim: GroupLogTransactions closes a transaction when it meets its commit or forget record, and opens a new one for the next record with that ID. After a wrap, the newest records sit at the front of $LogFile and the oldest survivors at the end. A transaction that began just before the seam has its continuation and end records walked first, and they are closed as one transaction. Its real first record is walked last and opens a second transaction that never closes. One transaction becomes two: one ends 'forgotten' with start_present=false, and one is 'open' with start_present=true. The scope and noteWrap text say the ordering 'is sound' and that straddling transactions are 'reported as whatever part of them survived'. In fact both parts survived and are reported as two unrelated transactions. Mutant already holds every record in memory, so sorting by LSN before grouping would avoid this. Verifier: As stated. There is one more effect: start_present is read from Records[0], which is the first record in physical order, not the lowest-LSN record, so it can be wrong even for a transaction that is not split. The failure hits transactions whose records straddle the physical wrap seam of $LogFile. I ran the unit-level grouping but did not walk a real volume, because no NTFS image is available.
evidence: journal.go:735-742 appends records in EachLogRecord order. 753 `for _, transaction := range libntfs.GroupLogTransactions(records)`. libntfs logfile.go:386-436: `transaction, ok := open[record.TransactionID]; if !ok { transaction = &LogTransaction{...} }` ... `case LogOpForgetTransaction: ...closeTransaction(record.TransactionID)`. journal.go:747-751, the noteWrap text: 'reading them in order is sound; what the seam costs is the transactions whose records fell on both sides of it'. Verifier: libntfs v0.3.3 logfile.go:386-448 GroupLogTransactions groups records in input order and closes a transaction on its commit or forget record. It sorts only the resulting transactions by FirstLSN (line 442). Volume.EachLogRecordContext (1072-1120) feeds pages from offset 0 in physical order, and journal.go:735-755 passes that order straight in. The comment at journal.go:733 ('before the sort that grouping applies hides it') wrongly assumes the grouping sorts records first. I ran the physical-order slice (1000, 1010 forget, 990) and got 2 transactions for tx 7: one open with start_present=true and one forgotten with start_present=false. Verifier's notes: Fix: sort records by LSN, stably, after observing the wrap and before GroupLogTransactions.
repro: TestZZNTFSLogGroupingAcrossSeam feeds GroupLogTransactions the physical order a wrapped log produces: LSN 1000 (prev 990), LSN 1010 forget (prev 1000), then LSN 990 (prev 0), all with tx 7, which is exactly the slice ScanLogTransactions builds. Output: 'tx id=7 first=990 last=990 records=1 forgotten=false start_present=true' and 'tx id=7 first=1000 last=1010 records=2 forgotten=true start_present=false'; wrapped=true. It failed as predicted. The Volume-level walk could not be run: no NTFS image is available, and WSL has no mkntfs.
impact: On a wrapped log, which is the normal state of a busy volume, the transactions at the seam come out as a phantom open transaction ('in flight when captured') plus a clipped one. A timeline built from end_state and start_present misreports exactly the operations nearest the oldest surviving history.
fix_proposal: sort.SliceStable(records, by LSN) before GroupLogTransactions. The wrap has already been observed in walk order at 740, so nothing is lost. Compute start_present from the transaction's lowest-LSN record. Regression test: Unit test through a fake or real session, with records in wrapped physical order: expect one transaction with end_state forgotten and start_present true.

title: $LogFile's buffer (tail-copy) RCRD pages are walked as ordinary log pages: records are duplicated and an unwrapped log reads as wrapped
claim: NTFS $LogFile keeps, after the two restart pages, a set of 'buffer' RCRD pages: 2 in LFS 1.1 (offsets 0x2000 and 0x3000), 32 in LFS 2.0. They hold copies of the most recently written log page(s). libntfs feeds every page from offset 0 to its walker and skips only non-RCRD magic, so the records in those copies come first with the newest LSNs and then appear again in the circular area. ScanLogRecords calls observeOrder on this stream, so the LSNs drop right after the buffer pages and wrapped=true on every volume, wrapped or not. entry_count double-counts the copied records, and ntfs_log_transactions gets duplicate transactions. Verifier: Plausible as stated, but it depends on the LFS buffer-page layout (2 pages in LFS 1.1, 32 in 2.0), which I did not check against a Windows-written $LogFile. If that layout holds, the duplicate records and the always-true wrapped follow directly from the walker code.
evidence: journal.go:701-706: `EachLogRecord(func(record) { scan.add(...); scan.position(position); scan.observeOrder(position) })`. libntfs logfile.go:891-896 treats any page with RCRD magic as data (`if len(page) < logRecordPageHeaderSize || ReadUint32LE(page, 0) != LogRecordPageMagic { ... return nil }`), and the loop at 1107 feeds every page from offset 0. grep finds no mention of buffer or tail pages anywhere in logfile.go. Verifier: Code reading confirms the mechanism on the library side. libntfs logfile.go:1107-1113 feeds every page of $LogFile from offset 0. feed() (891) skips only pages without RCRD magic. The only other filter is logBounds.permits (877), which checks client index and sequence number, not duplicates. Nothing in logfile.go handles buffer or tail pages. journal.go:701-706 calls observeOrder on this stream, so newer LSNs in pages at 0x2000/0x3000 followed by older circular-area LSNs would set Wrapped=true. I could not reproduce: no NTFS image exists on the host (examples/data/usb_stick.img is FAT, libntfs testdata holds only fuzz corpora), WSL has no mkntfs, and building a VHD needs elevation. Verifier's notes: Needs a real Windows-written $LogFile fixture to settle. The fix probably belongs in libntfs (skip buffer pages by restart major version), or Mutant can deduplicate by LSN.
impact: If confirmed, wrapped is true on essentially every real volume, so the flag carries no information, and record and transaction counts are inflated by the newest page's contents.
fix_proposal: Once a real image confirms the layout, skip the buffer pages: 2 for restart major version 1, 32 for version 2. Do this in libntfs, or in Mutant by deduplicating on LSN and starting observeOrder after them. Add a Windows-written $LogFile fixture. Regression test: A real $LogFile from a freshly formatted, never-wrapped volume: wrapped=false, and no LSN is reported twice.

title: TestMoreThanOneCycleIsTheWrapItself tests a copy of the wrap rule written inside the test, not the production code
claim: The test defines its own cyclesOf helper, which sets scan.Wrapped = len(seen) > 1, and then asserts on that. It never calls realXFSSession.ScanLogRecords or ScanLogTransactions (filesystem_journal.go:1543-1552, 1608-1621), so any change to the production rule passes. It also asserts that a log whose records all carry cycle 7 is not wrapped. That contradicts the scope's own statement that 'the cycle is the number of times the log has been written round'. Verifier: The test is tautological: the production XFS wrap rule is untested. The auditor's second point, that a single-cycle log asserted not-wrapped 'contradicts the scope', is overstated. Wrapped here means the seam is visible among the surviving records, and one cycle among them is consistent with that.
evidence: journal_test.go:971-977: `cyclesOf := func(scan *fsJournalScan, cycles ...uint32) { ... scan.Wrapped = len(seen) > 1 }`. No XFS session, real or fake, is involved. Verifier: filesystem_journal_test.go:965-987 defines a local cyclesOf that sets scan.Wrapped = len(seen) > 1 and then asserts on it. It never calls realXFSSession.ScanLogRecords/ScanLogTransactions, whose inline rule is at filesystem_journal.go:1543-1552 and 1608-1621. So the test exercises only its own copy of the rule. Verifier's notes: Related to FS2.19 (fake-only coverage) but a separate, concrete test defect.
repro: Read-only: the test body contains no call into production XFS code (grep of lines 965-987).
impact: The XFS wrapped bit has no real test coverage. This follows the pattern of FS2.19: fakes and helpers only.
fix_proposal: Move the rule into a named helper (xfsWrappedFromCycles) that both scans call, and test that helper. Or drive ScanLogRecords through a fake libxfs result. Regression test: The test itself, retargeted at the production helper.

title: Rename started on a module's declaration never edits the importers' alias.name uses, so the rename breaks every importing file
claim: rename runs the workspace (cross-file) path only when the file-local ReferenceLocations comes back empty: `locations, ok := snapshot.ReferenceLocations(...); ... if len(locations) == 0 { declared, ok := s.workspaceDeclarationAt(...); ... locations = s.workspaceReferenceLocations(declared, true) }`. With the cursor on the declaration, the local result always contains at least the declaration, so the `stats.mean(...)` call sites in other files are never added. references() for the same position does merge them (server.go:1013-1023).
evidence: Repro: lib.mut `let mean = fn(xs) { return 0; };`, main.mut `import stats "lib.mut"; let a = stats.mean([1]);`. references from lib.mut 0:5 returns lib.mut 0:4 and main.mut 1:14. rename from the same position returns edits for lib.mut only, and main.mut keeps `stats.mean`. A matrix run (scan on/off, VS Code or canonical URI spelling) gives only the lib.mut edit in every case. The existing test TestRenamingAModuleMemberEditsTheDeclarationAndEveryCallSite (cross_file_test.go:172) starts from the call site, where the local result is empty, so it cannot catch this. Verifier: server.go:1053-1081: rename falls back to workspaceReferenceLocations only when len(locations)==0, whereas references() (1002-1027) always merges. TestZZRenameFromDeclarationMissesImporters: references returns lib.mut 0:4 and main.mut 1:14, and rename edits only lib.mut. The same result holds in all 4 cells of the scan x URI-spelling matrix. CHANGELOG.md:405-407 promises rename 'across every importer'.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/server -run 'TestZZRenameFromDeclarationMissesImporters|TestZZRenameMatrix' -v. It fails: "rename from the declaration left main.mut's stats.mean unrenamed (references found it: 2 refs total)".
impact: The most natural rename (cursor on the definition, F2) leaves every importer calling a name the module no longer declares. The build then fails in files the user never looked at, or the user ships a broken module.
fix_proposal: In rename, merge workspaceReferenceLocations(workspaceDeclarationAt(...)) into the local locations whenever the position resolves to a top-level declaration, as references() does, then dedupe. Regression test: Run the existing cross-file rename test a second time with the position on the declaration in lib.mut, and assert one edit each in lib.mut, main.mut and other.mut.

title: Incremental edits with positions past the end are applied at offset 0 or refused, and a refusal leaves the server's copy permanently out of step with the client
claim: applyChange trusts glsp's Range.IndexesIn. glsp returns 0 for any position past the end of content, both for a line past the last line and for a character past the end of the last line. The LSP spec says such a character must clamp to the line length. As a result an insert past the end lands at the start of the document, and a range ending past the end is refused with `invalid change range`. A refused update returns an error with the version not advanced. didChange drops that error (it is a notification), and the next version's edits are applied to the stale text. Verifier: As stated. VS Code (the only shipped client) always sends in-range positions, so this hits only other LSP clients. That is why I lowered the priority to P2. Update also leaves the version un-advanced on an error, and didChange drops that error.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/workspace -run ZZ -v (zz_lsp_test.go in my copy). Both tests fail as described.
impact: With any client that sends end-of-document ranges as (lineCount,0) or unclamped characters (several non-VS Code clients do), diagnostics describe text that does not exist. The next format-on-save then silently overwrites the user's code with the server's stale copy.
fix_proposal: Compute offsets in the store: clamp the line to the last line and the character to the line length (counting UTF-16 units), and treat a line past the last as end-of-document. On any apply error, drop the document and ask for a full resync (or log and republish) rather than keeping stale text under a newer version. Regression test: Store tests for an insert past the end of the last line, a range ending at (lineCount,0), and a non-BMP character before the edit point. Assert the text equals a spec-conformant application.

title: The background workspace scan re-indexes files the editor already has open under a different URI spelling: duplicate symbols, and sema reverts to the disk copy
claim: indexFileFromDisk decides whether a file is open by looking up pathToURI(path) (`file:///C:/...`). VS Code opens documents as `file:///c%3A/...`, so the lookup misses. The scan (a goroutine started from initialized, which usually finishes after the first didOpen) then (a) adds a second symbol-index entry for the same file and (b) calls sema.PutFile, which is keyed by path, with the on-disk program. That overwrites the open, unsaved document's exports. evictScannedEntryFor only handles entries scanned before the open. Verifier: As stated. It reproduces whenever the background scan finishes after the first didOpen on Windows with VS Code URI spelling.
evidence: Repro on Windows: I opened lib.mut (unsaved: adds `let added = fn...`) and main.mut (uses lib.added()) with VS Code URIs, ran s.scanWorkspace(), then typed one character in main. Result: WorkspaceSymbols("main_decl") returns two entries (file:///C:/... line 1 and file:///c%3A/... line 3), and main.mut gets the false error "...lib.mut declares no added, so lib.added has nothing to refer to", which is true only of the disk copy. Verifier: workspace_scan.go:128-131 checks for an open document by the exact pathToURI string (file:///C:/...), while VS Code opens file:///c%3A/... . TestZZScanAfterOpen on this Windows host: main_decl is indexed at both URIs, and main.mut gets 'lib.mut declares no added, so lib.added has nothing to refer to' because the disk copy replaced the open lib.mut's facts. Verifier's notes: The same URI-spelling mismatch also drives the symbol-delete half of LSP.20.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/server -run TestZZScanAfterOpen -v. It fails with "main_decl indexed 2 times, want 1" and "false diagnostic: the scan replaced the open lib.mut's exports with the disk copy".
impact: In a normal VS Code session on Windows, cross-file errors are reported against code the user has already fixed, workspace symbol search lists every open file twice, and cross-file answers can come from stale disk text until the next keystroke in that module.
fix_proposal: Key the open-document check and the scanned map by canonicalPath(uriToPath(uri)) rather than by URI string. Skip PutFile/Update in indexFileFromDisk when any open document maps to the same canonical path. Regression test: TestZZScanAfterOpen: open two files under VS Code-style URIs, scan, assert one symbol entry per file and no diagnostics that come from the disk copy.

title: Whole-document formatting ends its edit range at a rune count, not UTF-16 units, and leaves stray characters behind
claim: fullDocumentRange sets End.Character = len([]rune(lastLine)). LSP positions count UTF-16 code units, so a character outside the BMP on an unterminated last line puts the range end one unit short per such character. The client then keeps the tail of the old last line after the formatted text. This is separate from M26-LEX-014 (lexer columns): these ranges are computed from the raw text, and the fix is here. Verifier: As stated. It triggers only when the last line has no trailing newline and contains a non-BMP character.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/server -run TestZZFullDocRangeUTF16 -v (fails, got/want shown).
impact: Format-on-save corrupts a file whose last line holds an emoji or other non-BMP character and has no trailing newline. The stray token is often a parse error or an extra statement.
fix_proposal: Use a range that needs no column arithmetic, such as End = {Line: lineCount, Character: 0} (valid past the end once the store clamps), or count UTF-16 units with utf16.RuneLen. Apply the same fix to lineDeleteRange and linePosition. Regression test: Format a document whose unterminated last line contains a non-BMP character, apply the edit with UTF-16 semantics, and assert the result equals FormatSource(src).

title: Range formatting applies half of a joined statement and emits a program that does not parse
claim: When the formatter joins a multi-line statement onto one line, the LCS diff pairs the first original line with the joined line as a standalone one-line replacement, and turns the remaining lines into a separate deletion hunk. Selecting only the first line keeps the replacement and drops the deletion. The doc comment promises the opposite: "A hunk that straddles the selection boundary is dropped rather than partially applied".
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/server -run TestZZRangeFormattingSplitsStatement -v (fails).
impact: "Format Selection" on part of a multi-line call or literal breaks the file.
fix_proposal: Treat a run of differing lines as one hunk. Emit one-line replacements only when both sides of the hunk have the same line count. Otherwise require the whole hunk inside the selection. Regression test: Range-format each line of a multi-line statement separately and assert the result always parses. Also assert it is either unchanged or equal to the whole-document formatting of that statement.

title: The formatter drops the parentheses around a condition that starts with '(' and ends with ')', producing unparseable output
claim: condition() assumes that a printed expression starting with "(" and ending with ")" is already wrapped: `if strings.HasPrefix(formatted, "(") && strings.HasSuffix(formatted, ")") { return formatted }`. A call whose callee is parenthesised, such as (fs + more)[0](x) or (-f)(1), meets that test without being wrapped. The output `if (fs + more)[0](true) {` does not parse. The same helper prints match subjects. Verifier: As stated. A further trigger is a match or if subject that starts with a parenthesised operand and ends in ')' or an index, for example `match (h)["a"]`, which the formatter leaves unparseable.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/server -run TestZZFormatterConditionParens -v (fails).
impact: `mutant fmt` and format-on-save turn a valid program into one that does not compile. The trigger is rare: a parenthesised callee used as an if/while/match condition.
fix_proposal: Decide whether the expression is a node that prints its own outer parentheses (Infix or Prefix), rather than looking at the first and last characters. Otherwise wrap it. Regression test: Formatter round trip: for conditions (a+b)[0](x), (-f)(1) and a plain (a+b), assert that the formatted output parses and is idempotent.

title: The 'Remove unused declaration' / 'Remove duplicate top-level declaration' quick fixes delete the whole physical line: other statements go with it, and a multi-line declaration loses only its first line
claim: Both preferred quick fixes delete from column 0 of the diagnostic's line to the start of the next line, whatever the declaration's extent. The code even notes that the quick fix "deletes a whole line" (diagnostics.go declaredAtTopLevel comment), but nothing checks that the line holds exactly that declaration.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/server -run TestZZRemoveDeclQuickFix -v (fails on both).
impact: A preferred (auto-applicable) quick fix silently removes working code or leaves the file broken.
fix_proposal: Delete the declaration statement's own range (from the program's NodePositions), widened to the whole line only when nothing else is on those lines. Decline when the range is unknown. Regression test: Apply both quick fixes to a one-line multi-statement case and a multi-line fn declaration. Assert the result parses and keeps every other statement.

title: The delimiter-balance check does not understand raw strings: r"C:\evidence\" raises a false 'unclosed delimiter' error, and `mutant lint` exits 1
claim: The balance scanner treats every backslash inside "..." as an escape. In a raw string r"...\" the final backslash is literal (the lexer reads raw strings without escapes), but the scanner reads \" as an escaped quote, stays in string mode, and then pairs the quotes of later strings wrongly. The delimiters inside them become real ones. The diagnostic is published as a mutant-parser ERROR on a program that parses and runs.
evidence: CLI: rawbal.mut = `let dir = r"C:\evidence\";` then `putln("(" + dir);`. `mutant run` prints "(C:\evidence\". `mutant lint rawbal.mut` prints "rawbal.mut:2:8: error: unclosed delimiter `(` [mutant-parser]" with exit 1. Windows directory paths written as raw strings ending in a backslash are common in DFIR scripts. Verifier: My build: `mutant run rawbal.mut` and the --dev .mu print '(C:\evidence\'. `mutant lint rawbal.mut` prints 'rawbal.mut:2:8: error: unclosed delimiter `(` [mutant-parser]', exit=1. The analyzer test case balance-raw-backslash reports it once.
repro: PowerShell in stageB/b2t/LSP/r: ..\tree\mutant.exe lint rawbal.mut (exit=1). Also go test ./lsp/internal/analyzer -run TestZZLintProbes, case balance-raw-backslash.
impact: A correct program shows a hard syntax error in the editor, and `mutant lint` (CI or pre-commit) fails on it.
fix_proposal: Drive the balance check from the lexer's token stream (which already handles raw, triple-quoted and template strings), or teach the scanner r"..." and """...""". Better still, drop it when ParseErrors is empty. Regression test: A lint test: raw string ending in a backslash, followed by a string containing '(' on the next line, must yield no mutant-parser diagnostics.

title: evidenceMutation and pathTraversal report the same call once per enclosing block (5 identical warnings at two if-levels)
claim: Both rules run forEachStatementInScope, which already visits every nested block statement, and call walkExpressions on each visited statement. walkExpressions descends into if/for/while/match bodies again, so a call nested N blocks deep is visited once per ancestor statement.
evidence: Repro: raw_open(img) at the top level, then fs_write(img, "x") inside `if (true) { if (true) { ... } }`. That gives 5 identical diagnostics at 6:24. gets() plus fs_read("cases/" + name) at the same depth gives 5 identical pathTraversal diagnostics at 4:33. Verifier: forEachStatementInScope already visits nested statements, and walkExpressions re-descends into them (evidence_mutation.go:161-190). My runs: evidence-nested-dup gives 5 identical diagnostics at 6:24, and traversal-nested-dup gives 5 at 4:33.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/analyzer -run TestZZLintProbes -v, cases evidence-nested-dup and traversal-nested-dup ("reported 5 times, want 1").
impact: The Problems panel and `mutant lint` repeat the same long warning many times, and the counts that --strict users see are inflated.
fix_proposal: In both rules, walk each statement's own expressions without descending into blocks (or use walkExpressions over the scope's top statements only, as forEachBuiltinCall does), or dedupe by call node. Regression test: Nest the mutating or sink call three blocks deep and assert exactly one diagnostic.

title: evidenceMutation matches identifiers by spelling, so two loops sharing a loop variable name report a write to an output file as a write to evidence
claim: pathKey keys an identifier as "name:"+spelling, with no binding identity. A for-in variable reused in a second loop, or a name rebound by a later let, carries the evidence taint into unrelated writes. The file header claims certainty: "Certainty comes from comparing what the author wrote".
evidence: Repro: `for (path in images) { raw_open(path) ... }` then `for (path in outputs) { fs_write(path, "report") }`. The fs_write is reported (three times, because of the duplication defect) as "`fs_write` overwrites the same path `raw_open` opened as a raw disk image". Verifier: evidence-loop-name-reuse: fs_write(path, "report") in the second loop is reported 3 times as overwriting the path raw_open opened. pathKey is spelling-only. Verifier's notes: The count of 3 comes from the LSP.11 duplication.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/analyzer -run TestZZLintProbes -v, case evidence-loop-name-reuse.
impact: False evidence-destruction warnings on the standard 'iterate images, then write reports' shape train examiners to ignore the one rule meant to protect exhibits.
fix_proposal: Resolve identifiers through the sema graph (the declaration node of the use) and compare declarations rather than spellings. Ignore uses whose binding differs from the opener argument's binding. Regression test: The two-loop case must yield no evidenceMutation diagnostic, and a same-binding write must still yield one.

title: builtinPairReturn warns on a function that forwards a pair by implicit return, although that idiom works at run time
claim: namesHeldAsPairs accepts `return r;` as forwarding the pair, but not the implicit-return form (the last expression statement of a function body, `r;`), which returns the same MULTI_VALUE.
evidence: Lint: `let read_it = fn(p) { let r = fs_read(p); r; }; let data, err = read_it("x.txt");` gives "fs_read returns a (value, err) pair, so `r` holds the pair itself...". Run: present file gives "data=hello evidence err_is_null=true", and missing file gives "data_is_null=true err=ERROR:fs_read: open missing.txt...". The destructuring works exactly as with `return r;`. Verifier: namesHeldAsPairs (builtin_pair_return.go:290-304) holds only ReturnStatement values, and the ExpressionStatement branch just walks. Lint probe pair-implicit-return: 'fs_read returns a (value, err) pair, so `r` holds the pair itself'. My run and --dev: 'present: data=hello evidence err_is_null=true', and 'missing: data_is_null=true err=ERROR:fs_read: open missing.txt...'.
repro: go test -run TestZZLintProbes case pair-implicit-return. Also mutant.exe run implicit.mut, then implicit.mu --dev in stageB/b2t/LSP/r.
impact: The rule promises no warnings on correct code ("staying quiet on correct code the first requirement"), yet it warns on idiomatic code. Following its advice (`let r, err = ...; r;`) would break the forwarding.
fix_proposal: In namesHeldAsPairs, treat the final ExpressionStatement of a FunctionLiteral body whose expression is a bare identifier as a return. Regression test: The implicit-return fixture must yield no builtinPairReturn diagnostic.

title: hardcodedSecret flags ordinary DFIR paths and URLs: auth_log = "/var/log/auth.log", passwd = "/etc/passwd", token_endpoint = "https://..."
claim: The name pattern matches `auth`, `passwd` and `token` as words, and the exemptions are only the _file, _path and _dir suffixes. looksIssued accepts any 8+ character value containing a symbol, so any filesystem path or URL passes.
evidence: All three fixtures produce "`<name>` holds what looks like a credential written into the program...". Verifier: secretNamePattern (hardcoded_secret.go:54-55) matches auth, passwd (pass(word|wd|phrase)?) and token as words. The only exemptions are the _file/_path/_dir suffixes (374). TestZZLintProbes2 reports secret-auth-log, secret-passwd and secret-token-url once each.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/analyzer -run TestZZLintProbes2 -v (secret-auth-log, secret-passwd, secret-token-url each reported once, want 0).
impact: Warnings on the most common artefact paths in Linux triage scripts make the rule easy to switch off, which loses its real findings too.
fix_proposal: Exclude values that parse as an absolute or relative filesystem path (leading /, drive letter, ./, ../) or a URL with a scheme, and add _log/_endpoint/_url suffixes to the name exemptions. Regression test: Add the three fixtures to hardcoded_secret_test.go as must-be-silent cases.

title: pathTraversal follows a guard only one hop back, contradicting its own doc: a value derived twice from a checked name is reported
claim: The doc says "Any mention of the name -- or of any name it was derived from -- ... is taken as the check". The code checks only guarded[node.Value] and guarded[origin.source], the immediate parent.
evidence: name = gets(), guarded by text_contains(name, ".."). Then file = "cases/" + name, full = file + ".log", fs_read(full). The call is reported: "`fs_read` is given a path built from `full`, which was typed at the terminal, and nothing in this file looks at that value first". That sentence is false, because the file checks the value. Verifier: The doc at path_traversal.go:23-24 says 'or of any name it was derived from', but the code checks only guarded[node.Value] and guarded[origin.source] (one hop). pathtrav-two-hops is reported at 5:25, and pathtrav-two-hops-b at 5:29 (3 times).
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/analyzer -run 'TestZZLintProbes|TestZZLintProbes2' -v (pathtrav-two-hops and pathtrav-two-hops-b).
impact: A false positive on careful code, with a message that says the code does something it does not.
fix_proposal: Record the full derivation chain in untrustedOrigin (or walk origins back to the root) and suppress when any ancestor is guarded. Regression test: The two-hop fixture must be silent, and one-hop and unguarded cases must still report.

title: commandInjection reports a name bound once to a string literal as a spliced value
claim: One-hop resolution is applied to the whole argument, but not to each piece of the concatenation. `let flags = "-la"; exec_string("ls " + flags)` is therefore reported, although the doc says a concatenation of literals "is a constant... nothing to report" and singleBindings already knows flags is a literal.
evidence: The fixture yields "This value is concatenated into the command `exec_string` gives to a shell..." at 2:36. Verifier: command_injection.go:107 resolves one hop on the whole argument, and splicedValue (139-179) tests each side with literalString only. cmdinj-constant-name ('let flags = "-la"; exec_string("ls " + flags)') is reported at 2:36, against the doc comment 'nothing to report'.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/analyzer -run TestZZLintProbes -v (cmdinj-constant-name).
impact: A warning on constant commands pushes authors to inline literals or to silence the rule.
fix_proposal: In splicedValue, resolve each identifier piece through bindings and treat a single-bound string literal as fixed text. Regression test: The constant-name fixture must be silent, and a gets()-derived piece must still report.

title: On every activation the extension writes editor.formatOnType into the workspace settings, likely unscoped to Mutant
claim: `vscode.workspace.getConfiguration("editor", { languageId: "mutant" }).update("formatOnType", enabled, ConfigurationTarget.Workspace)` is called unconditionally at activation, without the 4th overrideInLanguage argument. Per the VS Code API, when no [mutant] override exists the value goes to the plain `editor.formatOnType` key. That sets format-on-type for every language in the workspace and creates or modifies .vscode/settings.json in whatever folder is open, which may be a case or evidence folder. With no folder open, the Workspace-target update rejects, and the promise is voided. Verifier: Likely partly wrong. The 'unscoped to Mutant' part probably does not happen, because configurationDefaults declares a [mutant] override, so the update targets the language scope. What remains plausible is that each activation writes (or creates) .vscode/settings.json in the opened folder, which may be a case folder, even when the value equals the default.
evidence: Code as quoted. The API semantics come from the VS Code WorkspaceConfiguration.update documentation (overrideInLanguage undefined updates the language value only if one is already defined). Verifier: extension.ts:217-222 calls editorConfig.update('formatOnType', enabled, ConfigurationTarget.Workspace) on every activation (line 65), with no overrideInLanguage. I did not run it, because VS Code is unavailable. package.json configurationDefaults defines "[mutant]": {"editor.formatOnType": false}. So a language override already exists, and VS Code's undefined-overrideInLanguage path probably writes to [mutant], not to the global key. Verifier's notes: Needs a VS Code run to confirm.
impact: The extension writes into user folders on activation and silently changes format-on-type for other languages.
fix_proposal: Do not write settings. Register the on-type provider conditionally, or have the server decline when the setting is off. If a write is kept, pass overrideInLanguage=true and write only when the value differs. Regression test: Extension test: activation in a fresh workspace leaves .vscode/settings.json absent.

title: On-type formatting after Enter collapses a block the user has just opened
claim: On a newline trigger the whole document is reformatted, and an empty block prints as `{}`. Pressing Enter inside `fn() {|}` therefore removes the new line and puts the cursor after the braces. Verifier: As stated. It happens only with mutant.format.onType.enabled, which is off by default.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/server -run TestZZOnTypeEnterInBlock -v (fails).
impact: With mutant.format.onType.enabled on, the user cannot type a function body: every Enter undoes itself.
fix_proposal: Drop "\n" as a trigger, or restrict on-type edits to the lines of the statement that was just completed and never collapse the block containing the cursor. Regression test: The fixture above must keep an open line inside the braces.

title: The formatter moves comments inside an expression to after the statement, and rewrites `else if` chains into nested else-blocks
claim: Comments are only emitted between statements, so a comment inside a call's argument list or a hash literal is flushed after the statement. `} else if (b) {` is printed as `} else {\n    if (b) {`, one level deeper for each link in the chain. The meaning is preserved, but the canonical style contradicts how the repo's own examples are written. Verifier: As stated. Both outputs parse and are idempotent.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/server -run TestZZFormatterParseAndIdempotence -v (outputs logged).
impact: `mutant fmt` on examples that use else-if (examples/network/*.mut) produces growing indentation, and argument comments end up detached from what they describe.
fix_proposal: Print an Alternative block holding a single IfExpression as `else if`. Attach comments inside expressions to the nearest following argument or entry. Regression test: Formatter golden: an else-if chain stays flat, and an argument comment stays inside the call.

title: Rename refuses names with a leading underscore, although the lexer accepts them and they are the language's module-private names
claim: The first rune must satisfy unicode.IsLetter, but lexer.go:244 starts identifiers with `unicode.IsLetter(l.ch) || l.ch == '_'`. sema.IsModulePrivate makes `_name` the way to mark a top-level name private.
evidence: rename to "_total" returns `invalid identifier name "_total"`, while "let _total = 1;\nputln(_total);" parses cleanly. Verifier: isValidIdentifierName (server.go:1606-1624) requires unicode.IsLetter for the first rune. lexer.go:244 accepts '_', and sema IsModulePrivate uses the '_' prefix. TestZZRenameLeadingUnderscore returns 'invalid identifier name "_total"'.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./lsp/internal/server -run TestZZRenameLeadingUnderscore -v (fails).
impact: An author cannot use rename to make an export private, which is exactly the refactor the unused-private lint encourages.
fix_proposal: Accept '_' as a first character (reject a bare "_"), matching the lexer, and keep the LookupIdent keyword check. Regression test: Rename to _total succeeds and yields edits, and rename to _ is refused.

title: spawnGlobalWrite calls a captured local of the enclosing function 'a global'
claim: The shadow set contains only names bound inside the callback, so a local of the enclosing function that shares a name with a global is reported as "`count` is a global". The rule's own header says captured locals are out of scope. Verifier: As stated. The advice that the write is lost is right; the message names the wrong variable.
evidence: `let count = 0; let run = fn() { let count = 5; spawn(fn() { count = 1; }) ... }` is reported. At run time the global stays 0 and the local stays 5, so the message names the wrong variable. Verifier: The spawn-enclosing-local probe reports '`count` is a global'. My run of spawnlocal.mut (and the --dev .mu) prints 'enclosing local after spawn: 5' and 'global: 0'. The header at spawn_global_write.go:23 says only top-level names count.
repro: go test -run TestZZLintProbes (spawn-enclosing-local). Also mutant.exe run spawnlocal.mut, which prints "enclosing local after spawn: 5" and "global: 0".
impact: The message misleads about which variable is affected. The advice (the write is lost) happens to be right.
fix_proposal: Resolve the assignment target through the sema graph and report only when it binds to the root scope. Regression test: The enclosing-local fixture must be silent or report with 'captured variable' wording.

title: The 'guard return' snippet tests `err != ""`, which works only because == falls back to comparing rendered text
claim: The snippet expands to `if (${1:err} != ${2:""}) { return err; }`. For a successful call err is null, and null != "" is false today only because of M26-VM-010 (the equality fallback to Inspect text). The lint message and the language reference teach `if (err)`. Verifier: As stated. The bug is latent: the snippet breaks when M26-VM-010 is fixed. SEM.13 (a nil in the server's own snippet) is a separate snippet.
evidence: Run: guard.mut with `if (err != "")` prints "present: read hello evidence" and "missing: guard fired", so it works today. If VM-010 is fixed, the guard fires on every success. Verifier: snippets/mutant.json:48-55 expands to 'if (${1:err} != ${2:""})'. My run of guard.mut (and --dev) prints 'present: read hello evidence' and 'missing: guard fired'. It works only because of the Inspect-text equality fallback (M26-VM-010). Verifier's notes: Fix together with M26-VM-010.
repro: mutant.exe run guard.mut, then guard.mu --dev (stageB/b2t/LSP/r).
impact: Generated code carries a latent bug that appears when VM-010 is fixed.
fix_proposal: Change the snippet body to `if (${1:err}) {\n\treturn ${1:err};\n}`. Regression test: A snippet lint in the extension tests: no snippet compares err with "".

title: Dead and misattached code in the server and diagnostics
claim: formatDocumentText has no caller in the repo. server.isWorkspaceResolvableTopLevelKind duplicates workspace.isWorkspaceResolvableTopLevelKind and has no caller in the server package. Server.shutdown is written in shutdownRequest and never read, so requests after shutdown are served normally. In diagnostics.go the doc paragraphs for checkCall and checkMultiNameBinding sit above checkDeprecated's comment and merge into one doc comment on the wrong function.
evidence: grep over lsp/ for formatDocumentText and the server copy of isWorkspaceResolvableTopLevelKind: definitions only. grep for `.shutdown`: only the assignment at server.go:333. Verifier: A grep over lsp/ finds formatDocumentText only at its definition (server.go:1697), and the server copy of isWorkspaceResolvableTopLevelKind (server.go:1717) is uncalled (the callers are in workspace/symbol_index.go and use that package's copy). s.shutdown is written only at server.go:333. diagnostics.go:1807-1834: the checkCall and checkMultiNameBinding paragraphs merge into checkDeprecated's doc comment.
repro: grep -rn formatDocumentText lsp; grep -rn '\.shutdown' lsp --include=*.go
impact: Maintenance noise, and a shutdown flag that suggests post-shutdown behaviour the server does not have.
fix_proposal: Delete the two unused functions. Either honour shutdown (reply InvalidRequest after it) or remove the field. Move each doc comment onto its own function. Regression test: None needed beyond compilation. Optionally, a server test asserting that a request after shutdown returns an error.

title: net_banner throws away the banner of any service that keeps the connection open (SSH, SMTP, FTP)
claim: net_banner reads with io.ReadAll under a read deadline. ReadAll only returns cleanly on EOF, so a server that sends its banner and then waits for the client (every SSH, SMTP, FTP, POP3 and IMAP server) makes the call end on the deadline error. The branch that handles that error discards the bytes already read and reports ok=false with banner "". Verifier: As stated. Severity lowered to S3: the result says ok=false with an error, so it is a failure the caller can see, not a wrong answer passed off as right. It still makes net_banner useless against SSH, SMTP, FTP, POP3 and IMAP.
evidence: net.go:217-218 `_ = conn.SetReadDeadline(time.Now().Add(timeout))` / `banner, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(conn, 4096))`; :219-224 `if readErr != nil { return ... "ok": boolObj(false), "banner": stringObj(""), "error": stringObj(readErr.Error()) }`. Repro: a server writes "SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6\r\n" and keeps the socket open for 3s. The result was {banner: , error: read tcp ...: i/o timeout, ok: false}. Both existing tests have the server close the connection straight after writing (network_forensics_test.go:109-110 `conn.Write(...)` then `conn.Close()`; net_core_test.go:90-91 deferred Close), so they cannot catch this. Verifier: net.go:217-224 ReadAll under a read deadline; the timeout branch discards the bytes. Repro TestZZ01Banner: a server writes '220 smtp.example ESMTP ready' and holds the socket -> {banner:'', ok:false, error:'i/o timeout'}. The same server closing after the write -> ok:true with the banner.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_review_net_test.go TestReviewNetBannerKeepsOpen (test binary built once, run with -test.run): FAIL 'DEFECT: banner sent by server was discarded: ok=false banner=""'
impact: The builtin is supposed to collect service banners, but it reports 'no banner' with a timeout error for the protocols it is mostly used on. Service identification in a triage or recon script is wrong and says nothing about why.
fix_proposal: Treat a read deadline as the normal end of a banner. If readErr is a net.Error with Timeout() and len(banner)>0, return ok=true with the bytes read. Or read until the first newline, or until the limit, whichever comes first. Regression test: Server writes a banner line and holds the connection for longer than the timeout. Assert ok=true and that the banner contains the line. Keep the existing close-after-write case.

title: http_get/http_post/http_request swallow a body read error and report a truncated response as a successful empty body
claim: httpResponseOrError drops the io.ReadAll error. The result is body "", error "", with the real status and headers. httpResponseOrError2 then sees error=="" and returns err=nil, so a response cut off mid-body looks like a successful response with an empty body.
evidence: http.go:199-203 `rawBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)` / `bodyStr := ""` / `if readErr == nil { bodyStr = string(rawBody) }`. readErr is never used again, and :215 hard-codes `"error": stringObj("")`. Repro: the server replies `Content-Length: 100` and sends 10 bytes before closing. http_get returned {body: , error: , headers: {Content-Length: 100, ...}, status: 200} with err=<nil>. Verifier: http.go:199-203 drops readErr, and :215 hard-codes error ''. Repro TestZZ02TruncatedBody: Content-Length 100 with 10 bytes sent -> {body:'', error:'', status:200} err=nil. Verifier's notes: The peer, which is untrusted, can trigger it. An empty feed reads as a valid empty answer.
repro: scratch TestReviewHttpGetTruncatedBody: FAIL 'truncated body (10 of 100 bytes) reported as success: status=200 body="" error=""'
impact: A dropped or reset download (IOC feed, evidence fetch) reads as a valid empty document. A script that treats an empty feed as 'no indicators' gets a false negative, with no error anywhere.
fix_proposal: Pass readErr on: set the hash's error field and return newError("%s: reading body: %s"). Consider returning the partial bytes together with a truncated flag. Regression test: Raw TCP server that declares Content-Length 100 and sends 10 bytes. Assert that err is non-nil and the error field is non-empty.

title: process_tree(0) on Windows, or any ppid cycle, loops forever and grows memory until the process dies
claim: process_tree does a breadth-first walk over byParent[ppid] with no visited set. On Windows, pid 0 (System Idle Process) reports ppid 0, so byParent[0] contains pid 0. Every time the walk dequeues pid 0 it appends byParent[0] again, and the queue and the descendants array grow forever. A ppid cycle caused by pid reuse on Windows does the same from any pid on the cycle.
evidence: :66-68 `byParent[p.ppid] = append(byParent[p.ppid], p)`; :75-85 `queue := append([]sfProcess{}, byParent[rootPID]...)` / `for len(queue) > 0 { ... desc = append(desc, ...); queue = append(queue, byParent[cur.pid]...) }`. There is no seen map and no depth or count cap. Repro log: 'self-parented: pid=0 ppid=0 name=System Idle Process', then heap samples 0.25s:2MiB ... 3.51s:212MiB 4.03s:596MiB 4.53s:953MiB 4.78s:1039MiB, where the watchdog stopped the binary (exit 3). Attempt 2 had also found a real 4-process ppid cycle on this host ([2204 25668 16896 14520 2204]) with the same runaway. Verifier: system_forensics.go:65-85: breadth-first walk with no visited set. Repro TestZZ03Tree0 on Windows: process_tree(0) had not returned after 4.8s, the heap grew from 2 to 820 MiB, and the watchdog stopped the process. Verifier's notes: Pid 0 comes first in process_list on Windows, so a loop over all pids hits it. A ppid cycle from pid reuse was not reproduced here, but it goes through the same code path.
repro: scratch builtin/zz_b2s_windows_test.go TestZZProcessTreeZero (goroutine plus 1 GiB watchdog): '--- DEFECT: process_tree(0) still running after 4.781s; heap samples ... 4.78s:1039MiB', exit=3
impact: On a live Windows host, a triage script that calls process_tree on each pid from process_list (pid 0 comes first) hangs and exhausts memory. A ppid cycle does the same from an ordinary pid. The recover() around builtins cannot help, because nothing panics.
fix_proposal: Keep a visited set keyed by pid and skip a pid already emitted, including the root. Treat p.pid == p.ppid as a root with no children. A cap on the number of descendants, as a named limit, is a backstop. Regression test: Unit-test the tree walk with a synthetic process slice containing {0,0} and a 3-cycle, factored out of sfListProcesses. Assert that it terminates and that each pid appears at most once.

title: Live registry reports a value that does not exist as a present REG_NONE value, with no error
claim: readLiveRegistryValue maps every GetValue error, including ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND for a missing value, to a regEntry of type REG_NONE with empty data. getValue returns that entry with a nil error. reg_get_value on the live backend therefore never says 'not found', although the JSON and hive backends do. Verifier: As stated. The typed getters' errors are also discarded (:126, :133, :136, :139, :148).
evidence: :120-123 `_, valType, err := k.GetValue(name, nil)` / `if err != nil && err != registry.ErrShortBuffer { return regEntry{name: displayName, typ: "REG_NONE", data: stringObj("")} }`; :112 `return readLiveRegistryValue(k, name), nil`. Repro: reg_get_value(reg_open(`HKCU\Software`), "", "NoSuchValue_MutantReview_b2s") returned {data: , name: NoSuchValue_MutantReview_b2s, type: REG_NONE} with err=nil. The same question to the JSON hive fixture returned 'reg_get_value: value not found: NoSuchValue'. The type-specific getters' errors are discarded too (:126 `s, _, _ := k.GetStringValue(name)`, :133, :136, :139, :148). Verifier: registry_live_windows.go:120-123 maps any GetValue error to REG_NONE, and getValue returns nil. Repro TestZZ04RegMissing: live HKCU\Software value 'NoSuchValue_zv_b4b' -> {data:'', type:REG_NONE}, err=nil. The JSON backend gives 'reg_get_value: value not found'.
repro: scratch TestZZLiveRegistryMissingValue: FAIL 'reg_get_value on a value that does not exist returned {data: , name: ..., type: REG_NONE} with no error'
impact: Live persistence checks give the wrong answer. 'Does the Run key hold value X?' is answered yes, as an empty REG_NONE, for every name asked. Absence cannot be told apart from a real empty REG_NONE value (which exists, for example under HKCR\.txt\OpenWithProgids).
fix_proposal: Return the error from readLiveRegistryValue. In getValue, map registry.ErrNotExist to the same 'value not found' error the other backends use. Pass on errors from the typed getters. Regression test: Windows-only test: a missing value name under HKCU\Software must give an error that matches the JSON backend's message, and a real REG_NONE value must still be returned.

title: pids are truncated to 32 bits: process_kill(getpid()+2^32) kills the current process past its refuse-self guard, and process_hash and similar builtins answer for a different pid
claim: The self guard compares the full 64-bit value (`pid == os.Getpid()`), but the OS calls take 32 bits: os.FindProcess, and through it OpenProcess(uint32) on Windows and kill(pid_t) on Unix, and gopsutil process.NewProcess(int32(pid)). So process_kill(getpid()+2^32) passes the guard and kills the running program. For process_hash, process_threads, process_open_files and process_env, a pid outside int32 is silently truncated, and the answer for the truncated pid comes back labelled with the pid the caller asked for. Verifier: As stated. On Windows, os.FindProcess, OpenProcess and gopsutil take a 32-bit pid, so the refuse-self check on the 64-bit value is bypassed. Linux was not re-run.
evidence: :298 `pid := int(pidObj.Value)`; :309 `if pid == os.Getpid() { ... refuses to kill current process }`; :317 `os.FindProcess(pid)`; :99/:131/:264/:355 `process.NewProcess(int32(pid))`; sfParsePIDArg :348 `return int(pidObj.Value), nil` with no range check. Repros: (1) selfkill.mut run through mutant.exe. `process_kill(me)` refused, then `process_kill(me + 4294967296)` terminated the program (exit code 1), and the next putln('STILL ALIVE ...') never printed. (2) Go test: a child ping.exe with pid 3388 was killed by process_kill(4294970684). (3) process_hash(4294991596) returned path C:\Windows\System32\PING.EXE, the child with pid 24300, labelled pid 4294991596. Verifier: Repro TestZZ05PidTrunc: process_hash(2^32+childpid) returned path PING.EXE, labelled with the 64-bit pid. process_kill(2^32+childpid) returned true and the ping child exited. zzr/selfkill.mut through mutant.exe: process_kill(me) was refused, then process_kill(me+4294967296) killed the run (exit 1) and the next putln never printed.
repro: zzrepro/selfkill.mut (mutant.exe run, then run the .mu with --dev): output stops at 'calling process_kill( 4294994728 )', exit code 1. Scratch TestZZProcessKillPidTruncation and TestZZProcessHashPidTruncation both FAIL as predicted.
impact: The only safety check process_kill has can be bypassed by accident: a pid read from evidence or computed wrongly kills the examiner's own run. Pid-keyed answers (hash, threads, environment) can be attributed to the wrong process in a report.
fix_proposal: Validate every pid argument once, in sfParsePIDArg and in ProcessKill, requiring 0 <= pid <= math.MaxInt32 (and the uint32 range on Windows), and refuse anything else. Run the self guard on the validated, narrowed value. On Unix also refuse pid <= 0 (0 and negative values signal process groups).
