Regression test: process_kill(getpid()+2^32) and process_hash(2^32+childpid) both return an error. Use a child process for the kill case.

title: Live registry drops the data of every type outside the six it knows (REG_RESOURCE_LIST etc.), against the reg_get_value contract
claim: The reg_get_value metadata promises that 'Binary values (REG_BINARY, and types the reader does not recognise) also carry data_bytes'. The live backend's default branch returns data "" and no raw bytes, so a 140-byte REG_RESOURCE_LIST reads as empty. The code comment admits the regf backend does it differently. Verifier: As stated. The code comment admits the difference from the regf backend, but the metadata promise is still broken.
evidence: :150-154 `default: // An unrecognised type reports no data on a live key ... that difference predates this and is left alone here.` / `return regEntry{name: displayName, typ: fmt.Sprintf("REG_TYPE(%d)", valType), data: stringObj("")}`. Repro: the raw registry API reported `.Translated type=8 size=140`, and reg_get_value(live `HKLM\HARDWARE\RESOURCEMAP\System Resources\Physical Memory`, ".Translated") returned {data: , name: .Translated, type: REG_TYPE(8)} with no data_bytes. Verifier: registry_live_windows.go:150-155 default branch. Repro TestZZ06RegType8: raw .Translated is type 8 with 140 bytes. reg_get_value(live) -> {data:'', type:REG_TYPE(8)} with no data_bytes. metadata.go:2051 promises data_bytes for 'types the reader does not recognise'. Verifier's notes: P2, not P1: it affects only uncommon value types.
repro: scratch TestZZLiveRegistryDropsOtherTypes: FAIL '140 bytes of REG type 8 reported as empty data with no data_bytes'
impact: Evidence present in the live registry (REG_NONE blobs used for persistence, resource lists, REG_LINK targets) is reported as empty. The same key exported to a hive file and read through the regf backend gives different data.
fix_proposal: In the default branch, fetch the raw bytes (k.GetValue(name, buf) with the size from the first call), hex-encode them into data and set raw. That gives data_bytes, as the regf backend and the metadata already promise. Regression test: Windows-only: read a type-8 or REG_NONE value that has data. Assert that data_bytes is present and its length equals the raw size.

title: process_memory_scan on the self process always finds the pattern, because the pattern argument is in the memory being scanned
claim: Only the self process can be scanned, and the scan covers every readable region of the process, including the heap that holds the pattern string, its []byte copy and the Mutant VM's constants. Any pattern therefore matches at least once. A fresh random pattern that exists nowhere else was reported found 6 times on Windows (attempt 2 got 2 on Linux under WSL). The scan cannot answer 'not present'.
evidence: :230 `if int(pidObj.Value) != os.Getpid() { ... self process only }`; :235 `sfScanSelfMemory([]byte(patternObj.Value), maxMatches)`. The []byte copy and patternObj.Value both sit in scanned regions (memscan_windows.go:29-31 accepts any MEM_COMMIT page that is not NOACCESS or GUARD). The existing test system_forensics_test.go:124 scans for a needle it put in memory itself and asserts a match, so it cannot fail. Verifier: Repro TestZZ07MemScan: a fresh random 'zv-<24 hex>' pattern -> matched=4 on Windows. The pattern argument and its []byte copy sit in the scanned heap. The metadata does not mention this.
repro: scratch TestZZMemoryScanFindsAnyPattern: 'process_memory_scan(self, fresh unique pattern) matched=6' -> FAIL
impact: 'Is this IOC string resident in memory?' always comes back yes. The result is worthless as a finding, and matched>0 is misleading when quoted in a report.
fix_proposal: Report which matches fall inside the scanner's own buffers, or exclude them: hold the pattern in one known allocation and skip matches at that address and at the chunk buffer. At minimum, document that self-scan matches include the query itself and return the pattern's own address so a caller can discount it. Cross-process scanning is the real fix. Regression test: Scan for a pattern built at runtime (for example the hex of random bytes) that exists nowhere else, and assert that the addresses exclude the argument's own storage. Replace the test at system_forensics_test.go:124 with one that can fail.

title: http_conn_read_request/_head and http_conn_read_response/_head read an unbounded request line and header section from the peer
claim: The 32 MiB cap ('so a hostile stream can't OOM us') is applied only to bodies, through io.LimitReader in requestToHash and responseToHash. http.ReadRequest and http.ReadResponse on mc.buffered() have no header limit (net/http enforces MaxHeaderBytes only inside http.Server), so a peer that sends one very long header line makes the interception proxy buffer all of it.
evidence: :70 `req, err := http.ReadRequest(mc.buffered())` (the same at :85, :105, :144); :25 `const maxHTTPBodyBytes = 32 << 20 // 32 MiB cap so a hostile stream can't OOM us.`; :326 `io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(req.Body, maxHTTPBodyBytes))`, body only. Repro at two sizes under the 1 GiB watchdog: a 16 MiB header grew the heap by 48 MiB, a 64 MiB header grew it by 135 MiB (ratio 2.8, about 2x the input), and both were accepted ('ok, X-Pad len=67108864'). Attempt 2 measured an 800 MiB peak for a 256 MiB header. Verifier: mitm_http.go:70/85/105/144 call http.ReadRequest/ReadResponse with no header budget. Repro TestZZ08HeaderUnbounded: an 8 MiB X-Pad header grew the heap by 12 MiB, a 32 MiB header by 69 MiB, and both were accepted. Verifier's notes: A network peer, which is untrusted, can trigger it. This is resource exhaustion, not an embargo item.
repro: scratch TestZZHttpConnReadRequestHeaderUnbounded: FAIL 'heap growth scales with header size (48 MiB -> 135 MiB, ratio 2.8)'
impact: Any client of a Mutant net_serve or MITM handler can exhaust the examiner's memory with one connection. With maxServeHandlers=1024 concurrent handlers the effect multiplies.
fix_proposal: Wrap the reader in a per-message header budget before ReadRequest and ReadResponse, for example with a named maxHTTPHeaderBytes of 1 MiB: an io.LimitedReader over the buffered reader whose limit is reset before the body is read. Or pre-read the head with a bounded scan for CRLFCRLF. Regression test: Peer sends 'X-Pad: ' followed by (maxHTTPHeaderBytes+1) bytes. Assert an error and that heap growth stays under a small multiple of the limit.

title: net_pcap_analyze, net_capture_raw and net_os_fingerprint allocate whatever a pcap record header asks for, up to 4 GiB per packet, from a 40-byte file
claim: pcapgo.Reader bounds CaptureLength only by the file's own snaplen (uint32 from the header) and by orig_len, both of which the attacker controls, and then does make([]byte, CaptureLength). None of the three builtins sets a snaplen ceiling, so a crafted 40-byte capture allocates incl_len bytes before the read fails. Verifier: As stated. Also, all three returned err=nil for this truncated record: the short read comes back as io.EOF and is treated as a clean end of capture, so a truncated capture is silently accepted.
evidence: pcapgo read.go: `r.snaplen = r.byteOrder.Uint32(buf[16:20])`, then in ReadPacketData `if ci.CaptureLength > int(r.snaplen) {...}` / `data = make([]byte, ci.CaptureLength)`. net.go:408/505/791 `pcapgo.NewReader(file)` with no reader.SetSnaplen and no size check against the file size. Repro: a 40-byte file with snaplen 0xffffffff and incl_len 32 MiB allocated 32 MiB, and with incl_len 128 MiB allocated 128 MiB, in each of the three builtins (TotalAlloc delta, under the watchdog). Verifier: gopacket v1.1.19 pcapgo read.go:116/126/134 trusts the header snaplen, and net.go never calls SetSnaplen. Repro TestZZ09Pcap: a 40-byte pcap with snaplen 0xffffffff and incl_len 16 MiB and then 64 MiB -> TotalAlloc grew by 16 and 64 MiB in each of net_pcap_analyze, net_capture_raw and net_os_fingerprint. Verifier's notes: Triggered from evidence input, up to about 4 GiB of transient allocation per call.
repro: scratch TestZZPcapHeaderDrivenAllocation: FAIL for net_pcap_analyze, net_capture_raw and net_os_fingerprint ('allocates by the file's incl_len: 32 MiB then 128 MiB for a 40-byte file')
impact: A hostile capture file in an evidence set can make a triage run allocate up to 4 GiB per call (incl_len 0xffffffff), which kills a small analysis VM, and the growth comes from the evidence itself.
fix_proposal: After NewReader, call reader.SetSnaplen(min(header snaplen, a named maxPcapPacketBytes such as 256 KiB, the largest real link MTU plus a margin)), or compare each record's length with the remaining file size before reading. Record the new limit in the limit budget. Regression test: The same 40-byte crafted file must return an error with TotalAlloc growth below 1 MiB.

title: http_get/http_post/http_request route through HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY from the environment
claim: The configuration policy forbids environment-variable configuration, and the policy guard only catches direct Getenv-style calls. httpClient has no Transport, so net/http's DefaultTransport reads HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY and sends every request through whatever proxy the environment names, without the examiner being told. (On Linux, SSL_CERT_FILE/SSL_CERT_DIR likewise decide TLS trust for these calls and net_tls_connect; attempt 2 started but did not finish that repro.) Verifier: As stated. This breaks the published configuration policy.
evidence: :14 `var httpClient = &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}`, where Transport nil means DefaultTransport, which is Proxy: ProxyFromEnvironment. Repro: with HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:<port> set in the process, http_get("http://ioc-feed.mutant-review.invalid/list.txt") was received by the local 'proxy' ('GET http://ioc-feed.mutant-review.invalid/list.txt HTTP/1.1'), and its forged body 'from-the-proxy!!' came back as status 200 with err=nil. Verifier: http.go:14 has a nil Transport, so DefaultTransport and ProxyFromEnvironment are used. Repro TestZZ10ProxyEnv (run alone): with HTTP_PROXY set to a local listener, http_get('http://ioc-feed.zv-b4b.invalid/list.txt') reached the listener, and its body 'FROM-PROXY!' came back as status 200 with err=nil. docs/CONFIGURATION_POLICY.md Rule 2 permits reading a foreign variable only where the value is 'observed, never obeyed'. Verifier's notes: security=false: only someone who controls the examiner's environment can use it, and such a party is already privileged. SSL_CERT_FILE on Linux was not re-run.
repro: scratch TestReviewHttpGetObeysProxyEnv, run alone because the stdlib caches the proxy env: FAIL 'environment variable HTTP_PROXY redirected http_get through 127.0.0.1:62585'
impact: Whoever controls the examiner's environment can see, and for plain HTTP rewrite, everything the scripts fetch or post, including IOC feeds and uploads. That is the environment-driven behaviour the owner decision rules out.
fix_proposal: Give httpClient an explicit Transport cloned from DefaultTransport with Proxy: nil. If proxying is ever wanted, add a flag. Consider an explicit RootCAs source for the same reason, and extend the policy guard to flag http.Client values with a nil Transport and uses of DefaultTransport. Regression test: With HTTP_PROXY set to a local listener, http_get to an unroutable host must not reach the listener.

title: net_serve dies on the first accept error, including the stale deadline a previous net_accept leaves on the listener
claim: NetServe returns on any Accept error. net_accept sets a deadline on the raw listener and never clears it, so after one timed-out net_accept, net_serve fails at once with 'i/o timeout'. Transient errors such as EMFILE and ECONNABORTED also end the server, where http.Server retries them with backoff. Verifier: As stated. The EMFILE/ECONNABORTED retry part was established by code reading only.
evidence: serve.go:87-89 `conn, err := ml.ln.Accept()` / `if err != nil { return ... "net_serve: accept failed: %s" }`; secure_net.go:465 `ml.raw.SetDeadline(time.Now().Add(...))`, which is not reset afterwards. Repro: net_accept(l, 20) timed out, then net_serve(l, ...) returned immediately with 'net_serve: accept failed: accept tcp 127.0.0.1:62058: i/o timeout'. Verifier: Repro TestZZ11ServeAfterAccept: net_accept(l,20) timed out, then net_serve(l,...) returned at once with 'net_serve: accept failed: ... i/o timeout'. serve.go:86-90 returns on any Accept error, and secure_net.go:465 leaves the deadline set.
repro: scratch TestZZNetServeAfterAcceptTimeout: FAIL 'net_serve returned at once instead of serving'
impact: A long-running collector or MITM service stops at the first file-descriptor spike or after a poll-then-serve pattern. The doc promises it 'only returns on a listener error'.
fix_proposal: Clear the listener deadline at the start of NetServe (ml.raw.SetDeadline(time.Time{})). Retry temporary accept errors with capped backoff, and return only when the listener is closed. Regression test: net_accept with a short timeout, then net_serve: a client must still be dispatched.

title: A net_serve handler that fails or panics never closes its connection; the client hangs and the handle and file descriptor leak
claim: run() only logs a handler runtime error, or recovers a panic, and returns. The connection registered by NetServe is neither closed nor removed from connRegistry, so each failing connection leaks a socket, and the peer waits until its own timeout. Verifier: As stated. The line numbers are wrong: serve/serve.go is 145 lines long; the recover is at :99-103 and the Run error log at :128-130.
evidence: serve.go:294-296 `if err := machine.Run(); err != nil { fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "[net_serve] handler error ...") }`, with no close; :265-269 recover logs only; builtin/serve.go:91 `id := registerConn(conn, ml.isTLS)`. Nothing removes it on the error path. Repro: the handler reads, then calls a non-function. The log showed '[net_serve] handler error (conn 1): vm_runtime_error ... calling non-function', and the client's read was still blocked 4s later. Verifier: Repro serve/zz_verify_test.go TestZZ12FailedHandler: a handler that raises a runtime error left the client read blocked until its 3s timeout. The same handler without the error gave EOF in 18ms. run() only logs the error or panic.
repro: scratch serve/zz_review_serve_test.go TestReviewFailedHandlerLeaksConnection: FAIL 'handler failed but the server side of the connection is still open 4s later'
impact: One buggy code path, or a hostile input that triggers a runtime error in the handler, leaks a descriptor per connection until accept fails with EMFILE, which by the finding above then stops the server.
fix_proposal: In the NetServe goroutine, after NetServeRunHook returns (or in run's deferred recover) with an error or panic, call removeConn(connID) and close it if the handler has not already done so. Keep caller ownership for the success path, which the net_spawn hand-off relies on. Regression test: A handler that raises a runtime error: the client must see EOF within a second, and lookupConn(id) must fail.

title: net_serve/net_spawn compile handlers without the module and macro pipeline, so a handler that uses import or a macro fails although mutant run compiles it
claim: prepare() parses and compiles the one file directly (parser, then compiler.NewWithState, then Compile). It skips module.Load/Link and macro expansion, which generator.buildByteCode does for every normal compile. Handlers are documented as 'the Mutant program run for each connection', yet an import fails with 'undefined variable' and a macro with 'macro definitions must appear at the top level'. Verifier: As stated. Severity lowered to S4: the failure is loud and happens at net_serve/net_spawn time, and no wrong result is produced.
evidence: serve.go:236-251 `p := parser.New(lexer.New(string(src)))` ... `comp.Compile(program)`, with no module.Load and no evaluator.DefineMacros/ExpandMacros (compare generator/generate.go buildByteCode). Repro: a handler with `import "helpers.mut"; putln(helpers.greet());` compiles through generator.CompileForDebug, but prepare reports 'compile error: undefined variable: helpers'. A handler with `let twice = macro(x) {...}; putln(twice(21));` compiles through the generator, but prepare reports 'macro definitions must appear at the top level, and are expanded before compilation'. Verifier: Repro serve TestZZ13Prepare: generator.CompileForDebug accepts both an import handler and a macro handler. prepare() fails with 'undefined variable: helpers' and with 'macro definitions must appear at the top level'.
repro: scratch serve/zz_b2r_prepare_test.go TestB2rHandlerWithImportCompilesLikeAProgram and TestB2rHandlerWithMacroCompilesLikeAProgram: both FAIL as predicted
impact: Handler code cannot share libraries with the main program. A program that 'serves itself' works under mutant run but not under net_serve. The error messages blame the author's code.
fix_proposal: Reuse the generator's buildByteCode path (module graph, link, macro expansion, then compile) in prepare, exported as needed. Resolve relative imports against the handler's directory. Regression test: Keep the two scratch tests, which assert that prepare succeeds for an import handler and a macro handler.

title: net_spawn work is silently dropped when the program that spawned it finishes
claim: spawn starts `go run(...)` and returns true. The goroutine is not tracked by anything the runner waits on (builtin/tasks.go WaitForTasks only counts spawn() tasks), so when the main program ends the process exits and the worker is killed partway. net_spawn has already returned true. Verifier: As stated. The line numbers are wrong: the spawn is at serve/serve.go:135-141.
evidence: serve.go:305 `go run(handlerPath, 0, arg)`, with no WaitGroup and no liveTasks.Add. Repro with mutant.exe: spawn_main.mut calls net_spawn("worker.mut", "payload") and prints 'spawned: true'. worker.mut sleeps 800 ms and then writes worker_done.txt. After the run, plus a 2 s wait, worker_done.txt did not exist. Running worker.mu on its own created it. Verifier: zzr/spawn_main.mu through mutant.exe printed 'spawned: true' and exited 0. Two seconds later worker_done.txt did not exist. worker.mu run on its own wrote it. serve.go:139 `go run(...)` is not tracked by anything the runner waits on.
repro: zzrepro/spawn_main.mut and worker.mut: 'spawned: true', 'worker_done after spawn run: False', 'worker_done after standalone run: True'
impact: Background collectors or exporters started with net_spawn from a script that does not end in net_serve never finish, and nothing reports it. The docs describe the builtin only as 'returns immediately'.
fix_proposal: Register net_spawn goroutines with the same live-task accounting WaitForTasks uses, so the runner waits for them at exit. Or document that the caller must keep the program alive, and return a handle that can be joined. Regression test: A runner-level test: main spawns a worker that writes a file after a delay, and the file must exist when mutant exits.

title: http_get/http_post/http_request follow redirects, including to another host, and report the final response as the answer for the URL asked
claim: The client uses Go's default CheckRedirect, which follows up to 10 hops across hosts and schemes (https to http included). The result has no final URL or redirect chain, so a script cannot tell that the status and body came from somewhere else. POST is also silently turned into a GET on 301/302/303.
evidence: :14 `&http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}` with no CheckRedirect; :211-216 the result holds only status, body, headers and error. Repro: server A replies 302 to server B's /landing, and http_get(A/ioc) returned {body: body-from-the-OTHER-host, status: 200}, with result keys [status body headers error]. Verifier: Repro TestZZ15Redirect: server A 302 -> server B /landing; http_get(A/ioc) returned body 'from-B', status 200, with no final URL field.
repro: scratch TestB2rHttpGetFollowsCrossHostRedirectSilently: FAIL 'redirect to another host followed silently'
impact: IOC and evidence fetches can be answered by a different host (a parked domain, a captive portal, an attacker's redirect), and the provenance of the result is lost.
fix_proposal: Record resp.Request.URL as final_url, plus the redirect count, in the result. Consider refusing cross-host or scheme-downgrade redirects unless an option allows them. Regression test: A cross-host 302: assert that final_url equals B's URL, or that the call is refused.

title: http_parse_request/response and http_conn_read_* silently truncate a body over 32 MiB, and the rebuilt message keeps the original Content-Length
claim: requestToHash and responseToHash read at most 32 MiB of body and return no error and no truncated flag. The headers still carry the original Content-Length, so http_build_request or http_build_response produce a message whose declared length disagrees with its body. In an interception proxy that desynchronises the next hop.
evidence: :326 `bodyBytes, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(req.Body, maxHTTPBodyBytes))`, with the rest of the body neither read nor reported. Repro: a raw POST with Content-Length 33555456 parsed to body len 33554432 with no error, and http_build_request of that hash emitted 'Content-Length: 33555456' followed by a 33554432-byte body. Verifier: Repro TestZZ16ParseTrunc: a declared body of 33555456 bytes parsed to a 33554432-byte body with err=nil. http_build_request emitted 'Content-Length: 33555456' followed by the 33554432-byte body.
repro: scratch TestReviewHTTPParseRequestTruncates: FAIL 'body silently truncated from 33555456 to 33554432 bytes, no error and no truncated flag'
impact: A captured upload or download is recorded incomplete as if it were whole, and a relayed message is malformed.
fix_proposal: Read up to limit+1 bytes. If more than the limit arrives, return an error (or truncated=true together with the declared length) and point callers to the *_head builtins for streaming. Regression test: A body of limit+1 bytes must give an error or truncated=true.

title: ws_read_frame/ws_write_frame cannot relay a frame faithfully: RSV1 (permessage-deflate) is dropped and FIN is forced on
claim: The documented use is 'read one frame, inspect/rewrite it, write it to the other side'. ws_read_frame discards the RSV bits (no field for them), and ws_write_frame always writes 0x80|opcode. A compressed frame is relayed as uncompressed garbage, and the first fragment of a fragmented message (FIN=0) is relayed as a complete message, after which the continuation frame is a protocol error.
evidence: :61-64 `fin := header[0]&0x80 != 0` / `opcode := header[0] & 0x0f`, with RSV bits 0x70 never surfaced; :156 `b.WriteByte(0x80 | opcode) // FIN + opcode`. Repro: wire 0xC1 (FIN+RSV1, text) was relayed as 0x81; wire 0x01 (FIN=0, text) was read as fin:false and relayed as 0x81. Verifier: Repro TestZZ17WS: wire 0xC1 read and rewritten came out as 0x81. Wire 0x01 was read as fin:false and rewritten as 0x81. websocket.go:61-62 drops the RSV bits, and :156 always writes 0x80|opcode.
repro: scratch TestZZWSFrameRoundTrip: FAIL 'first byte 0xC1 became 0x81', 'first byte 0x01 became 0x81 (fin read as false)'
impact: A WebSocket MITM built on these primitives corrupts traffic from any browser that negotiates permessage-deflate (the default in Chrome and Firefox) and breaks fragmented messages.
fix_proposal: Return rsv1, rsv2 and rsv3 from ws_read_frame, and accept optional fin and rsv arguments (or a frame hash) in ws_write_frame so a relay can round-trip the header byte exactly. Regression test: Read, then write, for 0xC1 and 0x01 frames: the first byte must be identical.

title: cmd_run with the cmd shell runs only the first line and reports ok=true
claim: cmd_run joins the builder's lines with "\n" and passes the result as one `cmd.exe /C <command>` argument. cmd.exe stops at the first newline, so every later line is silently dropped while the result says ok=true and exit_code 0. PowerShell runs all lines.
evidence:
builtin/command_exec.go:86 `command := strings.Join(builder.lines, "
")`; security/command_exec.go:113-114 `return cmdExecutable, []string{cmdFlagExec, command}, nil`. Repro: lines ["echo FIRST_LINE", "echo SECOND_LINE"] with shell cmd gave stdout "FIRST_LINE
", ok: true. The same builder with shell powershell printed both lines. Related to the ledger's M26-TMP-005 (bash) and M26-TMP-008 (cmd quoting), but the fix is different: the join lives in the builtin and needs a per-shell separator. Verifier: Repro TestZZ18CmdRun: shell cmd with lines [echo FIRST_LINE, echo SECOND_LINE] -> stdout 'FIRST_LINE
', ok=true. Shell powershell printed both lines. command_exec.go:86 joins the lines with '
'. Verifier's notes: Related to M26-TMP-005 and M26-TMP-008, but a separate root cause: the line join in the builtin, not argv quoting.
repro: scratch TestReviewCmdRunMultiLineCmd: FAIL 'second line never ran (stdout="FIRST_LINE\r\n") yet ok=true'
impact: A multi-step collection built with cmd_builder("cmd") runs step 1 only and reports success.
fix_proposal: Join per shell: ' & ' or ' && ' for cmd and batch (or write a temporary .cmd file), '\n' for PowerShell and bash. Or refuse more than one line for cmd. Regression test: cmd_run with shell cmd and two echo lines: stdout contains both.

title: process_modules(0) on Windows returns the calling process's own modules
claim: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot treats th32ProcessID 0 as 'the current process', so process_modules(0), meaning System Idle Process, lists mutant.exe's own DLLs. uint32(pid) also wraps negative pids.
evidence: :18-19 `windows.CreateToolhelp32Snapshot(windows.TH32CS_SNAPMODULE|windows.TH32CS_SNAPMODULE32, uint32(pid))`, with no pid==0 guard. Repro: process_modules(0) returned 14 modules including the test binary itself. Verifier: Repro TestZZ19Modules0: process_modules(0) returned 15 modules, including the test binary itself (Toolhelp32 treats pid 0 as the current process).
repro: scratch TestZZProcessModulesZero: FAIL 'process_modules(0) (System Idle Process) reports the calling process's own modules'
impact: A script that walks process_list, where pid 0 comes first, and records each process's modules attributes Mutant's own DLLs to System Idle Process in the report.
fix_proposal: Refuse pid <= 0 (and pids outside uint32) with an error, and route through the same pid validation as the pid-truncation finding. Regression test: process_modules(0) returns an error on Windows.

title: net_udp_scan and net_connect_scan accept a zero or negative timeout and report every port closed with no error
claim: timeoutMs is never validated. For UDP, SetDeadline(now+0) expires before the reply arrives. For TCP, a negative DialTimeout fails at once. Both return a normal result with empty port lists. Verifier: Partly right. For TCP, timeout 0 means no timeout in net.DialTimeout, and the scan found the port. Only a negative timeout fails silently for TCP. For UDP, both 0 and a negative timeout report nothing open.
evidence: :162 `timeout := time.Duration(timeoutMs.Value) * time.Millisecond`; :172 `_ = conn.SetDeadline(time.Now().Add(timeout))`; :115/:120 the same for TCP. Repro against a local UDP echo port: timeout 500 gave responsive_ports [port], while timeout 0 and timeout -1 gave [] with err=nil. Against a listening TCP port: timeout 500 gave open_ports [port], timeout -1 gave [] with err=nil. Verifier: Repro TestZZ20ScanTimeout: UDP echo port with timeout 500 -> [port]; with 0 and with -1 -> [] and err=nil. Listening TCP port with -1 -> [] and err=nil. Verifier's notes: Only the script author can trigger it. P3.
repro: scratch TestZZScanNonPositiveTimeout: FAIL for udp 0, udp -1 and tcp -1
impact: A typo or a computed timeout produces a clean 'nothing open' result.
fix_proposal: Reject timeoutMs <= 0 with an argument error, as validatePortRange does for ports. Regression test: Both scans with timeout 0 and -1 return an error.

title: http_get/http_post/http_request buffer the whole response body with no size cap
claim: io.ReadAll(resp.Body) has no bound, unlike the 32 MiB cap the mitm builtins use. A large or endless response is read into memory, up to the 30 s client timeout, and then copied again into a string.
evidence: :199 `rawBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)`. Repro: a 48 MiB response was returned in full (body length 50331648). Verifier: Repro TestZZ21NoCap: a 40 MiB response was returned whole (body length 41943040). http.go:199 is an unbounded io.ReadAll. Verifier's notes: Same pattern as TOOL.04 (lua_run_http), but different code, so not a duplicate.
repro: scratch TestReviewHttpGetNoSizeCap (48 MiB): FAIL 'http_get buffered the full 50331648-byte body in memory (no cap)'
impact: A hostile or misconfigured endpoint can exhaust the examiner's memory. The limit policy expects every read of this kind to be bounded by a named constant.
fix_proposal: Read through io.LimitReader(resp.Body, maxHTTPBodyBytes+1), and return an error or truncated=true when the limit is exceeded. Regression test: A 48 MiB response gives an error or truncated=true, and the body is at most the limit.

title: process_env on Windows folds the hidden '=C:' per-drive entries into one empty-named variable
claim: Windows environments carry entries such as '=C:=C:\\dir' and '=ExitCode=...'. The split on the first '=' gives key "" and value 'C:=C:\\dir'. Every such entry overwrites the same key, so all but one are lost and the survivor has a garbled value. Verifier: As stated. It only shows when the process inherits cmd.exe's hidden per-drive variables.
evidence: :279-283 `idx := strings.Index(line, "=")` ... `pairs[line[:idx]] = stringObj(line[idx+1:])`. Repro: os.Environ held ["=ExitCode=00000000" "=O:=O:\\project\\mutant"], and process_env() had key "" = "O:=O:\\project\\mutant". Verifier: Repro TestZZ22Env launched through cmd.exe: os.Environ held 3 entries starting with '=' (=C:, =ExitCode, =O:). process_env() had one key '' with value 'O:=O:\project\...'; the other two were lost. When the test was launched from Git Bash there were no '=' entries.
repro: scratch TestZZProcessEnvDriveVars: FAIL 'process_env has an empty-named variable ... built from 2 '='-prefixed entries'
impact: Per-drive working directories, which are useful live-response context, are lost or garbled.
fix_proposal: Split at strings.Index(line[1:], "=")+1 when the line starts with '=', so the key is '=C:'. Regression test: Windows-only: process_env() contains a key that starts with '=' and has no empty key.

title: http_request silently ignores a Host header
claim: Headers are applied with req.Header.Set, but Go's client ignores Header["Host"] and sends req.Host (taken from the URL). A caller's virtual-host header is dropped without an error.
evidence: :84-86 `for k, v := range headers { req.Header.Set(k, v) }`. Repro: headers {Host: vhost.example}, and the server saw Host="127.0.0.1:62581". Verifier: Repro TestZZ23Host: headers {Host: vhost.example}; the server saw Host '127.0.0.1:<port>'.
repro: scratch TestReviewHttpRequestHostHeader: FAIL 'Host header in http_request headers was silently dropped'
impact: Virtual-host probing and SNI/Host mismatch checks give the default host's answer.
fix_proposal: When the key equals 'Host' ignoring case, set req.Host = v. Regression test: The server observes r.Host equal to the supplied header.

title: process_kill metadata says non-SIGKILL signals are ignored on Windows; the code refuses them
claim: The platformNote says 'other signal numbers are ignored', but the implementation returns an error for any signal other than 9 on Windows.
evidence: metadata: `platformNote: "On Windows only SIGKILL semantics are honored; other signal numbers are ignored."`; system_forensics.go:314-315 `if len(args) == 2 && sig != syscall.SIGKILL { return ... "process_kill on windows only supports SIGKILL semantic" }`. Verifier: metadata.go:1830 platformNote says other signals are 'ignored'. Repro TestZZ24KillSig: process_kill(999999, 15) on Windows returned the error 'process_kill on windows only supports SIGKILL semantic'.
repro: Code reading only. The generated CAPABILITY_REFERENCE carries the same wrong sentence.
impact: Scripts written from the docs that pass SIGTERM fail on Windows.
fix_proposal: Change the note to 'refused on Windows' (the code's behaviour is the safer one). Regression test: The metadata note matches the Windows behaviour. A doc-consistency test could assert the phrase.

title: Type inference gives if, while and for-in bodies their own scope. The VM and sema do not, so the argument-type lint flags programs that run correctly
claim: inferTypes opens a child typeEnv for every block, if arm, while body and for-in body, and it binds for-in names in that child env. The VM does neither. A `let` in an if arm or a loop body rebinds the outer name, and a for-in binding stays bound after the loop. sema/graph.go:352-355 says the same thing. After such a block, inference therefore reports the OUTER type. argumentTypeIsCertain trusts any identifier that is never the target of `=`, and a second `let` is not an assignment. So str_upper(x) is flagged on programs that run and print the upper-cased string. The rule's own contract is that no correct program is ever flagged. Verifier: As stated. Downgraded to S4: the false positive is warning-level (lint exits 0) on a program that shadows a name inside a block or loop. In the if case lint also emits a 'duplicate top-level declaration' warning, but the for-in and while cases draw only the false type warning.
evidence: infer.go:166-170 `case *mast.BlockStatement: child := newTypeEnv(env)`. infer.go:185-188 `case *mast.WhileStatement: // Its own scope, matching the loop's own scoping in both engines: a let in the body is not visible after the loop.` That is false for the VM, and the evaluator does not scope if-blocks either (evaluator.go:262 evalBlockStatement reuses env). infer.go:195-218 binds the for-in names in `child`. sema/graph.go:352-355: 'A block does not open a scope ... A for (v in xs) binding is defined in the enclosing scope, not the body, which is what the VM does'. builtin_params.go:259-264: 'an identifier that is never assigned to anywhere in the document, so the type recorded at its binding is the type it still holds ... to guarantee no correct program is ever flagged.' Hover shows the same wrong type (`identifier x : int`). Verifier: infer.go:166-223 opens a child typeEnv for block/for/while/for-in and binds for-in names in the child; argumentTypeIsCertain (builtin_params.go:250-264) trusts any identifier that is never assigned. Own repro r/scope1.mut `let name = 42; if (len("ab") == 2) { let name = "alice"; } putf("A=%v\n", str_upper(name));` runs and prints A=ALICE; `mutant lint` warns 3:26 'argument 1 to str_upper must be STRING, got INTEGER'. scope2.mut (for-in rebinding t, and a while-body let u) prints B=q C=zz, and lint warns twice. sema/graph.go:352-355 documents the VM model (no block scope). The zero-false-positive guarantee is stated only in a code comment, not in a published doc. Verifier's notes: The evaluator/VM loop-scope disagreement the auditor mentions is not in the ledger and belongs to CMP/EVL.
repro: CLI (scratch r/scope.mut): `let x = 5; if (true) { let x = "hello"; } putf("if: %v\n", str_upper(x));`, plus the same shape for for-in, while, and an if inside a fn. The run prints `if: HELLO`, `forin: B`, `while: INNER`, `fnif: S`. `mutant lint scope.mut` prints 4 x `warning: argument 1 to str_upper must be STRING, got INTEGER` (3:28, 6:31, 10:31, 11:71) and exits 0. Go: tree/lsp/internal/analyzer/zz_sem_test.go TestZZScopeFalsePositive fails for if, for-in, while and in-fn-if, as predicted.
impact: The editor draws a false warning squiggle on working code, and `mutant lint` reports it too, which breaks the rule's documented zero-false-positive guarantee. Hover, completion detail and inlay type hints after such blocks show the wrong type.
fix_proposal: In argumentTypeIsCertain, treat an identifier as certain only if the file declares that name exactly once (any let, loop binding or parameter) and never assigns it. Then, or as well, make infer.go follow sema's scope model: no env for blocks, if arms or loops, and bind for-in names in the enclosing env. Correct the while comment. Note for the CMP/EVL owners: the evaluator's loopEnv (evaluator.go:479-600) scopes while and for-in bodies but the VM does not, so the two engines disagree on the loop cases. Regression test: argTypeMessages must be empty for the four programs in TestZZScopeFalsePositive. Control: `let x = 5; str_upper(x);` still fires.

title: Solver-narrowed parameter kinds reach the argument-type diagnostic through a user function's inferred return type
location: lsp/internal/analyzer/infer.go:428-449 (solved kinds seeded into the body env; return type from functionReturnType); lsp/internal/analyzer/fn_solver.go:24-27; lsp/internal/analyzer/builtin_params.go:320-327
claim: The solver's parameter kinds are documented as display-only: they 'must never feed a diagnostic'. The only guard is reassignedNames, which marks parameter NAMES uncertain. But inference seeds a solved kind into the function body, joins the returns into the function's return type, and types `let s = f(...)` from that. `s` is a plain never-assigned identifier, so argumentTypeIsCertain trusts it. The solver ignores type guards: it narrows v to INTEGER from `v & 255` even behind `if (type_of(v) == "STRING") { return v; }`. So a correct program is flagged. Verifier: As stated. It needs an operator or builtin that narrows the parameter to a single kind (& does, + does not). Calibrated S4, like SEM.01.
evidence: fn_solver.go:24-27 'The whole thing is display-only ... it must never feed a diagnostic'. infer.go:438-443 `paramType = solvedParams.kinds[i].asType()` then `child.set(p.Value, paramType)`. infer.go:448-449 `ret := inf.functionReturnType(n.Body); return Type{Kind: TypeFunction, Ret: &ret}`. infer.go:410-411 types the call as *ft.Ret. builtin_params.go:323-327 'Excluding the names here is what makes "solved types are display-only" a property of the code ... a solved parameter could not have produced a diagnostic anyway.' Test log: `solved low_byte params=[v] kinds=[4]` (ksInt), `TypeOf(s) = int`. The control, the same function with `return v;` in place of `v & 255`, draws nothing. A second source of wrong narrowing was read but not run: fn_solver.go:217-219 keys byName by bare name file-wide, so a nested function that reuses a top-level function's name supplies the constraints for every caller. Verifier: infer.go:428-449 seeds solved parameter kinds into the body env and sets Ret from functionReturnType. infer.go:410 types the call as *ft.Ret. reassignedNames excludes only parameter names. Own repro r/solver3.mut: `let norm = fn(a) { if (type_of(a) == "STRING") { return a; } return a & 15; }; let r = norm("xy"); str_upper(r)` prints D=XY, and lint warns 'must be STRING, got INTEGER'. With `a + 1` (solver2.mut) there is no warning, because + does not narrow to numeric. Go TestZZ02Solver shows the same message. Verifier's notes: Different root from SEM.01: the solver leaks through the return type, not through scoping.
repro: CLI (r/solver.mut): `let low_byte = fn(v) { if (type_of(v) == "STRING") { return v; } return v & 255; }; let s = low_byte("abc"); putf("solver: %v\n", str_upper(s));` prints `solver: ABC`. `mutant lint` prints `solver.mut:6:32: warning: argument 1 to str_upper must be STRING, got INTEGER`. Go: TestZZSolvedTypeReachesDiagnostic fails as predicted.
impact: A false diagnostic on correct code, the same promise as the finding above broken through a different path. The code comment that is supposed to guarantee display-only is wrong.
fix_proposal: Keep solver output out of any type a diagnostic can read. Either run a second inference pass without solver seeding and use it for argumentTypeIsCertain/TypeOf in diagnostics, or restrict 'certain' identifiers to lets initialised by a literal or a builtin call. Scope byName by declaration (the sema graph) rather than by bare name. Regression test: TestZZSolvedTypeReachesDiagnostic: argTypeMessages must be empty for the low_byte program.

title: Building the name graph is quadratic in file size: every field read rescans the whole program, and Diagnostics pays it on each keystroke
claim: sema asks the StructOf oracle once for every `p.x` whose left side resolves. The analyzer's oracle first calls structTypeNameForDeclaration, which walks every statement of the program recursively to find the declaring identifier. So the build is O(field reads x file size). Snapshot.Graph() is built inside Diagnostics, so the cost lands on the keystroke path, on the jsonrpc2 reader goroutine that serves every request. Verifier: As stated. The input is the author's own file (trusted), and the cost is editor latency on the single dispatch goroutine.
evidence: struct_type.go:29-33 `for _, stmt := range s.Program.Statements { if typeName, ok := s.structTypeNameInStatement(stmt, target); ok {`. It is called unconditionally first at resolver.go:171. graph_walk.go:339 `declared := b.lookupType(b.structOf(holder.Ident), KindStruct)`. Measured (functions of the form `let fN = fn(r) { return r.size + r.offset; };`): graph build 20 ms / 84 ms / 356 ms at 500 / 1000 / 2000 functions (25 / 50 / 100 KB), a factor of 4.2 per doubling. Diagnostics(default config) took 30 / 97 / 360 ms. Attribution: nil oracle 4.5 / 13 ms, trivial oracle 8 / 8.5 ms, structHeldBy 101 / 409 ms. structTypeNameForDeclaration alone took 143 ms for 3000 calls and 559 ms for 6000. The earlier attempt's trail recorded 3.0 s at 200 KB and 48.7 s at 400 KB. That was not re-run here: the 1 GiB watchdog and time budget kept this run to small sizes. The workspace scan limit is 1 MiB. Verifier: resolver.go:167 structHeldBy calls structTypeNameForDeclaration (struct_type.go:25-35), which walks every statement, once per field read. TestZZ03Quadratic (n x `fn(q){ return q.alpha + q.beta; }`): Graph 34/103/416 ms and Diagnostics 39/115/440 ms at 19/39/79 KB. That is x3-4 per doubling, run under a 1 GiB watchdog.
repro: Go (heap watchdog): tree/lsp/internal/analyzer/zz_sem_test.go TestZZGraphBuildQuadratic and zz_sem3_test.go TestZZGraphOracleAttribution; timings as above.
impact: Every keystroke in a 100 KB script with many field reads costs about 0.4 s of diagnostics, and about 3 s at 200 KB. The language server stops answering hovers and completions meanwhile, because it has a single dispatch goroutine.
fix_proposal: Build a map from declaring *ast.Identifier to struct-literal name once per snapshot, in one walk (or reuse the inference map, which already records struct types for let names), and make structHeldBy an O(1) lookup. Regression test: A test asserting that Graph() for 2000 functions costs less than 2.5x the cost for 1000 (or a benchmark with a budget).

title: Workspace.RemoveFile has no caller, so a deleted module keeps resolving for the rest of the session
claim: RemoveFile is documented to 'forget a file, as when it is deleted or closed without ever having been on disk'. Nothing calls it (git grep finds only the definition). The watched-file Deleted branch clears the symbol index and s.scanned but leaves sema's facts. resolveImport accepts any file that has facts, so an import of the deleted file still resolves. Go-to-definition jumps into the missing file, completion offers its members, and member refusals are decided on stale facts, while the build fails with 'module not found'.
evidence: server.go:306-310 `case lsp.FileChangeTypeDeleted: s.safeSymbolDelete(change.URI); s.mu.Lock(); delete(s.scanned, canonicalPath(path))` has no s.sema.RemoveFile. workspace.go:220-225: resolveImport's `indexed` checks only `w.facts[key]`. Verifier: git grep finds no non-test caller of sema.Workspace.RemoveFile. The server.go:307-310 Deleted branch only drops the symbol index and scanned. TestZZ04Deleted (server): after removing util/helpers.mut and sending didChangeWatchedFiles Deleted, then re-analysing main: factsKnown=true, ModuleMemberDefinition ok=true pointing at the deleted file, and zero diagnostics.
repro: Go: tree/lsp/internal/server/zz_sem_server_test.go TestZZDeletedModuleStillResolves opens main.mut (`import stats "lib/stats.mut"; let m = stats.mean([1]);`), deletes lib/stats.mut, sends didChangeWatchedFiles Deleted and re-analyses main. Result: `facts still known=true definition ok=true uri=.../lib/stats.mut completions=[mean]`. FAIL as predicted.
impact: Until restart, the editor confidently navigates to and completes from a module that no longer exists, and never hints that the import is broken.
fix_proposal: Call s.sema.RemoveFile(string(change.URI)) in the Deleted branch, and in didClose when the document has no file on disk. Add a server test for it. Regression test: TestZZDeletedModuleStillResolves: after the delete event, Facts is unknown and ModuleMemberDefinition returns false.

title: Import cycles and duplicate namespaces are computed by sema but never published to the editor
location: sema/workspace.go:23-30, 290-293, 309-313, 400-439 (Diagnostics and Closure have no production caller); lsp/internal/server/server.go:1317-1318 (publishDiagnostics = analyzer.Diagnostics only)
claim: DiagImportCycle is documented as 'the editor reports it and carries on'. bindingsLocked says 'Diagnostics reports the second' of two imports binding one alias. Neither Workspace.Diagnostics nor Workspace.Closure is called outside tests and parity tests, and publishDiagnostics sends only analyzer.Diagnostics. A file the build refuses (import cycle, duplicate namespace) shows nothing, or only an 'unused import' hint.
evidence: `git grep` for `.Diagnostics(`, `.Closure(`, DiagImportCycle and DiagDuplicateNamespace outside sema/ finds only analyzer.Diagnostics call sites (server.go:1318, api.go:126) and tests. workspace.go:24-25 '...the editor reports it and carries on'. workspace.go:291-293 'The first wins, matching the compiler, and Diagnostics reports the second.' Verifier: Neither Workspace.Diagnostics nor Workspace.Closure has a non-test caller. publishDiagnostics (server.go:1317-1318) sends analyzer.Diagnostics only, and the analyzer and server have no cycle or duplicate-import logic. sema TestZZ05Computed produces 'import cycle: c.mut -> d.mut -> c.mut' and 'two imports bind the name "m"'. server TestZZ05Published: c.mut publishes [] and e.mut publishes only 'unused import m', although m.one is used. Verifier's notes: The cycle message uses lowercased canonical paths (seen in the repro), which is moot while it is unpublished.
repro: Go: tree/lsp/internal/server/zz_sem_server2_test.go TestZZImportRefusalsNeverPublished. a.mut<->b.mut cycle: `published=[] ... sema.Closure cycle diags=1`. dup.mut (`import "x/util.mut"; import "y/util.mut";`): `published=["unused import util: ..."] sema.Diagnostics=1`. FAIL for both, as predicted. tree/sema/zz_sem_test.go TestZZImportRefusalsComputed shows sema produces 'import cycle: ...a.mut -> ...b.mut -> ...a.mut' and the duplicate-namespace sentence.
impact: The editor is silent on two import errors the build refuses. For the duplicate it suggests the import is merely unused.
fix_proposal: Merge sema.Workspace.Diagnostics(key) (hold back DiagUnresolvedImport until the scan completes) and the Closure cycle diagnostics whose Module == key into publishDiagnostics. Render the cycle chain from ModuleFacts.Path, not canonical keys: closureLocked builds it from lowercased keys. Regression test: TestZZImportRefusalsNeverPublished: the published diagnostics for a.mut contain 'import cycle' and for dup.mut contain 'two imports bind'.

title: sema declares for-in bindings before walking the iterable, but the compiler compiles the iterable first
claim: The walk's header says it follows the compiler's binding order. For a for-in it declares Key/Value, then walks node.Iterable. The compiler compiles node.Iterable (compiler.go:1508) before it defines the bindings (1516-1520). So in `for (xs in xs)` the iterable resolves to the loop binding: go-to-definition is wrong, the outer `let xs` is reported unused, find-references and rename miss the iterable, and `for (y in y)` gets no undefined-name diagnostic although the compiler refuses it.
evidence: graph_walk.go:52-57 `for _, name := range []*ast.Identifier{node.Key, node.Value} { ... b.declare(name.Value, name, rng, KindLoopBind) } b.expression(node.Iterable, nil)`. graph_walk.go:7-14: 'Both are the compiler's rules, and changing either here would change what the editor says about a program without changing the program.' compiler.go:1508 `if err := c.Compile(node.Iterable)` precedes compiler.go:1516 `valueSymbol := c.symbolTable.Define(node.Value.Value)`. Verifier: graph_walk.go:49-58 declares Key/Value before walking node.Iterable. compiler.go:1508 compiles the Iterable before Define at 1516-1520. r/forin2.mut (`let items=[4,5]; for (items in items)` inside a fn) prints F=4 F=5, and lint warns 'unused declaration items'. Go: definition of the iterable goes to line 2 (the binding), not line 1 (the let), and references of the outer let number 1. forin3.mut `for (z in z)` gets compiler error 'undefined variable: z' while lint is silent.
repro: CLI: r/forin.mut (`let main = fn() { let xs = [1, 2]; for (xs in xs) { putf("%v\n", xs); } }; main();`) prints 1 and 2. `mutant lint` prints `forin.mut:2:7: warning: unused declaration xs`. r/forin_undef.mut `for (y in y) {...}` gives compiler error `undefined variable: y`, and lint prints nothing. Go: TestZZForInIterableResolution: definition of the iterable goes to line 2 (the binding), 'unused declaration xs', and no undefined diagnostic. TestZZForInRenameMissesIterable: ReferenceLocations of the outer xs returns 1 location (want 2). Both FAIL as predicted.
impact: Wrong definition and references. Renaming the outer variable leaves the iterable pointing at nothing, which breaks the build. There is a false 'unused' warning, and a missing error on a program that does not compile.
fix_proposal: Walk node.Iterable before declaring the bindings in graph_walk.go:49-58. Regression test: A sema test: in `let xs = [1]; for (xs in xs) {}` the iterable's reference targets the let. `for (y in y) {}` records y as unbound.

title: A function declared inside another function gets no signature help, no function hover card and no parameter inlay hints
claim: functionLiteralForBindingIdent searches for the let that declares a function, but functionLiteralInExpressionForIdent returns immediately on a FunctionLiteral instead of searching its body. A helper declared inside `main` is therefore never found. The same walk in struct_type.go:123-126 does descend, as does the MacroLiteral arm in this very function (signature_help.go:465-468). HoverText, signatureInformationForCall and InlayHints all depend on it.
evidence: signature_help.go:343-345 `case *mast.FunctionLiteral: return nil, false`. Verifier: signature_help.go:343-345 `case *mast.FunctionLiteral: return nil, false`. TestZZ07Nested: top-level wrap gives sig 'wrap(body, tag)', the function hover card and 2 param hints. The same helper nested in run() gives sig <none>, hover 'identifier wrap : fn' and 0 param hints.
repro: Go: TestZZNestedFunctionSignature. Top level: `signature="pad(text, width)" hover="function pad(text, width)" paramHints=2`. Nested in main: `signature="" ok=false hover="identifier pad : fn" paramHints=0`. FAIL as predicted.
impact: Every local helper, a common shape in scripts built around a main function, loses signature help, its hover card (doc comment, solved types) and its parameter hints.
fix_proposal: In functionLiteralInExpressionForIdent, recurse into node.Body with functionLiteralInStatementForIdent, as struct_type.go does. Regression test: Signature help on a nested `pad(` returns `pad(text, width)`, and hover returns the function card.

title: Builtin calls never get parameter-name inlay hints, and the test that claims to cover them passes on an unrelated type hint
claim: InlayHints promises parameter-name hints for 'both user functions and builtins'. builtinSignatureInformation labels every builtin parameter with an offset pair (`Label: spans[i]`), and InlayHints skips any label that is not a string. So no builtin call ever gets a hint. TestInlayHintsBuiltinParameters accepts any hint that has a Kind, and the `: []int` TYPE hint on its `let xs = [1, 2];` satisfies it.
evidence: inlay_hint.go:83-88 `// ParameterInformation.Label is string | [uint, uint]; we only emit hints for the plain-string form. label, ok := sig.Parameters[i].Label.(string); if !ok || label == "" { continue }`. language_teach.go:318 `param := lsp.ParameterInformation{Label: spans[i]}`. inlay_hint_test.go:37-41 `if h.Label != "" && h.Kind != nil { foundNamed = true }`. Verifier: language_teach.go:318 labels builtin params with offset spans, and inlay_hint.go:83-88 skips non-string labels. TestZZ08BuiltinHints: str_repeat("ab", 3) gives no hints, and `let s = str_upper("a")` gives only the type hint ': string'. A user fn gives 'a:' and 'b:'. inlay_hint_test.go:37-41 accepts any hint with a Kind, so the push test passes on the ': []int' type hint.
repro: Go: tree/lsp/internal/analyzer/zz_sem2_test.go TestZZBuiltinParameterHints. `push(xs, 3)` gives only `0:6 type ": []int"`, `str_repeat("ab", 3)` gives [], and the user function `add(1, 2)` gives `left:`, `right:`. FAIL as predicted.
impact: The advertised builtin parameter hints never appear, and the regression test cannot detect it.
fix_proposal: When a ParameterInformation label is a [2]UInteger, slice the signature label and strip the `...` prefix and `: TYPE` suffix to get the name. Change the test to require Kind == InlayHintKindParameter on the call's line. Regression test: `str_repeat("ab", 3)` yields parameter hints on both arguments.

title: Member completion treats the LSP character (UTF-16 code units) as a byte offset, so any non-ASCII text earlier on the line breaks `x.` completion
claim: offsetForPosition adds pos.Character to the line's byte offset. The comment says 'Characters are treated as bytes'. LSP 3.16 (glsp protocol_3_16) positions are UTF-16 units, so after an `é` or `→` in a string on the same line the offset falls short of the dot and memberAccessAt finds no receiver. This is the inbound half of M26-LEX-014. That finding's fix (compute UTF-16 columns in the lexer, or convert outbound ranges in protocol/converters.go) does not touch this byte slicing of Source, so the fix here is different. Verifier: As stated. Related to M26-LEX-014 (outbound columns), but this is the inbound conversion in a different function with a different fix, so it is not a duplicate.
evidence: member_completion.go:144-146 '// ... Characters are treated as bytes, matching the rest of the analyzer's ASCII-oriented position handling.' member_completion.go:156 `target := i + int(pos.Character)`. Verifier: member_completion.go:156 `target := i + int(pos.Character)`, with a comment saying characters are treated as bytes. TestZZ09UTF16 with the cursor at the UTF-16 end of `putln("<s>", p.`: 'ab' gives [lat lon]. 'ñ' (13 UTF-16 units, 14 bytes) and '日本' give ok=false and no items.
repro: Go: TestZZMemberCompletionUTF16 on `struct Point { x; y; }; let r = Point{...};` then `putf("<c> %v", r.` with the cursor at the UTF-16 end of the line. c="e": items x,y. c="é": ok=false with no items. c="→": ok=false with no items. FAIL as predicted.
impact: Field, enum-variant, module-member and builtin-family completion silently stop working on any line with non-ASCII text before the cursor, for example a message string.
fix_proposal: Convert (line, UTF-16 character) to a byte offset by walking the line's runes (utf16.RuneLen), and share the helper with whatever fixes M26-LEX-014. Regression test: TestZZMemberCompletionUTF16 returns x,y for all three labels.

title: Signature help and completion describe the builtin when a user function of the same name shadows it
claim: signatureInformationForCall checks builtin.GetBuiltinByName before it resolves the name in scope, so for `let max = fn(first, second, third) {...}; max(1, 2, 3)` it shows the builtin max. The VM calls the user's function. CompletionItemsAt adds every builtin to `seen` first and then skips a user binding whose name is already seen, so only the builtin item is offered. Hover gets this right, because it resolves the binding first (analyzer.go:136-147).
evidence: signature_help.go:92-96 `if builtin.GetBuiltinByName(fn.Value) != nil { if sig, ok := builtinSignatureInformation(fn.Value); ok { return sig, true }`. analyzer.go:356 `if _, ok := seen[bind.name]; ok { continue }`. Verifier: signature_help.go:92-96 checks GetBuiltinByName before resolveDefinition. r/shadow2.mut `let min = fn(a, b, c) { return c; }; min(9, 8, 7)` prints E=7 (the user fn runs). TestZZ10Shadow: sig 'min(value: INTEGER|FLOAT, ...values: ...)', completion detail 'builtin · min(...)', while hover shows 'function min(a, b, c)'.
repro: CLI: r/shadow.mut prints `max: 1`, so the user function runs, and lint reports nothing. Go: TestZZShadowedBuiltinSignature gives signature `max(value: INTEGER|FLOAT, ...values: INTEGER|FLOAT) -> INTEGER|FLOAT` while hover says `function max(first, second, third)` (FAIL as predicted). TestZZShadowedBuiltinCompletion: the only `max` item is `builtin · max(value: ...)`.
impact: Signature help, and the completion detail, describe parameters the called function does not have.
fix_proposal: In signatureInformationForCall, resolve the identifier with resolveDefinition (or isBoundAt) first, and fall back to the builtin only when nothing binds it. In CompletionItemsAt, let a visible user binding replace the builtin item. Regression test: TestZZShadowedBuiltinSignature expects `max(first, second, third)`.

title: The incoming call hierarchy drops calls made at the top level of the same file, although the comment says they are reported
claim: The comment says top-level calls 'are collected under a zero caller and reported separately. The server names it after the file'. The loop instead skips every ref with From == nil, and nothing else collects them. The server does name cross-file top-level callers `<file>` (server/call_hierarchy.go callerAt), so same-file top-level calls are the only callers never shown. In scripts, those are most calls.
evidence: call_hierarchy.go:71-73 comment. call_hierarchy.go:77 `if !ref.InCallPosition || ref.Target != node.ID || ref.From == nil { continue }`. Verifier: call_hierarchy.go:71-77: the comment says the zero caller is reported, but the loop skips From == nil. server crossFileIncomingCalls handles only other files' MemberCallSites. TestZZ11Incoming: work() is called once in boss and 3 times at top level, and IncomingCalls returns boss with 1 site (total 1, want 4).
repro: Go: TestZZIncomingCallsFromTopLevel on `let helper = fn() {...}; let main = fn() { return helper(); }; helper(); helper();`. It reports one caller, main, with 1 site. There are 3 call sites. FAIL as predicted.
impact: 'Show incoming calls' misses the file's own top-level calls, so a function looks unused or under-used.
fix_proposal: Group From == nil refs under a file-level CallNode (the server already builds the `<file>` item), or return them in a separate slice for the server to render. Regression test: IncomingCalls reports 3 call sites for helper, including a file-level caller with 2.

title: The parameter solver stops after 8 rounds over Go map order, so the same document gives different signatures from one analysis to the next
claim: solveFunctionParams ranges over the `solved` map, whose order is randomised, and caps the fixpoint at 8 rounds. The comment says 'the cap is a guard against a bug rather than an expected exit'. A pass-through chain longer than the rounds needed in an unlucky order does not converge, and whether it converges depends on map order. Verifier: As stated. It only shows up on pass-through chains of roughly 9 or more functions.
evidence: fn_solver.go:222-224 `for round := 0; round < 8; round++ { changed := false; for _, fn := range solved {`. fn_solver.go:196-198 'the cap is a guard against a bug rather than an expected exit'. Verifier: fn_solver.go:222-224 ranges over a map with an 8-round cap. TestZZ12SolverOrder, a 12-function pass-through chain analysed 60 times: 'h0(y)' 46 times, 'h0(y: STRING)' 14 times. A 5-function chain is stable (60/60).
repro: Go: TestZZSolverChainNondeterministic, a 14-function chain `f0(x) -> f1(x) -> ... -> str_upper(x)`, with signature help on `f0("a")` over 40 fresh analyses: `map[f0(x):39 f0(x: STRING):1]`. FAIL as predicted.
impact: Hover, signature help and inlay types for user functions flicker between keystrokes, and usually miss the fixpoint.
fix_proposal: Iterate functions in source order, and loop until nothing changes. Sets only shrink, so the total number of parameter bits bounds the rounds. Regression test: 40 analyses of the chain all give `f0(x: STRING)`.

title: The 'if guard return' snippet inserts `nil`, which Mutant does not have
claim: The snippet's default expansion `return ${2:nil};` does not compile ('undefined variable: nil'), and the server's own lint flags it as an error. The extension's equivalent snippet uses `${1:err}`.
repro: CLI: r/snip.mut (the default expansion) gives `compiler error: undefined variable: nil`. `mutant lint` gives `snip.mut:3:12: error: undefined identifier nil`. Go: TestZZGuardSnippet logs the same diagnostic.
impact: Accepting the snippet's default produces a program that does not build, from the editor's own teaching feature.
fix_proposal: Use `${2:err}`, matching the extension's snippet. Regression test: Expanding every snippet with its defaults yields no undefined-identifier diagnostic.

title: Semantic tokens overlap on one-line fn/struct/enum, and struct and enum declaration names are painted as variables
location: lsp/internal/analyzer/analyzer.go:830-835 (whole-node token types), 1110-1115 (tokenLength default), 938-949 (no override for the declaration Name)
claim: FunctionLiteral, StructStatement and EnumStatement get a token covering the whole node whenever it fits on one line. That token overlaps every lexical and identifier token inside it. The client capability overlappingTokenSupport is never checked, and LSP 3.16 forbids overlap otherwise. The multi-line form gets no such token, so the same construct colours differently depending on line breaks. The declared name (`Point` in `struct Point {`) has no override and is painted `variable`, while `Point{...}` uses are painted `type`.
evidence: analyzer.go:830-835 `case *mast.FunctionLiteral: return ..."function"; case *mast.StructStatement: return ..."type"; case *mast.EnumStatement: return ..."enum"`. analyzer.go:1111-1114 default length `rng.End.Column - rng.Start.Column` on one line. analyzer.go:938-943 overrides only s.Fields. Verifier: analyzer.go:830-835 gives whole-node token types. TestZZ14Tokens: `struct Box { w; h; };` produces type(0:0+21) overlapping variable('Box'), the enum likewise, and `let sq = fn(n){...}` produces function(0:9+23) over inner tokens. The two-line struct has no overlap. The declared names are painted as variable. The repo never checks overlappingTokenSupport.
repro: Go: TestZZSemanticTokens. `struct Point { x; y; };` gives `0:0+23=type("struct Point { x; y; };")` followed by `0:7+5=variable("Point")`, which overlaps. `enum Colour { Red, Green };` gives `0:0+27=enum(...)` and `0:5+6=variable("Colour")`. `let f = fn(x) { return x + 1; };` gives `0:8+23=function("fn(x) { return x + 1; }")` over `x`, `+` and `1`. The two-line struct gives only `variable("Point")`. FAIL for the three one-line cases, as predicted.
impact: The token stream violates the protocol for common one-liners, and type names are coloured as variables at their declaration.
fix_proposal: Drop the whole-node tokens. Override StructStatement.Name as type, EnumStatement.Name as enum and the let name of a function as function. Regression test: A decoded token stream has no overlaps, and the declaration name token is type/enum.

title: DeclID.Seq is a uint16: the 65,537th same-name declaration in one scope wraps to 0 and takes the first one's identity
claim: declareIn stores seq+1 in a uint16 with no check, and files the node under b.g.nodes[node.ID]. At 65,536 repeats, declaration 65,537 gets Seq 0 and replaces the first in the node map, and uses of both merge under one ID. The file is 720 KB, under the workspace scan's 1 MiB cap. Verifier: As stated. Only a generated file can reach this.
evidence: id.go:124 `Seq uint16`. graph.go:572-573 `seq := b.seq[key]; b.seq[key] = seq + 1`. graph.go:593 `b.g.nodes[node.ID] = node`. Verifier: id.go:124 Seq uint16, and graph.go:572-573 increments without a check. sema TestZZ15SeqWrap, 65,537 `let k` (720,917 bytes): first.Seq=0 and last.Seq=0 give the same ID, and NodeFor(first.ID) returns the declaration on line 65538.
repro: Go: tree/sema/zz_sem_test.go TestZZSeqWrap (65,537 x `let x`). Result: `file bytes=720913 decls=65537 first.Seq=0 last.Seq=0 same-id=true`. UsesOf(first) returns 2 ranges (lines 2 and 65539), and NodeFor(first.ID) returns the declaration on line 65538. FAIL as predicted.
impact: Rename and find-references on the first declaration also edit uses of the last. Only generated files can reach this.
fix_proposal: Widen Seq to uint32 (DeclID.String already formats via uint64), or saturate and stop recording. Regression test: TestZZSeqWrap: first and last IDs differ, and UsesOf(first) has 1 range.

title: The private-member refusal says 'private to this program' when the import's target is not indexed
claim: resolveModuleMember raises the underscore refusal before it checks that the module is known, which is deliberate. With an unresolved import the key is "", and displayName("") returns 'this program'. So the squiggle says the name is private to the file the reader is in, not to lib/stats.mut. The compiler's sentence names the module. Verifier: As stated. Refusing early is by design; only the wording is wrong.
evidence: resolve.go:255 `privateMemberRefusal(alias, name, ctx.moduleName(key))`. workspace.go:449-451 `if key == "" { return "this program" }`. Verifier: resolve.go:249-256 checks the private name first (deliberately), and workspace.go:449-451 displayName("") returns 'this program'. TestZZ16Private: `import m "pkg/mathx.mut"; putln(m._secret);` with the module unindexed gives 'm._secret is private to this program: ...'.
repro: Go: tree/lsp/internal/analyzer/zz_sem2_test.go TestZZPrivateRefusalWording (`import stats "lib/stats.mut"; putln(stats._total);` with lib not indexed) gives `stats._total is private to this program: a top-level name beginning with _ is visible only inside the module that declares it`.
impact: A misleading error message while a workspace is still scanning or an import is missing.
fix_proposal: When the namespace's key is empty, name the import spelling, for example `lib/stats.mut`. Regression test: The message names `lib/stats.mut`.

title: The document-link range for a triple-quoted string covers two quote characters on each side
claim: StringLiteralRefs trims one character from each end of any single-line literal, assuming a one-character delimiter. A `"""..."""` literal keeps two quotes on each side inside the underline. Verifier: As stated. Cosmetic.
evidence: document_link.go:32-35 `if start.Line == end.Line && end.Character >= start.Character+2 { start.Character++; end.Character-- }`. Verifier: document_link.go:32-35 trims one character per side. TestZZ17Links: `"""logs/a.txt"""` underlines `""logs/a.txt""`, while a plain string underlines 'logs/a.txt'.
repro: Go: tree/lsp/internal/analyzer/zz_sem5_test.go TestZZStringLinkRanges on `let p = """data/x.log""";` gives value `data/x.log` and underlines `""data/x.log""`. A plain `"data/x.log"` underlines correctly.
impact: The clickable link underline is visibly misplaced. This is cosmetic.
fix_proposal: Trim by the literal's delimiter length (3 for a triple-quoted token). Regression test: The triple-quoted case underlines exactly `data/x.log`.

title: The Lua 5-second cap does not stop a script inside a string function
claim: lua_run_string/file/http bound a script with `context.WithTimeout(..., 5*time.Second)` and `state.SetContext(ctx)`. gopher-lua checks that context only between VM instructions. A single call into a Go library function such as string.find with a backtracking pattern never looks at it, so one call runs for as long as the pattern takes. RUNTIME_INTEGRATION.md:93-99 says 'a script that runs long (or loops forever) is aborted'. Verifier: As stated. RUNTIME_INTEGRATION.md:9-16 and :99-104 name the 5-second cap as what contains an untrusted script (lua_run_http), and one Go-side pattern call ignores it.
evidence: `local s = string.rep("a", N) return tostring(string.find(s, ".-.-.-b"))`: N=200 took 2.79s and returned ok=true. N=400 took 43.4s: the deadline was noticed only after the call returned (ok=false). N=1600 did not return within 60s. Doubling N costs about 15x. The existing timeout tests (executor_test.go:106, and none in builtin/lua_test.go) use only a pure-Lua `while true do end`, which is the one shape the context does stop. Verifier: lua_run_string with `string.find(string.rep("a",N), ".-.-.-b")`: N=200 took 5.38s and N=300 took 27.6s, both ok=false only after the call returned. N=1600 did not return within 15s. The context is checked only between VM instructions. Verifier's notes: builtin/zz_verify_test.go TestZZLuaTimeoutNotHonouredInsideGoFunction. I used sizes 200/300 and a 15s guard instead of 400/60s to spare the shared host.
repro: builtin/zz_tool_test.go TestZZLuaTimeoutNotHonouredInsideGoFunction (the call runs in a goroutine with a 60s guard). FAIL: `lua_run_string did not return within 60s despite its 5s cap`.
impact: A script fetched by lua_run_http, or a rule file, pins a CPU core and blocks the calling Mutant program indefinitely. RUNTIME_INTEGRATION.md names the sandbox as the mitigation for untrusted scripts, and this sandbox cannot be interrupted.
fix_proposal: Replace string.find/match/gmatch/gsub/rep in the sandbox with wrappers that refuse inputs past a size/complexity budget, or run the pattern functions with a step counter. Document that the cap is between instructions until that lands. Regression test: TestLuaRunStringCapStopsPatternBacktracking: the N=1600 script must return ok=false within about 6s.

title: A Lua script's memory has no bound
claim: runLuaSource sets a time cap and nothing else. A script can allocate as much as the process can, in one call, well inside the 5 seconds. Verifier: As stated. The docs promise no memory bound, but they do tell users to rely on the sandbox for untrusted scripts, and a large string.rep from lua_run_http can take the process into a fatal out-of-memory (inferred; not run on the shared host).
evidence: `string.rep("x", N*1024*1024)`: 16 MiB -> TotalAlloc +16 MiB, 128 MiB -> +128 MiB, both ok=true. The growth is linear with no ceiling. The earlier attempt's trail shows 1 GiB succeeding in 0.28s. gopher-lua strRep (stringlib.go:392-400) calls strings.Repeat(str, n) directly, so a large n asks the Go runtime for n bytes at once; past what the host can commit, that is a fatal, unrecoverable out-of-memory rather than a Lua error (not run, for the shared host). Verifier: string.rep 16 MiB -> TotalAlloc +16 MiB, 128 MiB -> +128 MiB, both ok=true. Growth is linear, with no budget anywhere in runLuaSource. Verifier's notes: TestZZLuaMemoryUnbounded ran under a 1 GiB watchdog.
repro: builtin/zz_tool_test.go TestZZLuaMemoryUnbounded under a 1 GiB heap watchdog: 16 and 128 MiB both allocated and returned ok=true.
impact: An untrusted script (lua_run_http, lua_run_file) can take the host process down with a runtime fatal error that no recover or result hash can report.
fix_proposal: Wrap string.rep (and the table constructors reachable from loops) with a per-state byte budget, and set gopher-lua's RegistryMaxSize/CallStackSize explicitly. Refuse a count whose product with #s passes the budget before calling strings.Repeat. Regression test: TestLuaRunStringRefusesOversizedRep: string.rep("x", 2^30) returns ok=false with a budget error and allocates less than the budget.

title: lua_run_http reads the whole response with no size limit
claim: `body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)` then `string(body)` then Load: the remote endpoint decides how much memory the call takes. The only bound is httpClient's 30s timeout (http.go:14).
evidence: A local httptest server returning an N MiB script: 8 MiB -> TotalAlloc +34 MiB, 64 MiB -> +287 MiB, both ok=true, about 4.5x the body with no ceiling. builtin/http.go:199 has the same io.ReadAll pattern (BLT area, not in the ledger); the fix here is Lua-specific because a script needs a much smaller cap. Verifier: An httptest server returning an 8 MiB script -> +34 MiB; 64 MiB -> +287 MiB; both ok=true. lua.go:64 calls io.ReadAll with no LimitReader and never checks resp.StatusCode. Verifier's notes: Related to NET.21 (http.go:199, the same io.ReadAll pattern), but this is a separate call site with its own fix, so it is not a duplicate.
repro: builtin/zz_tool2_test.go TestZZLuaRunHTTPBodyUnbounded under the 1 GiB watchdog.
impact: A hostile or misconfigured endpoint makes lua_run_http allocate several GB within the 30s timeout.
fix_proposal: Read through io.LimitReader(resp.Body, maxLuaScriptBytes+1) and refuse a larger body. Also check resp.StatusCode, since today a 404 page is loaded as Lua. Regression test: TestLuaRunHTTPRefusesOversizedScript.

title: Neither REPL can call a function defined on an earlier line
claim: Each line compiles with NewWithState(symbolTable, constants), then `byteCode = mutil.EncryptByteCode(byteCode, replPassword)` and `constants = byteCode.Constants`. EncryptByteCode (mutil/util.go:37-45) XORs the instructions of every COMPILED_FN constant in the pool with a keystream seeded by this line's instruction length. Functions compiled on earlier lines are already encrypted, so each later line encrypts them again under a different key. When the next line calls one, the VM decrypts with one key and gets garbage opcodes.
evidence: CLI REPL: `let add = fn(a, b) { a + b };` then `add(1, 2);` -> `vm_runtime_error ip=0 op=opcode_214: unknown opcode 214: this program was built by a newer version of mutant`. The same on one line prints 3. Web REPL: the same two lines -> `unknown opcode 227 ...`. Strings bound on earlier lines survive ("hello" reads back), so the defect is specific to function constants. No existing test evaluates a function across two Eval calls (webrepl/repl_test.go:100-114 defines and calls on one line). Verifier: Terminal REPL: `let add = fn(a, b) { a + b };` then `add(1, 2);` -> 'unknown opcode 214: this program was built by a newer version of mutant'. On one line it prints 3. Web REPL: 'unknown opcode 227'. A string bound earlier still reads back. repl.go:461-462 and webrepl/repl.go:106-107 re-run EncryptByteCode over the whole accumulated constant pool on every line. Verifier's notes: repl/zz_verify_test.go TestZZReplFunctionAcrossLines FAIL, TestZZReplSameLineControl PASS; webrepl/zz_verify_test.go TestZZWebReplFunctionAcrossLines FAIL.
repro: repl/zz_tool_test.go TestZZReplFunctionAcrossLines (FAIL), TestZZReplSameLineControl (PASS); webrepl/zz_tool_test.go TestZZWebReplFunctionAcrossLines (FAIL).
impact: Defining a helper and then using it, the basic REPL workflow, fails in both the terminal and the browser REPL. The error message wrongly blames a newer mutant version.
fix_proposal: Encrypt only the constants this line added (constants[len(previous):]), or keep the plaintext pool and encrypt a copy per line. Share one helper between repl and webrepl so the two cannot drift. Regression test: TestReplFunctionDefinedOnOneLineRunsOnTheNext, one each for repl.Start and webrepl.Eval, covering a closure, a recursive function and a function called three lines later.

title: mutant fmt rewrites a file that does not parse and changes its string literals
claim: handleFmtCommand writes whatever api.Format returns. For a file with parse errors, FormatSource falls back to normalizeDocumentWhitespace, which strips trailing spaces and tabs from every line, including lines inside a triple-quoted string, and turns a lone CR into LF. The command prints `formatted:` and exits 0, so a broken file is silently rewritten and its string data changes. gofmt refuses a file that does not parse. Verifier: Right about the behaviour. The whitespace-only fallback for unparsable input is documented as a design choice in docs/LSP_EXTENSION_LLD.md:470. The defects are that the fallback strips whitespace inside string literals, and that the CLI writes the fallback result to disk and reports success for a file that does not parse. The tutorial places `mutant fmt` 'in the gofmt tradition', and gofmt refuses such a file.
evidence: badfmt.mut = `let banner = """` / `row one   ` / `row two` / `""";` / `putln(len(banner));` / `let broken = ;`. `mutant fmt badfmt.mut` -> `formatted: badfmt.mut`, exit=0, and the file now reads `row~one` (the three trailing spaces inside the literal are gone). The same file without the broken line keeps `row~one~~~`. Verifier: r2/badfmt.mut has a triple-quoted literal with 'row one   ' plus a line 'let broken = ;'. `mutant fmt` prints 'formatted: badfmt.mut', exits 0, and the literal line becomes 'row one'. The same file without the broken line keeps the three spaces. Verifier's notes: P2 rather than P1: only files that already fail to parse are affected. Severity/priority raised from S3/P2 by duplicate LSP.07.
repro: CLI in scratch r1: PowerShell script writing badfmt.mut, running `mutant.exe fmt badfmt.mut`, and printing the file with spaces shown as ~.
impact: `mutant fmt .` over a working tree edits every file that currently fails to parse and alters literal data such as banners, templates and expected-output strings, while reporting success. --check likewise reports whitespace diffs for files it cannot format.
fix_proposal: In handleFmtCommand, report the parse errors for a file that does not parse, leave it untouched and set exit 1 (expose ParseErrors through lsp/api). Keep the whitespace fallback for editor-side formatting only, if at all. Regression test: TestFmtRefusesAFileWithParseErrors: the file bytes are unchanged and the exit code is 1.

title: graph query outline renders a shared enclosed declaration once per path, exponentially
claim: outlineRows guards against cycles with onPath, which its comment says was added after a one-edge self-loop consumed 9 GB. It does not guard against a declaration reached through more than one ENCLOSES parent. Each parent re-renders the shared subtree, so a store whose nesting is a DAG yields 2^depth rows. Verifier: As stated. Severity lowered because it needs a hand-crafted or damaged store: the exporter writes a tree.
evidence: A store with L levels of two declarations, each enclosing both of the next level: L=10 (20 declarations, 36 edges) -> 2046 rows in 51ms; L=12 -> 8190; L=14 -> 32766; L=16 (32 declarations) -> 131070 rows in 324ms. That is 4x per two levels, rows = 2^(L+1)-2. The earlier attempt measured L=22 -> 8,388,606 rows in 24s; about L=30 (60 declarations) would need billions of rows. Verifier: Diamond ladder: L=10 -> 2046 rows, L=12 -> 8190, L=14 -> 32766, L=16 -> 131070 (192ms). The row count is 2^(L+1)-2. outlineRows guards only the current path (onPath), not nodes already rendered. Verifier's notes: cli/zz_verify_test.go TestZZOutlineDiamondLadder, under a 1 GiB watchdog.
