repro: cli/zz_tool_test.go TestZZOutlineDiamondLadder under a 1 GiB heap watchdog; FAIL at every size.
impact: The code treats a store as possibly damaged (the self-loop fix). The same damage in DAG form, from a hand-edited store or a future exporter, hangs `mutant graph query outline` and exhausts memory.
fix_proposal: Keep a visited set for the whole outline (not just the path). Render a declaration's subtree once, and at every later parent emit a one-line 'also enclosed by X, shown above' marker. Or refuse a store where any declaration has more than one ENCLOSES parent. Regression test: TestOutlineRendersASharedChildOnce: the diamond ladder at L=16 yields at most about 2*declarations rows. Fixed: outlineRows became an outliner that keeps, beside the path set, the set of declarations already rendered anywhere in the answer: each is rendered in full once and named in one line under every further encloser, and the answer notes how many were. A declaration enclosed only from inside a cycle, reached from no root, was left out of the outline while the headline counted it; it is now rendered at the top level.
regression_test: cli TestOutlineRendersADeclarationWithTwoEnclosersOnce (the diamond ladder at L=16: at most 2 rows per declaration); cli TestOutlineListsADeclarationOnlyACycleEncloses

title: A debug session launched with noDebug still stops at every breakpoint
claim: noDebug only suppresses stop-on-entry: `vm.DebugOptions{StopOnEntry: args.StopOnEntry && !args.NoDebug}`. Breakpoints sent afterwards are still bound and still stop. protocol.go says NoDebug means the session 'simply never stops', and DEBUGGING.md says 'Run without stopping for anything'.
evidence: A five-iteration loop with a breakpoint on the loop body, launched with {"noDebug": true}, then setBreakpoints and configurationDone: the session stopped 5 times. Verifier: A launch with {noDebug:true}, then setBreakpoints on the loop body, stopped 5 times over 5 iterations. session.go:281 applies NoDebug only to StopOnEntry. protocol.go:108-110 says it 'simply never stops', and DEBUGGING.md:84 says 'Run without stopping for anything'. Verifier's notes: dap/zz_verify_test.go TestZZNoDebugStillStopsAtBreakpoints.
repro: dap/zz_tool_test.go TestZZNoDebugStillStopsAtBreakpoints -> FAIL `a noDebug launch stopped 5 times`.
impact: VS Code's Run Without Debugging (Ctrl+F5) sends noDebug and still sends breakpoints, so the program halts at each one and waits for a continue that the UI does not offer in that mode.
fix_proposal: When NoDebug is set, record it on the session and answer setBreakpoints with verified:false and a message, or skip binding in vm.Debugger. Also ignore pause/step. Regression test: TestNoDebugLaunchNeverStops (a breakpoint is set and zero stopped events arrive before terminated).

title: A '==N' hit condition behaves as '>=N'
claim: parseHitCondition's comment says 'the forms with an operator mean what they say', but `==` and `=` fall through to the bare-count branch, which returns skip=N-1, meaning stop on every arrival from the Nth on. SkipHits cannot express 'exactly N' at all. Verifier: As stated. Only the == and = forms are wrong; the bare-count semantics are documented.
evidence: parseHitCondition("==2") -> skip=1 ok=true, the same as ">=2". A breakpoint with hitCondition "==2" in a five-iteration loop stopped 4 times, not once, and was bound verified=true with no message. Verifier: parseHitCondition("==2") and ("=2") both give skip=1, the same as ">=2". Over 5 arrivals the breakpoint stopped 4 times and was bound verified=true with no message. A bare count meaning 'Nth onwards' is documented (DEBUGGING.md:97), but the comment says operator forms 'mean what they say'. Verifier's notes: TestZZEqualsHitCondition FAIL; TestZZParseHitCondition shows the parse table.
repro: dap/zz_tool_test.go TestZZEqualsHitCondition (FAIL: 4 stops, want 1) and TestZZParseHitCondition (table of parses).
impact: A user asking for the second arrival only is stopped on every arrival after it, with no warning that the operator was not honoured.
fix_proposal: Either implement equality (a max-hits field on vm.BreakpointSpec) or refuse `==`/`=` with the same 'not understood' note the other unsupported forms get. Fix the comment. Regression test: TestHitConditionEqualsStopsExactlyOnce, or TestHitConditionEqualsIsRefusedWithANote.

title: db_index_prop reports success on a node that does not exist
claim: DbIndexProp passes the script's node id straight to g.IndexNodeProperty and returns true. graphene does not check that the node exists, so a mistyped or stale id writes an index entry that points at nothing and the call reports success. db_add_edge does check (it refuses `edge references non-existent node`).
evidence: db_index_prop(h, 999999, "k", "v") -> true, err=nil, on both the in-memory and the disk backend. On disk, db_open_disk with verify_on_open:true afterwards accepts the store (nodes: 1), so nothing ever reports the dangling entry. metadata.go:2193 promises 'true once the property has been indexed'. Verifier: db_index_prop(h, 999999, "k", "v") -> true, err=nil, on both the memory and the disk backend. After that, a disk reopen with verify_on_open:true is accepted (nodes: 1). Verifier's notes: TestZZDbIndexPropOnMissingNode FAIL; TestZZDbIndexPropMissingNodeVerifyOnOpen logs the reopen being accepted.
repro: builtin/zz_tool_test.go TestZZDbIndexPropOnMissingNode (FAIL for both backends); zz_tool2_test.go TestZZDbIndexPropMissingNodeVerifyOnOpen (reopen accepted).
impact: A script that indexes evidence properties against a wrong node id gets a success and a store whose index disagrees with its nodes.
fix_proposal: Check g.GetNode(id) (or run a Tx that fails on a missing node) before indexing, and return `db_index_prop: node %d does not exist`. Regression test: TestDbIndexPropRefusesAMissingNode. Fixed: db_index_prop looks the node up with GetNode and refuses `node N does not exist` before indexing, then indexes directly. Not through a transaction, although a commit would check the node itself: on a disk store a commit is an fsync, measured at 5us -> 430us a call, and no db_* builtin deletes a node while graphene's lock keeps other writers out, so the window it would close is unreachable. (The first text of this row, landed in dc3e3bb, described the transaction version that was measured and reverted.)

title: test, lint and fmt silently skip a directory argument whose name starts with a dot
claim: Both walkers return filepath.SkipDir for any directory whose d.Name() starts with '.', and WalkDir hands the root itself to the callback first. A directory the user named explicitly, such as `.hidden`, is skipped whole. Both walkers also `return nil` on a walk error, so an unreadable subdirectory is skipped silently.
evidence: `.hidden/bad_test.mut` holds a failing assert_eq. `mutant test .hidden` -> `no *_test.mut files found`, exit 0, while `mutant test .hidden/bad_test.mut` -> 1 failed, exit 1. `mutant lint .hidden` -> no output, exit 0, while `mutant lint .hidden/lintme.mut` reports two errors, exit 1. Verifier: `mutant test .hidden` -> 'no *_test.mut files found', exit 0. `mutant test .hidden/bad_test.mut` -> 1 failed, exit 1. `mutant lint .hidden` -> no output, exit 0. `mutant lint .hidden/lintme.mut` -> 2 diagnostics, exit 1. The root passed to WalkDir itself matches the dot-name skip rule. Walk errors are swallowed with `return nil`. Verifier's notes: CLI run in b4b/TOOL/r2.
repro: CLI in scratch r2 (PowerShell): test and lint on the directory versus on the file.
impact: A CI step or examiner pointing test or lint at a dot-directory gets a green result with nothing checked.
fix_proposal: Apply the skip rule only when path != root, and count walk errors into the exit code instead of ignoring them. Regression test: TestCollectFilesWalksAnExplicitDotDirectory for both collectors.

title: mutant fmt and lint accept any file named on the command line
claim: collectMutantSourceFiles appends every non-directory argument without checking the extension, so `mutant fmt notes.md` runs the Mutant formatter over Markdown and writes the result back.
evidence:
notes.md = "# Title
line one  

| a | b |   
". `mutant fmt notes.md` -> `formatted: notes.md`, exit 0, and the bytes are now LF-only with trailing spaces stripped (23-20-54-...-0A-0A-7C-...-7C-0A). Verifier: notes.md = '# Title
line one  

| a | b |   
'. `mutant fmt notes.md` prints 'formatted: notes.md', exits 0, and leaves the bytes LF-only with trailing spaces stripped. collectMutantSourceFiles appends any non-directory argument.
repro: CLI in scratch r1 (PowerShell), comparing the file bytes before and after.
impact: A mistyped path or shell glob (`mutant fmt *`) edits non-Mutant files, including Markdown whose trailing double space is a line break.
fix_proposal: Refuse a file argument that does not end in .mut, or say 'skipping X: not a .mut file' and exit non-zero. Regression test: TestFmtRefusesANonMutantFile.

title: Without --enable-macros the REPL refuses any line containing 'quote' or 'macro'
claim: macroCheck is a case-insensitive substring test for "macro", "quote" and "unquote" over the whole line, string literals and identifiers included. A matching line is refused and never compiled.
evidence: `let q = "a quote";` -> `Macros are experimental features...`, then `q;` -> `undefined variable: q`. `let macroCount = 2;` is refused the same way. Verifier: `let q = "a quote";` is refused with 'Macros are experimental...', and then `q;` gives 'undefined variable: q'. macroCheck (repl.go:1055-1060) is a case-insensitive substring test over the whole line. Verifier's notes: TestZZReplMacroWordRefused FAIL.
repro: repl/zz_tool_test.go TestZZReplMacroWordRefused -> FAIL.
impact: Ordinary code that mentions these words, such as a string about quoting or a variable named quoteCount, cannot be entered in the default REPL.
fix_proposal: Detect macros from the parsed AST (a MacroLiteral node, or a call to quote/unquote) rather than from the text. Regression test: TestReplAcceptsTheWordQuoteOutsideAMacro.

title: The terminal REPL forgets struct and enum declarations between lines
claim: Each line compiles with a fresh compiler that knows only the symbol table and constants. StructDefs/EnumDefs from earlier lines are not handed back. webrepl/repl.go:47-51 and :101 already fix this with SeedTypeDefinitions; the terminal REPL was not given the same fix. Verifier: As stated. The nil-deref on the next line is the CMP-001 let-binding mechanism (M26-CMP-001) triggered by the failed line.
evidence: `struct Point { x; y; };` then `let p = Point { x: 1, y: 2 };` -> `compiler error: undefined struct type: Point`, and then `p.x;` -> `vm_runtime_error: recovered panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference`. Verifier: `struct Point { x; y; };` then `let p = Point{...}` -> 'compiler error: undefined struct type: Point'. Then `p.x` -> 'recovered panic: ... nil pointer dereference'. The terminal REPL never calls SeedTypeDefinitions; webrepl does (webrepl/repl.go:101). Verifier's notes: TestZZReplStructAcrossLines FAIL.
repro: repl/zz_tool_test.go TestZZReplStructAcrossLines -> FAIL.
impact: Types cannot be used in the terminal REPL unless declared on the same line as every use, while the browser REPL accepts the same session.
fix_proposal: Carry structDefs/enumDefs across lines and call comp.SeedTypeDefinitions exactly as webrepl does, ideally through one shared session type. Regression test: TestReplStructDeclaredOnOneLineIsUsableOnTheNext.

title: Piped input to the terminal REPL is not executed
claim: newInteractiveLineReader enables readline whenever in and out are os.Stdin and os.Stdout, without checking that they are terminals. With stdin piped, the readline path reads nothing and the REPL ends at once with exit 0, running none of the input. Verifier: As stated. Verified on Windows only.
evidence: `"putln(12345);`nlet a = 2;`na + 40;`n" | mutant.exe` -> exit 0, output contains neither 12345 nor 42, and ends at the first `>>` prompt. The same lines through repl.Start with a bytes.Reader (scanner path) run normally. Verified on Windows only; the readline cause is inferred from the code path taken. Verifier: Piping `putln(12345); let a = 2; a + 40;` into mutant.exe from PowerShell -> exit 0; the output has neither 12345 nor 42 and ends at the first '>>'. newInteractiveLineReader (repl.go:546-551) chooses readline whenever in/out are os.Stdin/os.Stdout, without checking for a terminal.
repro: PowerShell pipe into the scratch mutant.exe (r1), checking for 12345 and 42 in the output.
impact: Scripted use (`mutant < session.txt`, a heredoc) silently does nothing and reports success.
fix_proposal: Use readline only when stdin is a terminal (readline.IsTerminal / golang.org/x/term) and fall back to the scanner otherwise. Regression test: A CLI test that pipes two lines into the built binary and expects both results.

title: REPL completion never offers the session's own names
claim: Completion takes Symbols from `env.Keys()`, but env is a fresh object.Environment that nothing ever writes to. The session's bindings live in the compiler symbolTable. The web REPL uses r.symbolTable.GlobalNames() (webrepl/repl.go:187, 195).
evidence: `let myvariable = 3;` then `:complete myva` -> `No completion candidates.` Verifier: `let myvariable = 3;` then `:complete myva` -> 'No completion candidates.' env at repl.go:379 is a fresh Environment that nothing ever writes to. Verifier's notes: TestZZReplCompleteUserSymbol FAIL.
repro: repl/zz_tool_test.go TestZZReplCompleteUserSymbol -> FAIL.
impact: Tab completion and :complete offer only builtins, never the variables and functions the user has defined.
fix_proposal: Pass symbolTable.GlobalNames() (as webrepl does) and delete the unused env parameter threaded through vanity/handle*Command. Regression test: TestReplCompleteOffersSessionGlobals.

title: The browser-safe builtin set admits builtins that read or write host files
claim: The rule is that 'a builtin is browser-safe unless it needs the host', but the path heuristic matches only parameter names like path/file/dir. lua_run_string is allowed and registers mutant.read_file (builtin/lua.go:163-175), which reads any host file, and os is opened (lua.go:129). record_seal(source, record, ...) reads and writes host paths under names the heuristic does not match. WASM_REPL_REFERENCE says lua_run_string runs with 'no io/os libraries ... so it is pure in-memory computation'. Verifier: As stated. In a real browser, host I/O fails with ENOSYS, so the practical exposure is off-browser reuse of webrepl.
evidence: webrepl.New(): `fs_read(...)` -> `undefined variable: fs_read` (refused), while `lua_run_string("return (mutant.read_file('<tmp>/host-secret.txt'))")` -> "HOST-FILE-CONTENTS". The safe list includes [runtime integration] lua_run_string, [classified records] record_seal and [chain of custody] case_open. Verifier: In webrepl.New(), fs_read is refused ('undefined variable'), but lua_run_string("return (mutant.read_file('<tmp>/host-secret.txt'))") returns 'HOST-FILE-CONTENTS'. The safe set also includes record_seal, case_open and the ledger_* writers. WASM_REPL_REFERENCE.md:429-431 says lua_run_string has 'no io/os libraries' and is 'pure in-memory computation', but os is opened (lua.go:129) and mutant.read_file reads the host. Verifier's notes: webrepl/zz_verify2_test.go TestZZWebReplLuaReadsHostFile FAIL; TestZZWebReplSafeByCategory dumps the set.
repro: webrepl/zz_tool2_test.go TestZZWebReplLuaReadsHostFile (FAIL) and TestZZWebReplSafeByCategory (dump).
impact: In a real browser the host reads fail with ENOSYS, so the practical exposure is small. Under Node-hosted wasm, or any reuse of webrepl off the browser, the 'safe' set reads and writes host files, and the reference documents otherwise.
fix_proposal: Add lua_run_string to explicitDeny (or give the web REPL a Lua state without mutant.read_file), and deny record_seal/case_open etc. by a metadata flag such as TouchesHost rather than by parameter name. Correct WASM_REPL_REFERENCE.md. Regression test: TestBrowserSafeExcludesEveryBuiltinThatOpensAHostPath, driven by a metadata flag.

title: wasmreplserve serves a stale REPL binary and never rebuilds it
claim: ensureWasmBinary rebuilds only when mutant_repl.wasm is missing or lacks the 4-byte magic. Any older build is served forever after the source changes. syncWasmExec meanwhile overwrites wasm_exec.js on every start from the PATH go's GOROOT, so the JS glue and the served wasm can come from different Go versions. Both files are written into examples/wasm-repl, where they are neither tracked nor git-ignored. Verifier: As stated. This is a developer-only tool.
evidence: A 4-byte file containing only the magic 00 61 73 6d passed prepareExampleFiles unchanged ('wasm after prepare: 4 bytes'), while wasm_exec.js was re-synced (16992 bytes). `git check-ignore examples/wasm-repl/mutant_repl.wasm examples/wasm-repl/wasm_exec.js` -> rc=1 (not ignored). Verifier: A 4-byte file holding only the wasm magic passed prepareExampleFiles unchanged, while wasm_exec.js was re-synced (16992 bytes). `git check-ignore` on both files -> rc=1; only index.html is tracked. Verifier's notes: cmd/wasmreplserve/zz_verify_test.go TestZZStaleWasmIsServed FAIL.
repro: cmd/wasmreplserve/zz_tool_test.go TestZZStaleWasmIsServed -> FAIL.
impact: A developer testing a web REPL change sees the old REPL, or a mismatched wasm_exec.js, with no message. Running the server also dirties the working tree.
fix_proposal: Rebuild when any Go source under webrepl/, cmd/replwasm/ or their dependencies is newer than the artifact (or always rebuild; go build caches). Take wasm_exec.js from the same toolchain that built the wasm. Add both files to .gitignore. Regression test: TestPrepareRebuildsAWasmOlderThanItsSource.

title: lua_run_* renders whole numbers in exponent form
claim: luaValueToString formats every LNumber with strconv.FormatFloat(v, 'g', -1, 64), so any whole number of a million or more comes back in exponent form. Lua's own tostring, and RUNTIME_INTEGRATION.md's 'numbers stringify to their obvious text form', give the digits.
evidence: `return 1000000` -> "1e+06"; `return tostring(1000000)` -> "1000000"; `return 123456789` -> "1.23456789e+08"; `print(2500000)` -> "2.5e+06"; `return 7` -> "7". Verifier: `return 1000000` -> '1e+06'; `return 123456789` -> '1.23456789e+08'; `print(2500000)` -> '2.5e+06'; `tostring(1000000)` -> '1000000'. lua.go:204-205 formats with FormatFloat 'g', -1. RUNTIME_INTEGRATION.md:61 promises 'obvious text form'. Verifier's notes: TestZZLuaNumberRendering FAIL.
repro: builtin/zz_tool_test.go TestZZLuaNumberRendering -> FAIL.
impact: A scoring or parsing script that returns a file size, offset or count of a million or more hands the caller exponent text, and to_int or an equality check on it then misreads the value.
fix_proposal: Render numbers the way gopher-lua's LNumber.String does: an integral value as an int64 when it fits, otherwise %.14g. Regression test: TestLuaRunStringRendersIntegersAsDigits.

title: mutant.version() in Lua reports 2.1.0
claim: Both Lua APIs return the literal "2.1.0", documented as 'returns Mutant version for compatibility checks'. The build is global.Version = "2.5.0" (global/const.go:23).
evidence: `return mutant.version()` -> "2.1.0" from lua_run_string and from the patch VM. examples/lua/lua_run_string_example.mut:3 prints it. Verifier: mutant.version() returns '2.1.0' from lua_run_string and from the patch VM; global.Version is 2.5.0. examples/lua/lua_run_string_example.golden:3 records 2.1.0, so the fix must update that golden. Verifier's notes: Same class as M26-LSP-001 (fixed) but a different site, so not a duplicate.
repro: builtin/zz_tool_test.go TestZZLuaVersion and runtime/lua/zz_tool_test.go TestZZPatchVersionAndCapability -> FAIL.
impact: A script gating on version reads a release three versions old. It is the same drift class as M26-LSP-001, but in a different file with a different fix.
fix_proposal: Return global.Version in both places, and add a test that compares against it. Regression test: TestLuaVersionMatchesGlobalVersion.

title: mutant test --json leaves out file counts of zero, although the code says every count is written
claim: The Totals comment says 'every count inside it is then written even when it is zero, and a CI check reading totals.tests_failed never has to distinguish absent from none', but Files, FilesFailed and FilesNotRun are tagged `omitempty`. Verifier: As stated. Calibrated to S5: the JSON schema is documented nowhere in docs/, so only the code comment is contradicted, and a consumer that treats a missing count as 0 gets the right answer.
evidence: A passing run emits `{"kind":"summary",...,"totals":{"files":1,"tests":1,"tests_failed":0,"tests_skipped":0}}` with no files_failed. A failing run emits files_failed:1. A file that fails to compile has tests_failed:0, so files_failed is the count that matters, and it is the one that disappears at zero. Verifier: `mutant test --json good` summary: totals {files:1,tests:1,tests_failed:0,tests_skipped:0}, with no files_failed. A failing run shows files_failed:1. test_runner.go:380-382 tags these omitempty, contradicting the comment at :373-376.
repro: CLI in scratch r2: `mutant test --json good` (passing) versus `mutant test --json plain` (failing).
impact: A CI consumer reading totals.files_failed gets a missing field on success. That is exactly the 'absent vs none' puzzle the comment says was designed away.
fix_proposal: Drop omitempty from files, files_failed and files_not_run (or document which are optional). Regression test: TestJSONSummaryAlwaysCarriesFileCounts.

title: A DAP header line is read with no length limit
claim: maxMessageBytes (16 MiB) caps the body 'because anything may be on the other end of a pipe', but readFrame reads each header line with `c.reader.ReadString('\n')`, which buffers without bound until a newline arrives. Verifier: As stated. The peer is the editor, or a local process on the 127.0.0.1 listener.
evidence: A header line with no newline: 8 MiB -> TotalAlloc +24 MiB, 32 MiB -> +96 MiB, linear with no cap. Verifier: A header line with no newline: 8 MiB -> TotalAlloc +24 MiB; 32 MiB -> +96 MiB; err=EOF only at end of input. The 16 MiB cap (maxMessageBytes) applies only to the body. Verifier's notes: TestZZHeaderLineUnbounded.
repro: dap/zz_tool_test.go TestZZHeaderLineUnbounded.
impact: A misbehaving client, or a local process on the --port listener, can grow the adapter's memory without limit. This is the case the body cap exists to prevent.
fix_proposal: Read header lines through a bounded reader (e.g. ReadSlice with a 4 KiB limit, refusing longer lines). Regression test: TestReadFrameRefusesAnOverlongHeaderLine.

title: The REPL panics at start when the current user cannot be resolved
claim: welcome() does `user, err := user.Current(); if err != nil { panic(err) }` only to print a greeting. On a host where the uid has no passwd entry (containers run with an arbitrary uid, and cgo-off builds read /etc/passwd), user.Current fails and `mutant` with no arguments crashes with a Go panic. Verifier: The REPL panics at start on Linux/cgo-off only when the uid has no passwd entry AND $USER or $HOME is unset. That is narrower than 'the uid has no passwd entry'.
evidence: The code path is unconditional, and the release builds are CGO_ENABLED=0, which uses the pure-Go /etc/passwd lookup. Verifier: repl.go:646-649 panics on a user.Current error. In Go 1.26.2 os/user/lookup_stubs.go current(), a cgo-off build falls back to $USER/$HOME when the uid has no passwd entry, and returns an error only when one of them is empty. Example: `docker run -u 12345`, which usually has no USER. Verifier's notes: Cannot be reproduced on this Windows host without changing the environment.
impact: The REPL cannot start at all in some container deployments.
fix_proposal: Fall back to a generic greeting when user.Current fails; never panic for cosmetics. Regression test: Make the lookup injectable (var currentUser = user.Current) and test that welcome survives an error.

title: Misleading and dead code in the Lua patch API and the compile path
claim: (1) mutant.can_use_builtin is documented as 'check if patch has capability' and always returns true. (2) luaToObject/luaToObjectValue have no caller in the tree, and they convert any integral float with int64(n), so 1e300 and 9.3e18 become -9223372036854775808. (3) LoadBytecode's comment says it takes 'plaintext Lua 5.2 bytecode (e.g., from luac)', but gopher-lua's Load compiles source text, and the tests pass source. (4) get_global can never return anything: the only caller passes `Globals: map[string]object.Object{}`. (5) cli/cli.go says 'Pass nil for privateKey - Generate() will create a new one. In production, you'd load a persistent key', while generate.go:36/44-45 loads or bootstraps the persistent local key.
evidence: The grep for luaToObject finds only its definitions. TestZZLuaToObjectHugeNumber logs `1e+300 -> INTEGER -9223372036854775808`; TestZZPatchVersionAndCapability logs can_use_builtin("exec_command") = true. Verifier: api.go:56-60: can_use_builtin always pushes true. luaToObject has no caller outside its own definitions, and luaToObjectValue(1e300) -> INTEGER -9223372036854775808. vm.go:78-79 says the LoadBytecode input is 'Lua 5.2 bytecode', but it is compiled as source. cli/cli.go:34-35 claims 'Generate() will create a new one', but generate.go:44-45 loads or bootstraps the persistent key. Verifier's notes: TestZZLuaToObjectHugeNumber and TestZZPatchVersionAndCapability logs.
repro: runtime/lua/zz_tool_test.go TestZZLuaToObjectHugeNumber, TestZZPatchVersionAndCapability.
impact: A reader, or a patch author, is told about capabilities, bytecode and key handling that do not exist.
fix_proposal: Delete can_use_builtin (or implement it), delete luaToObject*, and fix the LoadBytecode and cli.go comments. Either feed real globals to APIContext or drop get_global. Regression test: none (deletion); a policy grep that no exported Lua API function returns a constant.

title: mutant test runs every test file in one process and never resets builtin's process-global state, so one file's open case fails the next file
claim: runTestFileAt builds a fresh VM per file but the builtin package's process-global state (custodyStore/custodyActive, ledgerHandles, recordHandles, disclosureKeys, the audit chain auditLog, taskRegistry, channel/conn/listener registries, the graphene label registry, ~35 stores in all) is never reset between files. A test's outcome depends on which files ran before it in the same `mutant test` invocation. The reset functions that exist (resetCustodyForTesting custody.go:1252, resetLedgerForTesting ledger.go:803, resetRecordsForTesting record.go:1346, resetProgramIdentityForTesting custody_seal.go:95) are unexported and only Go tests call them. Verifier: As stated. Test results depend on file order whenever a file leaves custody, ledger or record state open. I did not reproduce the other leaks (manifest cross-recording, passphrase cache) separately, but the same unreset globals cause them.
evidence: test_runner.go:83 `for index, file := range files { report := runTestFileAt(file, modulePaths, options)`; runTestFileAt only does `machine := vm.NewWithPasswordAndGlobalStoreMode(...)`, `machine.Run()`, `builtin.WaitForTasks()`, with no builtin reset. custody.go:346-351 `if custodyStore.session != nil && !custodyStore.session.Closed { ... "case_open: case %q is still open; close it with `case_close()` before opening another"`. Repro run in the scratch copy with the CLI built by go1.26.2 (CGO_ENABLED=0): a_test.mut = `test("file A opens a case", fn() { let c, e = case_open("CASE-A", "alice"); assert(is_null(e), "case_open failed"); });` b_test.mut = the same with CASE-B/bob plus `case_close();`. `mutant test b_test.mut` gives `ok b_test.mut (1 test)`. `mutant test .` gives `ok a_test.mut` then `FAIL b_test.mut ... case_open failed: ERROR:case_open: case "CASE-A" is still open`. Verifier: Re-ran in b4c/ARCH/leak with mutant.exe built from HEAD by go1.26.2 (CGO_ENABLED=0). `mutant test b_test.mut` -> ok. `mutant test a_test.mut` -> ok. `mutant test .` -> ok a_test.mut, then FAIL b_test.mut: 'case_open: case "CASE-A" is still open; close it with `case_close()` before opening another', exit 1. test_runner.go loops over the files in one process and builds a new VM for each file, but it never resets the builtin package's globals. The reset helpers (resetCustodyForTesting etc.) are unexported and only Go tests call them. No doc promises that each test file is isolated. Verifier's notes: The script author triggers this against their own tests; the failure is loud or depends on order. S3/P2 is right.
repro: In a scratch dir, write the two files above, then run `mutant.exe test b_test.mut` (passes) and `mutant.exe test .` (b fails because of a).
impact: Order-dependent test results: a file passes alone and fails in the suite, or the reverse. The same leak silently records file B's evidence opens into file A's case manifest (custodyActive stays true), carries the audit chain head across files, and keeps cached passphrases and record keys. A suite of custody/disclosure tests cannot be trusted to test each file on its own.
fix_proposal: Give builtin one exported `ResetProcessState()` (or a per-run Session object that owns these stores) that closes leaked handles with a warning and clears the custody, ledger, record, disclosure, task and registry state. Call it from runTestFileAt before each file. Longer term, move the stores into a per-run context that the VM carries, so pmap/spawn/serve share it on purpose rather than by accident. Regression test: A Go test in the main package that writes the two .mut files above to t.TempDir(), runs the test runner over the directory, and requires both to pass. A second case covers a leaked ledger handle and a leaked record key.

title: gets() under `mutant debug` (stdio, which VS Code uses) reads the DAP protocol stream: a request frame is consumed as program input and never answered
claim: Program output was made injectable (builtin.SetOutput, which dap uses to turn putln into output events), but program input was not. builtin's package-level `stdinReader = bufio.NewReader(os.Stdin)` reads the same os.Stdin that dap.Serve reads protocol frames from. A debuggee's gets() races the adapter for stdin, and each read it wins swallows up to 4096 bytes of protocol. Verifier: As stated. Under stdio `mutant debug`, gets() takes a DAP frame as program input, and that request is never answered.
evidence: gets.go:14 `var stdinReader = bufio.NewReader(os.Stdin)`; cli_debug.go:79 `dap.Serve(os.Stdin, os.Stdout, options)`; extension.ts:149 `new vscode.DebugAdapterExecutable(mutantCliPath(), ["debug"])` (stdio). Repro: a Go DAP client (scratch dapc/main.go) spawns `mutant.exe debug prog.mut`, sends initialize/launch/configurationDone, then 10 `threads` requests 300 ms apart. For control.mut (putln; sleep_ms(3000); putln), 10 of 10 threads requests were answered, in two runs. For gets.mut (`let line = gets(); putln("gets returned: " + line);`), the adapter emitted an output event `gets returned: Content-Length: 47` and 9 of 10 threads requests were answered, in both runs. Verifier: I rebuilt the auditor's DAP client in b4c/ARCH/dap. It spawns `mutant.exe debug prog`, sends initialize, launch and configurationDone, then 10 threads requests 300 ms apart. gets.mut: the adapter emitted the output event 'gets returned: Content-Length: 47' and answered 9 of 10 threads requests. control.mut (no gets): 10 of 10. builtin/gets.go keeps a package-level bufio reader on os.Stdin, and cli_debug.go serves DAP over os.Stdin. Verifier's notes: This is related to M26-RUN-011 (stdin shared with --password-stdin) but is a different consumer. It is not a duplicate.
repro: Build scratch dapc (the Go client), then `dapc.exe mutant.exe gets.mut` vs `dapc.exe mutant.exe control.mut`.
impact: Debugging any program that reads stdin in VS Code (the default adapter transport) loses editor requests: the editor waits forever on the swallowed request, and the program gets protocol text as its input. docs/DEBUGGING.md:66 presents stdio as the normal transport and gives no warning.
fix_proposal: Add builtin.SetInput(io.Reader) mirroring SetOutput. dap installs a reader that is either empty (gets returns EOF with a clear error: 'stdin is the debug protocol; use --port or a launch `stdin` file') or fed from a launch-configuration file. Build stdinReader lazily from the installed reader. Regression test: A dap package test that serves over an io.Pipe, launches a program calling gets(), sends two requests, and asserts both responses arrive and gets() returns an error rather than protocol bytes.

title: The static-analysis layer (sema, compiler, LSP) links the whole 65k-LOC builtin runtime for names and metadata: the language server is 70.7 MB with grpc, OPA, sqlite and every forensic library
claim: sema imports builtin for one call, `builtin.GetBuiltinByName(flat) != nil` (a name-existence check). The LSP analyzer and server use only builtin.Builtins' names and the metadata API (BuiltinParamDoc, ParamKind, ReturnSpec, TypedSignature, PlatformSupport, TeachingDoc) and never call an implementation. The metadata lives in files that compile standalone (metadata.go, names.go, signature.go import only "strings"), but it shares a package with every builtin implementation, so every consumer links the runtime. Verifier: Mostly as stated. Correction: the LSP also uses ClassifiedSinks/ClassifiedSources (builtin/classified.go) and GetBuiltinByName/Builtins (builtin.go). So metadata.go, names.go and signature.go alone are not enough for a spec package; a names-only registry and the classified lists must move too.
evidence: `go1.26.2 list -deps`: ./sema 657 packages (424 non-std, 35 aoiflux); ./compiler 658; ./lsp/cmd/mlsp 667 (434 non-std); ./parser only 80 (4 non-std). The built mlsp.exe is 70,763,520 bytes (mutant.exe is 73,441,280) and `go version -m` lists 82 module deps, including google.golang.org/grpc, open-policy-agent/opa, modernc.org/sqlite, gopsutil, gopacket, saferwall/pe and all 9 aoiflux libs. Extraction test in the scratch copy: metadata.go, names.go and signature.go copied into a new package `builtinmeta` built cleanly with 42 total deps. The mlsp binary also runs builtin's init() (audit.go:113 installs the audit sink) and the package initialisers of every dependency. Verifier: go1.26.2 list -deps: ./sema 657 packages, ./compiler 658, ./lsp/cmd/mlsp 667, each with 35 aoiflux packages and mutant/builtin; ./parser 80. sema's only use of builtin is resolve.go:234 GetBuiltinByName. The rebuilt mlsp.exe is 70,764,032 B, and `go version -m` lists grpc v1.83.2, opa v1.19.0, modernc sqlite v1.56.0 and gopacket. LSP uses of builtin are names, metadata, Param*, ReturnSpec, TeachingDoc, PlatformSupport, ClassifiedSinks/Sources and GetBuiltinByName. Verifier's notes: Priority lowered to P3. This is architecture and binary-size debt with no wrong behaviour.
repro: CGO_ENABLED=0 go1.26.2 list -deps ./sema | wc -l; build ./lsp/cmd/mlsp and check its size; copy the three files into a new package and build it.
impact: Each per-platform VS Code extension package ships about 70 MB of runtime it never executes. The editor, the compiler's static checks and anything importing sema pick up the attack surface and init() side effects of network, OPA and sqlite code. The sema and analyzer test binaries rebuild whenever any builtin implementation changes.
fix_proposal: Move names.go, metadata.go and signature.go (plus a names-only set generated from Builtins) into mutant/builtin/spec, which has no internal imports. builtin imports spec. sema, lsp and compiler's name resolution import spec only. Keep a consistency test that spec's name set equals builtin.Builtins' names. Regression test: A policy test asserting that `go list -deps ./lsp/cmd/mlsp ./sema` contains no github.com/aoiflux/* package and not mutant/builtin.

title: CONTRIBUTING describes the engine architecture wrongly: the evaluator does not run the REPL, and there are no longer three gob registration lists
claim: CONTRIBUTING.md:181-182 says 'the tree-walking evaluator (`evaluator/`), which runs the REPL and macro expansion', and :187-189 says 'Bytecode format changes touch three separate gob registration lists — `runner/runner.go`, `generator/generate.go` and `compiler/linetable_test.go`.' Both are false at HEAD. Verifier: As stated. The evaluator runs macro expansion (in the generator, repl and webrepl), not the REPL. There is one gob list, in serialize/gobtypes.go.
evidence: REPL: repl/repl.go:438-439 calls only evaluator.DefineMacros/ExpandMacros, then :452 `comp := compiler.NewWithState(...)` and :465 `machine := vm.NewWithGlobalStoreAndPassword(...)`. The web REPL is the same (webrepl/repl.go:94-95), and docs/WASM_REPL_REFERENCE.md:62 says the tree-walker was replaced. evaluator.Eval has 0 production callers outside the evaluator package. The only production entry points are DefineMacros/ExpandMacros (generator/generate.go:239-240, repl, webrepl). Gob: there is one list, serialize/gobtypes.go GobTypes(), registered through serialize.RegisterGobTypes() (sync.Once), which runner.go:331, generate.go:318, mutil/util.go:352,362 and compiler/linetable_test.go:185 all call. None of those files has its own list. Verifier: CONTRIBUTING.md:181-189 (read in the scratch copy) says the evaluator 'runs the REPL and macro expansion' and names three gob registration lists. repl/repl.go:438-439 and webrepl/repl.go:94-95 call only evaluator.DefineMacros/ExpandMacros, then compile and run on the VM. The only gob.Register in the tree is serialize/gobtypes.go:72. No non-test code outside evaluator/ calls evaluator.Eval. Verifier's notes: The gob-list sentence is the same defect as DOC2.11 (which also covers .gitattributes). The evaluator/REPL claim is unique to ARCH.05. Merge the gob half into whichever survives.
repro: grep -rn 'gob.Register' --include=*.go . (only serialize/gobtypes.go:72); read repl/repl.go:430-470.
impact: A contributor adding a gob type goes looking for three lists that do not exist. A contributor changing REPL behaviour edits the evaluator, which the REPL does not execute. The rule 'a new operator must land in both engines' then puts the cost of the whole language on an engine whose only production job is running macro bodies at compile time.
fix_proposal: Rewrite the paragraph: the evaluator runs macro bodies at compile time (generator, repl, webrepl), and everything else runs on the VM. Gob types are registered in serialize/gobtypes.go GobTypes() only. Separately decide whether the evaluator must keep full-language parity or can be scoped to what a macro body may do. That decision sets how much of parity/ (65 tests, 4,359 LOC) stays mandatory. Regression test: none (doc); optionally a policy test that no file other than serialize/gobtypes.go calls gob.Register.

title: The byte-code container type lives in compiler, so the VM, mutil and the Lua runtime depend on the compiler, sema and builtin
claim: vm imports compiler only for compiler.ByteCode (10 refs), BytecodeVersion, BytecodeVersionNamedBuiltins and NormalizeVersion. mutil imports it only for ByteCode. So the runtime layer (vm, mutil, runtime/lua) transitively depends on compiler -> sema -> builtin, and the VM cannot be built or tested without the compiler. Verifier: As stated. runtime/lua does not import compiler directly; it reaches it transitively.
evidence: `grep -n 'compiler\.' vm/*.go mutil/*.go` (non-test) returns only ByteCode/BytecodeVersion*/NormalizeVersion references plus one comment (vm.go:1159). `go list -deps ./vm ./runtime/lua ./mutil` includes mutant/compiler and mutant/sema. Verifier: Non-test vm/ and mutil/ reference compiler only as ByteCode (12), BytecodeVersion (2), BytecodeVersionNamedBuiltins (2), NormalizeVersion (3) and one comment. go list -deps ./vm, ./mutil and ./runtime/lua all include mutant/compiler, mutant/sema and mutant/builtin.
repro: the grep and go list above
impact: An inverted dependency: a change to sema or compiler internals rebuilds and retests the VM, and a cycle blocks any future move of compile-time checks that need VM types. Low severity; it is technical debt.
fix_proposal: Move ByteCode, the version constants and NormalizeVersion into code/ (the instruction-format package, which already holds the opcodes). compiler produces code.ByteCode, vm consumes it, and vm drops its compiler import. Regression test: A policy test asserting that `go list -deps ./vm` contains neither mutant/compiler nor mutant/sema.

title: builtin/ is one 65k-LOC package whose filesystem and custody clusters are separable, but newError's package-path match and the shared helpers block a split
claim: A go/ast identifier scan of the 135 non-test files shows clusters with narrow interfaces. The filesystem/disk-image cluster (16 files, 18,293 LOC) uses only 3 custody hooks (custodyRecordOpen, custodyRecordOpenAt, custodyRecordTouch), 2 format helpers and 1 net helper, besides names and the shared result helpers. The custody/ledger/disclosure/record cluster (19 files, 14,077 LOC) uses back into fs only fsRegion, fsHashAlgorithm and formatTime, and uses graphdb's DATA and type helpers. Two things block a split. (1) newError derives err.context by matching `strings.Contains(frame.Function, "mutant/builtin.")` and camel-casing the Go function name, so a builtin moved to mutant/builtin/fs keeps its context only because "mutant/builtin/fs." still contains "mutant/builtin."? No: "mutant/builtin/fs.X" does not contain "mutant/builtin.", so its errors would silently fall back to context "builtin". (2) About 25 shared constructors (newError, resultAndError, intObj, stringObj, makeHashObject, boolObj, hashValueByStringKey, optString, ...) sit in the unclassified 'other' cluster (76 files, 17,702 LOC). Verifier: As corrected by the auditor's own note. A function in mutant/builtin/<sub> does NOT match "mutant/builtin.", so moving a builtin to a subpackage would silently degrade its err.context to "builtin". Nothing is wrong today; this only blocks a future split. I did not re-derive the cluster edge counts.
evidence: Cluster edges from the scratch clus/main.go scan: fs->custody 3 identifiers, fs->formats 2, fs->net 1, custody->fs 3 (formatTime fsHashAlgorithm fsRegion), custody->graphdb 4, net->custody 1 (refuseClassified), graphdb->custody 2 (ledgerIsMarked refuseClassified). builtin.go:799 `if strings.Contains(frame.Function, "mutant/builtin.") {`. The context-guessing itself is already known as M26-BLT-017 (23 names wrong; my scan reproduced the same 23 mismatches). Verifier: builtin.go:799 matches strings.Contains(frame.Function, "mutant/builtin."). In a scratch subpackage mutant/builtin/zzfs, a Go test printed frame "mutant/builtin/zzfs.fsOpen" with contains=false, so a builtin moved to a subpackage would fall back to context "builtin". builtin/ has 135 non-test files and 65,328 LOC (counted). Verifier's notes: The mechanism is M26-BLT-017's (guessing the name from the frame). Fixing BLT-017 by passing the registered name removes the blocker.
repro: go run the scratch clus tool over tree/builtin
impact: Every builtin change recompiles and retests the whole package (127 test files, 41,654 test LOC). Nothing breaks today, but any package split will silently degrade error contexts unless newError is fixed first.
fix_proposal: First make error context explicit: pass the registered name from the dispatch site, which also fixes BLT-017. Then extract a small builtin/core (result/hash/option helpers plus the custody hook interface). Then move fs (and later custody) into subpackages, with the Builtins registry in the top package importing them. Regression test: A test that every Builtins entry's error context equals its registered name (the BLT-017 regression test) is the prerequisite guard.

title: MODULES.md promises that any polymorphic build strips the source layout, but a default-mutation .mu carries every module's file name and source text
claim: MODULES.md:228-230 says: "The file-to-line map is debug information. `mutant release` and any build with polymorphic mutation strip it along with the rest, so a released artifact does not carry the layout of your source tree." The code strips only for release. compiler.go:293 reads "Polymorphism does not strip." generate.go:132 calls `bytecode.StripDebugInfo()` only `if stripDebug`, and stripDebug is the `release` flag. `mutant gen` defaults to --mutation 5, so the ordinary .mu a user hands over carries SourceFile, SourceText, LineTable and ModuleSpans for every module. The comment at generate.go:116 ("Polymorphism strips them too, unconditionally") repeats the false claim. Verifier: As stated for the doc: MODULES.md:228-230 and the generate.go:116-117 comment falsely say polymorphic builds strip debug info. Only `mutant release` strips, which is deliberate and in the CHANGELOG. A .mu from `mutant gen` at any mutation level carries SourceFile, the full concatenated source text of every module (comments included), line tables and module spans. Anyone holding the run password (every recipient in tutorial s7) can recover that text.
evidence: I built with `mutant gen --src tb.mut --dev --mutation 10` (tb.mut imports lib/math.mut), copied only tb.mu to an empty directory w/iso as moved.mu, and ran `mutant moved.mu --dev`. The traceback printed `at divide(a=1, b=0) (lib\math.mut:2:9)` and quoted the source line `2 | 	return a / b;`, plus `at <main> (tb.mut:4:14)` with `4 | putf("%d\n", math.divide(1, 0));`. No source file existed in that directory, so the file names and source text are inside the artifact. Verifier: Ran gen --src tb.mut (imports lib/math.mut, has a comment line) --mutation 10 --password-file; copied only tb.mu to an empty dir and ran it: the traceback names lib\math.mut:2:9 and tb.mut:5:14 and quotes both source lines. generate.go:132 calls StripDebugInfo only if stripDebug (release). compiler.go:292-297 says 'Polymorphism does not strip'. ByteCode.SourceText is every module's source concatenated (module/link.go:50-53,113), so comments ship too. The CHANGELOG states it on purpose: 'Debug information is unconditional in development artifacts and stripped only by mutant release'; 'the program's source text travels with the artifact'. Verifier's notes: security=false: the behaviour is intended and published in the CHANGELOG, and the text is only readable with the password. A doc fix closes it. The owner may still choose to strip source text from gen artifacts (it conflicts with COMPARISON.md's 'analysis itself is protected'), but that is a design choice, not an embargo item.
repro: In a scratch copy: lib/math.mut = `let divide = fn(a, b) {\n\treturn a / b;\n};`; tb.mut imports it and calls math.divide(1, 0). Run `mutant gen --src tb.mut --dev --mutation 10`, copy tb.mu to an empty directory, and run it with --dev. The traceback names lib\math.mut and quotes its source.
impact: Someone who ships a .mu (the artifact the tutorial and README present as the encrypted deliverable), relying on the documented stripping, gives every recipient who holds the run password the full source text, module file names and import layout. COMPARISON.md sells 'The analysis itself is protected' and names mutation as part of that.
fix_proposal: Either strip debug info whenever mutationLevel > 0 (the engine already remaps line tables, so only the SourceText/ModuleSpans/names need dropping), or correct MODULES.md:228-230 and generate.go:116-117 to say that only `mutant release` strips, and that a .mu from `mutant gen` carries the source text of every module. Regression test: Generator test: Generate with release=false and mutationLevel=5, decode the artifact, and assert the documented contract. Either SourceText, ModuleSpans and fn.Name are empty, or (if the doc is changed) a docs test asserts that MODULES.md does not claim polymorphic builds strip.

title: STRUCTURED_DATA example 6.3 teaches `let updated, err = push(...)`, the pattern the language reference calls WRONG, and the example fails
claim: The gzip half of example 6.3 builds its array with `let updated, err4 = push(big_records, { "id": i, ... }); big_records = updated;`. push returns one array, so the two-name binding takes it apart. After the first iteration big_records is a HASH, not an array. MUTANT_LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md:214 and TUTORIAL_30_MIN.md:232 both label this exact line 'WRONG'. The example never reaches its gzip round trip.
evidence: I extracted the fence verbatim to s2.mut and ran it under --dev. The base64, hex and url lines print as documented, then: `[json_stringify error] ERROR:argument to `json_stringify` could not be converted to JSON: unsupported value type for JSON: ERROR_OBJ at s2.mut:39:22`. The 'original bytes / compressed bytes / gunzip round-trip ok' lines never print. The fence is untagged (```), so the D1 compile test never sees it. Verifier: Extracted STRUCTURED_DATA.md:351-403 verbatim to s63.mut and ran it under --dev. The base64, hex and url lines print, then '[json_stringify error] ... unsupported value type for JSON: ERROR_OBJ at s63.mut:39:22'. The gzip lines never print. push has one return (metadata.go:414), and LANG_REF:214 labels this exact pattern WRONG. Verifier's notes: Lowered to P2: a documentation example with no guarantee behind it. The fix is trivial.
repro: Extract the third ``` block after '## Examples' in STRUCTURED_DATA.md to s2.mut, then run `mutant --dev s2.mut && mutant --dev s2.mu`.
impact: The structured-data guide teaches the destructuring mistake the rest of the docs warn about, and the program it shows fails.
fix_proposal: Replace the two lines with `big_records = push(big_records, {...});`. Tag the example fences as ```mutant so the D1 compile test and a run check cover them. Regression test: Docs test that runs (not only compiles) the STRUCTURED_DATA examples and asserts that no output line starts with '[json_stringify error]' / '[gunzip error]'. Alternatively, lint the fences with builtinSingleReturn as an error.

title: The tutorial's install path (go build / go install) produces a binary on which the tutorial's own `mutant release` step fails
claim: Section 1 installs with `go build ./...` and `go install`, and the page promises that 'Everything below is a command that was run and an output that came back.' Section 7 then runs `mutant release --src triage.mut --password-file ./case-42.key` and shows `./triage.exe` producing output. A binary built that way has no embedded runtime assets (git ls-files releaseassets/data contains only placeholder.bin), so the release step fails. Verifier: As stated. Also, the error the user actually hits is the 'is invalid' variant, which gives no remedy.
evidence: I built with `CGO_ENABLED=0 go1.26.2 build -o mutant.exe .` (the same thing go install builds) and ran `mutant release --src triage.mut --password-file pw.txt`. Output: `Compiling release build...` then `unable to generate release mode builds: embedded runtime asset for windows/amd64 is invalid: open data/windows_amd64.bin: file does not exist`, exit 1. No triage.exe was produced. Neither the tutorial nor the error says that `mutant gen assets` plus a rebuild, or scripts/build.*, is needed. Verifier: Plain `go1.26.2 build -o mutant.exe .` of the HEAD archive, then `mutant release --src hello.mut --password-file pw.txt`, prints 'unable to generate release mode builds: embedded runtime asset for windows/amd64 is invalid: open data/windows_amd64.bin: file does not exist', exits 1, and produces no binary. git ls-files releaseassets/data lists only placeholder.bin. TUTORIAL_30_MIN.md:28-33 installs with go build/go install. The 'invalid' error path (releaseassets/assets_runtime.go:31-33) names no remedy; only the 'missing' path does. Verifier's notes: Distinct from M26-RUN-008 (no arm64 runtimes) and M26-RUN-009 (gen assets toolchain). README's source install (go install) has the same gap, but README also points to the build scripts.
repro: In a clean archive of HEAD: go build -o mutant.exe . ; mutant release --src triage.mut --password-file pw.txt
impact: A new user following the 30-minute tutorial fails at 'Ship it', the step the tutorial is built around, and the error does not name the fix.
fix_proposal: Change the tutorial's install step to the build script (./scripts/build.sh --host-only), or add a step that runs `mutant gen assets` and rebuilds before section 7. Make the release error name that remedy. Regression test: A docs test asserting that TUTORIAL_30_MIN.md's install block uses the build script whenever the page contains `mutant release`, and a CLI test asserting that the missing-asset error text names `mutant gen assets` / scripts/build.

title: json_stringify writes a FLOAT with an integral value as an integer, so 5.0 does not round-trip as FLOAT as STRUCTURED_DATA promises
claim: STRUCTURED_DATA.md:482-484 says: "`5` decodes to `INTEGER`, `5.0` decodes to `FLOAT`. Round-tripping through `json_stringify` preserves that shape." objectToJSONValue returns a Float's float64 to encoding/json, which writes 5.0 as `5`. That text parses back as INTEGER. Verifier: As stated. The type change also changes later arithmetic: a re-imported 5.0 becomes 5, so 5/2 gives 2, not 2.5.
evidence: s9.mut: `let b, e2 = json_parse("5.0"); putln(type_of(b)); let s, se = json_stringify(b); putln("rt=", s);` prints `FLOAT` and then `rt=5`. The same happens to the doc's own example 6.1 data: bob's `"score":42.0` would re-serialise as 42. Not in the ledger. M26-DAT-018 covers integers above MaxInt64 only. Verifier: j.mut: json_parse("5.0") gives FLOAT, json_stringify gives "5", and json_parse of that gives INTEGER. builtin/json.go:68-69 passes the float64 to encoding/json, which writes integral floats without '.0'. STRUCTURED_DATA.md:482-484 promises the round trip preserves the shape. Verifier's notes: Raised S4 to S3: a silent wrong result in an edge case, and a broken doc promise. Not DAT-018 (above MaxInt64) and not BLT-010 (cache round trip).
repro: mutant --dev s9.mut && mutant --dev s9.mu (prints INTEGER FLOAT FLOAT FLOAT, then rt=5)
impact: A value's type changes through a JSON round trip (FLOAT becomes INTEGER), for example in an exported and re-imported report. The doc promises the opposite.
fix_proposal: In objectToJSONValue, emit a Float whose value is integral and finite as json.Number(strconv.FormatFloat(v,'f',-1,64)+".0") (or use 'g' and append '.0' when there is no '.', 'e' or 'n'). Otherwise, drop the round-trip sentence from STRUCTURED_DATA.md. Regression test: builtin test: json_stringify(json_parse("5.0")) == "5.0" and type_of(json_parse(json_stringify(5.0))) == FLOAT.

title: The docs say `if (c) { ... };` needs its semicolon and that the formatter repairs missing ones; the canonical form has none and fmt deletes it
claim: LANGUAGE_REFERENCE:941 says 'Semicolons are required to terminate statements -- including statements whose value is a block, e.g. `let f = fn() { ... };` and `if (c) { ... };`. The language server's formatter enforces this canonically (it repairs missing semicolons ...)'. TUTORIAL:198-200 repeats it ('at the top level, `if (c) { ... };`. If you forget one, `mutant lint` tells you exactly where'). ExpressionStatement.RequiresSemicolon returns false for `*IfExpression, *MatchExpression`, so the canonical form of an if or match statement has NO semicolon.
evidence: semi.mut contains `if (c) { putln(1); };` and `if (c) { putln(2); }`. `mutant fmt --stdout semi.mut` prints both as `if (c) {\n    putln(1);\n}` with no ';', and prints `match (m) {...}` without one too. `mutant lint semi.mut` reports nothing for the `if` without ';' (it warns only on the let/putln lines). The tutorial's own triage.mut goes through `mutant fmt --stdout` with its `if (err) {...};` rewritten to `}`. Verifier: semi.mut holds `if (c) { putln(1); };`, `if (c) { putln(2); }` and `match (m) {...};`. `mutant fmt --stdout` prints all three without ';'. `mutant lint semi.mut` reports nothing and exits 0. ast/expStatement.go:28-31 exempts IfExpression and MatchExpression from RequiresSemicolon. LANG_REF:941 and TUTORIAL:198-200 give `if (c) { ... };` as the required form. Verifier's notes: Same sentence as M26-LEX-007, but a distinct false claim (if/match canonical form), and the two are best fixed together. Not EX.07 (workshop files).
repro: w/tut/semi.mut: mutant fmt --stdout semi.mut ; mutant lint semi.mut
impact: Readers are taught a rule the formatter then undoes, and are told lint will catch a missing ';' that lint does not flag. The part saying semicolons are 'required' at all is M26-LEX-007.
fix_proposal: Reword both passages: `let`/expression statements take ';'; `if`, `match` and loop statements end at '}' and a trailing ';' after them is removed by `mutant fmt`. Drop `if (c) { ... };` from the examples. Regression test: Docs test: every `if (...) { ... };` example in the language reference and tutorial is unchanged by api.Format, or the prose no longer lists if as needing ';'.

title: A program that ends with putln prints an extra blank line; the Cookbook says nothing extra appears and the Tutorial's shown outputs omit it
claim: COOKBOOK Traps: 'The program's last value is printed ... End with `putln(...)` and nothing extra appears.' putln returns null, and the runner prints `last.Inspect()` plus "\n" unless the value is a void MultiValue. Null's Inspect is "", so a program ending in putln writes one more empty line. The tutorial's 'command that was run and an output that came back' blocks show no such line.
evidence:
I captured stdout bytes with Process.StandardOutput. a.mut = `putln("x");` gives 120,10,10 ("x

"). b.mut = `putln("x"); let _ = 2 + 3;` gives 120,10,53,10, which matches the doc's '5' claim. c.mut ending `hashset_close(...)` gives "true
", which matches the doc. hello.mut from the tutorial prints `hello from mutant`, `[2, 4, 6]` and then an empty line. Verifier: Captured stdout bytes. a.mut `putln("x");` gives 120,10,10. b.mut `putln("x"); let _ = 2 + 3;` gives 120,10,53,10. runner/runner.go:517-523 writes last.Inspect()+"
" unless the last value is a void MultiValue; putln returns Null, which inspects as "". COOKBOOK.md:800 says 'End with putln(...) and nothing extra appears'. The tutorial output blocks omit the blank line. Verifier's notes: Related to, but not the same as, M26-EVL-002 (function address printed) and M26-RUN-006 (empty program panic).
repro: printf 'putln("x");\n' > a.mut; mutant --dev a.mut; capture stdout of `mutant --dev a.mu` as bytes
impact: Every program's output carries a trailing blank line, which breaks exact-output comparisons and pipelines that expect the documented output. The trap section tells readers the opposite.
fix_proposal: In runner.go, skip printing when the last value is Null (as for a void MultiValue), and keep 'nothing extra appears' true. Otherwise, correct COOKBOOK.md:800 and the tutorial output blocks. Regression test: main_exit_code/runner test: a program `putln("x");` writes exactly "x\n" to stdout.

title: DETAILED_EXPLANATIONS ('Current Behavior') describes env configuration, a reachable 'delay' action and two probe stages in every mode, none of which is current
claim: Line 10: 'Policy decides action using mode/profile/env configuration.' Line 11: 'Action can be warn, delay, or terminate.' Lines 21-24: 'Runner checks happen at two stages: pre-decode, pre-execution.' In the code, ResolveTamperResponse (response_policy.go:129-138) returns warn for dev or non-secure and otherwise defaultTamperResponseForProfile. The profile is fixed at standard (QUICK_REFERENCE.md:51), which returns only terminate or warn (profile.go:53-63), so TamperResponseDelay is unreachable. No environment variable is read anywhere, an owner-settled rule the policy guard enforces. runner.go:160-168 runs the pre-execution pass only `if secureMode`, and EXECUTION_MODES.md:43 says --compat gets '1 -- pre-decode only'. Verifier: As stated. TamperResponseDelay is handled at response_policy.go:154 but no resolver produces it.
evidence: response_policy.go:129-138 and profile.go:48-64 as quoted. `grep Getenv|LookupEnv security/response_policy.go security/profile.go` finds nothing. runner.go:163 `if secureMode { if err := enforceAntiRev(secureMode, "pre-execution")`. Verifier: A scratch test in security/ ran ResolveTamperResponse over dev x secure. It returned only warn or terminate, never delay, with the profile fixed at standard (profile.go:18-20 returns a constant). The policy files read no environment (the LookupEnv calls in security/ are detector signals). runner.go:160-168 runs the pre-execution pass only if secureMode, as EXECUTION_MODES.md:43 says. Verifier's notes: DOC3.06 and DOC3.11 cover the same class in other security docs (SECURITY_LLD etc.), not DETAILED_EXPLANATIONS. Consider batching the fixes.
repro: Read the cited lines. Also, `mutant hello.mu --compat --password-file pw.txt` prints no pre-execution probe line.
impact: The 'current behavior' explainer contradicts the owner's no-env-vars rule and EXECUTION_MODES.md. It teaches a delay response that cannot happen, and an extra probe stage that compat runs do not get.
fix_proposal: Rewrite section 1 as 'mode decides (profile fixed at standard): warn or terminate', and section 2 as 'two stages in secure mode, pre-decode only under --compat/--dev'. Remove 'env'. Either remove TamperResponseDelay or state that it is unreachable. Regression test: The policy/ docs guard could ban 'env configuration' in docs/*.md. A unit test asserts ResolveTamperResponse never returns delay.

title: COOKBOOK says `mutant gen` produces 'the Go program' for someone without Mutant; it produces an encrypted .mu that needs Mutant
claim: "To ship the analysis to someone who does not have Mutant installed, see §7 of the tutorial: `mutant gen` produces the Go program, `mutant release` produces a signed standalone binary for a named target." `mutant help gen` says 'Compile source into encrypted bytecode' and 'The compiled .mu lands beside the source. Run it with: mutant hello.mu ...'. A .mu cannot run without the mutant binary.
evidence: The `mutant help gen` output is quoted in the claim. TUTORIAL_30_MIN.md:470-479 itself says 'The recipient needs `mutant` and the password'. Verifier: COOKBOOK.md:787-789 says '`mutant gen` produces the Go program' for shipping to someone without Mutant. gen writes an encrypted .mu, and TUTORIAL:470-479 says 'The recipient needs mutant and the password'.
repro: mutant help gen
impact: It points a reader who wants to ship to a machine without Mutant at the wrong command.
fix_proposal: Replace with: '`mutant gen` produces an encrypted .mu (the recipient needs mutant and the password); `mutant release` produces a standalone binary for a named target.' Regression test: none practical beyond a docs grep for 'produces the Go program'

title: README states a 409-builtin standard library (registry has 659) and clones from a different repository than every other doc
claim: README.md:19: 'Batteries included: a **409-builtin** standard library'. builtin/names.go registers 659, and MUTANT_LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md:965, WHAT_IS_MUTANT.md:19, COMPARISON.md:14 and TUTORIAL:378 all say 659. The gendocs prose-count guard looks for 'N builtins', so the hyphenated '409-builtin' is exactly the rewording the reference (lines 967-972) says walks past a drift gate. README.md:39 clones `https://github.com/gaurav-gogia/mutant`, while `git remote -v` is `git@github.com:aoiflux/mutant.git` and TUTORIAL:29, CONTRIBUTING:25, SECURITY.md:12 and the extension's package.json all use aoiflux/mutant. Verifier: As stated. Whether the old URL redirects was not checked over the network.
evidence: python count of `= "..."` in builtin/names.go: 659. `git -C /o/project/mutant remote -v` shows origin git@github.com:aoiflux/mutant.git. `grep gaurav-gogia/mutant` finds only README.md:39 outside CHANGELOG. Verifier: README.md:19 says '409-builtin'. builtin/names.go has 659 BuiltinName consts. The gendocs guard regex is `(\d+)\s+builtins` (cmd/gendocs/prose_counts_test.go:50), which misses the hyphenated form. README.md:39 clones github.com/gaurav-gogia/mutant, while git remote is aoiflux/mutant and TUTORIAL:29 and the CHANGELOG links use aoiflux.
repro: grep -n '409' README.md; git remote -v
impact: The front page understates the library by 250 builtins. The clone URL may point at an old or renamed repository (not checked over the network: PLAUSIBLE that GitHub redirects).
fix_proposal: Change the README to '659 builtins' (or a phrasing the gendocs guard reads) and extend the guard to 'N-builtin'. Use https://github.com/aoiflux/mutant. Regression test: gendocs prose-count test regex also matching `(\d+)-builtin`; docs test asserting a single clone URL across README/TUTORIAL/CONTRIBUTING.

title: Language reference says `match x { ... }` without parentheses 'parses cleanly as a struct literal'; it is a parse error
claim: "`match x { ... }` without them parses cleanly as a struct literal named `x` and means something else entirely." The parser requires '(' after match and rejects the form. Verifier: As stated. The sentence reads as the rationale for requiring parentheses, but it states the current behaviour, and that statement is wrong.
evidence: e22.mut `let x = 1; let r = match x { 1 => 2 }; putln(r);` gives `parser errors: expected next token to be (, but got IDENT instead`. Verifier: m.mut `let r = match x { 1 => 2 };` gives 'parser errors: expected next token to be (, but got IDENT instead'. LANG_REF:336-338 says it 'parses cleanly as a struct literal'.
repro: mutant --dev e22.mut
impact: The stated reason for the rule is wrong. A reader expecting a silent misparse gets a clear error, so the harm is small.
fix_proposal: Say that the parentheses are required and that omitting them is a parse error. Regression test: none

title: Triple-quoted strings: the reference lists 'three things' that happen, but a fourth (dropping the whitespace-only closing line and the newline before it) is undocumented
claim: The doc says 'Three things happen to the text' (drop the newline after the opener, dedent, CRLF->LF). stripBlockIndent also removes the last line when it is whitespace-only (`lines = lines[:len(lines)-1]`), so the text has no trailing newline.
repro: b1.mut in the DOC1 scratch directory (the tq= line)
impact: A reader who writes a block to a file expecting a final newline gets none.
fix_proposal: Add the fourth rule: 'when the closing """ is alone on its line, that line and the newline before it are dropped'. Regression test: none

title: WHAT_IS_MUTANT credits security/crypto.go with 'deterministic options where appropriate'; there is no deterministic encryption path
claim: 'The encryption layer lives in security/crypto.go: password-based AES-GCM encryption, deterministic options where appropriate, ...'. AESEncrypt always derives the key with Argon2id from a password and random salt (crypto.go:29-70). The only deterministic branch is in deserializeMetadata and AESDecrypt, where it exists to reject such data ('this data was encrypted deterministically and cannot be decrypted with password mode'). generate.go:29-34 records that the 'deterministic encryption' claim 'was never true of the code'.
evidence: No producer sets UsePasswordKDF=false: grep finds only crypto.go:63 (true), 178 (true on parse) and 194 (false on parse of legacy data). Verifier: grep UsePasswordKDF: it is set true at crypto.go:63 (encrypt) and 178, and false only at 194 when parsing legacy metadata, which AESDecrypt then refuses (crypto.go:82). No deterministic encryption producer exists. WHAT_IS_MUTANT.md:201 lists 'deterministic options where appropriate'. Verifier's notes: Similar family to DOC3.07 (deterministic dev key in SECURITY_LLD) but a different doc and a different claim.
repro: grep -rn UsePasswordKDF --include=*.go .
impact: The security overview describes a mode that does not exist.
fix_proposal: Delete the bullet, or reword it to 'legacy deterministic artifacts are recognised and refused'. Regression test: none
