evidence: README.md:17 quoted above; examples/modules/main.mut:25,29 `import "lib/report.mut";` / `import numbers "lib/stats.mut";`; `mutant test --cover examples/modules` passes 12 tests over the imported modules. Verifier: examples/project/portscan_service/README.md:17 'Mutant does not have an `import` statement'. examples/modules/main.mut:25,29 use `import`, and the sweep reports main.mut 'run, reproducible; matches golden'. docs/MODULES.md exists.
repro: grep -n import examples/project/portscan_service/README.md examples/modules/main.mut
impact: The one example billed as 'how a Mutant project is split across files' tells readers the language's module system does not exist. (M26-NET-013, net_serve handlers compiled without the module pipeline, is the true, narrower limit.)
fix_proposal: Say that import composes files at compile time (see docs/MODULES.md), and that net_serve handlers are the exception: they are compiled per connection from a path and cannot use import yet (M26-NET-013). Regression test: Docs grep test: no file under examples/ contains 'does not have an `import`'.

title: email_attachment_triage triages a message with no attachment, while the shipped phish.eml has one
claim: The attachment-triage example parses an inline single-part text message, so its golden records 'attachments: []' and 'email_urls: []'. It never shows an attachment. examples/data/phish.eml (multipart/mixed, invoice.pdf.exe attachment, a phishing URL) is in the tree, and no email example reads it. Verifier: As stated. This is a demo coverage gap only, so S5.
evidence: email_attachment_triage.mut:3 `let raw = "From: ...Subject: Invoice Attached\n\nPlease see attached invoice.";`. Golden: 'email_parse: {attachments: [], ...}' / 'email_urls: [] err:'. Probe zz/p8.mut on phish.eml: `attachments: [{filename: invoice.pdf.exe, mime: application/octet-stream; ..., sha256: bfdf5e72..., size: 128}]`, `urls: [{host: update.svc-cdn.top, ...}]`. Verifier: email_attachment_triage.mut:3 parses an inline single-part message; its golden has attachments: [] and email_urls: []. zz/v8.mut: email_parse(fs_read(phish.eml)) -> 1 attachment, invoice.pdf.exe. phish.eml is used by forensics/chain_of_custody.mut and COOKBOOK, but by no email example.
repro: Scratch tree zz/p8.mut (fs_read phish.eml -> email_parse / email_urls), compiled and run as above.
impact: The example's golden holds an empty result where the named capability should appear, so a regression in attachment extraction would not change it.
fix_proposal: Read examples/data/phish.eml, print the attachment name/size/sha256, and run detect_suspicious_files-style name checks on it. Re-record the golden. Regression test: sweep --golden with a golden listing invoice.pdf.exe.

title: The project's own linter flags 49 ignored (value, err) errors across 17 example files, including workshop tools
claim: `mutant lint examples` reports 49 warnings of the form '`X` can fail, and this `err` is never read before it is rebound or the scope ends ... the program carries on with that and reports success'. They spread over 17 files: 11_verdict 6, persistence_triage_commands 6, ws_echo_handler 6, graph_detection_timeline 5, concurrent_server_handler 4, incident_graph 3, fs_example 3, sigma_rules 3, decode_payload 2, and others. The examples teach the pattern the linter warns against.
evidence: mutant lint examples: 358 lines, 49 matching 'is never read before it is rebound'. Per-file counts from `grep 'is never read before' | cut -d: -f1 | uniq -c`. E.g. graph_detection_timeline.mut:7 `let p, err = db_add_artifact(...)` followed by :8 `let f, err = ...`, with err never tested. Verifier: `mutant lint examples` in the scratch tree: 49 warnings of the form '... is never read before it is rebound' across 17 files, for example graph_detection_timeline.mut:7,8,9,11 (db_add_artifact / db_add_relation errors rebound unchecked).
repro: Scratch tree: .\mutant.exe lint examples > lint.txt; grep -c 'is never read before it is rebound' lint.txt -> 49.
impact: Readers copy the example's error handling. incident_graph.mut, for instance, indexes proc["node_id"] after an unchecked db_add_artifact. Low severity, but it conflicts with the stated '(value, err) idiom' teaching goal.
fix_proposal: Test each err or bind `_` on purpose. Add `mutant lint examples` (no ignored-error warnings) to the release gate. Regression test: A test running the lint analyzer over examples/ and requiring zero ignored-error diagnostics (or an allowlist with reasons).

title: Sigma keyword searches silently miss any value nested deeper than 24 levels, and the rule reports a clean no-match
claim: allValues says it 'flattens every string the event carries', but sigmaCollect returns early at `if value == nil || depth > 24 { return }`. A keyword that sits deeper than 24 levels is never compared, so sigma_match/sigma_scan return matched=false, and fields_missing stays empty. Keyword searches have no field to report missing, so nothing tells the examiner the event was only partly searched. The same event is accepted whole by json_parse (maxNativeDepth = 256) and is fully reachable by a field search, which has no depth cap. Verifier: As stated. The depth guard also protects the stack, so the fix should report truncation (or raise an error) rather than just remove the cap. Realistic events seldom nest more than 24 levels, which keeps this at S3.
evidence: sigma_engine.go:994-995: `// allValues flattens every string the event carries, once, for keyword searches.`; :1005-1007: `func sigmaCollect(value object.Object, out *[]string, depth int) { if value == nil || depth > 24 { return }`. format_native.go:39 `maxNativeDepth = 256`. Verifier: builtin/sigma_engine.go:1005-1007 sigmaCollect returns at `depth > 24`. My scratch test builtin/zz_verify_test.go TestZZSigmaDepth ran the rule `keywords: ['mimikatz']` against {a:{a:...'sekurlsa mimikatz run'}}. At depth 1, 23 and 24 it reported matched=true. At depth 25 and 30 it reported matched=false with fields_missing=[]. A field search on a.a...a (30 levels) against the same event reported matched=true, so only keyword searches are capped. Verifier's notes: Not a duplicate of ART-016/017/018. Those are other defects in the sigma semantics.
repro: builtin/zz_lim_test.go TestZZSigmaKeywordDepth (scratch copy). Rule `detection: keywords: ['mimikatz'], condition: keywords`, with the event {a:{a:...{a:'sekurlsa mimikatz run'}}} nested d levels. Output: d=1 matched=true; d=24 matched=true; d=25 matched=false; d=26 matched=false; d=40 matched=false. fields_missing=[] every time.
impact: The detection answers 'no hit' on an event that holds the keyword, with no signal that the search was cut short. That is a wrong forensic answer reported as right. Deeply nested JSON (cloud audit logs, wrapped EDR telemetry) can reach this depth after json_parse, which allows 256.
fix_proposal: Name the depth as a documented limit. When it is hit, either raise an error or record a truncation (for example add 'keywords:depth' to fields_missing, or a 'truncated' flag) instead of returning nothing. Align it with maxNativeDepth so any event the parsers accept is searched whole. Regression test: sigma_match with a keyword at nesting maxNativeDepth-1 must match, or must report truncation; it must never return matched=false with no indication.

title: CONFIGURATION_POLICY says binary-format bounds are tested by fuzzing; the tree has no fuzz targets
claim: The Limits section excuses binary-format offsets from the guard because 'their bounds are tested by fuzzing instead'. No Go fuzz target exists anywhere in the tree, so the stated alternative check does not exist. That leaves every parser offset bound unchecked by either mechanism. Verifier: As stated. The CHANGELOG's release-gate entry repeats the claim: the gate 'runs ... fuzzing', but with no targets its fuzz step can only print SKIP.
evidence: CONFIGURATION_POLICY.md:290-293: 'The guard is a floor, not a proof. ... binary-format offsets are deliberately not guarded, and their bounds are tested by fuzzing instead.' `git grep -n -E 'func Fuzz|\*testing\.F' HEAD -- '*.go'` returns nothing. The review's own docs/review/2.6.0/baseline.md:35 says: 'fuzz targets | SKIP: no `-FuzzTime`, and there are no fuzz targets yet'. The ledger holds many parser-offset defects that fuzzing would have found (ART-005, ART-011, ART-024, NET-009, FS2-003). Verifier: `git grep -n -E 'func Fuzz|\*testing\.F\b' HEAD -- '*.go'` returns nothing. docs/CONFIGURATION_POLICY.md:290-293 says binary-format offsets 'are tested by fuzzing instead'. scripts/release_gate.sh:126-141 and release_gate.ps1:171-188 list Fuzz* targets and print 'SKIP: no fuzz targets' when none exist. CHANGELOG.md:21 lists 'fuzzing' among the checks the gate runs. Verifier's notes: Different from DOC2.12, which is about the fuzz step writing into the working tree.
repro: git grep -n -E 'func Fuzz|testing\.F\b' HEAD -- '*.go' -> no output.
impact: A reader, or a Stage F planner, concludes that parser bounds are covered by fuzzing and does not guard them. The documented safety net does not exist.
fix_proposal: Either add fuzz targets for the binary parsers (hive, plist, jumplist, lnk, prefetch, evtx, pcap, protobuf/cbor/msgpack, record/grant parsers), or change the sentence to say the offsets are neither guarded nor fuzzed yet. Regression test: A cmd/gendocs doc-claim test that fails when CONFIGURATION_POLICY mentions fuzzing and `testing.F` appears in no _test.go file.

title: The limits reference and policy claim every limit is named and listed; the generated list holds none of Mutant's runtime limits
claim: The preamble says, in the present tense, that every value that bounds what Mutant does 'is a named constant ... marked with a //mutant:limit directive ... This is the list of them', and that 'A limit that is not listed here is a bare literal somewhere in the source'. CONFIGURATION_POLICY repeats it and adds 'the reference names the flag beside the value'. The generated list has 4 entries. Three are testkit/goroutines.go values used only by tests, since testkit is imported by no non-test file. The fourth is limitscan's own failure-message width. Zero of Mutant's runtime limits appear. Many named, documented-in-prose runtime limits (maxHTTPBodyBytes, maxConnReadBytes, sqliteMaxRows, MaxRecordHeader, dap maxMessageBytes) are neither listed nor bare literals, which contradicts the second sentence. No flag is named although --polymorphic-level (main.go:23 defaultPolymorphicLevel) and the sweep flags override limits. Verifier: As stated. One mitigation: the preamble's second paragraph does point to the budget in policy/limit_budget.go, so a careful reader learns that unlisted limits exist. It still wrongly calls all of them bare literals and presents the list as complete.
evidence: docs/LIMITS_REFERENCE.md:17 '4 limits in 2 packages.' Tables list only policy/limitscan maxShownExpression and testkit GoroutineSettleTimeout/goroutinePollInterval/goroutineStackBuffer. The scan in the scratch copy returned '174 findings, 4 limits, 0 formats'. builtin/mitm_http.go:25 `maxHTTPBodyBytes = 32 << 20` is named and absent. `go run ./cmd/gendocs -check` in the scratch copy reports 'docs/LIMITS_REFERENCE.md is up to date', so the gap is in the claim, not staleness. Verifier: docs/LIMITS_REFERENCE.md reads '4 limits in 2 packages': policy/limitscan maxShownExpression plus three testkit values. No non-test .go file imports mutant/testkit (git grep). The preamble (cmd/gendocs/limits.go:19-28) says 'Every value that bounds what Mutant will do ... is a named constant ... This is the list of them', and CONFIGURATION_POLICY.md section 6 repeats it. builtin/mitm_http.go:25 maxHTTPBodyBytes and builtin/sqlite_builtins.go:23 sqliteMaxRows are named constants with no directive (N1 budget entries). They are neither listed nor bare literals, which contradicts 'a limit not listed here is a bare literal'. Verifier's notes: P1 only because the generated document ships with 2.6.0 and the fix is a wording change.
repro: Scratch copy: limitscan.Scan("..") -> 174 Findings, 4 Limits, 0 Formats, 410 files; gendocs -check up to date.
impact: An examiner or reviewer reading the reference to find what bounds a run finds nothing about any of the 144 real limits (see measurements) and is told the list is complete.
fix_proposal: Until the budget is empty, say so in the preamble: print the count still unnamed (len of Findings) and point at policy/limit_budget.go. Drop test-only packages (testkit, policy) from the reference, or label them. Reword 'a limit not listed here is a bare literal' to cover named-but-undirected constants. Regression test: gendocs test: the preamble's completeness sentence is rendered only when the scan returns zero findings; otherwise the rendered text states the outstanding count.

title: The limit guard cannot see whole classes of limits, and real limits in the tree fall through each gap
claim: (G1) N1 only fires for names containing a limit word, and a limit used through an identifier is never a literal, so a limit named without max/limit/timeout/size is invisible forever. (G2) Comparisons need a strong name, or a weak name plus a value of at least 1024, so count caps under 1024 and caps on unlisted names pass. (G3) Float thresholds pass. (G4) A bare time unit (time.Millisecond, time.Minute) has no literal and passes, and so does a divided duration. (G5) A limit held in a non-limit-named variable passes. (G6) Compound loop conditions (`i < n && i < 5000`) pass. (G7) Equality bounds pass. (G8) Plain literal arguments below 65536 pass. (G9) Channel buffers below 1024 pass. (G10) Hex is exempt in L7 fields as well as in comparisons, though the policy documents only the comparison exemption. The empty-budget target therefore does not mean every limit is named. Verifier: The blind spots are real, but they are mostly documented design. CONFIGURATION_POLICY.md:290-292 says 'The guard is a floor, not a proof. It recognises limits by shape and by name, so a limit in a shape none of the rules describes is not caught.' Two things remain. First, the list of real unnamed limits the guard can never surface (processProtectionTerminateConfidence, auditRetained, TimingLoopIterations, ledgerRetainedSegments, the float entropy thresholds, ioc :88 `>20`, and others) must be added to the Stage F work list by hand. Second, the L7 hex exemption is deliberate (limitscan.go:572) but the policy doc does not state it.
evidence: Real unflagged sites (absent from the scan's 174 findings): runner/runner.go:38 `const processProtectionTerminateConfidence = 80` (the score threshold that decides to terminate the process, used at :229); builtin/audit.go:77 `auditRetained = 4096` (the audit chain's memory cap); security/antitamper_constants.go:48 `TimingLoopIterations uint64 = 200000`; builtin/ledger.go:178 `ledgerRetainedSegments = math.MaxInt32`; builtin/prefetch_builtins.go:137 `volCount > 256`; builtin/jumplist_builtins.go:199 `pathChars > 2048`; builtin/detection.go:434/436 `ent > 7.8` / `ent > 7.2`; security/antitamper_detectors.go:109 `time.Sleep(time.Millisecond)`; lsp/internal/server/server.go:466 `WorkspaceSymbols(params.Query, 100)`; builtin/ioc_builtins.go:88 `if bits-ones > 20` (the twin of the flagged :87 maxHosts). Verifier: policy/zz_verify_test.go ran limitscan.ScanSource over the auditor's 17 G1-G10 snippets plus three controls. The controls each produced 1 finding: `const maxFoo = 80` (N1), make 4096 (L1) and 5*time.Second (L3). All 17 gap snippets produced 0 findings. The real sites exist: runner.go:38/229 processProtectionTerminateConfidence, audit.go:77 auditRetained, ledger.go:178 ledgerRetainedSegments. Verifier's notes: The severity drops from S4 to S5 because the documentation states the limitation.
repro: policy/zz_lim_test.go TestZZGuardGaps (scratch copy) runs limitscan.ScanSource over 17 snippets modelled on the sites above (G1-G10). Every one returns findings=0. The full Scan output (policy/zz_findings.txt) has no entry at any of the cited file:line.
impact: Limits that decide whether Mutant kills itself, how much audit history it keeps, or how long it sleeps will never reach LIMITS_REFERENCE or the budget. The Stage F work list built from the budget alone misses them.
fix_proposal: Add rules: (a) any package-level numeric const referenced as the non-literal side of a </<=/>/>= comparison, as a make size, or as a LimitReader/Buffer cap must carry a directive, whatever its name; (b) a bare time unit passed to Sleep/WithTimeout/After/NewTicker/SetDeadline or assigned to a *Timeout field; (c) float literals compared against anything; (d) literal args to calls whose parameter is named limit/max. Pin each in TestTheLimitGuardCatchesEachRule, and document the hex exemption for L7. Regression test: Extend TestTheLimitGuardCatchesEachRule with the G1-G10 snippets from TestZZGuardGaps as 'catches' cases.

title: The per-file count budget lets a new unnamed limit in whenever another limit in the same file is named in the same change
claim: The budget is a number per file, not a list of known findings. Naming one existing literal and adding a new bare literal in the same file keeps the count equal, so the guard passes. This breaks the stated contract 'more fails because a new literal limit appeared'.
evidence: limit_guard_test.go:49-51: 'Each file may hold exactly as many unnamed limits as policy.LimitBudget says: more fails because a new literal limit appeared'. The comparison is only `got, allowed := len(byFile[file]), LimitBudget[file]`. Verifier: In my scratch copy I replaced 5*time.Second in builtin/net.go:315 with a documented //mutant:limit duration const and appended `func zzNewUnnamedLimit() []byte { return make([]byte, 1<<24) }`. go test ./policy -run 'TestUnnamedLimitsStayWithinBudget|TestLimitDirectivesAreWellFormed' reported PASS. Control: I undid only the rename, which left the new make in place, and the guard failed with 'builtin/net.go holds 4 unnamed limit(s); its budget is 3', listing net.go:1039 L1 1<<24. The check is only `len(byFile[file])` against LimitBudget[file] (limit_guard_test.go:69).
repro: Scratch copy: in builtin/net.go (budget 3), replaced `5*time.Second` at :315 with a documented `//mutant:limit duration` const zzDNSTimeout and appended `func zzNewUnnamedLimit() []byte { return make([]byte, 1<<24) }`. `go test -run 'TestUnnamedLimitsStayWithinBudget|TestLimitDirectivesAreWellFormed' ./policy/` -> PASS. A new unnamed 16 MiB allocation got past the guard.
impact: During Stage F, while limits are being named file by file, new unnamed limits can slip in unnoticed. The ratchet only holds for changes that touch one kind of literal.
fix_proposal: Budget by fingerprint rather than count: store rule+func+normalised text per finding (e.g. map[string][]string), fail on any finding not in the list and on any listed entry that no longer occurs. Regression test: A guard self-test that builds a two-file ScanSource result with one finding swapped for another and asserts the budget check reports the new one.

title: The Lua patch sandbox declares a 64 MB memory cap that nothing enforces
claim: SandboxConfig.MaxMemoryMB is set to 64 by DefaultSandboxConfig ('returns a secure default configuration'), and ExecutePatches uses that config for every Lua patch. Nothing in the tree reads MaxMemoryMB, so a patch can allocate without bound. M26-TOOL-011 covers the separate builtin/lua.go path; this is the runtime/lua sandbox that the runner uses. Verifier: As stated. Only the author who embeds and encrypts the patch can trigger it, so the harm is a false claim in the config rather than an exposure to untrusted input.
evidence: The grep for MaxMemoryMB finds only the field (vm.go:15), the default (vm.go:33) and a test literal (executor_test.go:108). Execute (vm.go:123-127) applies only `vm.config.MaxExecutionMS`. Verifier: runtime/lua/vm.go reads MaxMemoryMB nowhere. The only references are the field (:15), the default of 64 (:33) and a test literal. Execute applies only MaxExecutionMS. ExecutePatches (executor.go:51) uses DefaultSandboxConfig. My scratch test runtime/lua/zz_verify_test.go TestZZLuaMem ran with MaxMemoryMB=64: string.rep of 16 MiB returned 16777216 with err nil, and string.rep of 96 MiB returned 100663296 with err nil, TotalAlloc +96 MiB. Verifier's notes: Not a duplicate of M26-TOOL-011, which covers builtin/lua.go's runLuaSource. Nearby but not re-reported: the auditor's observation (a), that AllowedLibs is validated but never restricts anything because Open calls OpenLibs(), is true by reading vm.go:60-73. It belongs with the TOOL/SEC owners.
repro: runtime/lua/zz_lim_test.go TestZZSandboxMemoryCapIsNotEnforced (1 GiB heap watchdog): DefaultSandboxConfig, `string.rep('x', N*1024*1024)`. N=16 -> result 16777216, err nil, TotalAlloc +16 MiB. N=128 -> result 134217728, err nil, TotalAlloc +128 MiB, twice the declared 64 MB cap.
impact: The declared bound is false. Patches are author-embedded and encrypted, so the exposure is limited, but anyone reading the config believes memory is capped.
fix_proposal: Either enforce it (gopher-lua has no allocator hook; wrap string.rep/table growth or poll runtime memory from the context goroutine) or delete the field and the claim. Name whichever value remains as a //mutant:limit. Regression test: A sandbox test that allocates 2x MaxMemoryMB and expects an error.

title: The LSP's drift test for the range/CIDR thresholds compares the mirror to its own copy, so it cannot fail when the builtin moves
claim: The comment says 'If either implementation moves its cap, the thresholds here are wrong ... [this test catches it]', but the test checks maxRangeLength against the literal 10_000_000 and maxCIDRHostBits against 20. It never reads the builtin's values, which are function-local consts or bare literals. A change to the builtin cap leaves the test green and the diagnostic lying. The same concept is also written three times: builtin maxRange, the lsp maxRangeLength, and the test literal.
evidence: unbounded_resource_test.go:168 `if maxRangeLength != 10_000_000 {`; :171 `if maxCIDRHostBits != 20 {`. collections_builtins.go:256 `const maxRange = 10_000_000` (local). ioc_builtins.go:88 `if bits-ones > 20 {` (a bare literal). Verifier: unbounded_resource_test.go:167-174 compares the analyzer's own constants against literals. In my scratch copy I changed builtin/collections_builtins.go:256 to `const maxRange = 5_000_000` and ioc_builtins.go:88 to `> 16`. go test ./lsp/internal/analyzer -run TestUnboundedResourceThresholdsMatchTheBuiltins still reported PASS.
repro: Scratch copy: changed collections_builtins.go:256 to `const maxRange = 5_000_000` and ioc_builtins.go:88 to `> 16`, then ran `go test -count=1 -run TestUnboundedResourceThresholdsMatchTheBuiltins ./lsp/internal/analyzer/` -> PASS. Both files were restored afterwards.
impact: Once the builtin caps change, the editor warns about calls that now work, or misses ones that now fail. The editor-parity rule promises it will not.
fix_proposal: Export the caps from builtin (MaxRangeLength, MaxCIDRHostBits, as //mutant:limit consts, which also removes two budget entries) and have the analyzer reference them directly (lsp already imports mutant/builtin), then delete the mirror test. Regression test: Compile-time reference: the analyzer uses builtin.MaxRangeLength, so no separate copy exists to drift.

title: *_read_file whole-file ceilings differ by filesystem with no stated reason: 32 MiB on exFAT, 1 GiB on NTFS/ext/HFS, none on XFS beyond the volume's claimed capacity
claim: Only xfat_read_file applies Mutant's maxInMemoryReadBytes (32 MiB). The other five pass straight to library ReadAll: libntfs caps at 1<<30, libext at min(1 GiB, image size), libhfs at DefaultMaxAlloc 1 GiB, libfat at the located chain length, and libxfs only rejects sizes above the superblock's own claimed capacity, which a crafted image controls. The metadata for every one says it 'allocates for the file's whole length before reading a byte ... bounded by what a library will read into memory'. The same script therefore refuses a 40 MiB file on exFAT and returns it on NTFS, and a crafted XFS inode can request an allocation as large as its superblock claims. Verifier: The per-filesystem ceilings differ as described: 32 MiB on exFAT, 1 GiB on NTFS/ext/HFS, the chain length on FAT. The metadata partly documents this ('bounded by what a library will read into memory'). The part that matters is XFS. xfs_read_file allocates the inode's recorded di_size bounded only by the superblock's self-declared capacity, so a crafted image could plausibly drive a multi-GiB allocation and a fatal out-of-memory. That is the same class as M26-FS2-003 and M26-ART-005. I have not reproduced it. Also, libxfs ReadFileData silently truncates a short read (out[:n]).
evidence: filesystem_parsers.go:2170-2174 (xfat) `if size := entry.Size(); size > maxInMemoryReadBytes {`, with the comment 'the same 32 MiB ceiling the *_read_at builtins apply'; :2143/2157/2214/2225 `return f.ReadAll()`; :2229 `return s.volume.ReadFileDataByPath(cleanPath)`. libntfs@v0.3.3 file.go:638 `if f.size > 1<<30`; libext@v0.3.0 file.go:158 `defaultReadAllLimit = 1 << 30`; libhfs@v0.3.2 config.go:25 `DefaultMaxAlloc = int64(1) << 30`; libxfs@v0.4.1 directory.go checkPlausibleSize (capacity from sb.NumberOfBlocks*BlockSize). Verifier: Code read. Only realXFATSession.ReadFile checks maxInMemoryReadBytes (filesystem_parsers.go:2170). The NTFS, FAT, ext and HFS readers call the library's ReadAll: libntfs@v0.3.3 file.go:639 refuses sizes > 1<<30, libext@v0.3.0 file.go:158 defaultReadAllLimit 1<<30, libhfs@v0.3.2 config.go:25 DefaultMaxAlloc 1 GiB. XFS calls libxfs@v0.4.1 ReadFileData (directory.go:131-151), which runs `make([]byte, int(inode.Size))` after checkPlausibleSize. That check only compares against sb.NumberOfBlocks*BlockSize, and sb dblocks (volume.go:908) is never checked against the image's real length. A crafted XFS image can therefore ask for an allocation as large as its own superblock claims. Not reproduced: the repo has no XFS image, and libxfs's module testdata holds only manifests. Verifier's notes: If a crafted XFS image confirms the out-of-memory, raise this to S2/P1, in line with FS2-003. The fix is to apply maxInMemoryReadBytes (or one named whole-file limit) before calling the library.
impact: Results for the same file depend on which filesystem held it. On XFS the memory ceiling is whatever the evidence claims. Up to 32x more memory per call than the documented 'in-memory limit' of the *_read_at family.
fix_proposal: Apply maxInMemoryReadBytes (or one named whole-file limit) in the shared read path of all six ReadFile implementations, checked against the recorded size before calling the library, and document it in metadata and LIMITS_REFERENCE. Regression test: Per filesystem, a fixture file one byte over the named limit: *_read_file errors and names the limit, and *_read_file_at/*_extract_file still reach it.

title: The same concept is capped at different values in different places with no stated reason (line length, nesting depth, frame size, decompression)
claim: Max line length for line-oriented evidence is 4 MiB (bodyfile), 8 MiB (hashset, syslog), 64 MiB (ndjson), or the bufio default 64 KiB (email_urls, known as ART-014). Max nesting depth is 24 (sigma, silent), 32 (hive ri, protobuf, silent), 64 (CBOR, DER, classified walk), 100 (bplist), 256 (json/yaml/msgpack native, XML, MFT path), and unbounded for toml and XML plist (known DAT-004, ART-009). The max framed message is 16 MiB for DAP but uint32 (4 GiB) for the LSP's jsonrpc2 VSCodeObjectCodec on the same Content-Length framing. Decompression is 1000x input capped at 1 GiB for gzip/zlib/tar, but a fixed 64 MiB for prefetch MAM, independent of input size (a few-hundred-byte file may declare 64 MiB, about 200,000x). Only the ndjson and native caps carry a written reason. Verifier: The values differ as listed. Correction: the claim that only the ndjson and native caps carry a written reason is wrong. The prefetch cap (prefetch_builtins.go:177-179, 'Real prefetch files are a few MB at most') and the hashset ('NSRL lines can be long') and syslog ('tolerate long lines') buffers carry reasons too. The unbounded toml/msgpack/XML-plist depth and the email 64 KiB sub-items are already in the ledger as M26-DAT-004, M26-ART-009 and M26-ART-014.
evidence: bodyfile_builtins.go:35 `scanner.Buffer(make([]byte, 64*1024), 4*1024*1024)`; hashset_builtins.go:42 `8*1024*1024`; syslog_builtins.go:51 `8*1024*1024`; format_text.go:749 `maxNDJSONLine = 64 << 20`; sigma_engine.go:1006 `depth > 24`; hive_builtins.go:123 `depth > 32`; format_binary.go:211 `maxProtobufDepth = 32`; plist_builtins.go:237 `depth > 100`; dap/transport.go:28 `maxMessageBytes = 16 << 20`; jsonrpc2@v0.2.2 stream.go:160 `strconv.ParseUint(line, 10, 32)` then `io.LimitReader(stream, int64(contentLength))`; prefetch_builtins.go:181 `maxPrefetchDecompressed = 64 << 20`, applied at :184 against the declared size only. Verifier: Spot-checked values: bodyfile_builtins.go:35 4 MiB; hashset_builtins.go:42 and syslog_builtins.go:51 8 MiB; format_text.go:749 64 MiB; hive_builtins.go:123 depth 32; format_binary.go:211 32; plist_builtins.go:237 100; dap/transport.go:28 16 MiB; jsonrpc2@v0.2.2 stream.go:160 ParseUint(...,32) with LimitReader at :169; prefetch_builtins.go:181 64 MiB checked against the declared size. Verifier's notes: An architectural observation for Stage F naming. No single defect.
repro: Code read only. Each value is quoted above.
impact: A script's behaviour on the same input shape depends on which builtin reads it (error, silent truncation, or success). Stage F cannot choose shared names without a decision per concept.
fix_proposal: In Stage F, define one named limit per concept (maxEvidenceLineBytes, maxDocumentDepth, maxFrameBytes, and the shared decompression ratio) in one place, and reference it everywhere. Where a value legitimately differs, say why in the directive's prose. Regression test: A policy test listing the canonical limit per concept, which fails when a Scanner.Buffer or depth comparison uses anything else.

title: Completion requests build documentation for all 659 builtins twice and throw one copy away (about 10 ms and 6.7 MB per request)
claim: The completion handler always runs `items := analyzer.New().Analyze("").CompletionItems()` and then overwrites items with snapshot.CompletionItemsAt whenever a snapshot exists, which is the normal case. Both calls rebuild all ~659 builtin completion items from scratch. Each rebuild renders builtinHoverText and builtinCompletionDetail markdown (analyzer.go:328-336), which is static data. All of this runs on the single jsonrpc2 dispatch goroutine, and editors send completion requests on almost every keystroke.
evidence: server.go:406-414: `items := analyzer.New().Analyze("").CompletionItems()` / `if snapshot != nil { ... items = snapshot.CompletionItemsAt(params.Position) }`. analyzer.go:328-333 runs `for _, b := range builtin.Builtins { ... Detail: builtinCompletionDetail(b.Name) ... builtinHoverText(b.Name) ...}` on every call. CPU profile of the empty call: CompletionItemsAt is 60% of the samples, builtinHoverText 36%, callableCard.render 20%, TypedSignature 12.6%. The rest is GC. Verifier: lsp/internal/server/server.go:404-416. completion() always runs `items := analyzer.New().Analyze("").CompletionItems()` and then overwrites items with snapshot.CompletionItemsAt(...) whenever a snapshot exists. analyzer.go:311-336 rebuilds every keyword and builtin item, including the builtinHoverText and builtinCompletionDetail markdown, on every call. My test, lsp/internal/analyzer/zz_verify_test.go TestZZVerifyCompletionCost, measured the server path at 10.72 ms/op, 6,723,550 B/op and 72,757 allocs/op. The snapshot-only path was 5.84 ms/op, 3,356,519 B/op and 36,337 allocs/op. So half the work is thrown away, and the other half is static data rebuilt on every request. Verifier's notes: This is separate from M26-SEM-004, which is the cost of building the name graph. Handlers run on the single jsonrpc2 reader goroutine (see the lsp-transport memory note), so the cost queues behind keystrokes.
repro: Scratch tree/lsp/internal/analyzer/zz_perf_test.go, BenchmarkZZCompletionRequest -count=4: server_path_both 9.6-11.0 ms/op, 6.72 MB/op, 72,757 allocs/op; snapshot_only 5.0-7.8 ms/op, 3.36 MB/op, 36,337 allocs/op. BenchmarkZZEmptyCompletion (the discarded half) 4.5-5.1 ms/op, 3.37 MB/op.
impact: Every completion stalls the language server for about 10 ms plus GC. Hovers, diagnostics and the next didChange queue behind it on the single dispatch goroutine, and this adds to the per-keystroke cost that M26-SEM-004 describes.
fix_proposal: Compute the keyword and builtin completion items once, with sync.Once at package level, since they depend only on static metadata. Copy the cached slice and append the snapshot's bindings in CompletionItemsAt. In server.completion, only build the fallback list when snapshot == nil. Regression test: A benchmark or budget test: two consecutive CompletionItemsAt calls allocate less than 10% of the first; and server.completion with a snapshot does not call Analyze (for example, allocations per request below 1 MB).

title: Each integrity probe hashes the whole running function, so a hot loop in a large main body runs about twice as slow
claim: Every 64 + jitter%31 steps, runIntegrityProbes calls verifyCurrentFrameIntegrity, which computes `sha256.Sum256(fn.Instructions)` over the whole current function. The per-step cost therefore grows with the size of the function the loop runs in, not with the work done. Top-level scripts keep their loops in main, and main can hold up to 64 KiB of instructions (jump operands are 16-bit). M26-VM-012 covers the sweep across frames (depth); this is the per-probe cost across function size, a separate mechanism that also runs at depth 1. Verifier: The mechanism is as stated. The magnitude at HEAD is about 1.35-1.4x for a loop inside a 56 KB main, not 2x. The 'about twice' figure only holds once M26-VM-001's value round-trip cost is removed. Only unusually large top-level scripts or functions (tens of KB of bytecode) are affected.
evidence: vm.go:2591 `actual := sha256.Sum256(fn.Instructions)`, reached from vm.go:1646 every nextProbeInterval() = integrityEvery(64) + jitter%31 steps (vm.go:173-179). There is no caching and no incremental or chunked verification. Verifier: vm/vm.go:1632-1663. runIntegrityProbes calls verifyCurrentFrameIntegrity every integrityEvery(64) + jitter steps. verifyFrameIntegrity (vm.go:2579-2596) computes sha256.Sum256(fn.Instructions) over the whole function, with no chunking or caching. My test, vm/zz_verify_test.go TestZZVerifyProbeVsMainSize, ran at HEAD with 5 runs each and reports medians. The same 10,000-iteration loop with a 53-byte main took 211 ms with probes on and 195 ms with them off. With main padded to 56,109 bytes it took 351 ms on and 257 ms off. Probe overhead therefore grows with function size: about 8% on the small main and about 37% on the 56 KB main. Verifier's notes: Related to M26-VM-012, but that finding is the number of frames per sweep. This one is function size per probe at depth 1. They are distinct mechanisms and share one fix site (verifyFrameIntegrity). They could be fixed together.
repro: Scratch BenchmarkZZProbeVsMainSize runs the same 10,000-iteration `s += i` loop, with main padded by K dead statements after it, and compares probes on against integrityEvery=0. On the M26-VM-001 prototype VM (fix tree), 6 runs each: K=0 (53-byte main) was about 68-82 ms with probes on and 71-86 ms (median ~82) with probes off, so no difference. K=4000 (56,109-byte main) was 202-243 ms (median ~220) on versus 87-132 ms (median ~120) off, so probes roughly double the loop. At HEAD the same K=4000 case was 325-337 ms on versus 255-356 ms off. That is noisy, because HEAD's value round trip dominates, and the probe share grows once M26-VM-001 is fixed.
impact: After M26-VM-001 is fixed, tight loops in a large top-level script spend about half their time re-hashing the program. Before that fix it is a 10-30% tax, hidden by the larger cost.
fix_proposal: Verify a rotating fixed-size chunk per probe, for example 4 KiB at a moving offset, against per-chunk digests computed at registration. Full coverage is then amortized over len/4096 probes and the cost per probe is constant. Alternatively, cap the bytes hashed per probe and keep the full-function hash for the sweep. Regression test: vm: the 10,000-step loop with a 56 KB main must cost within 1.3x of the same loop with a 53-byte main, with probes on.

title: regex_* builtins compile the pattern on every call, so a per-line match costs about 4x a precompiled match
claim: RegexMatch, RegexFind and the other regex builtins call regexp.Compile(pattern) on every invocation. Scripts pass the same literal pattern in a loop over lines or events, so the compile repeats once per line. Verifier: As stated. I measured about 8 us of compile overhead per call on this host.
evidence: regex.go:19 `re, err := regexp.Compile(pattern)` inside RegexMatch, and the same line at :37, :72, :101 and :119 for the sibling builtins. There is no cache. Verifier: builtin/regex.go:19, 37 and the sibling builtins call regexp.Compile(pattern) on every invocation, with no cache. I found no doc describing per-call compilation as intended; the sigma note in CAPABILITY_REFERENCE is about sigma rules, not regex_*. My test, builtin/zz_verify_test.go TestZZVerifyRegexCompileEachCall, used a URL pattern over a 118-byte log line. RegexMatch took 10,154 ns/op, 6,639 B/op and 62 allocs. A precompiled MatchString took 1,993 ns/op with 0 allocs, so the builtin is about 5x slower. Verifier's notes: Today this is dwarfed by the per-load VM cost (M26-VM-001).
repro: Scratch tree/builtin/zz_perf_test.go, BenchmarkZZRegexMatch -count=3, an IOC/URL pattern over a 120-byte log line: the builtin took 15.6-21.1 µs/op, 11.1 KB/op and 81 allocs/op; a precompiled re.MatchString took 4.1-4.6 µs/op with 0 allocs. The ~13 µs difference per call is the compile.
impact: A million-line log scan pays about 13 s of pure recompilation. This is secondary to M26-VM-001 today and becomes significant once the VM overhead drops.
fix_proposal: Add a small bounded LRU (for example 64 entries, keyed by the pattern string) of compiled *regexp.Regexp. Regexp is safe for concurrent use. Report compile errors exactly as now. Regression test: builtin: 1,000 regex_match calls with the same pattern allocate less than 2x what one call allocates (or a benchmark budget).

title: The Classified field moved every encrypted value from the 48-byte into the 64-byte allocation class
claim: Stage A's baseline lead is correct. Adding `Classified *Classification` to object.Encrypted grew the struct from 48 to 56 bytes. Go's allocator rounds 56 up to the 64-byte class, so every stored scalar, string or bytes value costs 16 more bytes. The field is only ever non-nil for BYTES. Verifier: As stated. The cost is 16 B more per stored value. baseline.md found no significant time difference.
evidence: unsafe.Sizeof(Encrypted{}) = 48 at v2.5.0 and 56 at HEAD (scratch object/zz_size_test.go, run in both trees). This matches baseline.md's +16 B/op on GlobalMemoryModeRuntime_IntegerSetGet (304 -> 320) and ArraySetGet (424 -> 440), and the +9% B/op on MapVsPMap. Verifier: `git show v2.5.0:object/encObj.go` shows Encrypted as {Value []byte; EncType ObjectType(string); Seed int64}, which is 48 bytes. HEAD adds Classified *Classification. My test, object/zz_verify_test.go TestZZVerifyEncryptedSize, reports sizeof(Encrypted)=56 against 48 for the old layout. Heap allocation of &Encrypted{} is 64 B/op against 48 B/op for the old layout. This matches baseline.md:241 (304 -> 320 B/op) and baseline.md:250-252, which records it as an unverified lead. Verifier's notes: The field itself is deliberate: the doc comment explains why the mark travels beside the ciphertext. Only the size-class side effect is the finding.
repro: go1.26.2 test ./object -run ZZEncryptedSize -v in the v250 and tree copies: `sizeof(Encrypted)=48` and `sizeof(Encrypted)=56`.
impact: About 5-9% more heap churn per stored value, and more GC work. The time difference was not statistically significant in baseline.md.
fix_proposal: Keep Encrypted at 48 bytes. Carry the mark in a separate EncryptedBytes type or a wrapper used only by the BYTES arm, or pack EncType as a small integer instead of a string (16 bytes -> 1) to make room. Regression test: object: assert unsafe.Sizeof(Encrypted{}) <= 48.

title: The evidence read-only guard does not scan the file that opens every filesystem image, nor the file that writes recovered files, and syscall.Open passes it
claim: docs/EVIDENCE_HANDLING_POLICY.md says the guard 'is what makes the assertion true' behind case_manifest's `integrity.evidence_read_only: true`, and that the list covers raw/ewf/vhdi/ntfs/fat/xfat/ext/hfs/xfs images and deleted-file recovery. The list names 21 files. It omits 12 evidence files added in Phases 2-3, including builtin/filesystem_region.go, whose line 182 `img, err := os.Open(path)` opens the image for every *_open family, and builtin/filesystem_recover.go, whose fsWriteEvidenceFile (lines 1128 and 1146) is the only code in the evidence path that creates and removes files. The other ten are disk_image_extents, filesystem_capabilities/deleted/journal/report/slack/stream/verify/xattr and fs_forensics. The guard also matches mutators by selector name only: syscall.Open or windows.CreateFile with a write flag, and os.NewFile, are not in fsMutators, and only a call named OpenFile has its flags checked. Verifier: As stated. The hand-maintained list is a documented soft edge. What is wrong is the doc's statement of current coverage and the court-facing manifest claim that rests on it. No actual write to evidence exists today.
evidence: The listing loop `git ls-files builtin/filesystem_*.go builtin/disk_image_*.go builtin/fs_*.go builtin/table_*.go`, checked against evidence_policy.go, printed LISTED for 4 files and UNLISTED for 12. The probe run, with a control, is in repro. Verifier: Re-ran the listing loop: 12 of the 16 builtin/filesystem_*, disk_image_*, fs_* and table_* files are missing from EvidenceReadOnlyFiles, including filesystem_region.go (os.Open of the image at :182, used by every *_open) and filesystem_recover.go (fsWriteEvidenceFile, OpenFile O_WRONLY|O_CREATE|O_EXCL plus os.Remove at ~1128/1146). Probe in the scratch copy: os.OpenFile(p, os.O_RDWR, 0) plus a write in filesystem_region.go, and syscall.Open(p, O_RDWR) under an alias in the listed archive.go. TestEvidenceCodeNeverWrites PASSED. Control: os.OpenFile(O_RDWR) in archive.go made it FAIL. The code (evidence_policy.go:28-30) and the doc (sec 2) both admit that an omission is not caught. But doc sec 2 also says the list currently covers ntfs/fat/ext/... and deleted-file recovery, and that the guard 'is what makes the assertion true' behind case_manifest's evidence_read_only:true. That claim is false for the Phase 2-3 files. Verifier's notes: DOC3.02 is the same root defect. TEST.01 is the survivor because it is more complete: it also covers filesystem_recover.go and the syscall.Open/selector-only gap.
repro: In the scratch copy I appended `func zzWriteImage(p string) { f, _ := os.OpenFile(p, os.O_RDWR, 0); f.Write([]byte{0}) }` to builtin/filesystem_region.go. I added `import zsys "syscall"` and `func zzOpenWritable(p string) { fd, _ := zsys.Open(p, zsys.O_RDWR, 0); _ = fd }` to builtin/archive.go, which is listed. `go1.26.2 test ./policy/ -run TestEvidenceCodeNeverWrites -v` printed PASS. Control: after adding `os.OpenFile(p, os.O_RDWR, 0)` to archive.go the test FAILED with 'builtin/archive.go:895 (zzCtl2): OpenFile with a writable flag'.
impact: A write-capable open added to the code that opens every filesystem image would pass go test and the release gate, while every case manifest keeps stating evidence_read_only:true. The policy document says the guard exists to prevent exactly that.
fix_proposal: Derive the list rather than hand-maintain it. For example, fail when a builtin/*.go file calls os.Open/fsRegion openers or returns a *_open handle and is absent from EvidenceReadOnlyFiles, or scan all of builtin/ with a small allowlist of files that legitimately write. Add filesystem_recover.go with an EvidenceWriteAllowlist entry for fsWriteEvidenceFile, since O_EXCL is what keeps it off the evidence. Add syscall.Open, unix.Open, windows.CreateFile and os.NewFile to the mutator rule, judging flags as OpenFile's are. Regression test: A policy test that parses a synthetic file containing os.OpenFile(p, os.O_RDWR, 0) and syscall.Open(p, syscall.O_RDWR, 0) and expects 2 findings, plus a test that every builtin file calling os.Open on a path argument is either listed or explicitly exempt.

title: The gate's gofmt step ignores gofmt's exit status, and the bash twin deletes every CR, so a syntax error and TEST-001's own defect both pass
claim: Both twins decide the gofmt step on gofmt -l's stdout alone. When gofmt cannot parse a file it prints to stderr, exits 2 and writes nothing to stdout, so the step reports PASS. In the .sh twin, `echo "$unformatted" >"$log"` then truncates the step log and erases that stderr. Three committed Go files are compiled by no gate step except cross-compile, which --quick skips: examples/data/make_usb_stick.go and examples/lua/lua_http_server_example.go (//go:build ignore) and cmd/replwasm/main_wasm.go (js/wasm). A syntax error in any of them passes the whole gate. The .sh twin also copies files with `tr -d '\r'`, which deletes every CR and not only the CR of a CRLF pair. A blob git stores with CRs therefore passes the .sh gofmt step on Linux, where nothing converts line endings, even though the comment says the step judges 'the content git stores'. That blob shape is the one TEST-001 found: lexer.go stored with CR CR LF. The .ps1 twin replaces only CRLF and still flags it, so the two twins disagree on the same tree. Verifier: As stated. Practical reach: an ordinary package with a syntax error also fails go vet and go test. The pass-through matters for //go:build ignore files and js/wasm files (and --quick, which skips cross-compile), and for committed-CR blobs on a Linux host.
repro: I made a scratch git repo holding the TEST-001 lexer.go blob and broken.go, and ran the release_gate.sh gofmt_lf function, extracted verbatim, through the gate's step capture (gaterepo/drive.sh). It returned exit=0, note empty, and an empty log. I also ran the .ps1 step body verbatim under pwsh 7.6.6 on a repo holding broken.go. It printed 'STEP RESULT: PASS (files: broken.go; gofmt exit 2)', with gofmt's parse error on stderr.
impact: The gofmt step can report PASS on a tree that does not parse. On Linux it cannot detect the committed-CR class of defect that made 26 files fail in Stage A, so which twin runs decides whether TEST-001 recurs silently.
fix_proposal: Fail the step when gofmt exits non-zero: check $? in bash (capture stdout to a file, keep stderr, and append to the log rather than truncating it), and $LASTEXITCODE in PowerShell. Build the LF copies from what git stores, not from the working file with every CR stripped: `git archive`/`git cat-file` for tracked files, or strip only the CR of a CRLF pair in both twins. Regression test: policy/gate_guard_test.go: run the gofmt step of the host's twin against a temp repo holding (a) a file that does not parse and (b) a blob with CR CR LF, and expect FAIL for each.

title: The TEST-008 fix can be bypassed: the bash twin compares paths case-sensitively, and the PowerShell twin does not resolve junctions or symlinks
claim: The refusal of a log directory inside the repository compares path strings. release_gate.sh resolves symlinks with pwd -P but compares case-sensitively (`case "$(absolute_path "$LOG_DIR")/" in "$ROOT_PHYSICAL"/*`). On a case-insensitive filesystem (macOS APFS by default, NTFS under Git Bash, /mnt/c under WSL), --log-dir spelled with different case names the same directory and is accepted. release_gate.ps1 uses GetUnresolvedProviderPathFromPSPath, which never resolves a junction, symlink or subst drive, so a log directory reached through one is accepted. In both twins a relative --log-dir is resolved after `cd "$REPO_ROOT"` / Set-Location, that is against the repository and not the caller's directory. `--log-dir out` run from elsewhere is therefore refused as 'inside the repository' (sh:36-38, ps1:43-45). Verifier: Both bypasses are real. Downgraded because the consequence is the TEST-008 symptom: gofmt-lf copies inside the module, guards counting twice, and a spurious gate FAIL. So a bypass makes the gate fail in the safe direction, never pass falsely, and only for an operator who spells the path oddly. The relative-path quirk is surprising but safe.
evidence: Both bypasses ran against the working-tree scripts. The control spelling was refused with exit 2 and the directory was not created. The two other spellings were accepted, and the gate ran and created the directory inside the repository. Verifier: absolute_path plus the case check extracted from release_gate.sh. The exact-case path inside a scratch repo was REFUSED. The same path upper-cased (Git Bash on NTFS) was ACCEPTED. The ps1 check logic run verbatim: the direct path was REFUSED, and a junction j->repo was ACCEPTED. A relative --log-dir resolves against the repo and is refused.
repro: Git Bash, scratch repo gaterepo/repo holding the working-tree release_gate.sh: `bash .../repo/scripts/release_gate.sh --go go-nonexistent --quick --log-dir .../GATEREPO/REPO/inside-logs` exited 1 after running its steps and created gaterepo/repo/inside-logs. The same command with the exact case exited 2 with the refusal. pwsh 7.6.6: created junction gaterepo\j -> gaterepo\repo and ran `pwsh -File repo\scripts\release_gate.ps1 -Go go-nonexistent -Quick -LogDir gaterepo\j\junction-logs`: exit 1, and gaterepo\repo\junction-logs exists. With -LogDir gaterepo\repo\direct-logs it exited 2.
impact: The failure TEST-008 describes, with gofmt-lf copies compiled as part of the module and guards counting files twice, is still reachable by an ordinary spelling on macOS and through junctions or subst drives on Windows. The new regression test exercises only the exact-case, direct path.
fix_proposal: Compare identities rather than strings. In bash, create the directory in a temp location first, or walk up from its deepest existing ancestor and compare each directory with the repository using `[ dir -ef "$ROOT" ]`. In PowerShell, resolve the deepest existing ancestor with [IO.Directory]::ResolveLinkTarget / Get-Item .Target, or compare file IDs, and compare OrdinalIgnoreCase on every OS whose filesystem is case-insensitive. Resolve a relative --log-dir against the caller's working directory, captured before cd. Regression test: Extend TestGateRefusesALogDirInsideTheRepository with the same probe directory spelled in upper case (all hosts), and on Windows through a junction created in t.TempDir() to the repository's policy directory.

title: The TEST-005 fix covers scripts/ only; lsp/build.sh is still committed 100644, and the docs tell users to run ./lsp/build.sh
claim: TestShellScriptsAreCommittedExecutable reads `git ls-files --stage -- scripts` and so checks only scripts/*.sh. lsp/build.sh is recorded as 100644 in the index and at HEAD. Its own usage line (lsp/build.sh:24) and three documentation sites invoke it directly as ./lsp/build.sh or ../lsp/build.sh. A Linux or macOS checkout fails that with 'Permission denied', the defect TEST-005 fixed for the four scripts under scripts/. scripts/package-vscode-extension.sh:127 runs it through `bash`, so packaging is unaffected. examples/workshop/evidence/build_evidence.sh is also 100644 but is documented as `sh .../build_evidence.sh`.
evidence: `git ls-files -s lsp/build.sh` gives 100644 1f7d964f...; `git archive HEAD lsp/build.sh | tar -tv` shows -rw-rw-r--. docs/LSP_EXTENSION_ONBOARDING_60_MIN.md:46 reads `./lsp/build.sh --host-only`. Verifier: git ls-files -s '*.sh': lsp/build.sh and examples/workshop/evidence/build_evidence.sh are 100644. scripts/*.sh are 100755. I extracted the HEAD archive (autocrlf off) onto the WSL native fs: -rw-r--r--, and ./lsp/build.sh --help gave 'Permission denied', exit 126. Docs invoke it directly: LSP_EXTENSION_ONBOARDING_60_MIN.md:46, mutant-vscode-extension/README.md:159,175. TestShellScriptsAreCommittedExecutable reads only `git ls-files --stage -- scripts`. Verifier's notes: A sibling of M26-TEST-005, not a duplicate. That row is scoped to scripts/ and FIXED there; this is a file the fix left out. On /mnt/c (drvfs) every file shows 777 and archive output there carries CRLF, so the repro must use the native Linux fs.
repro: `git archive HEAD lsp/build.sh` extracted in WSL Ubuntu (wsl.exe -e bash scratch/wsltry.sh): `ls -l` shows -rw-r--r--; `./lsp/build.sh --help` prints './lsp/build.sh: Permission denied' with exit=126.
impact: The LSP onboarding and extension README instructions fail on the first command on Linux and macOS. The regression test added for TEST-005 cannot see this, because it only looks at one directory.
fix_proposal: Record lsp/build.sh (and build_evidence.sh, for consistency) as 100755 with a mode-only index change, as TEST-005 did. Widen the guard to `git ls-files --stage -- '*.sh'` across the repository, with an explicit allowlist for scripts documented to be run through sh/bash. Regression test: TestShellScriptsAreCommittedExecutable over every tracked *.sh; it fails today on lsp/build.sh.

title: The no-env-config guard is blind to environment reads through library defaults and non-listed APIs; two such reads are in the shipped binary
claim: TestNoEnvironmentAccessOutsideAllowlist recognises only the selectors Getenv/LookupEnv/Setenv/Unsetenv/ExpandEnv/Environ/Clearenv, a dot-import of os/syscall, and .Env writes. It cannot see an environment read made by a library or standard-library function on the caller's behalf. Two are in production: `var httpClient = &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}` (builtin/http.go:14) leaves Transport nil, so http_get/http_post/http_request obey HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY through DefaultTransport's ProxyFromEnvironment (M26-NET-010), and the guard passes. security/key_bootstrap.go:23 `os.UserHomeDir()` makes HOME/USERPROFILE choose the directory the signing key pair is read from and written to. Other one-token routes it passes: `os.ReadFile("/proc/self/environ")`, a func value `http.ProxyFromEnvironment`, and any Go package placed in a directory named `dist` or `node_modules`, which the walk skips by basename anywhere in the tree (policy/env_guard_test.go:28-33).
evidence: The guard passes at HEAD while NET-010 (CONFIRMED) shows proxy variables changing where HTTP builtins connect. During my test run with USERPROFILE redirected to a scratch directory, the builtin tests created home/.mutant/keys/ed25519_private_key.hex there: the key-store location followed the environment. Verifier: Added builtin/zz_env_bypass.go with os.ReadFile("/proc/self/environ"), os.UserHomeDir() and http.ProxyFromEnvironment, and builtin/dist/x.go with os.Getenv("HOME"), which is skipped because any dir named dist is pruned. TestNoEnvironmentAccessOutsideAllowlist and TestNoMutantEnvironmentVariableNames both PASSED. Control: os.Getenv in zz_env_bypass.go gave FAIL 'builtin/zz_env_bypass.go:13 (zzCtl): Getenv'. CONFIGURATION_POLICY.md sec 5 lists exactly the selectors checked, so the selector list is documented. But line 10 says 'The rule is machine-enforced', and shipped behaviour already depends on env through library defaults. Verifier's notes: The production symptoms are separate rows: M26-NET-010 (proxy env) and DOC3.01 (HOME picks the key store). This finding is the guard gap, a distinct root. Note (2026-09-28): the M26-DOC3-001 fix removed the os.UserHomeDir read from security/key_bootstrap.go and taught the guard the standard-library calls that read the environment inside themselves (os.UserHomeDir, UserCacheDir, UserConfigDir, TempDir, the empty-directory temp calls, and os/user lookups where they fall back). What is left of this finding is a read made inside a library -- net/http's proxy default (M26-NET-010, and M26-DAT-030 through OPA), gopsutil's HOST_PROC (M26-NET-025) -- plus /proc/self/environ and the dist/node_modules pruning.
repro: In the scratch copy I added builtin/zz_env_bypass.go with `raw, _ := os.ReadFile("/proc/self/environ"); return string(raw), http.ProxyFromEnvironment`. `go1.26.2 test ./policy/ -run 'TestNoEnvironmentAccessOutsideAllowlist|TestNoMutantEnvironmentVariableNames' -v` gave both PASS. Control: adding `os.Getenv("HOME")` to the same file made it FAIL with 'builtin/zz_env_bypass.go:14 (zzCtl): Getenv'.
impact: docs/CONFIGURATION_POLICY.md presents the rule as machine-enforced, yet environment-driven behaviour has already shipped past the guard (NET-010). A green guard therefore does not mean 'no configuration from the environment'.
fix_proposal: Add the implicit readers to the rule: ProxyFromEnvironment, http.DefaultTransport/DefaultClient, an http.Client or Transport literal with no Proxy field set, UserHomeDir/UserConfigDir/UserCacheDir/TempDir, user.Current, and string literals naming /proc/self/environ. Classify each hit through EnvAccessAllowlist, so the HOME dependence is either justified in the allowlist or replaced by a flag. Skip `dist`/`node_modules` only at the repository root, or only when the directory holds no .go file that `go list ./...` builds. Regression test: A synthetic-source table test in policy, like TestTheLimitGuardCatchesEachRule, where each spelling above produces exactly one access finding.

title: Three more guards pass code that breaks their rule after a one-token respelling (disclosure, sema no-file-read, gate cgo)
claim: (1) The disclosure guard names calls by their source text. An aliased import (`import fm "fmt"`, then `fm.Sprintf(string(plaintext))`) is not 'fmt.Sprintf', and a method value (`render := b.Inspect; render()`) is not a call ending in '.Inspect'. Both pass in a DisclosureFiles member. (2) TestNameResolutionCannotReadAFile states that 'a package that imports nothing capable of opening a file cannot open one, on any path'. sema already imports mutant/builtin (sema/resolve.go:32), whose exported builtins (TarOpen, BinDWARFParse, ...) open files. It also imports path/filepath (sema/id.go:4, workspace.go:4), and filepath.Glob reads directories. archive/zip.OpenReader and go/parser.ParseFile(fset, name, nil, 0) open files too, and none of these is on the denylist. (3) TestEveryGateGoCommandChoosesCgo (the TEST-006 regression test) matches only the literal `"$GO" <cmd>` in bash and `& $Go <cmd>` / `-Exe $Go -Arguments @("<cmd>"` in PowerShell. `${GO} build` and `& $Go "build"` pass without CGO_ENABLED. Verifier: As stated. These are lint-grade gaps that need a deliberate respelling, and no plaintext leak exists. The sema test comment's structural guarantee ('imports nothing capable of opening a file') is false at HEAD.
evidence: All three bypasses and their controls ran in one scratch run, shown in repro. Verifier: One scratch run: view.go gained an `fm "fmt"` alias with fm.Sprintf(string(plaintext)) and a method value `render := b.Inspect; render()`. sema/zz_bypass.go used filepath.Glob, zip.OpenReader and parser.ParseFile(...,nil,0). release_gate.sh gained `run "$1" ${GO} build ./...` and .ps1 gained `& $Go "build" "."`. TestDisclosureCodeNeverRendersPlaintext ('scanned 13 files ... 0 findings'), TestNameResolutionCannotReadAFile and TestEveryGateGoCommandChoosesCgo all PASSED. Controls each FAILED: non-constant fmt.Sprintf, sema importing os, and `"$GO" build`. sema already imports mutant/builtin (resolve.go:32) and path/filepath (id.go:4, workspace.go:4).
repro: Scratch copy probes: builtin/view.go gained `import fm "fmt"`, zzLeak (fm.Sprintf of plaintext) and zzLeak2 (method value of Inspect). sema/zz_bypass.go calls filepath.Glob, zip.OpenReader and parser.ParseFile(..., nil, 0). release_gate.sh gained `zz_build() { run "$1" ${GO} build ./...; }` and release_gate.ps1 gained `function Invoke-ZZ { & $Go "build" "." }`. `go1.26.2 test ./policy/ -run 'TestDisclosureCodeNeverRendersPlaintext|TestNameResolutionCannotReadAFile|TestEveryGateGoCommandChoosesCgo'`: all PASS ('scanned 13 files ... 0 findings'). Controls: fmt.Sprintf(string(p)) in view.go, `"os"` imported in sema, and `run "$1" "$GO" build` each FAILED their test.
impact: Each guard is the only enforcement its policy has in a repository with no CI. Its green result proves less than its comment claims. For the sema guard the stated structural guarantee is already false at HEAD.
fix_proposal: Disclosure: resolve the import name of "fmt" per file and match on the resolved path. Treat any selector reference to Inspect (not only a zero-arg call) as a finding, and flag errors.New/fmt.Sprint/fmt.Sprintln of a non-constant as well. Sema: state the guarantee as 'imports no package on the denylist', or add path/filepath, archive/*, debug/*, go/parser, go/build, text/template, html/template and mutant/builtin, plus a check with go/packages that no reachable function in sema calls os.Open. Gate: match `\$\{?GO\}?` and quoted subcommands, or have the scripts route every go invocation through one function the test can check. Regression test: A synthetic-source table test per guard, like TestTheDisclosureGuardCatchesEachViolation, extended with the aliased-import, method-value, filepath.Glob/zip.OpenReader and ${GO}/quoted-subcommand spellings.

title: testkit.CheckGoroutines has no caller, so no test in the repository checks for goroutine leaks; with it, the known .tar.zst leak fails in 5 s
claim: testkit was added in 07c737a to report 'a leak ... by the test that caused it'. `git grep testkit.CheckGoroutines` finds no caller outside testkit's own test, and `git grep mutant/testkit` finds only the policy guard that forbids non-test imports. The checker works: wrapped around a tar_open/tar_read_bytes/tar_close of a .tar.zst with a 2 MiB last member, it fails the test and names the klauspost zstd decoder goroutines that M26-DAT-005 describes. The suite passes today because nothing calls it, and TestTarDetectsItsCompressionFromContent exercises zstd with no leak check.
evidence: The grep searches in claim, and the probe run in repro. Verifier: Outside testkit/, `git grep testkit -- '*.go'` finds only policy/testkit_guard_test.go (the import ban). I wrote builtin/zz_verify_test.go: CheckGoroutines, then writeTar zstd with a.txt and a 2 MiB random member, 4x TarReadBytes(a.txt), then TarClose. Result: FAIL, 'goroutines.go:53: 6 goroutine(s) outlived the test by more than 5s: github.com/klauspost/compress/zstd.(*Decoder).startStreamDecoder ...' (the M26-DAT-005 leak). LIMITS_REFERENCE.md:26-32 documents the helper's timeouts. Verifier's notes: ARCH.07 is the same root defect (testkit has no importer). TEST.07 is the survivor because it demonstrates the leak the helper would catch.
repro: Scratch builtin/zz_test_test.go: TestZZTarZstdEarlyMemberUnderTheGoroutineChecker calls testkit.CheckGoroutines(t), writeTar(t, "zstd", a.txt + 2 MiB random big.bin), TarOpen, TarReadBytes(a.txt) x4, TarClose. Result: 'goroutines.go:53: 9 goroutine(s) outlived the test by more than 5s: github.com/klauspost/compress/zstd.(*Decoder).startStreamDecoder...' FAIL. A control test that leaks `go func(){ time.Sleep(8s) }()` also fails. The same tar test without the checker passes.
impact: Goroutine leaks in handle-owning builtins (tar/zip, net_serve (M26-NET-012), spawn, channels) have no detector. The helper that would catch them ships unused, and LIMITS_REFERENCE.md documents its timeouts as if they were in force.
fix_proposal: Call testkit.CheckGoroutines at the start of the tests of every builtin that owns goroutines or handles (archive, net/serve/secure_net, channels, tasks, pmap/spawn in vm, the LSP server). Add a policy check that each such test file imports testkit, so it does not stay unused. Regression test: TestTarDetectsItsCompressionFromContent (and a zstd early-member read) under testkit.CheckGoroutines; it fails until DAT-005 is fixed.

title: The sweep's server mode passes a program that never listens: 'still running after --alive' is the whole check
claim: The comment on startAndStop says it draws the distinction a plain sweep cannot, because to that sweep 'a server doing its job and a program wedged in a loop look identical'. startAndStop does not draw it. It passes any process still alive after --alive (3 s) and never checks that anything listens or what the program printed. Check() requires only that the file lexically contains a net_listen/net_tls_listen/net_serve call, not that the call is reached, so an example that hangs, deadlocks or loops before binding passes as a server. Verifier: The alive-only check is the documented design: sweep/marker.go:34-37 says it 'confirms it is still alive after a moment'. What is wrong is the startAndStop comment (sweeper.go:114-117), which claims to draw the server-versus-wedged distinction, and the missing readiness check that leaves the 5 server examples unverified.
evidence: The run in repro reported ok for a program that never reaches its net_listen call. Verifier: zzex/wedged_server.mut carries a server marker, loops in `while (true) { spins = spins + 1; }`, and puts net_listen after the loop where it is never reached. `go1.26.2 run ./cmd/sweep --tree zzex --mutant .\mutant.exe --password reviewpass zzex` printed 'ok zzex/wedged_server.mut server, alive 3s ...' and '1 server | 0 failed'. check.go only requires the listener call to appear lexically.
repro: Scratch zzex/wedged_server.mut: `// mutant:sweep server -- serves a status page until interrupted` then `while (true) { spins = spins + 1; };` followed by an unreachable `net_listen("127.0.0.1:0")`. `go1.26.2 run ./cmd/sweep --tree zzex --mutant .\mutant.exe --password reviewpass zzex` printed 'ok    zzex/wedged_server.mut   server, alive 3s   serves a status page until interrupted' and '1 server | 0 failed'.
impact: The 5 server examples (and any future one) can regress to a hang or deadlock before binding and still pass the release gate's sweep step.
fix_proposal: Have a server example prove it is serving. Either the sweep passes a port it chooses (or reads the bound address the program prints) and dials it before --alive expires, or the program prints a readiness line that the sweep waits for. Regression test: cmd/sweep/sweeper_test.go: a server-marked program that loops before net_listen must FAIL; a program that binds and blocks must pass.

title: The success path of bin_dwarf_parse is never tested: its only test skips under every plain `go test` run
claim: TestBinaryImportsSectionsAndDwarf runs bin_dwarf_parse on os.Executable(), the test binary, and on any error calls `t.Skipf("dwarf may be unavailable in this test binary: %s", ...)`. `go test` links test binaries without DWARF unless -c or a profiling flag is given, so this skip is taken on every normal run, including the gate's. No other test or passing example calls bin_dwarf_parse: examples/binary/binary_analysis_example.golden records it failing (M26-EX-001). The function itself works: on a DWARF-carrying mutant.exe it returned compile_units 652. The same pattern, a missing precondition turned into a pass, covers two other skips. compiler/linetable_test.go:159 and generator/strip_debug_test.go:30 skip when examples/binary/static_bin_analysis.mut is renamed, and the generator one is the only test that release Generate strips debug info.
evidence: Full-suite run on this host: '--- SKIP: TestBinaryImportsSectionsAndDwarf ... bin_dwarf_parse: decoding dwarf section info at offset 0x0: too short'. `git grep BinDWARFParse -- '*_test.go'` finds only this site. Verifier: `go1.26.2 test ./builtin -run TestBinaryImportsSectionsAndDwarf -v` gave SKIP: 'bin_dwarf_parse: decoding dwarf section info at offset 0x0: too short'. `git grep BinDWARFParse -- '*_test.go'` finds only that site, and the example golden records an error (M26-EX-001). bin_dwarf_parse("mutant.exe") from a scratch program returned {compile_units: 652, format: pe}. After renaming examples/binary/static_bin_analysis.mut, TestCompileStripsDebugInfoWhenAsked (generator) and TestDebugInfoIsASmallShareOfTheArtifact (compiler) both SKIPPED and the packages reported ok.
repro: `go1.26.2 test ./builtin/ -v` in the scratch copy shows the SKIP above. Scratch program `let r, e = bin_dwarf_parse("mutant.exe");` printed 'result: {compile_units: 652, format: pe, path: mutant.exe}' with err empty. After renaming examples/binary/static_bin_analysis.mut in the scratch copy, TestCompileStripsDebugInfoWhenAsked and TestDebugInfoIsASmallShareOfTheArtifact both reported SKIP and their packages reported ok.
impact: A regression in bin_dwarf_parse's decoding or counting cannot fail the suite. Renaming one example silently disables the only wiring test of release-mode debug stripping.
fix_proposal: Build a small Go fixture with DWARF in the test (go build without -w into t.TempDir(), as goresym_builtins_test already does), or commit a tiny ELF/PE with .debug_info under testdata, and assert compile_units > 0. Replace the example-path skips with t.Fatalf, or with testdata copies, because the examples are part of the repository. Regression test: TestBinDWARFParseCountsCompileUnits on a fixture that carries DWARF, with no skip branch.

title: TestIsDebuggerPresent cannot fail
claim: The test calls IsDebuggerPresent() and only t.Logf's the result. Its comment says 'We don't assert a specific value'. It is counted as a passing test of debugger detection but asserts nothing. The same result under go test (no debugger) is knowable: false, unless a detector misfires, which is exactly what M26-TMP-002/TMP-010 describe. Verifier: As stated. The test's own comment says it is deliberately non-asserting, so in effect it is a panic smoke test that is counted as a detection test.
evidence: An AST scan of all *_test.go for Test functions with no t.Error/Fatal/Fail call and no helper taking t found 8. Six are known (M26-CMP-015, M26-EVL-017), deliberate measurement reports (TestParamKindCoverage, TestReturnCoverage), or panic-only 'survives' tests. This one and TestSemanticTokens... remain, and only this one asserts nothing it could assert. Verifier: security/security_test.go:14-24 only calls t.Logf. I ran it with the go1.26.2 SDK binary and a scratch HOME: 'IsDebuggerPresent() returned: false', PASS. There is no assertion at all.
repro: scratchpad/stageB/b3/TEST/scan/main.go run over the tree listed security/security_test.go:14 TestIsDebuggerPresent logs=1.
impact: Inflated test count. A detector that fires under go test on a clean host is not caught here.
fix_proposal: Assert false under `go test` with detectors unpinned, skipping explicitly when the process is under a debugger, or delete the test and rely on the detector unit tests. Regression test: The rewritten test itself, failing when a detector fires on a clean go test run.

title: build.sh records an empty hash in SHA256SUMS when hashing fails, although its comment says it refuses rather than record a hash of nothing
claim: write_checksums refuses a missing file but calls `printf '%s  %s\n' "$(sha256_of "$dir/$name")" "$name"`. Under set -euo pipefail a failing command substitution used as an argument does not stop the script, so when sha256_of fails ('No SHA-256 tool found', or a failing powershell.exe Get-FileHash) the line is written with an empty hash and the function returns 0. Verifier: A failing sha256_of produces an empty-hash line and a successful return. The comment's 'refusing rather than recording a hash of nothing' refers only to a missing file, which is handled. So this is an unhandled failure mode rather than a broken promise. sha256sum -c then fails loudly on the malformed line.
evidence: The harness run in repro wrote an empty-hash line and returned 0. Verifier: Extracted write_checksums verbatim under set -euo pipefail, with sha256_of stubbed to print an error and return 1. Output: 'No SHA-256 tool found.', 'checksums: .../SHA256SUMS', function returned 0, script exit 0. SHA256SUMS contains '  mutant-linux-amd64'.
repro: Extracted write_checksums verbatim into scratch/sums/drive.sh under `set -euo pipefail`, with sha256_of stubbed to print the error and return 1. Output: 'No SHA-256 tool found.', 'checksums: .../SHA256SUMS', 'write_checksums returned 0'; SHA256SUMS contains `  mutant-linux-amd64$`.
impact: A release directory can ship with a malformed SHA256SUMS. `sha256sum -c` reports it as improperly formatted rather than verifying, so it fails loudly for the downloader rather than silently.
fix_proposal: `local h; h="$(sha256_of ...)" || return 1; [[ $h =~ ^[0-9a-f]{64}$ ]] || { echo ... >&2; return 1; }` before printf. Regression test: A policy/gate-style test that sources write_checksums with a failing sha256_of and expects a non-zero return and no SHA256SUMS.

title: Off Windows, process protection measured nothing and passed like a clean host: six probes answered 'not supported' in the shape of a clean result
location: security/antitamper_windows_stub.go; security/antitamper_probe.go AntiTamperSignal; runner/runner.go enforceProcessProtection; builtin/security_status.go antiTamperSignalArrayObj
claim: iat_got, syscall_table, trampoline, process_injection, module_integrity and memory_page_anomaly read Windows process structures; on every other OS they answered detected false, confidence 0, detail 'not supported on this platform' -- the same shape as a probe that looked and found nothing. All five probes the runner's process protection runs are among them, and the runner reads only detected and confidence, so on Linux and macOS that stage checked nothing and passed exactly as it passes a clean Windows host, with nothing in the run to say so. CONFIGURATION_POLICY listed process protection as 'always on' without a platform. The unknown-probe answer and cpuid_hypervisor's failure path had the same shape: a sandbox-detector error was reported as 'no hypervisor signal'.
evidence: Found while checking the M26-TMP-001 fix on the owner's VMs with the Stage C build. On Fedora 40 (Hyper-V guest), sandbox_status and debug_status listed the six probes as detected false with 'not supported on this platform', and the first version of the new probe test passed there because it did not treat that detail as a non-measurement. On Windows 10 (build 19045) all fourteen probe rows carried a real measurement. With an explicit Measured field set by every existing constructor, the strengthened test failed on Fedora for all six probes and, on both hosts, for the unknown-probe answer.
repro: security/antitamper_detectors_test.go TestEverySupportedProbeMeasuresOrSaysItDidNot, built for linux/amd64 and run on the Fedora VM before the stubs changed, failed on iat_got, syscall_table, trampoline, process_injection, module_integrity and memory_page_anomaly ('says it measured, and reports "not supported on this platform"'); runner/process_protection_note_test.go TestProcessProtectionThatMeasuredNothingSaysSo failed before the note existed.
impact: A run on Linux or macOS in secure mode believed, and let its operator believe, that process protection had looked; a script reading probe_signals could not tell 'not detected' from 'not looked for'.
fix_proposal: Give a probe signal a measured bit beside detected, and have a run say when process protection measured nothing. Fixed: AntiTamperSignal.Measured; makeSignal sets it, and unmeasuredSignal (never detected, no confidence, a detail saying why) answers for the six Windows-only probes off Windows ('not measured on <os>: this probe reads Windows process structures'), for an unknown probe, and for cpuid_hypervisor when the sandbox detector fails. sandbox_status and debug_status rows carry measured. When none of the five process-protection probes measured, the stage still passes and the runner prints once per run '[security] process protection measured nothing on <os>: none of its probes (...) can run here'. ANTITAMPER_PROBE.md sections 3, 5 and 6 and the CONFIGURATION_POLICY row say process protection runs on Windows only. Verified on both VMs with the rebuilt binaries: Fedora shows the six rows measured false and the note once; Windows 10 shows all fourteen measured true and no note.

title: graph query callers and callees read every declaration record on a miss while the help lists them as index lookups
claim: answerUses, which answers callers and callees, calls allDeclarations on a name the index does not hold, to name the declarations that differ only in case -- the same scan where does. QueryQuestions declared both as costIndex, so `mutant help graph`, which builds its list of the questions that read every record from Cost, named only where and exported, and the answer to a missed callers or callees said nothing about having scanned. TestEveryQuestionThatCanScanSaysSoWhenItDoes pinned the list at two.
evidence: Found while adding `type`, which looks for other casings too. answerUses's miss branch: `all, scanErr := allDeclarations(g)`. QueryQuestions: {"callers", ..., costIndex}, {"callees", ..., costIndex}. The language reference said 'Two of them read every declaration record rather than an index'.
repro: Ask `callers Mean` of a store holding `mean`: the answer names mean (it scanned) and carries no note that it did; `mutant help graph` lists where and exported only.
impact: The help and the answer understate what two questions cost on a miss. The cost is milliseconds; the untruth is in a surface whose whole rule is that each answer says what it did.
fix_proposal: Declare callers and callees costIndexThen, and have their miss answers carry the scan note. Fixed: both are costIndexThen, both miss branches add missScanned (renamed from whereScanned), the help and MUTANT_LANGUAGE_REFERENCE list four questions that can scan, and `type` -- which looks for other casings among the struct and enum records only, found by their kind labels -- stays an index question.

title: graphene keeps no role on a commit, so a script's own ledger writes record who but not as what
verifier: Stage E1 2026-09-26 (read graphene v0.9.0 disk/store.go and disk/walbatch.go)
claim: store.TxContext has a RoleID field, and Mutant now begins every ledger commit with the examiner's role in it, but graphene v0.9.0 drops it: nextCommitMeta copies only ActorID from the context into batchMeta, which holds CommitSeq, UnixNano, ActorID, KeyID and Signature, and signedCommitData signs the same four. A role is persisted on a redaction record (RedactionRequest.RoleID) and on graphene's RBAC grants, never on a commit. A commit from ledger_add_node or ledger_add_edge therefore records the actor and not the role.
evidence: graphene@v0.9.0 disk/store.go:412 nextCommitMeta returns batchMeta{CommitSeq, UnixNano, ActorID: ctx.ActorID, Signer}; disk/walbatch.go:83 batchMeta has no role field; grep RoleID over disk/ finds only rbac.go, redact.go and custody.go. v0.9.0 is the latest release (go list -m -u).
repro: Open a ledger with {role: investigator}, ledger_add_node, close and reopen: nothing graphene exposes for the commit carries the role. The same ledger's ledger_redact_node record reports role investigator after the reopen (TestARedactionRecordKeepsItsRole).
