impact: Roles are attribution, not enforcement, and every disclosure-family and redaction record carries one, so what is lost is the role on a script's own nodes and edges. The docs say so rather than claiming every commit carries it.
fix_proposal: Upstream: carry RoleID in graphene's commit record (batchMeta, the WAL commit payload and signedCommitData, as a new payload version) and expose it where commit provenance is read. Mutant already passes the role in TxContext, so nothing here changes; add a test that a reopened ledger's commit reports the role once graphene does, and remove the caveat from role.go, ledger_open's metadata and DISCLOSURE_POLICY section 9.

title: A withdrawal on the examiner's own authority could write two Actor nodes for one name, after which every disclose_* write naming that examiner was refused
claim: disclosureTx.findOrAdd looks a node up with disclosureFind, which reads the committed graph and cannot see a node buffered earlier in the same transaction. E1 made disclosureWriteWithdrawal call actorNode twice in one transaction, once for the examiner (PERFORMED_BY) and once for the authority (AUTHORISED_BY), and the authority defaults to the examiner. When the ledger held no Actor node for that examiner -- one who had not disclosed anything through it -- the transaction added two Actor nodes with the same actor.id.
evidence: After the withdrawal, disclosureFind(Actor, actor.id, <examiner>) returns 'the ledger holds 2 Actor nodes ... written to by something other than disclose_*', and disclose_to_passphrase through the same examiner's handle is refused with that error. The E1 test did not see it: its withdrawing examiner had already disclosed, so the first findOrAdd found a committed node.
repro: TestOneNameIsOneActorNodeWithinATransaction: issue a disclosure as 'examiner', reopen the ledger as 'second examiner', disclose_withdraw with no options, then disclose_to_passphrase as 'second examiner'.
impact: The ledger stays sound and nothing is lost, but every later disclosure, withdrawal or reclassification recorded by that examiner is refused, and nothing a script can do removes the duplicate: schema nodes are not redactable.
fix_proposal: Stage E2: disclosureTx remembers every node findOrAdd buffers, by label, key and value, and finds it there before asking the graph; the second call returns the first node, compared on mustMatch like a committed one. Caught by case_attach, whose first attach adds the examiner as both the actor and the assignee in one transaction.

title: A case attached to one ledger could be written through another, whose empty lifecycle refused nothing
claim: E2 made the builtins that take the ledger ask that ledger for the case's lifecycle state (caseLedgerStateRefusal), and made case_assign and the evidence_* writers refuse a ledger other than the attached one (attachedToLocked). disclose_to_passphrase and disclose_reclassified check neither: given a second ledger opened by the same examiner, they read its lifecycle -- none, since the case was never registered there -- refuse nothing, and record the act in a ledger that is not the case's.
evidence: Case attached to ledger A, moved to in_review there; ledger B opened by the case's examiner under the same role. disclose_to_passphrase(B, record, view, recipient) issued and recorded a disclosure, and disclose_reclassified(B, new, old) recorded a reclassification, while A's lifecycle refuses both in review.
repro: TestACaseIsNotWrittenThroughAnotherLedger: openLifecycleRun, case_attach, class/view/record defined and sealed while active, forceLifecycle to in_review, a second ledger_open by the same examiner, then disclose_to_passphrase and disclose_reclassified through it. Failed on a01e378 with 'a disclosure through another ledger was not refused'.
impact: Every per-state refusal E2 introduced for disclosures and reclassifications could be stepped around by opening another ledger, and the case's record was then split between two ledgers with the lifecycle in one and the acts in the other. Not access control -- roles and states are asserted records -- but the record stopped being consistent with itself.
fix_proposal: Stage E4: custodySession.ledgerElsewhereLocked refuses a ledger other than the one the case is attached to (and, for a reopened handle of the same path, asks for case_attach with it). disclose_to_passphrase (through its preflight), disclose_reclassified, and the new role_assign and redaction_commit call it before any other ledger read.

title: ledger_patterns reported a match naming a node the ledger does not hold
claim: ledger_patterns refused a pattern with no edges, because every node then matches on its own and the result is a cross product rather than a subgraph match, but accepted a pattern with one node on no edge. That node matched every candidate on its own, and over a scope graphene's candidate builder takes the scope's ids as an unlabelled node's candidates without reading them -- so a returned match could name an id the ledger has never held.
evidence: A ledger with nodes 1, 2, 3 and edges 1->2, 2->3; the pattern {nodes 0, 1, 2 unlabelled; edge 0->1} over the scope [1, 2, 3, 999999] returned count 4 with the matches [1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 999999], [2, 3, 1], [2, 3, 999999]. Node 999999 is not in the ledger. The candidate builder (graphene v0.9.0 traversal/subgraph.go buildCandidates) appends the scope verbatim for an unlabelled pattern node, and only the pattern's edges are ever checked against the store.
repro: TestAPatternNodeNoEdgeTouchesIsRefused: readableTestLedger, then ledger_patterns with a 3-node pattern whose third node is on no edge, over a scope naming 999999, and a labelled variant over the whole graph. Failed on 7a53e67 with the four matches above where a refusal was expected.
impact: A read that reports a match is a claim that the entities matched are in the ledger and joined as the pattern says. A pattern with a node on no edge -- easy to write by mistake -- made that claim about an id the ledger does not hold, and about pairings that are a cross product rather than a subgraph. Nothing in the result said so.
fix_proposal: Stage E5: ledgerPatternFrom refuses a pattern node that is on no edge of the pattern (an edge from a node to itself counts), naming the node and why, alongside the existing refusal of a pattern with no edges. Every pattern node is then checked against the store through an edge, which is also what keeps an id a view does not show out of a match under ledger_under_view.

title: Three descriptions of the builtins that refuse classified plaintext left out db_add_relation, and one of them report_table and report_list
location: builtin/metadata.go:record_release summary; builtin/classified.go:package comment; docs/DISCLOSURE_POLICY.md section 10
claim: D2 (dc3e3bb) made db_add_relation refuse classified plaintext, and ClassifiedSinks lists it, held to the code by TestClassifiedSinksAreTheBuiltinsThatRefuse. The three places a reader learns which builtins refuse -- record_release's documentation, the header of builtin/classified.go and DISCLOSURE_POLICY section 10 -- still ended the list at db_add_artifact, and record_release's documentation also left out report_table and report_list, which refuse as well.
evidence: ClassifiedSinks() returns 16 names; record_release's summary named 13, classified.go's header and DISCLOSURE_POLICY section 10 named 15, and all three omitted db_add_relation.
repro: TestTheReleaseDocumentationNamesEverySinkAndSource fails on 56625aa: record_release's documentation does not name report_table, report_list or db_add_relation.
impact: The omission errs the safe way -- a reader told db_add_relation accepts classified plaintext finds it refused at run time -- but a list that describes a guard and is wrong about it is one a reviewer cannot rely on.
fix_proposal: Stage E6: all three lists name every sink; record_release's documentation also names record_search as a source, and TestTheReleaseDocumentationNamesEverySinkAndSource holds it to ClassifiedSinks and ClassifiedSources.

title: On Linux the process_* builtins read /proc from wherever HOST_PROC names
location: builtin/system_forensics.go ProcessEnv, ProcessOpenFiles, ProcessThreads, sfListProcesses, sfExecutableForPID; builtin/system_forensics_modules_linux.go sfProcessModulePaths (gopsutil v3.24.5 process.NewProcess, process.Processes)
claim: process_list, process_env, process_hash, process_modules, process_open_files and process_threads go through gopsutil's process package, which on Linux builds every path with common.HostProcWithContext: the context's EnvMap if it has one, otherwise os.Getenv("HOST_PROC"), otherwise /proc. Mutant passes no context (process.NewProcess, process.Processes), so the environment decides which directory these builtins read as /proc, and nothing in their output says it was not /proc. When HOST_PROC is not a mount point gopsutil decides a pid exists by signalling it, so a real pid's files can be replaced wholesale.
evidence: gopsutil v3.24.5 internal/common/common.go GetEnvWithContext and HostProcWithContext; process/process_linux.go builds 20 paths with HostProcWithContext; process/process_posix.go PidExistsWithContext falls back to signal 0 when HOST_PROC is not a mount. The policy guard cannot see a read made inside a library (M26-TEST-013).
repro: Scratch test in builtin, Linux binary run in WSL as uid 1000: with HOST_PROC unset, process_env(1) returned 'process_env: open /proc/1/environ: permission denied'; after t.Setenv("HOST_PROC", dir) with dir/1/environ holding 'PLANTED=by-HOST_PROC', process_env(1) returned {PLANTED: by-HOST_PROC} and no error.
impact: Whoever controls the examiner's launch environment on Linux decides what the live-response process builtins report -- the process list, a process's environment, its executable's hash, its modules, open files and threads -- and the examiner sees ordinary output. The same party as in M26-NET-010.
fix_proposal: Call the *WithContext variants with a context carrying common.EnvMap{common.HostProcEnvKey: "/proc"} (and any other HOST_* key a call reaches), so gopsutil never consults the environment. Regression test: with HOST_PROC pointing at a directory holding 1/environ, process_env(1) must not report that file.

title: A Rego policy's http.send connects through HTTP_PROXY and gives up after HTTP_SEND_TIMEOUT, both read from the environment
location: builtin/policy_engine.go validateRegoProgram, evalRegoQuery (rego.New with no capabilities); OPA v1.19.0 v1/topdown/http.go:649-662 (DefaultTransport clone), :266/:288 (HTTP_SEND_TIMEOUT read in init)
claim: policy_load, policy_eval, policy_allow, policy_rules and policy_trace evaluate Rego with OPA's whole builtin set, so a policy can call http.send; policy_load evaluates a policy's queries while validating it, so loading is enough. OPA builds http.send's transport by cloning net/http's DefaultTransport, whose Proxy is ProxyFromEnvironment, so HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY decide where the request goes -- M26-NET-010's defect through a second client -- and OPA's package init reads HTTP_SEND_TIMEOUT to set http.send's default timeout. A request that times out leaves the rule undefined, so the decision comes back empty with no error. The tls_client_cert_env_variable, tls_client_key_env_variable and tls_ca_cert_env_variable options also let a policy read any variable it names as TLS material (by reading).
evidence: OPA v1.19.0 v1/topdown/http.go: the client's transport is http.DefaultTransport.(*http.Transport).Clone() (:649-662); init() calls initDefaults() (:266), which reads os.Getenv("HTTP_SEND_TIMEOUT") (:288); :576-579 read the TLS variables a policy names. builtin/policy_engine.go passes only rego.Query, rego.Module, rego.Input and rego.QueryTracer.
repro: Scratch tests in builtin on Windows. (1) With HTTP_PROXY set to a local listener, policy_eval of a module whose decision is http.send({method: get, url: http://ioc-feed.mutant-review.invalid/list.json}).body: the listener received 'GET http://ioc-feed.mutant-review.invalid/list.json HTTP/1.1' and policy_eval returned {allow: true, decision: {from: the-proxy}}, the listener's forged body. (2) A policy calling a local server that answers after 2 s: without HTTP_SEND_TIMEOUT, policy_eval took 2.01 s and returned decision 200; with HTTP_SEND_TIMEOUT=200ms set at process start it took 200 ms and returned an empty decision and no error.
impact: Whoever controls the examiner's environment sees, and for plain HTTP rewrites, what a policy fetches, and can make a policy's http.send time out, which changes its decision without an error. The same party as in M26-NET-010.
fix_proposal: Take the network away from Rego: evaluate with rego.Capabilities or rego.UnsafeBuiltins leaving out http.send, since the http_* builtins exist for fetching; or, if a policy must fetch, give http.send a transport with Proxy: nil and a fixed timeout. Regression test: with HTTP_PROXY set to a local listener, policy_eval of a policy calling http.send must not reach the listener.
